subtopic: ATLANTIC ENTERPRISE PROGRAM
ATLANTIC ENTERPRISE PROGRAM
subsubtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-REJECTION OF CALAGRO CORPORATION PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the citizens of Prince Edward Island, and especially those of Prince County, are outraged by the federal Government's refusal to assist the greenhouse proposal made by Calagro Corporation.
Calagro Corporation had applied for interest rate buydowns and loan guarantees under the Atlantic Enterprise Program.
When the Government unveiled this program in February of 1986, it spoke of job creation. The Calagro project would have employed about 300 people during the construction period, and the plant would have required an operational staff of 150. In addition, the spin-off benefits for the local economy would have created more jobs.
April 28, 1987

The unemployment rate in Prince Edward Island is higher now than during the recession years. These jobs are badly needed, especially in the western part of Prince Edward Island.
We all remember the slogan: "Jobs, jobs, jobs"; but that has become another empty promise for Atlantic Canadians.
The federal Government's rejection of this proposal is a slap in the face, and it is one which will not be forgotten. The lack of support of both the provincial and federal Progressive Conservatives will be remembered.
This, Mr. Speaker, is not an empty promise.

subtopic: THE LATE MASUMI MITSUI
THE LATE MASUMI MITSUI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently we celebrated the seventieth anniversary of the Battle of Vimy Ridge. This past weekend a veteran of that battle passed away. His name was Masumi Mitsui, and he was a Japanese Canadian.
Masumi Mitsui was born in Japan, coming to Canada in 1908. He enlisted in the Canadian Army and was promoted to sergeant. He was wounded in action and awarded the Military Medal for Bravery.
He was one of 184 Japanese Canadians who served with our forces during World War I; 53 were killed and 91 were wounded.
In 1942, although he was a past-president of a branch of the Royal Canadian Legion, and although he had offered to serve again in the Canadian Forces after we declared war on Japan, Masumi Mitsui was forcibly taken from his farm and interned along with 22,000 other Japanese Canadians.
Since the end of World War II Masumi Mitsui had been working for the cause of Japanese Canadian redress. Now he is gone. How much longer will it take?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
subsubtopic: EARLY RETIREES-REQUEST THAT BILL BE SEVERED INTO TWO PARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) said on one of our radio stations it was the Opposition's fault that passage of legislation to provide refunds for early retirees was being delayed. Mr. Speaker, I have to say that this statement is as false as the image projected by the Conservatives. I suggest that the Conservative
Government split the Bill and call second reading of the Bill as far as the refund for 35,000 early retirees is concerned. The Liberal Party promises to facilitate same-day passage of second reading, report stage, third reading and royal assent, and we will even help the Government deliver unemployment insurance benefit cheques to the 35,000 early retirees, 13,000 of whom live in Quebec.

subtopic: TAX REFORM
TAX REFORM
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TAX DEDUCTIONS ON LOW-INCOME EARNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada are very concerned about where the Government is going on tax reform, particularly those living on low and modest incomes.
A letter from one Canadian in British Columbia said it well, and I quote:
I know we're all responsible for helping to reduce Canada's debt but it seems a
low wage earner is more responsible than a high wage earner.
To illustrate, he pointed out that his bi-weekly paycheque of some $250 had tax deductions which almost doubled from $4.90 in 1985 to $8.90 in 1986. In contrast, someone making a bi-weekly wage of $1,700 saw deductions for taxes increase by only $11.90 to $497.45.
I might remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that on December 19, 1984, he said the following:
We've made it quite clear we want to shift some resources from the upper
income brackets, from the wealthier people in this country to the needy in this
country, using the tax system.
My question to the Finance Minister is: When?

subtopic: VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PROVIDE MORE ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recognition for the importance of voluntary organizations is increasing in our society. It is estimated that Canadian men and women spend about 395 million hours annually on volunteer work in hospitals, with young people and the elderly, and on recreational organizations, to name just a few.
What would our society be without the contributions of these volunteers? Just think of all the expertise and competence that daily supports the work of hundreds of employees in the public, para-public and private sector. Mr. Speaker, in the past two years I have made several proposals for creating a special committee that would consider ways of providing more

April 28, 1987
adequate support for volunteer work in Canada. Recognition is not just setting aside one week a year. It also means providing material, physical and financial support, 12 months out of 12, to maintain our voluntary organizations.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I want to salute all volunteer workers during this special week, and I would urge all Canadians to show their appreciation.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY
THE ECONOMY
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN RATE OF GROWTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thanks to the progressive market oriented and financially sound policies of the Conservative Government, Canada's economy continues to forge ahead toward new record levels.
Latest Statistics Canada figures indicate a solid growth rate of 4 per cent for the first quarter. Leading the rebound have been the housing and auto industries. First quarter results show annualized housing starts at 237,000, up 11 per cent from the last quarter of 1986.
Employment grew at an annual rate of 3.2 per cent between January and March, and between September and March alone nearly 200,000 full-time jobs have been created.
These impressive figures demonstrate what can happen when Canadians roll up their sleeves and start working in concert with a Government which is truly deserving of their well placed confidence.

subtopic: WINTER OLYMPICS

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
subtopic: WINTER OLYMPICS
subsubtopic: OLYMPIC TORCH RELAY-OMISSION OF LABRADOR FROM ROUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Labrador are not being allowed to participate in the Olympic Torch Relay which is to begin the trek to Calgary this fall starting in St. John's. This is a disgraceful situation.
The torch will be carried all across the country and to other distant and northerly points including Whitehorse, Inuvik, and Yellowknife. Yet the Olympic torch relay will not even come close to Labrador, a very important and large part of the Province of Newfoundland, a land mass of 259,000 square kilometres and occupied by over 30,000 people. It is my belief that the people of Labrador should have a part in this and that
the torch should begin its journey in Labrador. How otherwise can it be called a national event?
The Government of Canada must step in and ensure that plans for the Olympic Torch Relay are revised to include Labrador and that Labradorians must be allowed to "Share the Flame".

subtopic: WORKERS' DAY OF MOURNING
WORKERS' DAY OF MOURNING
subsubtopic: RECOGNITION OF VICTIMS OF INDUSTRIAL ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, April 28 has been declared an annual day of mourning in recognition of the many Canadian workers who have been killed or disabled in industrial related accidents.
I had the privilege two years ago to be present in Sudbury with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lachine (Mr. Layton), at an early workers' memorial service in memory of miners who lost their lives as a result of a rockburst underground at the Falconbridge mine.
April 28 is a significant date because on that date in 1914 the first worker safety legislation in Canada was enacted by the Province of Ontario.
Earlier today a monument to commemorate workers was unveiled at Vincent Massey Park in Ottawa near the site of one of Canada's worst industrial accidents, the collapse of the Heron Road Bridge in 1966.
Our industrial and construction workers have and will continue to play an essential role in the growth and development of Canada. I ask all my colleagues and all Canadians to join today in recognizing their contribution.

subtopic: TAX REFORM
TAX REFORM
subsubtopic: HANDICAPPED TAXPAYER'S NON-DEDUCTIBLE EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote from another letter about our tax system. This time it is from a concerned citizen in Ottawa:
Thanks to our equitable tax system, out of a salary of $14,946.61, $2,358.40 is taken for tax, while those persons making far in excess of this amount pay no, or very little tax due to their fortunate position of having numerous tax writeoffs.
Due to a physical handicap (cerebral palsy) shoes alone cost me in excess of $700 per year which cannot be claimed.
I found living in a five foot by 8 foot room detrimental to my mental health and so have moved to a one bedroom apartment, cost $550 per month.
ParaTranspo costs in excess of $500 per year (Thank God there is such a thing).
As can be seen, there is not much chance of me being able to save for a time which in future may possibly see me in total physical handicapped situation ...
April 28, 1987

I do feel our tax system is unfairly balanced to those in upper income levels. So
much for tax reform!

subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL PRODUCTS
PHARMACEUTICAL PRODUCTS
subsubtopic: TESTIMONY SUPPORTING PASSAGE OF BILL C-22
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has become imperative that Bill C-22, the drug patent legislation, be passed without further delay.
Spokesmen for Quebec's Federation de I'age d'or have stated: "We are convinced that this amendment to the Patent Act is essential to promote research and discover new drugs to treat such diseases as cancer, Alzheimer's, AIDS and other cardiovascular conditions".
Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa said-listen to this, Mr. Speaker, and Members of the Opposition in particular should pay attention: "Montreal Mayor Dore and I have expressed our agreement to allow and encourage the federal Government to have its patent legislation passed because we know that this measure will pave the way for much larger research investments in Canada, particularly in Quebec".
The Montreal Board of Trade put it this way: "The greater Montreal region alone is expected to benefit from new investments exceeding $500 million, and this would create 750 jobs". New jobs, I might add.
We have the strong support of the Montreal Chamber of Commerce.
Quebec Industry and Commerce Minister Daniel Johnson wrote: "As we wait for this strategic and important decision for the industrial future of Quebec and Canada, you can count on my full co-operation".
Mr. Speaker, such testimony speaks much louder than the twisted positions taken by the NDP and Opposition Leader Turner.
Bill C-22 will free hundreds of millions of private investment dollars in Canada and create the kind of jobs our young graduates are anxious to have.

subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY
PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: CONGRESSIONAL INVESTIGATION OF UNITED STATES DRUG INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to inform the House and particularly
government Members that American legislators have started a Congressional investigation into the American drug industry, and Canada's current system is being held up as a model for the United States to follow.
In testimony before a Congressional hearing, the American Association of Retired Persons praised the Canadian system as: "an appropriate market-oriented model for moderating the trend in escalating prescription-drug prices".
This is just one more opinion in the growing list of people and organizations heaping praise on the current drug-pricing system in Canada, a system that was put in place by a Liberal Government under the leadership of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).
It is about time that the Government and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) acknowledged that the vast majority of Canadians do not support Bill C-22 and the changes to the Patent Act. Come election time, Canadians will remember who used closure to force this Bill through Parliament. They will remember who prevented witnesses from appearing before the committee. Most important, they will remember who raised prices for drugs by millions of dollars each and every year.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY OPENING OF SHIPPING SEASON
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY OPENING OF SHIPPING SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the St. Lawrence Seaway is now open for its 29th season. The great inland transportation system has had its share of troubles in past years but 1986 saw a trouble-free season with total tonnage up slightly over that of 1985. For our part, the federal Government has committed $175 million over the next seven years to prevent any further surprise mishaps.
The United States-Canada trade mission to Europe promoting the expanded use of the Seaway was described as being a big success. If the shippers, the carriers, and the seamen who man the ships will do their part by keeping the traffic moving through the season, the tonnage of movement through the Seaway should increase by some 3 to 5 per cent, and why not? The Seaway is already the most reliable, cost-efficient means of transporting bulk cargo goods of the world to the very heart of the North American continent, and vice versa.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION
CANADA POST CORPORATION
subsubtopic: CHAIRMAN'S LETTER TO CANADA LUTHERAN PUBLICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the editor of the Canada Lutheran, a

April 28, 1987
Oral Questions
religious publication, received the following letter from the Chairman of Canada Post concerning its second-class mailing privileges:
Upon a careful reading of the publication you have submitted in your application, I am unable to conclude that the content of Canada Lutheran is "devoted primarily" to one or more of the subjects enumerated in paragraph (b). Therefore I must conclude that your publication is best described by paragraph (a). As such, the exception provided by paragraph (i) is unavailable to you and your application is subject to the provisions of paragraph (h).
Your application fails because paragraph (h) takes away second class entitlement from any publication described in paragraph (a), if it is published by someone whose principal business is other than publishing and it is published for the purpose of advancing the publisher's principal business. When interpreting paragraph (h), it is important to note that the term "business" does not have a strictly commercial connotation. In the context of the Regulations, it is to be interpreted as the principal activity or purpose of the entity in question.
That clears it all up.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: FARM CREDIT CORPORATION-ENDING OF MORATORIUM ON FARM FORECLOSURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian grain economy is collapsing. Farm families are breaking up under the stress and strain of that pressure. Farm groups tell us that the situation is as bad as it was during the Great Depression. Yet this is the time chosen by the Government of Canada to start foreclosing on farms, kicking farmers off the land and kicking farmers when they are down.
Will the Prime Minister immediately reverse yesterday's mean-spirited decision by the Minister of Agriculture to start foreclosing on Canadian farms?

subtopic: AGRICULTURE

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt, and we on this side realize it, that it is a serious matter for Canadian agriculture. The federal Government has taken many initiatives to address that problem but let me try to put into perspective, if I can, the situation with the Farm Credit Corporation.
There are approximately 225,000 commercial farms in Canada. The announcement of the lifting of the foreclosure moratorium will affect approximately 50 farmers per month. By the way, those farmers have the option of having their cases referred to farm debt review boards or other programs this Government has initiated. So that a year from now, if the process goes ahead as planned, it will affect at the maximum about one-quarter of 1 per cent of all commercial farms in Canada.
In the meantime the federal Government is providing substantial financial assistance to farmers to see them through this very, very difficult time in the international grain markets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the speech of the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain). His desire to see the return of capital punishment seemed to turn on the whole question of law and order and what he called the protection of society. When it was brought up, as it has been many times and will be again, that capital punishment does not provide any real deterrence to murder, the Member said that justice, not utility, should be the basis on which we operate. I would be interested in hearing from the Hon. Member what standard of justice he uses. How does one determine what is just in a measure such as that? Is it the basis of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth? How does the Member determine justice?
The other question I would like him to address relates to protection of society. Opponents of the death penalty are very concerned that if the death penalty is reinstated it will mean that innocent people will be put to death. The Member said every precaution will be taken to ensure that this will not happen, but the Member knows that in some circumstances an innocent person will be put to death. People are very concerned about that, and Members of juries will be very concerned when accused murderers are facing trial. They will have very skilful lawyers working with juries, to play on the fears of jurors that they might condemn an innocent person. We have seen statistics which indicate that where there is capital punishment there is a higher rate of acquittal than in situations where there is not. It seems to me a very real possibility-a probability-that guilty people will be acquitted much more frequently under a capital punishment provision than otherwise. I would appreciate it if the Member would tell the House how he feels the acquittal of guilty murderers-juries do not want even the possibility of having condemned an innocent person to death- will lead to further protection of society?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me first comment that it is unfortunate that the Hon. Member for Cowichan- Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) will not in this particular instance be able to exercise a vote of conscience. My understanding is that his Party is voting in a block-

the Member feels he should rise on a point of order, then so be it, and I will be guided by your wisdom.
Let me come to the question of deterrence. As I pointed out at about one o'clock today, I do feel that deterrence is marginal, and it is very hard to determine exactly what deterrent effect this will have. We are speaking of a protection of society. I would gather it is a perspective that we see as individuals. It comes down to this conscience aspect of how we evaluate things morally within our own lives and how we see certain things evolving in society. I feel it is something that people should be free to express within themselves. It is something that should not be bound by Party lines or by dogma or doctrine. It is something that evolves from an individual's viewpoints, his upbringing, his spiritual views and his moral views.
In answer to the question of the Hon. Member, I would say that logically I am concerned about the innocent being prosecuted. Though I do not like to deal with statistics, members of the NDP have dealt with them considerably in this debate so I would say that statistics in Canada have shown that there is no proof that anyone in Canada has ever been put to death in error. I do not believe that anything we would institute would allow this kind of thing to happen. We would take the utmost of precautions. In the protection of society, there is always a risk, but it is so minuscule that I feel the protection of society far outweighs any risk we may take in this instance, given the heinous crimes and abominable situations we are facing at the hands of murderers.

Mr. Speaker, when one analyses the arguments put forward by proponents of the death penalty, one realizes that the bottom line is that those who support the death penalty do so on the basis of vengeance and retribution. It has been proven that capital punishment is not a deterrent. Given the fact that the status quo is such that the death penalty is not on the books, the onus rests on those who want to bring back the death penalty to prove that it is justifiable in today's society. Study after study has concluded that it is not a deterrent.
Does the Hon. Member believe it is appropriate that vengeance or retribution be the basis of our criminal justice system? Does he believe it is right that our criminal justice system should be based on the theory of an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth? If he thinks that that is morally right, perhaps he could indicate to me what other western nations have retribution as the basis of their criminal justice systems. Would the Hon. Member not agree that retribution has no place in the Canadian criminal justice system, that in fact there should be other principles that underlie our justice system, namely, the protection of society and the rehabilitation of those who would pursue a life of deviant behaviour?
I would admit that we all at times feel the need or desire to get even with someone who has committed a wrong, either toward us personally or toward the state collectively. However,

April 28, 1987
Capital Punishment
this is a human failing that we must overcome when we are talking about the criminal justice system, because if we were to allow vengeance to creep in and form the basis of our criminal justice system then we would in effect be saying that our criminal justice system is the law of the jungle. Would the Hon. Member not agree?

Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out earlier, I do not see this as being a form of revenge. Obviously the Hon. Member does, and that is the basic difference. This is why it is a question of the conscience, perception and perspective of each individual. It has never been proven that capital punishment is not a deterrent, as marginal and questionable as this particular area really is.
The Hon. Member asked what advanced nations have capital punishment. The answer is the United States of America, Ireland and Belgium, to name just a few.
There are those of us who believe that the protection of society is not a question of revenge or vengeance, but is merely a question of the ultimate crime being controlled. When I was a member of a law-enforcement agency, I recall an individual who had killed a child and was incarcerated. Through the system of parole he was released, according to the laws of the land. He was not on the street three months before he had killed again. I am not saying that in this particular case capital punishment would have been the penalty in the first instance, but had it existed it certainly would have been a deterrent to the second murder.
I do not want to base this entire debate on a question of revenge. It is a question of the protection of society and we have an obligation as legislators and leaders of the country to come forward with the protection that is needed today and in the future.

subtopic: CAPITAL PUNISHMENT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in such an important debate, so important in fact that after my election the first question put to me by a news reporter when I first arrived in Ottawa was wether I was for or against capital punishment. Canadians are following this debate with interest because it is very important, yet at the same time sad for me because nearly 15 years after the death penalty was abolished in Canada the Canadian Parliament reopens the debate with a motion aimed at restoring capital punishment.
During that time mankind was able to send men to the moon and in orbit in space. As Canadians we are very proud of the Canadarm sent to the moon to repair satellites. Our scientific achievements are well known, but after 15 years, since yesterday, publicly in this House, by debating the restoration of capital punishment we admit we have failed and that as citizens we have been unable to find solutions to provide better protection for our society and prevent certain kinds of murder from happening again.
Any way you look at them, Mr. Speaker, statistics show that the number of murders did not increase since the death penalty was abolished in Canada. In countries where capital punishment is still on the statute books statistics reveal that the number of murders did not decline either. So, Mr. Speaker, what is the point of restoring capital punishment in Canada?
We have a serious problem, a problem of society. How to protect society? How can we make sure that certain criminal acts will not be repeated? How can we make sure that the life of every human being on earth will be protected? That is the real issue of the debate. Those are the answers which we as parliamentarians must find and give people. But what are we up to? We want to restore the death penalty. And when I say it is sad, Mr. Speaker, it is because by so doing we admit we have failed in our duty, that we are unable to move forward, to better our society.
Killing those who have killed in order to prove that killing is wrong in today's modern society is absurd. As a parliamentarian I do not believe the state should have the power to kill someone. If killing is wrong, why should the state have the right to kill? That is what we are debating here today. People often argue that if the death penalty is reinstated that will dissuade people from committing murder. On statistical grounds alone that argument does not stand up. Most of the time even if murderers knew they would die they would still kill because they are not normal human beings. They are sick. That is what we should be addressing: how can we solve the problem, how can we cure those who need help instead of killing them?

Mr. Speaker, assuming that some day on our planet earth- there are even some scientists who are foreseeing this in the more or less distant future-there are more human beings than the planet can support, what will happen? Would the authorities decide to kill a lot of people to ease the problem? Or would they look at the problem as a whole to try and find a balance and save all human lives? That is the question, Mr. Speaker. Personally, I feel that by reinstating capital punishment in Canada after 15 years, we show that we are unable to find solutions in our modern society, to develop effective preventive mechanisms to reduce crime and to protect our society against unbalanced human beings.
Mr. Speaker, those who are in favour of reinstating capital punishment will certainly say that three out of every four Canadians agree with them. In my opinion and on the basis of the great many thorough discussions I have had with my Saint-Leonard-Anjou constituents, these polls mean that people want better protection. It is our penal code that should be revised.
Of course, we have penitentiaries. But are they part of the solution? In penitentiaries, we take criminals and lock them up
April 28, 1987

in small rooms. But is that a solution? Is that the way to cure them? Years ago, people felt that this was the solution. But today, have we considered all possibilities? Why do some people kill? If scientists can study and develop the technology to travel to the moon and throughout the universe, why can they not find out why some people kill instead of us wasting so much time and energy reinstating capital punishment in Canada after 15 years?
Mr. Speaker, I believe in life. I suggest that all human beings should be the right to live, even after committing a murder. It is our responsibility, as a society and as well-adjusted human beings, to find ways to help the murderer and to cure him, to protect both him and society, and not simply by locking him up to show him that everything is over, but maybe by truing to rehabilitate him. And it is my view, Mr. Speaker, that with all the scientific progress accumulated to date, if we really took the trouble, if we took the same amount of time available for this debate, if we used all the publicity enjoyed by this debate-and this is something I have been repeating for two and a half years, how many times have I been asked by the press whether I was for or against the death penalty. If we put all the emphasis enjoyed by the death penalty on finding a solution as to how to protect our society, how to rehabilitate and cure the people who kill, 1 think we would have a better society. This is where we should apply an ongoing effort, put all our energies to find a solution in the hope that some day our society will be better.
Mr. Speaker, of course this debate is very emotional. People who support capital punishment come up with examples- children that were killed, very young innocent children and women, all sorts of crimes that are really unacceptable. Of course there is no acceptable crime, but those crimes are most horrible. With capital punishment, they would like to say- Well, we found that individual guilty, we sent him to the gallows, the problem is solved. I do not think the problem is solved. First, we must ensure whether the convicted individual was the guilty one. How many people sentenced to die were innocent! Our judicial system is a human system, therefore subject to human error. There is that aspect. Think of the jury or the judge who sentenced someone to die and found a few years later they had erred. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, what their lives must be. So, the equation must be made on both side of the coin.
Those are horrible events, criminal acts with loss of life, but on the other side there is also the possibility of error. That has happened in history. Therefore, when someone says the solution is the death penalty, my answer is no, because statistics once more prove the opposite. Although some countries have capital punishment, the crime rate has not decreased. And here in Canada, the crime rate has not increased since we abolished capital punishment 15 years ago. We must therefore ask the question: Is that the right solution, and should we really, as a modern society, go over what was done 15 years ago, because this debate already took place twice in this House? Why should we, Mr. Speaker? I put it to
Capital Punishment
you: Why should we have this debate at this point, rather than debating our judicial system, looking at our Criminal Code, bringing in real reforms to our penitentiary system? That is the kind of debate we should have, Mr. Speaker, and that is where we should begin instead of moving backward. We are not making any progress, we are regressing.

What are the alternatives? How can we reduce the number of murders? No one, not even the most staunch supporter of the death penalty, argues that its reinstatement will prevent all murders. The declared aim is to reduce the murder rate. If our society is serious about that goal we must resist the temptation to adopt measures such as the death penalty which are illusory. Instead, our support must be directed toward effective alternatives.

We must find better alternatives. We must make sure that our criminals are put away until they are rehabilitated in order to protect society. Nowadays, of course, Canadians are concerned. It is true that they are asking for protection. Opinion polls indicate that quite clearly. However, as I said, Mr. Speaker, what they want is not the reinstatement of capital punishment but a more fair and equitable society that would reflect the history of mankind. And when at the beginning I said that I was sad, Mr. Speaker, I am really sad. For the past 15 years, since Parliament abolished capital punishment, we have made considerable scientific progress. We have sent human beings on the moon, we are exploring outer space, we have heart transplants and we have made so many incredible and marvelous scientific discoveries. How is it that after 15 years, we have to come back to capital punishment and have no other alternative than going backward?
This is not progress but regression. And on this issue, Mr. Speaker, I will continue to try to convince my colleagues that the reinstatement of capital punishment is not the best direction to take, but that we should find a better system and look at the structure of our penal and rehabilitation systems. Perhaps it is true, Mr. Speaker, that our rehabilitation system should be closely examined. It often happens that people undergoing rehabilitation commit other crimes. We have to consider the whole question. However, capital punishment would not solve those problems. It often happens that a murderer does not think about capital punishment. He is not a normal person.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell my colleagues that I will vote against the reinstatement of capital punishment.

Member to reflect on a very serious concern which I have with respect to the application of the death penalty, that being the fact that it is applied not to the rich and powerful in societies where it exists, but rather to those who are poor and, in many cases, are racial minorities.

Not only does capital punishment fail in its justification, but no punishment could be invented with so many inherent defects.

Similarly, the former Governor of Ohio, Michael Di Salle said this:
During my experience as Governor of Ohio, 1 found that the men on death row had one thing in common, they were penniless-the fact that they had no money was a principal factor in their being condemned to death.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member, who has spoken with great conviction against the death penalty and outlined a number of arguments, to comment as well on the unequal application of the death penalty in Canadian society.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not begin my remarks, as most of us are wont to do, by saying that I am pleased to take part in this debate, because I am not. My conscience dictates, however, that I must.
Sometimes it is casually said in light of the importance of an issue that it is a matter of life and death. However, I need not remind my colleagues in the House that the debate on which we are now embarking is a question of life and death.
I must state clearly and unequivocally that when it comes to such an issue of life and death, I opt in favour of life. If, as a society, we respect human life as sacred and inviolable, and if we recognize the rights of each person as primary, how can we do otherwise?
As has already been stated often, the death penalty in this country was abolished in 1976, even though by a narrow majority. However, if there is one thing that the people in this country want, it is a rule of law that is firm, strong, and predictable.
I take the position that it is incumbent upon those who want to restore the death penalty to justify the taking of life in the name of the state. The onus is on them, and it is a heavy onus, to prove why we should join that small band of countries that, by some means or another, inflict the death penalty.
The motion we have to address commences with these words:
That this House supports, in principle, the reinstatement of capital punishment-
That is what the debate is all about. Those first 11 words set out the real issue. As soon as anyone begins talking about first, second or third degree murder, or about hanging being too inhumane, that person is backing away from the real core issue.
[DOT]	(1600)
Does any Government have the right to sanction the killing of any person? It is a simple question but one which deserves more than a simple answer. Advocates of the death penalty will skip the moral issue, but can we? 1 have a letter on my desk, and I assume each Hon. Member received a copy of that
same letter, which was referred to yesterday. It was written by Leslie Parrott of Toronto whose daughter Alison was tragically abducted and murdered just last July. Mrs. Parrott writes in part:
It has more than ever convinced me that we as a society cannot ever and must
not ever condone killing, whether by state or by an individual, in any shape or
in any form.
She continues on to talk about victims' rights and states her belief that in no way can anyone's suffering be alleviated by the deliberate killing of another. Her message is clear and unconditional. Human life is sacred and killing is always wrong, who could have said it better?
We have already heard in the context of this debate several biblical quotations, beginning with the Book of Genesis, as justification for state killing. First let me say that the Roman Catholic Bishops, and practically all the councils of the other established churches, hold that it is abhorrent in the 1980s to turn to the Old Testament to justify a legal and moral position. If the church or synagogue or Christianity means anything today, the lessons to be learned are lessons of love. Love thy neighbour. Have compassion, understanding, charity and forgiveness. These are the teachings and principles of the church. If we take them away, we have not much left. The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away. Life is not ours to create and it is not ours to take.
Of course, arguments will be raised in favour of reinstatement, setting out, first, that there will be deterrence if the death penalty is there. To me, this is the only justifiable reason. If it can be shown that the death penalty has a deterrent effect then we might justify the return of the death penalty.
The second argument is that the penalty must suit the crime and, third, what about popular opinion which calls for reinstatement? There are other arguments such as the cost factor, but time will not permit me to address every one of these arguments.
First, with respect to deterrence, there are many who really believe that the death penalty has an effective deterrent ability for those who commit the crime of murder wilfully and with forethought, premeditated murder, but to me this is the last group which is likely to be deterred by the death penalty because theirs is the perfect crime and they will not be found out.
The facts are that in most western countries which have abolished the death penalty-and interestingly enough, Canada is included-the rate of murder has dropped or, put in another way, it has not climbed significantly since capital punishment was abolished.
A recent Statistics Canada report indicates that the rate of 2.19 per 100,000 in 1986 is the lowest homicide rate in 15 years, down from the 2.75 rate per 100,000 in 1976. In the United States currently 35 of the States have the death penalty. There are some interesting comparisons. For example,
April 28, 1987

Maine and Vermont are side by side with basically the same kind of people, income range and otherwise. Maine does not have the death penalty, Vermont does, yet Vermont's murder rate is slightly higher than that of Maine. It is the same with Rhode Island with no death penalty when compared with Connecticut, North and South Dakota, Virginia and West Virginia as well as with Oregon and Washington, which have a death penalty. In each case, the state which does not have capital punishment has a lower rate of murder although just slightly, than the state adjacent to it which does.
It is argued that the death penalty is needed to protect policemen and prison guards, and we all agree that policemen and prison guards have a difficult job and need all the protection which society-we, the people-can give, but I say to you, Mr. Speaker, in all sincerity, that the death penalty will not make their jobs one bit safer. The subculture in prisons will be there tomorrow as it was yesterday.
I do not want to enter into the numbers game but we did in fact have a bad year in 1962 while the death penalty was in place. In the year of our last hanging, 11 policemen were murdered. The high number since that date was in 1984 with six police murders, and at that time there was a substantial increase in the number of policemen serving their respective communities.
From 1961 to 1983, 14 prison guards were murdered with no clear indication of the deterrent effect of the death penalty. Indeed, the President of the Police Association of Ontario writes:
There is no concrete evidence to prove that it is or is not a deterrent and indeed
it is quite likely that we will never know with certainty if capital punishment
deters one who is contemplating murder.
I would ask my colleagues to note the reference to "one who is contemplating murder" since in this debate most of us are talking about premeditated and deliberate murder.
The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police has decided it is futile to base an argument of reinstatement on the grounds of deterrence. The point is simply that capital punishment has no material effect on the murder rate. It is not a deterrent and it fails completely to meet the test of justifying a return of the death penalty.
I turn next to the crime penalty aspect, the penalty must suit the crime. Retentionists will argue that legislation must make it safe for the public to walk the streets at night and at least with capital punishment a murderer will not commit a second offence. For them, the only just punishment for a murder, that most heinous of crimes, must be death. It is an appropriate means of justice-or so they say. Apart from death, there is no guarantee that a second offence will not take place-and I will not guarantee that it will not take place, either. But it is to be noted that the rate of occurrence of a second offence of the crime of murder is, thankfully, the lowest of all criminal offences.

In looking at these issues, one has to weigh the balance. Sometimes the cure is worse than the disease. While I have the greatest respect for our system of justice and our courts, I do not for one moment believe that that system rests on that delicate balance of an eye for an eye, or a tooth for a tooth, or an assault for an assault, or a rape for a rape, or a life for a life. Of course the penalty must suit the crime; but a life for a life concept is barbarous, outmoded, and revengeful. Yes, some convicted murderers, not executed, may murder again. But let us weigh the results of the restoration of capital punishment.
All of us have read the recently released study by Professor Freedman of the University of Toronto. We have a system of justice made up of people with feelings as strong as those held by the Members of this House. There is no doubt in my mind that the reimposition of the death penalty would have an effect on jurors. I have had a member of the Supreme Court of Canada say to me that, in the event that the death penalty is reinstated, he will resign before invoking that penalty.
Once again, the most frequent argument against the death penalty is the gross inequality of its application. I am convinced, as some of you are, that the wealth and status of the accused will have some bearing on the result. I am just as convinced that the death penalty, if imposed, would be imposed more frequently on the poor, the socially deprived, the disabled, or on the ethnic and social minorities.
Our courts are not infallible. Occasionally they do err. One of the reasons that lawyers are so very much concerned about this issue is that they know that false testimony is sometimes introduced into evidence; they know that there are cases of mistaken identity, cases of biased or circumstantial evidence. All of these things make it possible to convict an innocent person. It can happen. It has happened. No amount of compensation or expression of regret will ever bring back a life that the state mistakingly takes. What a terrible crime by the state against a citizen!
You may ask: What about the polls? I have to admit that my constituents read the polls and read the results, and they are just as concerned about the rise in crime generally as are people across the country. I know that a majority of Canadians favour the restoration of the death penalty.
Some of my colleagues have said that they will vote in accordance with the wants and the wishes of their constituents, and they ask why I do not do likewise.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I have come through three general elections, and in each one the issue of the reimposition of the death penalty has come up. It is a point that has been raised at candidates' meetings, general meetings, and in other forums. My answer has always been that I am opposed to the restoration of the death penalty. The people of St. Catharines do not expect me to change my religion or to vote against my conscience. I take some comfort in knowing my home community.

April 28, 1987
Capital Punishment
In this respect let me quote the words of Edmund Burke, who said: "Your representative owes you not his industry only but his judgment, and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it to your opinion".
Ours is not a "punch button" democracy. Each of us has been forced by the media to take a position on this question before having had the opportunity of engaging in a reasoned discussion or debate. Ours is not a country, either, of common referenda or plebiscites. We are expected to debate and fully reason any issue before the House before making a decision thereon. When the vote is finally taken on this issue, I expect the result to be a reasoned decision.
Those of you who were in the Chamber this morning to hear the words of the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) will know whereof we speak on this matter. For those who were not in the Chamber this morning for that speech, I commend it to you for your reading.
The real bottom line, as has been mentioned, is not the continued abolition or the reinstatement of the death penalty but our system of justice. It is our justice system that we have to look at and our justice system that we must be concerned with. I have always said that the taking of a life is the last thing that we should do, and I am not satisfied that we are anywhere close to having to take that last step.
One of the reasons that my constituents and your constituents feel as they do is that they are displeased and discouraged with our whole judicial system. They feel frustrated, ignored, and sometimes fearful for their own safety. They want to see that justice is being done. The public confidence in the judicial system is undermined by the discrepancies in sentencing. Confidence has to be restored in our parole system.
Canadians do not have faith in a system that they no longer understand. They read and hear little about it, and they do not believe that it reflects the kind of system that they were brought up under. Media coverage has led the people of Canada to believe that the crime rate is far in excess of what it is in fact, and they are now of the belief that only with the restoration of the death penalty will they be able to restore the law and order that was the norm in past times.
We are all concerned with violence in our way of life; far too many acts of homicidal violence take place in our society. But I sincerely do not believe that the return of the death penalty will resolve those problems. Rather, the problems of our society must be addressed by vigorous law enforcement measures, law reform measures.
Canadians want a society that is both just and humane. We want a criminal justice system that will respond effectively to the real needs of our citizens, who must be protected from crimes of violence. We, in our life-styles, cannot, at home and in our schools, continue a life of permissiveness without the counterbalance of restraint, discipline, and personal responsibility. Having disapproved of the use of the strap in our school system, the use of corporal punishment, we cannot now call for
capital punishment for the weaker among us who did not learn discipline and responsibility.
Society can, through its courts, express clearly and forcefully its profound condemnation of murder and other flagrant crimes against the person without resorting to the death penalty.
When the Lord put his mark upon Cain, the first biblical murderer, and cast him out of his family and into the wilderness, he did not kill him; he forced him into a life, remembering each day the wrong that he had committed.
This debate will be followed by a vote of conscience, free of dictate, partisan or Party loyalty. In good conscience, I shall cast my vote against the motion. I cannot do otherwise.

CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much regret that the Government has reopened the issue of capital punishment and made it necessary for me to participate in this debate.
During the last election I made it clear to my constituents that I am opposed to the reinstatement of the death penalty in Canada. My opposition is on moral grounds, on grounds bound to conscience. I believe that my constituents respect my decision and I would not be prepared to change my vote or my view on this issue even if that were the price of retaining my seat in the House of Commons.
A number of people during the course of this debate will be making a number of common arguments, and I basically support the arguments made by others who will be supporting the continued abolition of the death penalty. They will argue, and I agree, that capital punishment is not a deterrent and it is not, therefore, justifiable on that particular ground. They will argue, and I agree, that to restore capital punishment in Canada would be an uncivilized act and that we as Canadians should look at the precedent and practice of most western industrialized countries in western Europe, of Australia, New Zealand and all other countries in the OECD, with the exception of the United States, which have either banned the death penalty or in the case of Belgium and Ireland have not used it for a very long period.
April 28, 1987

They will note, as I note, that the murder rate was down in 1986 and that it has not risen in Canada since the death penalty was abolished 11 or 12 years ago. They will note, and 1 agree, that the chances of execution with the death penalty restored would very much depend on a person's social class, on how a person looked, whether he or she were of the middle class or seen as a loser, the court the person drew, the judge he or she drew, the lawyer, the jury, the defence lawyer, the jurisdiction in which the person appeared, whether or not he or she appeared before a jury, and a number of other factors like that. In other words, this application of a reinstated death penalty would be very unequal.
I noted, for example, in the statistics that the chances of being executed in the United States are a great deal greater if a person has murdered a white person rather than having murdered a black person. In the Republic of South Africa, that great example to us all, of the 115 executions in 1984, 113 were of blacks, only two were of whites. Your chances of being executed because you were black were something like 12 to 15 times greater than if you were white.
In my own constituency there was a tragic case a year or so ago, the death of Celia Ruygrok who was working in a halfway house in downtown Ottawa who was raped and then killed by a man who had a previous conviction for murder. That case has been brought forward. One cannot comment on it too greatly here except to express one's extreme condolences and regrets to Gerry Ruygrok and his wife, her parents and to all of those in the great, close-knit and loving family.
Gerry Ruygrok has expressed to my Leader and through him to this House his opposition to the death penalty. The evidence coming forward in the case and also before the inquest indicated that had our criminal justice system been working effectively, had parole been revoked, as it should have been in this case, then the incident could and should have been avoided. It seems to me that it is an example where we say we might have avoided this particular killing had there been the death penalty. The assailant would have been executed previously for his previous first offence. Therefore, this was an avoidable death.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is hypocritical of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who says he is against the death penalty, to be perfectly willing to let Parliament spend time on this debate on capital punishment, in the knowledge that it might result in legislation that in the final instance could mean the death penalty for some of our fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, it is the Pontius Pilate approach. I believe the Government should have shown some leadership on this issue, either by deciding that its policy would be to reinstate capital punishment or by deciding to do nothing.
We are told that 70 per cent of Canadians are in favour of the death penalty. But, Mr. Speaker, very few of those Canadians consider it a priority. Incidentally, two-thirds of
Capital Punishment
Canadians are opposed to the changes in the Patent Act being proposed by the Government, but the fact that the majority of Canadians object has not convinced the Government to drop the Bill. I agree that even if the Government is wrong about Bill C-22, it has the right and the duty, from time to time, to introduce legislation, even if that legislation is not supported by the majority of the people.
The Parliamentary Secretary who opened the debate said that now the Government had resolved the unemployment issue and dealt with Canada-U.S. relations and other problems it had been considering, it was time it kept its promise to hold a free vote on the death penalty.
Mr. Speaker, in seven provinces, the unemployment rate remains higher than it was during the recession from 1981 to 1983. An increasing number of jobs are part-time instead of full-time jobs, and some are for a short term only. In Newfoundland, the unemployment rate is 24 per cent. Among young people in Quebec, the unemployment rate is 16 or 17 per cent. The Government has yet to respond effectively to the youth unemployment problem that exists across the country. In fact, the recession is continuing. Mr. Speaker, there are all kinds of things for this Government to do. Ministers are complaining they do not have enough time to bring some very important Bills before Parliament and that we have many other Bills before the House that are just as important, but the Government will not be able to work on those Bills because Parliament is tied up with the death penalty.
Surely these other problems are more important than bringing back a measure which smacks of vengeance and which does not respond to the real problems of poverty, unemployment and the perception that there can and should be things done about security or law and order.
I would also point out that the scale of violence in Canada is grossly overestimated by many Canadians. One study that was done in Toronto indicated that Canadians felt that the murder rate in Canada was seven times higher than it actually is. In a single evening on the channels available in Metropolitan Toronto, more murders are perpetrated than occur in Metropolitan Toronto in an entire year. Most of the violence we see is fictional, and there is too much of it. From time to time, I feel thoroughly sickened by what I see on television. I see a set of values which, on the one hand is unduly commercial and appeals to people's vanity and greed, and on the other is perpetrating the myth that this is a violent society in which one can hardly dare to go out at night for fear of being attacked.
I have no problems when I walk anywhere in my constituency at any time of the day or night. There are some very limited areas in which I would recommend that a woman perhaps not walk at night, but in general our streets are safe. Our society in Canada is safe even though there are things we can and

April 28, 1987
Capital Punishment
should do, particularly with respect to the concerns, feelings and rights of victims.
I would like to put some statistics on the record to put the question of capital punishment into perspective. In 1983, there were over two million Criminal Code offences committed in Canada. That is too many, but that included speeding and other offences which I would suspect would probably make virtually every Member of Parliament one of those who from time to time may have violated the Criminal Code. Of those offences, 8 per cent or 172,000 were violent crimes.
To put things into perspective, it is interesting to note that for each policeman or policewoman on duty in Canada, there was an estimated one and a half to two violent crimes committed in the course of an average year. In other words, the perception of police always fighting crooks is incorrect. In fact, police are doing many other things as well and they do not, day after day, come into contact with violent crime.
Of that violent crime, something like one-third of 1 per cent were murders. The average between 1977 and 1983 was 589. Of those murders in the same seven years, on average 178 were first-degree murders, 170 were second-degree murders, and 140 were unreported.
The rate of conviction for murder is relatively low. It is running at about 19 per cent for first-degree murder and 29 per cent for second-degree murder. That translates to an average of 32 convicted first-degree murderers per year between 1977 and 1983 and 120 second-degree murderers. Assuming for the sake of argument that half of the first-degree convictions would in fact go to execution-and I do not know if that is realistic or not-then we are talking about perhaps 16 murderers per year who would actually hang, be electrocuted, be given an injection or be killed in some other awful way. One then must ask oneself about the biblical principle of the sanctity of human life and the Commandment: "Thou shalt not kill". We as a state would violate it whether one or 1,000 persons were executed for crimes of murder.
If there is to be deterrence, one must ask, what would be the rational response, supposing there is one, of someone who is on the verge of committing a crime which involves murder? There are 600 murders in a year and 32 convictions for first-degree murder, 16 of which might lead to a hanging. That is a 2.5 per cent chance of hanging and only that.
Most crimes are committed in passion, in anger, under the influence of drugs or under the influence of alcohol, but we are to assume that despite that, the criminal or potential criminal will stop, have a moment of lucidity and rationality, and say: "If I shoot this gun, then I might hang for the crime. There is a 2.5 per cent chance that I would hang, but 39 times out of 40 that I will not hang". Is that a deterrent? No, it is not. It is ridiculous to suggest that criminals think in those rational terms when murder is essentially an irrational act, but I would suggest that that is a very real factor.
I would like to read into the record a few letters which have come from my constituents. Despite the opinion polls, the mail
I am receiving from my constituents, which is substantial, is eight to one against the reinstatement of capital punishment and in favour of continued abolition. I have a letter here from young Elizabeth Monahan who lives in my riding. Her letter reads in part:
I am 11 years old, my name is Elizabeth and I am totally against the death penalty. You say it's wrong to kill somebody and then turn around and kill somebody yourself now does that make sense to you. What's the point of killing somebody?
We say that of murderers, we should say that of the state as well. She goes on:
And if you make a mistake and only find out too late what happens then, somebody's family is going to be pretty upset.
Another constituent who lives on Cartier Street has this to
say:
Dear Mike,
I take this opportunity to add my voice against the imposition of the death penalty in Canada. I have lived in this country, my new home, for about thirteen years and the absence of the death penalty was-is one of the many humane institutions I enjoyed.
I consider the death penalty as being nothing less than an act of collective vengeance, indeed legalized lynching.
I trust that you and your colleagues will do your best to prevent Canada from regressing into the barbaric age of "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth".
Another letter from a constituent reads as follows:
Dear Mike Cassidy,
I am writing to encourage you and all the other MPs to keep the death penalty out of Canada. I am opposed to any brutal or cruel punishments. 1 do not believe that fear will prevent murder. We see in the U.S. that the more fear, the more murders seem to occur. At least there is no solid statistical evidence that capital punishment works as a deterrent.
Families of victims deserve care & sympathy & support for their grief & anger. Those criminals who are out-of-control need restraint and also psychiatric care so they may change and not be tormented further by their own failings.
I hope you will follow your inner conscience & that it will lead you to oppose capital punishment, to support victims' rights to grieve & anger, and to call for further psychiatric help for all those who commit violent crime. I also feel tight gun control will minimize the number of murders we have.
Another letter from a constituent reads as follows:
Dear Mike
One issue concerns me more than any other facing Canada in the next few months. That issue is the death penalty. I had hoped the debate was behind us for good, the "hanging and flogging" wing of the Conservatives notwithstanding. Unfortunately, it is not.
He goes on to say:
We never should have to live again in a Canada which feels that legal murder is justice. All too much, the support on the other side is symptomatic of the kind of country people would like this to be-an Iran, a South Africa, a U.S.S.R., a China. No thanks, not my kind of Canada.
Another letter reads in part as follows:
We too know the death penalty is not a deterrent. Legalized killing of humans out of a sense of frustration at the lack of options or while pointing to the cost of prison sentences, is dehumanizing and demeans each of us individually.
Add to this the threat of executing an innocent party and you have a situation which is untenable on human, moral and legal grounds. We owe more to ourselves and our children.
April 28, 1987

We wish you well in your attempt to convince your colleagues to affirm the basic morality that civilization's history has been intent to show us, that killing people is antithetical to our existence. Teaching by example is the best tool we have to create Canada as a peaceful and secure society. The example that puts human blood on all our hands is the wrong one.
I could go on and on reading letters but I will only read a final letter from Mr. Ken Cunningham, the President of the John Howard Society of Ontario. He points out the number of organizations concerned with prison rights, the churches and the like, which have stood steadfastly in favour of abolition. Then he goes on to say the following:
As an organization which has worked for decades in the area of rehabilitation of offenders, we know that it is essential that the state's policies and practices model the behavior we expect of the offender. The death penalty, in our opinion is the ultimate hypocrisy. It does not reject violence, it embraces violence. It does not reject revenge, it elevates it to the status of law. It brutalizes us all. It removes the distinction between the murderer, who in his or her delusion feels justified in killing, and the rest of us, who in our delusions feel justified in killing the murderer.
I have quoted those views of my constituents at length and I subscribe to them.
This is a moral issue. The intensity of people opposed to reinstatement of the death penalty must be taken into account. I plead with my colleagues from all Parties. Listen to what Pope John Paul says. He calls for clemency and pardon for those who are condemned. The Canadian Council of Churches, representing 13 denominations, has said that it is implacably opposed to the death penalty. The Catholic Bishops in Canada have expressed very strong opposition. The Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) has come up with a handful of church people who are in favour. Of course there will be some. However, an overwhelming number of our moral and religious leaders say: Do not do it. Do not go backwards. They point out that the biblical precept of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth was put into the Bible to stop wanton vengeance for minor crimes at a time when the death penalty was prescribed for such things as swearing, blasphemy, sorcery, or fornication. There would not be many of us left if those penalties were enforced today.

My colleagues suggest they have never been guilty of those sins. 1 wish them well.
The concept of an eye for an eye was a measure of penal reform in those days. It was to prevent worse penalties from being imposed. For God's sake, whatever your religious faith may be today, let us be guided by the religious teachers who are still, praise the Lord, around. I am a Unitarian. I respect the teaching of the Christian churches without being a Christian. I believe those things should be carefully listened to.
I want to say a final word about the process. The amendment put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for
Capital Punishment
Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) would effectively allow the parliamentary committee set up under this resolution to go around the country to examine the issue without being committed to reinstatement. That would follow the precedent set on child care, star wars, acid rain, the rights of the disabled, and so on. That is a good precedent. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) quotes the McGrath Committee which recommended wider use of parliamentary committees. However, he neglected to point out that McGrath recommended that these committees conduct general inquiries when policy choices have not been made. It is an abuse for this Parliament to turn around and make such a profound decision without having inquired into it much, much further.
I believe the process is fundamentally flawed. If we have to bring it forward at all, and I wish we did not, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) could still respect his commitment to a free vote by sending a parliamentary committee out to investigate the issue. We have noted that several Members of Parliament have already changed their position. Having voted in favour of capital punishment, they are now opposed. That comes with deeper and more profound study and reflection on a very difficult issue. I believe a parliamentary committee, whatever its initial prejudice on the issue might be, could well come back and recommend against capital punishment, particularly when we note that this has been done in most other countries.

So finally, Mr. Speaker, I conclude by saying that I will vote against this resolution. For reasons of conscience I believe it is a moral question and I appeal to all my colleagues of all political Parties here in the House of Commons. If you have no doubt this is a measure which in the end is irreversible, and for this reason it is a bad way to make a decision when there is no consensus in the House of Commons. If there is no consensus, better live with the existing situation than restoring the death penalty and running the risk of legally killing certain people who have been found guilty of homicide, and then again change our point of view.
So I urge all those who may entertain some doubts to vote against this Government resolution.
