subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAR MEASURES ACT SUGGESTED REPEAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to move this motion asking the Government to consider the advisability of repealing the War Measures Act, and I appreciate the opportunity to debate the motion this afternoon. I am sorry that the motion was not made a votable motion because I think there are many Canadians who would support Parliament expressing itself on this particular long-standing piece of legislation.
There have been indications at various times that Governments were considering a change to this legislation, amendment of it to weaken its Draconian powers or, conceivably, replacement of it with other legislation, but that has not happened.
It is incumbent upon me this afternoon to speak for all those Canadians who, at various times, have said that the War Measures Act should not be on the statute books of a country which believes in the rule of law, that the War Measures Act should be replaced or, at the very least, should be removed from the books so that we might enter a better area of provision for emergencies perhaps, if that is necessary, but without having this particular power available to Canadian Governments.
The legislation itself, particularly in Section 6 of the Bill as it was originally passed in 1914, indicates the kinds of powers which Governments have. It reads:
6. The Governor in Council shall have power to do and authorize such acts and things, and to make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war. invasion or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it is hereby declared that the powers of the Governor in Council shall extend to all matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated, that is to say:-
April 28, 1987

(a)	censorship and the control and suppression of publications, writings, maps, plans, photographs, communications and means of communication;
(b)	arrest, detention, exclusion and deportation;
(c)	control of the harbours, ports, and territorial waters of Canada and the movements of vessels;
(d)	transportation by land, air, or water and the control of the transport of persons and things;
(e)	trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture;
(0 appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property and of the use thereof.
In this extensive clause are powers given to a Government of Canada to be invoked as a blank cheque to take practically any kind of action at all that it might think advisable in circumstances of emergency. We note that it is not only in situations of war, or even more, actual invasion of Canada, that these powers are available to Canadian Governments, but also in situations of insurrection in Canada, and not only actual situations of insurrection. The powers are available in a context of apprehended insurrection.
Anyone who thought in 1960 when the Bill of Rights was being debated in the House of Commons and when the then Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, resisted suggestions that his Bill of Rights should supersede this legislation, that this legislation would not be used in peacetime discovered only 10 years later how wrong they were. In October of 1970 when kidnappings occurred in the Province of Quebec, as I am sure we all remember, and when the Canadian Government became anxious about maintaining order, as it claimed, and there was concern about finding those who had perpetrated these acts, the Government chose to use the War Measures Act, not only as a symbol, but as the reality of its exercise of power in the Province of Quebec. There were those far beyond the borders of Quebec who saw possibilities in this. I was living in the interior of British Columbia in those days. I was most shocked to hear a mayor of Vancouver speaking at the time of the possibilities of dealing with people in his own province under the new realities which the War Measures Act proclaimed.
The War Measures Act very significantly provided a basis for other actions. The proclamation of the Act was the authority for the publication of regulations. The regulations which were published made certain associations which had been legal before the Act was invoked now illegal. They made any sort of involvement with those organizations which had been legal before now a matter of crime.
In these contexts we saw the worst reassertion in our time of principles which long stood, back in the 1920s and 1930s, as Section 98 of the Criminal Code. These provisions followed the Winnipeg sympathetic strike which had been resisted by the first leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation year after year and were finally repealed in the middle of the Great Depression after the Liberal victory of 1935. A decade and a half after those provisions had been put in the Criminal Code providing for action against political organizations they reappeared in this context in 1970.
War Measures Act
It was not only that kind of abuse of law by the Government of Canada that made the War Measures Act possible. We have still before us today, in the declaration of the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) that there is a need to redress the action against Japanese Canadians, the reality that the War Measures Act was the basis for moving against the Japanese Canadian population of British Columbia. Canadian citizens found themselves dispossessed and relocated. Many of them found themselves detained in the process and afterwards. They found their lives completely disrupted. In a somewhat similar way as those several hundred persons who were arrested in 1970 never obtained compensation, there has never been adequate compensation for the Japanese Canadians who experienced this under the War Measures Act beginning in 1942 and continuing for at least the next half a dozen years.
It was for those reasons that the Special Committee on the Participation of Visible Minorities, which did such yeoman work in the last couple of years of the previous Parliament, in its Recommendation No. 34 called upon the Department of Justice to "review the War Measures Act with a view to proposing the safeguards necessary to prevent a recurrence of the kind of mistreatment suffered by the Japanese in Canada during and after World War II". It was Japanese Canadians of course who suffered this, not Japanese citizens in Canada.
That was the recommendation of all members of the committee. I would go further, as I do in this motion, to call upon the Government to consider repealing the Act altogether. If we need some sort of emergency legislation, let it be properly drawn up. In this area of the Charter we need provisions which prevent the kind of arbitrary action which has been taken in the past. We need protection for the rights of Canadians.
In emergency legislation we need review mechanisms so that it is possible for those who have been detained or have otherwise suffered under the legislation to obtain compensation for what has been done to them. Nothing less than that is necessary. Individuals must have a basis for redress. It is not sufficient for the Government of Canada to act in this way. It is an abuse of rights and was such long before the Bill of Rights. It is tragic that the Bill of Rights was not regarded as being violated if action occurred under the War Measures Act. I am sorry to say that the provisions of the 1982 Charter allowing for reasonable departures from freedom, opens the same kind of possibility that we found in the fall of 1970.
O)
Recognizing the possibility for arbitrary exercise of power, which needs always to be constrained by the law of the land in order to have the rule of law truly prevail, I call upon the Parliament of Canada to urge the Government to consider a repeal of this War Measures Act of 1914 and give us carefully considered legislation in peacetime that will not be rushed through as was done by our predecessors in 1914, in giving a blank cheque to the Government of Canada.

April 28, 1987
War Measures Act

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAR MEASURES ACT SUGGESTED REPEAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) is to be congratulated for a most sensible suggestion that is, doing away with the War Measures Act, the subject of much controversy today. It is too severe an instrument to be used in circumstances short of war.
Perhaps what we should do is to look closely at the vacuum that would be left by this Act and see what should replace it. Maybe we need more precisely conceived and worded legislation to protect Canadians in many emergencies.
Since Roman times, Governments have recognized that they have a fundamental obligation to provide for the safety and security of their peoples in times of catastrophe. This dictum is summarized in the Latin phrase: Salus poluli suprema est lex, or, the safety of the people is the supreme law.
The Government of Canada recognizes this fundamental obligation and is committed to improving the national standard of emergency preparedness and developing the national capacity to provide for the safety and security of Canadians in emergencies of all kinds. This is done on the basis of partnership with the provinces, with mechanisms to provide comprehensive, joint planning and the formulation of co-ordinated arrangements for dealing with all aspects of emergencies falling under their respective jurisdictions.
Officials of Emergency Preparedness Canada, and other federal Departments have been addressing the entire question of legislation surrounding emergency response in Canada and during the course of their review a number of gaps in the legal framework for emergencies have become apparent, raising questions about the Government's ability to provide for the safety of Canadians during national emergencies.
The current statutory framework for authorizing emergency powers has some shortcomings.
The War Measures Act is generally conceded to be too broad and sweeping for peacetime public safety or public order emergencies. While it provides adequate powers for war or invasion, it includes few safeguards against abuse. Less provocative legislation for dealing with a deepening international crisis in not available.
Other statutes such as the National Defence Act, the Criminal Code, and several others Acts contain some provisions that could be applied to emergencies. In most cases these provisions are unnecessary for a minor emergency and likely to be very inadequate for a major emergency. Some would possibly be subject to challenge under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If invoked in combination, they would give rise to considerable confusion. Finally, few are adequately safeguarded. The Crown prerogative and the common law doctrine of necessity could possibly be used as the legal basis for taking emergency measures. However, the legal foundations of this approach are shaky and uncertain.
The Government could resort to the enactment of ad hoc legislation during an emergency, basing its legislation on the
"peace, order and good government" clause of the Constitution Act. However, the ad hoc approach could result in hasty and poorly drafted legislation if prepared in the heat of an urgent crisis. The process could be insufficiently rapid if Parliament were not in session, and would be impossible if Parliament were dissolved when the emergency arose.
Emergency legislation is an attribute of statehood. Canada is unique among industrially developed nations in not having comprehensive emergency legislation on its books. As well, all of our provinces and territories have legislation in place to deal with their responsibilities in emergencies.
As I said, I understand that the Government is reviewing the entire matter, and because revocation of the War Measures Act is on its agenda, I am certain that shortly we shall be discussing this matter publicly and in much greater detail.
There is no doubt that we in Canada must give greater attention to the entire area of emergency preparedness and to our ability to respond to crises. Emergencies take many forms and arise from many causes. They may be man-made in origin or may be the result of acts of God. They occur in peacetime and in war, and the range of precipitating causes encompasses natural disasters, such as epidemics, earthquakes, fire, floods, tornadoes or drought; technological mishaps such as industrial spills, pollution or major accidents; civil disturbances arising from revolts, terrorism or riots, conventional war and finally, the ultimate threat of nuclear attack.
The common factors in these disparate events are the sudden threat they pose to the community, the widespread harm they cause, and the need for prompt, often extraordinary measures to mitigate their effects and recover from them. In different ways and to varying degrees they may place in jeopardy the life and property of the individual, disrupt the peace, order and welfare of the community and, in the most extreme cases, threaten the continued existence of Canadian society itself.
Our ancestors lived in a less complicated age. With increasing population, especially in our urban centres, and with the threat of technological threats of all kinds mounting-ranging from chemical spills to the possibility of some madman launching a nuclear or biological attack-we are at the mercy of forces often beyond our control.
Our entire civilization seems to hang on an electrical thread. We saw what happened last summer when downtown Ottawa was without power for days; we know what happens in many emergencies when the power fails in the winter at temperatures of minus 40 degrees Celsius. Even in mid-summer, when tornadoes strike a community and the power goes off for a couple of days, freezers full of food can spoil. We have seen many instances in Canada when communities have been isolated because of floods and food has been airlifted in. Even those with freezers stocked with food found they had nothing to eat because it went bad. We saw what happened not too long ago in Montreal when fire put Air Canada's computerized reservation system out of action for days. Add to this incidents such as the Mississauga train derailment, when
April 28, 1987

escaping chlorine gas forced the evacuation of thousands, and it gives an idea of what kinds of things can happen in this country almost daily.
We are fortunate in having in Canada a sensible and effective emergency response system. Through the offices of Emergency Preparedness Canada, the agency responsible for co-ordinating the federal response to emergencies and for encouraging a uniform system of emergency response across the country, joint activities have been undertaken with provincial officials to evaluate current resources, both legal and material, assess actual needs, demarcate and co-ordinate respective responsibilities and to develop comprehensive plans for dealing with emergencies of any kind and of any scale.
The federal Government has concluded Memoranda of Understanding with all but three of the provinces and territories in order to demarcate respective responsibilities for emergency planning. A joint emergency preparedness program has been established with the provinces and territories to enhance the national emergency response capability and to encourage co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces and territories.
Further, disaster financial assistance arrangements have been put in place as a means of providing financial assistance to the provinces and the territories when the cost of dealing with the disaster would place an undue burden on the provincial economy. In general, the provinces and territories are well prepared to deal with the kinds of peacetime emergencies that have arisen in the past.
What we want in place of the War Measures Act is the kind of legislation other modern democratic states have had for many years.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAR MEASURES ACT SUGGESTED REPEAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate, but I am certainly not in support of this resolution. I think it would be the height of foolishness, if not idiocy, for a democracy that believes in the rule of law to disarm itself of the only method that it has consistent with the rule of law of dealing with crises.
Listening to the New Democratic Party and the arguments they raise that this should be repealed and that we should try to put something more modern and sensible in its place later, gives me one more reason to be glad that the Canadian people have never given the New Democratic Party the kind of support they have sought in election campaigns.
I have many reservations about the War Measures Act. If we had the wisdom that we have now when it was being drafted in 1914 it might have been a better and more moderate Act. I wish it were now possible to draft an improved version consistent with the principles which are fundamental to us in our democratic society today. However, the suggestion that that Act should be done away with, even if it means there is nothing in its place, is, to me, the height of irresponsibility. It is a way of betraying our democracy. It is a way of putting us into some predicaments.
War Measures Act
Let me give an example of one or two predicaments in which we would find ourselves if this New Democratic Party resolution succeeded. My colleague, the Hon. Member from Scarborough, referred to the derailment in Mississauga where a few tank cars full of chlorine gas fell off the tracks and might have killed a quarter of a million or more Torontonians, people living in the Mississauga area. The emergency team to which the Hon. Member referred, which is established and does work well with federal, provincial and municipal volunteers, and so on, would have arrived on the scene. It would have needed to commandeer some buildings in the area to use as hospitals. They would have had to rely on the Expropriation Act, which the federal Government introduced very proudly a few years ago, which gives 60 days' notice to the owners of that building, and if the owners of the building did not want to allow them in, they would have absolutely no authority to go in to establish hospitals.
There is nothing in the law of Canada, nothing in the law of necessity and nothing in the Crown prerogative, which permits the Government to take away a large building from its owner even if hundreds of thousands of Canadians are dying outside and need to be brought in and sheltered. Perhaps the owner would co-operate. Perhaps the owner could be spoken to and even pressured, but I do not believe that is the way to run the country even in a time of war.
I believe the country should be ruled by the rule of law, and the War Measures Act is consistent with the rule of law. The Act itself, as primitive as it is, requires the matter to be brought to the attention of Parliament. It has to be legislated. Procedures have to be set out in regulations. They have to be available for people to look at. Surely to God that is a better way to deal with the crisis which could have arisen and can arise any day of the week in this vast country of ours. To suggest that we should have nothing like the War Measures Act which could save hundreds of thousands of Canadians in a crisis situation is irresponsible.
Let me talk about the possibility of invasion. We may never be invaded. I hope we never are. But if we are invaded, how are we going to respond? I was once Solicitor General. Let us say we are invaded and have the problem of what to do with our prisons. Let us say there is a terrible tragedy of the sort which occurred in Europe. Should the prison guards have to stay on the job? Should the inmates continue to be fed three meals a day if the rest of the population is starving? Should they be moved somewhere? Should the prisons be used for prisoners of war if we are successful in capturing our invaders and want to use the prison for that purpose? Should the warden be able to turn his guards on the civil authority or on the military authority for wanting to use our penitentiaries for that purpose? That is ridiculous. How could we handle an invasion of that scale without having the possibility of rapidly reorganizing rights and freedoms and doing it according to some basis of rule of law.

April 28, 1987
War Measures Act
1 do not like the War Measures Act. I could visualize a better version being drafted. Elowever, to say we should do away with it, with nothing to replace it, is to say that there are circumstances where we are prepared not to have the rule of law at all.
I want to talk now about the Charter of Rights and Freedoms because I think the Charter of Rights and Freedoms must be reviewed as a very important constraint on the War Measures Act. Let us say that in a regrettable circumstance we are at war and some measures are introduced under the War Measures Act which establish press censorship. What if our military plans of defence of Canada come into the hands of the media? If they are printed, the enemy can buy copies of the daily newspapers and learn where Canadian troops are going to be deployed over the next few months. We could call in the media and order them, if we did not have the War Measures Act, not to print those plans, but we have absolutely no authority to do that. That would be an illegal act and, in my view, it would be an infringement on the rights of the press and a violation of the rule of law. Or we could introduce under the War Measures Act some program of censorship which would make it very clear that the authority defending our country in those circumstances would be legally able to order the media not to print any plans of the Canadian Armed Forces which fell into their hands. Without the War Measures Act we would have no legal way of doing that.
I will take my third example as a way of explaining what the Charter adds. Suppose people start writing letters to the editors complaining about the way in which the war is being conducted, about the way the Government is handling the powers it has, and the censor decides under the powers of the War Measures Act, because they are stated in very broad terms, that the Government does not need these critical articles to be printed in the newspaper. That, in my opinion, would be a violation of the Charter. The censor could not prevent the media from printing criticism of the Government, but it should be able to prevent the media from printing plans which show the way in which Canada will defend itself in the invasion, and I am still using my hypothesis of invasion. There is no way we could justify criticism of the Government being censored, whereas there would be justification for censoring the plans of the Canadian Armed Forces being printed in the media.
The Charter does add something, and when my friend regrets the fact that all we receive from the Charter is protection of things that are reasonable-we do not get the protection of everything or things that are not reasonable- frankly, it does not bother me very much. I am relieved that protection extends to what is reasonable. I voted for the Charter and I am quite sympathetic with the idea that rights which are asserted beyond the point of reasonableness in a democratic society and its circumstances are not protected. Therefore, to make a point, the War Measures Act has a lot to offer the Canadian people. Perhaps it could be improved. Perhaps it has been abused. I would say that with the Charter
of Rights and Freedoms there is a considerable restraint on the way it can be exercised. For a politician who wants to be taken seriously to argue there should be no War Measures Act, that Canada should have no lawful way of dealing with emergencies until perhaps Parliament brings in another law, in my view disqualifies that person from participating in the discussion of what the rule of law ought to mean in a democratic society.
I want to conclude by saying that I defend the use of the War Measures Act during the FLQ crisis. My friend, the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. MacLean), used the FLQ crisis as proof that the War Measures Act is a big mistake and not necessary. I was there and remember the circumstances. The City of Montreal and the Province of Quebec were demanding that the War Measures Act be introduced. Ordinary citizens were afraid to go to work. They were staying at home because of fear of terrorism in the streets of the city. I also remember the effect of the War Measures Act. It restored a sense of confidence and peace in the City of Montreal.
If the War Measures Act had been a more nuanced instrument, and it should be, there might have been able to be a more precise and relevant intervention into the normal rules and regulations of the community. However, that was the Act that we had. It was brought in and it accomplished what had to be accomplished. I feel that the War Measures Act proved itself in the FLQ crisis. That is far from saying it discredited itself during that FLQ crisis.
As a member of the Liberal Party who voted in favour of the imposition of that measure at the time, I honestly believe that history will show those whom Mr. Trudeau described as "bleeding hearts" to have been on the wrong side of the issue. These people were unwilling to have our society defend itself by the only means that it had at hand.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to echo the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) and by my Conservative colleague from Scarborough East (Mr. Hicks) to stress the need to repeal the War Measures Act.
Never twice without a third time, as the saying goes. Sadly enough, the War Measures Act made these words even truer. It will not be imposed a fourth time, three times is enough. A number of Canadians of Japanese origin and a lot of Quebecers are the living proof that the letter may not kill, but it certainly can cause serious injuries.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the War Measures Act and its built-in excesses has caused enough harm. It is a dangerous weapon which no longer has its place, even in a legislative arsenal.
Appropriately my learned colleagues have pointed out that in recent years all political Parties have spoken against this unfair law and for the need to draft new legislation.
April 28, 1987

I do not think it is necessary to emphasize the fact that the former administration did not keep this promise. What matters is that our Liberal colleagues join forces with our NDP colleagues and with us on the Government side to give Canada emergency measures worthy of this great country of ours. Our laws should reflect what we are-one of the most democratic nations in the world. This is how we are seen worldwide, and this is how we see ourselves.
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues who rose before me gave us a good idea of the kind of Bill which will replace the War Measures Act. Once it has been the subject of exhaustive consultations with the provinces, this Bill will provide the essential guarantees which are lacking in the current legislation. The War Measures Act will be subject to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Canadian Bill of Rights and the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights.
The interests of the provinces will also be adequately protected during emergencies. The consultation mechanisms provided under the proposed legislation are unprecedented in Canada's constitutional history, because they guarantee the provinces a major role prior to the declaration of a state of emergency.
Over the years, Mr. Speaker, the War Measures Act has given rise in this Chamber to comments where shame and anger were the predominant sentiments. That is why I want to say how proud I am of the steps being taken by our Government and why I want to share this sentiment with all the Members of this House.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAR MEASURES ACT SUGGESTED REPEAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that there is not a Member in this House who does not subscribe to the repeal of the War Measures Act and its replacement by a comprehensive safeguard of legislation with which to deal with a wider spectrum of possible national emergencies in an appropriate manner.
The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) will be gratified to know that this Government has every intention of presenting such legislation. The people of Canada and their elected representatives have for years been demanding that this blunt instrument be abolished. Its powers are too sweeping. On two of the three occasions on which it was invoked, it involved serious violation of fundamental freedoms in Canada.
Other modern states have had appropriate legislation to deal with national emergencies for years. Canada is lagging in this respect. Despite successive promises by the former Liberal Government, nothing was done about it. But the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has, on several occasions, promised to do away with the War Measures Act, a blunt instrument designed for another age, and replace it with something more in keeping with our times. It is on our agenda, and will be presented to this House.
We want to be sure, Mr. Speaker, that what replaces this infamous Act is right and appropriate for our society and for
War Measures Act
our times. It is not simply a matter of throwing out an inadequate piece of legislation. Our society is much more complex now than in 1914, when the War Measures Act was originally enacted.
I do not know whether you are aware, Mr. Speaker, but that Act was passed without dissent and after just one half hour of debate.
The emergency powers granted to the Government were not spelled out in the legislation. Rather, the Governor in Council was given broad powers to declare a state of emergency, and then to pass orders and regulations that could replace any statute of Parliament, all without Parliament ever having its say. Under the Act, a proclamation is considered conclusive evidence that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists.
In the spring of 1971, realizing that the existing Act was too imprecise to deal with emergencies in a modern democratic state, proposals for legislation were considered. The Government of the day proposed the appointment of a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to consider the enactment of such legislation. However, that committee was not appointed, and the legislation was never introduced. And so the War Measures Act, a totally inadequate and inappropriate Act, remains on the books.
One of the troublesome features of this Act, Mr. Speaker, is that in the past, regulations under the War Measures Act replaced statutes and normal laws, after an emergency was declared, without the consent of Parliament. We want to ensure that the new legislation brings Parliament further into the process and builds in other safeguards to protect the rights of Canadians should the legislation need to be invoked.
We have every intention of ensuring that the civil rights of Canadians will be considered first and foremost. We want to place limits on the use of the Act, and tailor it to specific emergency situations.
Some would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps we should just throw out the War Measures Act and pass emergency legislation when it is needed. I feel that that would be dangerous. Such an approach could lead to delays in responding to crises, and it would be impossible were Parliament not in session or dissolved when the emergency arose.
In addition, legislation rushed through in the heat of a crisis might be more likely to run roughshod over civil rights than would a properly safeguarded Act, calmly and carefully considered, by Parliament, using the instruments which Parliament has provided.
As we well know, Mr. Speaker, natural and man-made disasters are occurring with great regularity. Canadians who say it cannot happen here remind me of those who argued, in the 1920s, that there was no sense in Canada preparing for emergencies because we lived in a fire-proofed house far from inflammable materials.

April 28, 1987
War Measures Act
It is amazing how quickly developments can overtake the best prepared of organizations. One needs only to look at the recent New Brunswick floods, or the gas cloud that sent people to hospital in Calgary. Both New Brunswick and Alberta have superb organizations to look after the safety of their citizens. But things can happen out of the blue.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, did you know that more than 1,000 earthquakes occur in Canada annually? Because most of them happen in isolated spots, the damage is light, and they do not make headlines. But did you realize, Mr. Speaker, that scientists predict that within the next 25 years there could be an earthquake of catastrophic proportions in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia, in my own home area? An emergency preparedness official claims that such an event could be so disastrous as to be considered a national disaster.
For reasons such as these, we need to have in place national legislation, to identify very clearly the responsibilities of various orders of Government under crisis conditions of national proportions. The citizens of a society such as ours have the right to know in advance how their rights and freedoms might be limited in a serious emergency; and on the other side of the coin, what limits will be placed on government action.
I should like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by expressing our appreciation of the Hon. Member's efforts in bringing forward this proposal. I want to reassure him that the Prime Minister and this Government are committed to repealing the War Measures Act and replacing it with legislation that is fair and just. I can assure the Member that we will be doing that in the very near future.

We opposed then, as we do now, separatism. We opposed then, as we do now and always will, acts of terrorism. However, we understood the fears and concerns of the people of Quebec.

speechtext: Leave has been granted to the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) to move the adjournment of the House pursuant to Standing Order 29 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the current crisis facing Canadian grain producers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan J. Hovdebo (Prince Albert) moved:
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
That this House do now adjourn.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we have asked for this emergency debate because, as every Member of this House knows, and as anyone who is even remotely connected with agriculture knows, there is a crisis in the industry. All of agriculture is suffering these days but we are particularly concerned at this moment and for the next year about the grain industry. This debate is an attempt to bring before this House and the country the real crisis grain farmers are facing.
This crisis has been building for years, but during the last week or so there have been a number of events which have moved it from a crisis to an emergency. First, last week the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) announced an 18 per cent reduction in the initial prices for grain. Every farmer knows that that reduction was a minimum, because when the grain spreads are announced that drop will become greater. That 18 per cent decrease in grain prices comes on top of a 20 per cent decrease inflicted upon farmers last year. Even before that grain farmers across the country were feeling the pinch.
Second, yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced that he was removing the 18-month old moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures. That action puts at risk about 20 per cent of FCC borrowers who are in arrears. More than that, it sends a signal to financial institutions all across the country that the federal Government is removing its protection from farms. It sends a signal which indicates open season, not only on farms but on small businesses as well. It sends a signal that the Government will no longer make a commitment to retain the family farm.
Third, and perhaps this is the most devastating event of all, if you can call it an event, the Government has refused to commit itself to some kind of deficiency payment to make up for the reduction in grain prices. Many farm groups across the country, and many Members of this House, particularly in the Opposition, have attempted to get from the Government some kind of commitment which would assure farmers that some deficiency payment would be available.
Farmers realize that with the Government indicating much lower grain prices and that it will not commit itself to any level of deficiency payment, the crisis becomes an emergency. When the Government announces open season for farm foreclosures by removing the moratorium, the crisis becomes an emergency. The withdrawal of protection only applies to FCC loans, but every farmer in financial difficulty looked to that moratorium as a commitment by the Government to keep them on the farm. Why should a private bank go the extra mile to try and keep a farmer farming when the Government will not do it?
This crisis has manifested itself in many ways. First, we have had a large number of farmers leaving the farm. Quite often you will hear people say, well, it is not as bad this year as it was last year. It was not as bad last year as it was the year before. However, let us all remember that when a group of farmers leave the farm they do not come back. It is cumulative. Five hundred leave this year and 500 left last year and 1,000 farmers are off the land. If you extend it for three years, it goes up to 1,500, and so on.
The crisis has also manifested itself in a great deal of stress on the family farm, resulting in family breakup and discouragement for many farmers. Ordinarily spring is a time of great enthusiasm and renewal. Farmers are out cultivating, seeding, and this is the time the Government picks to take action it has taken and make the announcements it has made-lower prices, no protection. Many people think that life on a farm is not stressful; in ordinary and good circumstances that is possibly true. However, when your family depends on you, when the bank is looking over your shoulder and the Government is abandoning you, stress is something that you live with.
It is not that the Government has done nothing. It has done something. Previous Governments put in place the Western Grain Stabilization Program, and an insurance program. A drought relief program has been in place for many years. The current Government last year put in place a special grains program which supposedly gave $1 billion to grain farmers across the country. That promise was made last October. The money has not yet all materialized, but we expect it will come.

April 28, 1987
The Western Grain Stabilization Program pays for deficits incurred by farmers in the previous year. Those programs are in place and have helped but are not solving the problem. As one farmer told me, "they just keep you dangling a little longer but in the end you go under anyway".
How can the Government deal with lower prices set in an export market? They can negotiate, but Canada is basically a price-taker rather than a price-setter. Therefore, we must sell our grain on the world market at the available price. However, if the Canadian Government has a commitment to keep the agricultural industry viable it must take some action to ensure that farmers can survive. It must either guarantee the farmer a specific price for his grain or, if that is open to too many problems, guarantee him a basic return from his farm. All the Government really need do is assure the farmer that if he plants and harvests he can survive.
The Government says it has a debt review program in place and can, therefore, lift the moratorium. However, the review boards which have been put in place across the country have no teeth. They are unable to make judgments which will allow the farmer to remain on the farm if he is in trouble. The hated transition program makes no attempt to keep the farmer on the farm.
I think these two programs are an indication of the commitment which the Government has to the family farm. First, the Farm Debt Review Program does not have the mandate to keep the farmer on the farm. The Saskatchewan Farm Security Act has such a mandate and does everything to keep the farmer operating. The Farm Debt Review Board only brings the debtor and debtee together to talk.
The transition program is exactly that. The Government is spending money so that another 500 or 1,000 farmers can leave the farm. The moratorium should not have been removed until the Government had in place a debt relief program which would give the agricultural community confidence that it can survive and that the Government will help it to do so.

We can only ask whether we have a philosophical commitment to the family farm. Europe has such a commitment. In Europe subsidy programs have been put in place. Although we may not like them and may disagree with them, they have been put in place because of a commitment to keep the family farm operating. Subsidy programs may not work well for us, but they have chosen that method in Europe.
Japan as well guarantees their farmers a price for their products which will ensure them of a living wage. We do not necessarily want to mimic these programs, but they assure those farmers that they are wanted and that their Government is willing to commit a certain amount of funds to give the agricultural community the confidence it needs.
The Government apparently does not have the commitment to the agricultural community to allow farmers to plant and harvest crops with the assurance that they will receive enough return for the product to allow them to survive. Across the country we have been facing a situation for some time which requires, not a band-aid solution but a global solution which considers all the requirements of the farmer.
It does not help to reduce the price of diesel fuel if farm taxes are increased. It does not help to reduce the cost of fertilizer if, by the same process, the cost of chemicals is increased. All parts of the farming process are important. Doing something about each part will, in the end, impact upon the amount which the farmer will take home.
However, that will not solve the problem. Canada must take a good look at the entire agricultural industry and make the decision that we want the agricultural industry and the family farm to survive.

We have been attempting to get that kind of commitment for several months. The Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) and myself have asked this question at least twice a week for the last month, but have yet to receive a commitment. speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion this evening reflects a serious situation in much of Canadian agriculture, especially that part which is very dependent on grain and oil seeds. The area which is most responsible for that production in Canada is western Canada.
The Hon. Member opposite raised some concerns during his remarks that I would like to address. I do so with a certain sense of satisfaction, because it allows me to put on the record the kind of action the Government is taking in response to a very serious situation.
The Hon. Member raised three points. He talked about initial payments, about the concern over the Farm Credit Corporation's situation and the lifting of the moratorium on foreclosures, and he talked about the Government's refusal to commit itself to deficiency payments.
First I want to address the Farm Credit Corporation situation. I believe it is useful to put the over-all situation into some perspective, as I did in the House earlier today.
Of the approximately 225,000 commercial farmers in Canada, approximately 76,000 do business with the Farm Credit Corporation. It is no secret that some people have been having trouble keeping current and making payments to the Farm Credit Corporation. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) initiated a program whereby the FCC was instructed not to proceed with any foreclosure actions as far as Farm Credit Corporation clients were concerned.
In order to allay some of the concerns that have been raised by Members opposite during some of their observations and questions today, I want to outline as clearly as possible what the FCC is doing.
First, the Farm Credit Corporation will be able to deal with approximately 50 such situations a month. Those who find themselves in that unfortunate situation will meet with Farm Credit Corporation personnel on a one-to-one basis. They will have an opportunity to examine the current financial situation
and consider alternatives to see how that farm can stay in business. Each farmer will be given a proper opportunity to work out the problems which, above all, will be based on his ability to pay. These cases will then be referred to the Farm Debt Review Boards.
Hon. Members will know that Farm Debt Review Boards were established last summer and are operating in nine out of 10 provinces. They have met with considerable success, with an over-all success rate in excess of 50 per cent and more than 60 per cent in Alberta.
In order to assist farmers to stay on their land, they will consider such things as set-asides of both principal and interest, interest rate write-downs, and setting aside or writing down interest in arrears. Farmers will be able to consider a lease-back option where, if it looks as though the immediate Financial position is such that it could sustain outright purchase, farmers will be given an opportunity to engage in a lease-back. That is another option to help keep farmers on the land.
They will also have the option of buying the building site so that if it is judged that the farmer's operation is not viable he will have an option of buying his building site at less than market value. This is another way to help keep farmers on their farmsteads.
In addition, FCC has developed two innovative types of loans that attempt to address the over-all concern about interest rates. One is a commodity based loan and the other is shared risk mortgage.
Shared risk mortgages now operate at approximately 9.5 per cent. If we consider the commodity based loans for farmers strictly engaged in wheat production, this year they will be eligible for a loan at approximately 6 per cent. It is simply not the case that there is an open season on farmers, as suggested by the Hon. Member at the beginning of his remarks. The figures simply do not justify that assertion.
If the FCC continues to deal with approximately 50 cases per month, as it has indicated, in a year it will have dealt with a quarter of 1 per cent of all commercial farms in Canada.
This farm debt review process takes into account all those options which I said will be considered with the objective of keeping as many farmers on the land as possible. I hope that when Members understand the process that will be used to deal with people who are having problems in respect of FCC payments, it will allay some of the concerns that were raised about a wholesale abandonment of farmers and a lack of commitment to agriculture by the Government.
Let me address the situation as far as initial payments are concerned. It has been suggested that we should have kept initial payments at $130 per tonne for wheat and $80 per tonne for barley. I want to quote from people who deal with initial payments. Garf Stevenson of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool said: "The Pool agrees with the Government's decision to set initial prices to reflect world prices". Mr. Brunton of the

April 28, 1987
Alberta Wheat Pool said: "The Wheat Pool is all in favour of the Wheat Board setting an initial price that reflects real market conditions".
There is considerable support for the setting of initial prices in direct relation to the existing world prices. If that is not done, two concerns came through to us loud and clear. First, most farmers do not want to see the Wheat Board system of selling used as an income distribution system. They want to see the pooling system we use, which has worked so successfully for Canadian farmers for the past number of years, kept separate from the system of income distribution or income support. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) says no one said that but by implication that is exactly what was said when it was suggested that initial prices should be kept at a level which does not at all reflect actual world prices.
Hon. Members will know that the second concern which was raised is with the livestock industry, and that the secondary industries which use feed grain as an input operate on a North American market. They have to be competitive right across North America, and that means in the United States.
What do we do to the people who use barley, for instance, as an input in the livestock industry? The Hon. Member will know that in fact 60 per cent and sometimes higher of the barley grown in western Canada is fed to livestock. Therefore, if initial prices are kept higher than the world market, the domestic feed industry, which is a bigger customer for feed grain in western Canada than our export market, is forced to compete with an artificially high price based on world market expectation. That is why the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool exercised good judgment when he said that the Wheat Pool is all in favour of the Wheat Board setting initial prices that reflect real market conditions. That is exactly what we attempted to do.
I would like to speak now about what has been going on in agriculture. Let me try to put some semblance of balance into the situation. There is absolutely no question but that we face extremely low world market prices for grain and oil seeds, but there are other sectors of the Canadian agricultural economy which are not in that kind of situation. The beef industry, for instance, is in relatively good shape. Markets have improved considerably. I could say the same thing for the pork industry and for the supply managed industries, the feather industries and the dairy business. That is reflected in over-all estimates of Canadian farm income.
If we take the 1981 to 1984 average, we find that the net total revenue from all farm production in Canada is $6,165 billion. Last year it was up to $7 billion as opposed to $6.1 billion. This is net total revenue from all farm sources. If we want to talk about total receipts, then we are talking about a $20 billion industry. The projection for 1987 as far as all farm income is concerned is virtually the same as 1986. That is all
Canadian agriculture, for all commodities, no matter where in Canada.
Let us look at the situation which we all know is the most serious, what is going on in western Canada, the revenue from grain and oil seed production. That is where we have the problem. I will give some figures just to put the situation into context.
The 1981 to 1984 average was slightly over $3 billion. That is net total revenue, net income. In 1986 it dropped over $800 million to $2.2 billion. But the estimate for 1987 is that it will go up slightly to $2.5 billion. One can ask the question, how can we have net revenue go up when we are facing such very large declines in prices? It goes up for two reasons, Mr. Speaker.
First, the Government has taken the deliberate decision to assist the Canadian Wheat Board and other people who sell our grain commodities on the world market. In fact, we have been doing a very good job of selling. We increased our market share for the last crop year and we have the prospect of increasing our market share again this year. This year Canada, for the first time in a number of years, will account for in excess of 20 per cent of the world trade in wheat. That is a direct result of the Government supporting the Canadian Wheat Board in its efforts to sell.
The other reason the net revenue has gone up is because of the amount of support which has come largely from the federal Government. I would like to give some additional very startling Figures to show what has happened as far as federal support of agriculture in western Canada is concerned. From 1983 to 1987, it has gone up dramatically. The average income support from the federal Government from 1981 to 1984 was $336 million. In 1987, it is estimated to be $2.6 billion. We have responded tremendously to a very difficult situation.
Let me give you an example of some of the ways we have responded. With respect to the Special Canadian Grains Program, Hon. Members opposite ridiculed us last fall. One of the Members of the Provincial House in Saskatchewan called it "mythical". He said it would never happen. Hon. Members opposite said it was going to be a loan guarantee. They said it was not going to be cash. But it was cash, it is cash, and it came in record speed. The crop year starts on August 1. Two months into the crop year the Prime Minister announced in principle that $1 billion was going to be made available. He said that in the Throne Speech, if Hon. Members will remember. Four months into the crop year the details of how the money was going to be paid out was announced. It was announced in December at the Agricultural Outlook Conference. So that four months into the crop year for which the money was designed to help, this Government made available the details of how that money was going to be distributed. The first payment to western Canada went out in January. The final amount will be made available towards the end of May. That is three months before the end of the crop year. That full $1 billion will be made available three months before the end
April 28, 1987

of the crop year, which is exactly the time when that money is needed.
Farmers grow their crop during the summer season and sell it throughout the crop year which concludes on July 31. So the money would normally be received, if the price was higher, during that time period, and that is exactly when the $1 billion from the Special Canadian Grains Program is being made available.
Our response has been tremendous. Those of us who come from western Canada have long thought we have been left out of the decision-making process. Bureaucrats in Ottawa printed up forms and sent them out and we filled them in and sent them back. That did not happen this time. We sat down with farmers from right across the country, the majority of them from western Canada. That would be expected because the majority of the farmers who are in trouble come from western Canada; that is where most of the grain and oil seeds are produced. We sat down with the farmers and worked out a program together and on that basis I think we developed a very fair minded program.
The Hon. Member from Saskatchewan will know that Saskatchewan produces approximately 39 per cent of the grain. It received over 40 per cent of the benefit. Alberta produces 25 per cent or 26 per cent of the total grain. It received 26 per cent of the benefit. My own Province of Manitoba produces 15 per cent of the grain and it received 15 per cent of the benefit. It is a very fair minded approach to a very serious problem, and that approach resulted in money being put out at exactly the time of year it would have been received had prices been higher.
As far as the Western Grain Stabilization Act is concerned, one of the first things we did as the Government was to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to allow for interim payments prior to spring seeding. We have seen the affects of that in the last three years running. We had an interim payment in April, 1985, of, I believe, $450 million. We had an interim payment in April of 1986 of $580 million. We announced an interim payment 10 days ago of $705 million.
That is a tremendous amount of money to be made available at a critical time of the year for farmers' spring seeding. When we couple the $705 million with the remainder of the Special Canadian Grains Program, we get very close to $1.3 billion going into Western Canada at the most critical time of the year, spring seeding.
If we look at the amount of money going into Saskatchewan alone I believe we will see that it is $676 million, a tremendous amount of money being made available at a critical time of the year. So for Hon. Members opposite to get up and suggest that the Government has abandoned agriculture and that we have no concern about it bears absolutely no resemblance to the record of this Government in agriculture.

What have we done internationally? We have taken the lead-

-in attempting to arrive at some solutions. It was our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who sat down with farm leaders in Vancouver last year before he went to the Tokyo Summit to indicate to farmers that he would raise agriculture at the Summit, which happened. It was Canada which organized the five major wheat exporters getting together for the first time. We have been taking the lead. We played the lead role at the GATT meetings in Punta del Este, Uruguay, and agriculture will now be addressed as part of the main agenda of GATT. We have been taking the lead internationally in seeking a lasting solution to these problems.
Members opposite talk about us having no policy. We have policy. If I had another half hour I could go through all of the items that we have done internationally and cover the initiatives we have taken.

speechtext: Just tell us what the policy is for next year. That is what the motion is about.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
We are doing three things. First, we are seeking international solutions. Our Prime Minister is taking the lead in that respect. As he said today, we are getting some results. They may not be too dramatic, but they are steady.
Second, we have provided a tremendous amount of financial support, and I did not go into some of the things we have done in terms of reducing input costs. But we have taken considerable steps in reducing input costs. As I just pointed out, we have provided a tremendous amount of cash.
Third, and as important, we have encouraged and supported the Canadian Wheat Board in its over-all efforts to continue to sell our product around the world so that when these markets turn around-and we believe that they will-Canada will be in a position as a reliable supplier to maintain those markets and to supply them when prices go up. That is a decided difference from the approach of previous governments.
Some 15 years ago when we faced this situation in the early 1970s we had a Government which took us out of the international market, instituted a Local Initiatives Program, cut our production in half from one year to the next, and it was a disaster for us. It took us almost five years to recover our

April 28, 1987
production. That is not our approach. Our approach is to support a very important industry. We intend to do that through this very difficult time.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to speak in this emergency debate tonight concerning the current crisis facing grain producers. It was very interesting to hear the Minister talk about the controlled commodities such as dairy products and others. However, what the debate tonight concerns is the tremendous tragedy that is taking place in the western grain industry.
The Minister said that we will have a grain industry in this country with grain producers in two or three years when the market turns around. Most western farmers are not very certain in their own minds whether that will be the case. There is no commitment of a deficiency payment for the new crop year.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) told the House a few weeks ago, "We will spare no effort". I say to the Minister of Agriculture and to the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), go to your banker and try to get money to put in a crop and say, the Minister of Agriculture said he will spare no effort, and give the banker 65 cents, and he will give you a cup of coffee. But he will not give you a production loan. That is what this debate is all about tonight. It is about whether or not the Minister and the Government, who brag day in and day out about how much they have done for farmers, will put up the money and give the commitment in the new crop year to see that we have a viable and operating grain production industry in Canada.
Clearly, the two actions taken in the past week leave great uncertainty about that. Grain prices are down by 18 per cent, on top of 20 per cent last year. Last year when grain prices went down by 20 per cent the industry said that in constant dollars grain prices were at the same level as they were in 1933 when the Bennett buggies were being used and R. B. Bennett was sitting in the seat which the current Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) occupies. I am not saying that Tory times are hard times; but a great many western farmers must think that tonight, because grain prices have gone down by 18 per cent due to international forces, and there is no question about that.
For the Minister to trot out the canard that somebody is saying that initial prices should be set above world prices is patently ridiculous. What we want to know, and what American farmers and farmers in the European Economic Community already know, is what type of stabilization deficiency payment will be provided. They want to know that. Maybe they do not have to know the exact amount. The Minister could simply come clean and say, "Look, we are going to provide the same returns, that is, what the market provides, plus the Special Canadian Grains Program, or a new special grains program, plus even throw in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. We will give equivalent returns to what we gave last year".
The second thing about which farmers want some information is on the basis on which this will be paid. The Minister says that the farmers should only look at the market, that they should not assume that there will even be a program, which there probably will not be since there will be an election in Saskatchewan this fall. The Minister has said that they should not assume that there will be a special grains program, and that they should not assume on what basis it will be paid. It seems to me that a great many farmers might say that the only precedent they have is the one they had last year when it was paid on the basis of seeded acres.
A few weeks ago we had farmers from Lethbridge in southern Alberta saying, "What we will do this year is mind the land. We will do some recreational seeding. We can then say the land has been seeded. We will get the special grains program, if there is one, and if there is not one we will not have spent very much because we will not have put on any fertilizer, or worked up the land. We will not have used too much seed or too much weed control or anything else".
Surely, the Government owes it to the farmers of western Canada to tell them on what basis a deficiency payment, a special grains program, will be paid, as well as the amount. Surely, if the Government is to be fair it should come clean and give the farmers this information.
I believe that the pressure, not from us in opposition but from farmers from the three prairie provinces, will be enough that within a matter of a few weeks the Government will cave in and give this information so that farmers can go to their bankers, get their credit and know what is happening. American farmers know. They know exactly what the loan discount rate will be. They know what the target price will be. They know what the deficiency payment will be. They know on what basis conservation should be carried out, and so on. Western farmers do not know any of those things.
This afternoon I spoke to a western wheat grower who said that the crisis today is not so much with respect to the price of grain but the uncertainty of government policy. He said, "We do not know whether there will be a deficiency payment, or a special grains program, and we do not know on what basis".
Many believe that the payment should be completely neutral; that it should be on the basis of cultivated acreage. In that way, people would not be pressed to produce a certain crop, or even to seed unproductive acreage, unproductive land. But, no one knows on what the program will be based, or in fact whether there will be any program.
I was impressed by the fact that the Minister quoted the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. I talked to the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool today, and I can tell you that he is particularly concerned about this. It is for that reason he sent a special letter this evening to the Prime Minister, calling the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that the rural way of life in western Canada is in jeopardy.
April 28, 1987

He points out in his letter the critical economic situation confronting western Canadian families and communities.
This is a crisis that has far-reaching social and economic implications for the national economy, and particularly so for the west. The letter makes the point that programs must immediately be developed to keep families on the farm. What the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is highlighting is the lack of a program for restructuring the debt. He talks about the need for a deficiency payment, and about the acute need for a substantial deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year.
The Government has been stonewalling up to now. The pressure is now on, and eventually it will have to set out the parameters of a deficiency payment and the basis upon which it will be made. As a nation, we have to be prepared for at least two more years of massive payments from the public Treasury to meet the shortfall in the price of grain.
Several of us met with six U.S. Congressmen yesterday noon, and the same group met with the Minister. Those U.S. Congressmen made it perfectly clear that the U.S. Farm Bill is not going to be changed during the course of the Reagan administration, with the result that we are looking at least at the current crop year and the next crop year. In addition, they made it clear that the export enhancement program, a program about which my colleague from Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) will be speaking in more detail, is going to be strengthened, thus increasing the competition for Canadian Wheat Board sales. That simply translates into the fact that the farmer is going to get less money.
If we are to have our agricultural industry survive in the face of these things, we are going to have to provide more deficiency payments, more special grains programs.
I should like to now deal with the precipitous action taken by the Minister yesterday in lifting the foreclosure moratorium imposed upon the FCC. Like Members of this House, Canadian farmers will be less than impressed with the mathematics of the Minister when he said that one-quarter of 1 per cent of the farmers will be subject to foreclosure. The FCC, when it talks about economic farms in Canada, does not talk about 225,000 farms; rather, it talks about the farms with gross sales of about $20,000 per year. Perhaps the Hon. Minister does not read the FCC literature. In any event, it talks about a figure of 75,000, with gross sales of more than $20,000 per year.
The Minister's action will permit foreclosure proceedings to be commenced against those farmers whose FCC loans are in arrears. They represent about 35 to 40 per cent of the longterm debt in the agricultural sector. About 6,000 of the 75,000 accounts with the FCC have been in arrears for more than two years, and the experience with the FCC is that if a loan is in arrears for more than two years, it almost invariably leads to foreclosure.
So, we are not here talking about a one-quarter of 1 per cent, but roughly 8 per cent of the FCC loans which are certain to face foreclosure proceedings. Well, the Minister
says: "Don't worry about that; we are only going to foreclose on about 50 a month. The staff of the FCC cannot process any more than 50 a month. As a result, only 600 farmers a year have to worry about foreclosure."
The question I put to the Minister is: Which of the 600 of the 6,000 loans which are subject to foreclosure will be acted upon? That is what the banker is going to ask when the farmer applies for a production loan. Once the bank points out that the FCC is pursuing foreclosures, the farmer can respond: "Oh, don't worry about that. Charlie says that they are only going to close on 600 a year, and there are 6,000 altogether. If I am the last one subject to foreclosure, I will not be foreclosed on for 10 years."
And the banker, of course, would then say: "Well, the FCC has said they are going to foreclose. If you are going to be the last one foreclosed on, then you had better get a statement from the Minister for the Canadian Wheat Board saying that you will not be subject to foreclosure for 10 years."
That kind of thing, Mr. Speaker, just will not wash. If the Government is lifting the moratorium on foreclosures, then it is lifted. That will then lead to action on these loans. Regardless of how the Minister wants to sugar-coat it, that is the way it is.
This moratorium has been in place for 19 months. During that time, the Government should have put in place a debt restructuring program to solve the plight of farmers. Had they put in place a proper debt restructuring program, the moratorium need not have been in place at all. But the Government did not have such a program, and the moratorium bought time. In the meantime, however, no debt restructuring program was put in place.
The commodity-based mortgage that the Minister spoke of this evening was described to the Standing Committee on Agriculture today by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture as a program that should be sent to the Better Business Bureau to determine whether or not it meets the ethical criteria of a properly run program. That is how that organization viewed it.
I asked why it is that no one was taking advantage of it, and the answer I got was that people do not trust it; that it is too complicated. It is simply not a good program. That is evidenced in the fact that while there are 16,000 FCC loans in arrears, 6,000 of them for more than two years, only 1,200 farmers have taken advantage of that program.
The Minister talked about the Farm Debt Review Boards. I do not have the figures with me for all nine boards, but I can tell you that of 400 applications that have come before the Ontario board, agreement has been reached in 195 cases, and only in two cases has an agreement been signed.
In some cases, the banks have agreed to an agreement verbally but then welshed on it and went ahead with foreclosure proceedings. So, the Farm Debt Review Boards are not functioning that well. In my view, the moratorium should be maintained, and we should take the time to put in place much

April 28, 1987
better programs. We should modify and strengthen the commodity-based mortgage, or throw it out. More funds should be provided for the rescheduling of debt by the FCC. As well, we need help for other groups.
Tonight I spoke with the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the largest Wheat Pool in Canada. He spoke about a program which the pool is examining for rescheduling debt. That is what the Minister must look at. He must maintain this moratorium and put in place new programs for rescheduling debt. He is not kidding farmers. The crisis is facing western agriculture and much of eastern agriculture as well.
This is an historic event. Unless special programs are put in place to cope with it, we will see the loss of an entire way of life in prairie communities and rural communities across the country.
Action is needed now. The Government should come clean, give a commitment on a deficiency payment, stop foreclosures which will start on Friday of this week, and put in place a proper debt restructuring program. If the Government does not do so, the problems faced by western Canadian agriculture and agriculture in other parts of the country will be horrendous. People in the House and across the country who are concerned about agriculture are willing to make that commitment, and the Government must make that commitment now to our rural communities. It is absolutely essential.
