speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join in this debate with pleasure. The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), and I have debated the agriculture issue in the House over many years, sometimes on different sides of the House than the ones we occupy at present.
My memory is long regarding the policies of Parties on agriculture. I listened with care to the Hon. Members when they outlined the problem, the serious situation facing grain farmers in the Prairies and across Canada today. I waited with anticipation to hear how these Hon. Members would assist the Government in solving the problem.
The Hon. Member for Prince Albert said that he was not too sure whether we should do what Europe and the United States were doing. Then he said that maybe we should help farmers. I waited a little longer, and suddenly he sat down. He did not give us the NDP policy on how it would handle the crisis facing Canadian grain farmers. He left the impression that all Canadian farmers were in the can financially, which is simply not the case.
I listened to the Hon. Member for Algoma outline the problem. I waited for the so-called famous Liberal policy on agriculture to assist grain farmers through the serious problem. At the end of his speech he sat down, after saying
that special programs should be put in place to cope with it, meaning the farm problem. He also talked about commitment, a member of that Party talked about commitment. In two and a half years the Government has responded in more ways than the Liberals responded in the 20-odd years when they were in government. I will outline some of their responses.
However, let me deal with policy because it is important. When there is a problem, anyone can outline it, but a problem needs to be solved. When we were in opposition about the same time in the term of the former Liberal Government, I recall very well six or seven members of the Tory agricultural committee sitting down and drafting a 10-point policy to deal with the same problem. Grain prices were lowering. Interest rates were at 22 per cent. Inflation was double digit. Farmers were facing a serious financial crisis on the Prairies. As I said, we drafted a 10-point policy which we put before the Canadian people. We took that policy to Prince Albert. We promised it in the election, and it is already in place.
Where is the NDP policy? I looked all over for it. I thought it would come tonight. I searched the records and I found a few things which NDP Members say still stand.
They say that it might be necessary, as well, to take into public ownership some existing farm supply retail operations, farm assembly plants, meat packing plants, and canneries. That sounds very interesting. Would that solve the problem in the farm sector now?
Other proposals in the resolution would be tantamount to the state taking over agriculture, with farmers taking their marching orders from Ottawa. In its policy the NDP says that it would regulate the distribution, sale, and servicing of farm machinery to promote standardization. This is another NDP policy on agriculture.
They would also regulate food processing, wholesaling, and retailing industries in the public interest through the use of price controls. I wonder whether farmers would think this policy would solve the problems of grain farmers at the present time.
They went on to indicate the establishment of a public commission to determine a formula for farm unit size on a regional basis. Are they going to tell farmers what is the optimum size or the best size for their farms? Are they going to say that if they have a quarter section or more it ought to be sold off because it is not an NDP policy? I could continue, but it does not get much better.
However, the best one came from the Liberal Party. I want to deal with the policy of the Liberal Party because I do not have too much time. I searched for its policy. I had hoped the Hon. member for Algoma would stand and give us an indication of what it was.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: He left.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Yes, he left quickly. It seems that the Liberal Party has a policy which it announced a few weeks ago
April 28, 1987

in Winnipeg. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on April 11, 1987, because I think they said it better than I can. The article indicated that the authors of this feeble set of proposals were the members of an exclusive political group and that the task force consisted of two Members of Parliament, one being the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). I am pleased to see him here tonight. I know he will take part in the debate. Perhaps he will elucidate this policy because it is very necessary for him to do so. He was one of the authors. The other author was the Hon. Member for Algoma who just participated in the debate.
The article went on to refer to 11 Senators from western Canada, the leaders of the Saskatchewan and Alberta Liberal Parties, and three Alberta Liberal MLAs who all came from cities. They really had an excellent group!
Perhaps they should have used another western Member. They have one more about whom they forgot, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner).

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: He is a Toronto Member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Oh, I thought he was from Vancouver. He was a little farther west but apparently he did not participate in the Party's hearings. Maybe his interests are further away from agriculture.
The Winnipeg Free Press article continued:
Western Canadians who hope the Liberal Party might have learned something about their needs and aspirations during its two and one-half years out of office seem doomed to disappointment. Even the western members of the caucus remain sadly out of touch.
1 cannot argue with that, because I looked at its policy, its 17-page report. The article continued:
The 17-page report is an empty document offering ringing declarations of discredited party policy, outright distortions of economic reality and not a single firm proposal which would make any significant difference to the economy of western Canada.
It goes on and I will read only one more paragraph, but I would like to put this whole thing on the record. It says:
Western Canadians, of course, know all about mismanagement and a lack of understanding of their economy. They know all about the connection between political and economic decision making. They got a taste of both when the political decision of the previous Liberal Government led to the economic disaster of a National Energy Program which put a large part of the western Canadian oil industry out of business.
On and on it goes.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The Winnipeg Free Press'!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Yes, The Winnipeg Free Press. I went through the report too. I was pleased to get a copy and I did not see anything different from what was reported there.
Now, what do we have? We have the Hon. Senator-I do not think they have ridings so I will have to use his name- Hazen Argue. He put his great big cowboy hat on and is
driving around in an air-conditioned suburban talking about the terrible crisis on the prairie farms. Where was he when he was Minister in the Liberal Government and interest rates soared to 22.75 per cent? Was he driving around on the Prairies at that time?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. He was not, but now he is trying for perhaps a little press because Lord knows the Liberal Party policy needs a lot of help. I do not think the Liberals will get it from the Hon. Senator who is driving around in western Canada in his truck pulling a trailer, trying to get a little press for agriculture. Did the Liberal Party deal with fuel prices, Mr. Speaker? Did the Liberal Party bring fuel prices down for western farmers when all Canadian farmers were going through that crisis? No, prices went up. The Liberals added taxes like the Canadian ownership charge, the Canadian compensation charge. Fuel prices went up for farmers. But what did we do?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: You increased taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I am not kidding, and the Hon. Member should sit down and listen. What is the Liberal Party's policy? It is terrible. There is none. Interest rates were at 22 per cent, inflation was over 11 per cent and debt was rapidly increasing to over $20 billion. I sat in this House and watched the then Minister of Agriculture Mr. Whelan for 10 years. What did he do? He flashed his green hat around this country making speeches. I have a whole filing cabinet full of them. His speeches said nothing. What legislation was brought into this House? In 10 years we had 13 Bills, three of which dealt with farm credit, variable interest rates and borrowing outside of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: You fought western grain stabilization all the way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: We had a better idea. It is starting to hurt Members over there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Order, please. Could we allow the Hon. Member to continue his speech?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The facts are there and they hurt, Mr. Speaker.
What did we have? The then Minister of Agriculture tried to put out fires, but he had no ideas. Several of his Bills were renewing old acts which the Tories had brought in during the Diefenbaker years. The then Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, ended his term with a gem and that was Canagrex which was going to solve all the farmers problems. That is what we got out of the Liberal Government and a Minister who was Minister for however many years he was Minister.

April 28, 1987
Mr. Clark (Brandon

Souris): We had 20 per cent interest rates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Yes, we had a wonderful time with interest rates. It took this Government with the policy that we announced well in advance of the election to deal with the very serious problems that farmers faced for a long, long time.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Are they now all solved?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: No, we still have much to do but we are working. We know there are difficulties. Let me take Hon. Members through some of the policies that have been put in place and have assisted agriculture.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: If you don't, we will do it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: We talk about commitment. In the next five weeks $1.3 billion will be mailed out to western farmers through the Western Grain Stabilization Program and through the special grains program to assist farmers put crops in the ground.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Where is the Agri-bond, Stan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: We are working on that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: What about the PFRA Bill?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That is my Private Members' Bill and I would be glad if the Hon. Member would stand up and support it. Bring it forward and we will deal with it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: What about agricultural research?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I don't know if I will have time but I will talk about that too.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I will, though.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: In the Prince Albert declaration we said that we will remove the capital gains tax. We did that to the tune of a $500,000 exemption. We extended that to small business.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: You did it for everybody.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Absolutely. We do not show favouritism.
We removed the sales tax on farm fuels. This is reduced and will save farmers who farm 1,200 acres some $5,000 annually. We said we would change the western grain stabilization so that farmers could get the money when they need it at the beginning of the crop year. This is assisting them dramatically this year. An amount of $705 million will be sent out to farmers on April 20, 1987.
We said that we would change the Western Grain Transportation Act to remove the volume cap and to freeze the rate. We did that. Not only was the rate frozen but it was rolled back to
an average of $6 a tonne, which assisted greatly in the movement of grain out of western Canada.
We promised to increase sales and expand our markets for grains. We did, even in this difficult time of world surpluses, where the EEC assists its farmers to the tune of $36 billion and each of the individual states in the community assists probably as much, so that some $70 billion is going out to 11 million farmers in the European community. There are 340-odd million people paying the tax bill.
Let us go to the American economy. This year some $24 billion will assist farmers to export to try to take a market share. Through all of this, what was the Canadian Wheat Board doing? It was selling and increasing our market share. It was not leaving our bins full like we had under the Liberal Government which had a four bushel quota total in one year. Then we had a Prime Minister who came to western Canada and said "Why should I sell your grain?" That is what we got from the leadership of the Liberal Party. But we did not get that from this Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who says that our problem has to do with the subsidies and it ought to be included in the GATT negotiations. What happens, Mr. Speaker? That is where the problem is. That is leadership. It is not going out to western Canada and saying "Why should I sell your grain?" What kind of leadership did we have then for western Canadian farmers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: And then we got the LIFT.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: There are lots of examples of that type of leadership.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is better than the Gucci shoes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Under our Prime Minister, when the farmers were in difficulty a billion dollars was offered. Now the commitment is there if the farmers in the upcoming crop year face the same kind of difficulty. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his Budget said "We will be there". The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said "We will spare no effort". Given past examples, I would buy those kinds of promises and commitments any time over what we got from the two Parties on the other side. That is commitment. The budget on agriculture has been more than doubled. It was 50 per cent the first year, and there is a 60 per cent increase this year. Just a 1 per cent decrease in the interest rates saves farmers $130 million. How much have interest rates gone down in the last two and a half years? Four points. That is a saving for farmers.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Exchange rates are set in the States, not in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
We have hundreds of commitments. I give a rounding applause to the House of Commons because it has assisted. The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) are moving this legislation so as to assist farmers. Hundreds of commitments have been passed by this House of Commons under the
April 28, 1987

leadership of this Government to assist farmers. You would think, as we listen, regarding the difficulties in agriculture, that all farmers were in difficulty. That certainly is not the case. Some grain farmers are in difficulty. Others may get into difficulty. If you look at all the other types of agriculture, as the Minister of the Wheat Board pointed out, many are having an excellent year.
We find that many good borrowers are still coming to the Farm Credit Corporation. This year, it made some $300 million in loans. That was $70 million more that went out to the agricultural community than last year. Under commodity-based loans, another $300 million went out. Some $600 million-worth of loans went out to agriculture this year. These loans certainly would not have gone out to agriculture if everyone was in difficulty.
Comparing 1986 farm loans with those of 1985, one finds that year-over-year, almost $400 million more had gone out to agriculture. That shows that there is still a lot of good faith and many good borrowers, even with today's land prices and today's difficulties.
We have a problem and we will continue to deal with that problem which lies in the grain and oilseeds sector. I know these problems very well because my family went through bankruptcies. I know very well that it is difficult for any family to have to deal with a farm bankruptcy. As a Member of this House, I will do everything possible to see to it that as few farmers as possible have to face that very difficult trauma. Through the Farm Debt Review Board and the Farm Transition Program, we have offered even more assistance to those who will have to face that trauma.
This is not an easy time for any Member who represents a rural riding, but I will say in conclusion that I would far rather be here defending the policy of this Government than standing over there with the NDP and the Liberals defending their policies.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight we are participating in an emergency debate called for two basic reasons. First, during the Easter break, the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board announced a decline in the initial price for Canadian wheat for the coming crop year. This year the decline was 18 per cent for No. 1 wheat. The previous year, the Minister announced at a press conference that he was cutting the price of wheat by 19 per cent, so we are getting pretty close to seeing a 40 per cent decline in the price of No. 1 wheat in the last two years.
There was a 28 per cent decrease in the price of No. 1 feed barley last year, but the Minister was not content with that. This year he brought that down another 25 per cent, so we are talking about a decline of just over 50 per cent in the price of No. 1 feed barley in the last two years.
What triggered the emotional outcry both in the House and in the country was not just that, I believe. It was the additional
totally insensitive announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) on Monday morning that he would lift the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loans, a moratorium that had been in place since February 17, 1985.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Just plain stupid.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
It was plain stupid, it was insensitive and it was not something we expected from any Government, particularly a Government that claims to have its finger on the pulse of agriculture and that boasts of its close relationship with Canada's farmers.
In their defence, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board have said that this decision will put only 50 farm families out of business per month. This reminds me a little bit of the Zundel defence. He said that it was not six million but it was only 100,000 who were killed and therefore there was no problem. Fighting with the figures is not the point here and the Chair recognized that when he decided to declare this matter an emergency.
How do these 6,000 farmers who may be on that list of 50 a month feel? No one knows if they are at the top of the list, the bottom of the list or when their loans will be called. They are already under a great deal of pressure. There have been some partial studies done in Brandon, Manitoba, and in Ontario of the kind of stress farm families are under. The study done in the Province of Ontario published reports indicating that more than 30 per cent of the farm deaths in Ontario which occurred during the course of the study were due to suicide. That means that there is a suicide rate among farmers of between 10 and 12 times that of the Canadian average. In its insensitivity, the Government has placed even more pressure on these 6,000 farmers who are facing extreme financial stress according to the Farm Credit Corporation. The Government has made certain that that extreme financial stress is made just a little more difficult. Those are the reasons we put this item on the agenda for this evening.
We along with a great many farm organizations in Canada say that in the short term, and I address this to the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) who said that we did not mention anything about policy in this debate, there should be an announcement, loud, clear and now, telling farmers what sort of assistance the Government is prepared to provide in the coming crop year.
A billion dollars was added to net incomes from last year and in order to maintain those incomes at approximately the same level, we will need between $1.8 billion and $2 billion to hold the line. That is the kind of figure about which Canadian farmers want to hear. They want to know if there will be that kind of firm commitment. They do not want to hear vague promises about how the Government has permitted the Western Grain Stabilization Act to function or about how there was a $1 billion Special Grains Program announced in the midst of the Saskatchewan election when it appeared that the Conservative premier would lose the election. The farmers want to know what will happen in the 1987-88 crop year and if

April 28, 1987
the Government will maintain those levels of support and they want to know that now.
The Minister of Agriculture has been telling us in the House and through news releases that the farm organizations did not want to know about anything more than his vague promises of support and concern. We have received letters by mail and Telex in the last few days indicating that at least two of the very large farm organizations, one from Manitoba and one from Saskatchewan, have in fact demanded some kind of assurance. Many other organizations said as much after returning from that infamous meeting the Minister held back in March in which he said that the farm organizations did not really want anything more than to see his smile and shake his hand at the door.
In a letter dated today addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool asks all Members of Parliament to recognize a very critical economic situation confronting farmers and their families. It asks that programs be implemented immediately. The pool calls upon the Prime Minister to immediately develop programs through federal and provincial co-operation to keep families on their farms in productive capacities and, more to the point, it asks that early consideration be given to the acute need for a substantial deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year. That was said very clearly.
The same thing was said by the Keystone Agricultural Producers in Manitoba. On behalf of the grain producers in Manitoba, they call on the Government to announce as soon as possible an intention to introduce a similar program for the 1987-88 crop year with support levels at least equivalent to those of the 1986 program. The farmers want answers now and that is what this debate is all about.
The Minister of Agriculture said the reason he announced his lifting of the moratorium was because he had, in the time between September 17, 1985, and yesterday, initiated programs which would take care of the problem that approximately 20 per cent of farmers with loans outstanding presently face. He says the Government set up the Farm Debt Review Boards. It set up a transition program to assist people to leave agriculture if that is the only choice they have. The Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) referred to some of those programs tonight. He called them great successes. According to his figures, you would be led to believe that 50 to 60 per cent of the farmers who put their names in front of the Debt Review Boards maintained their farms and were successful in staying on the land.
Nothing could be further from the truth. What the Minister perhaps meant to say was that 50 per cent to 60 per cent were processed. Our information from those Debt Review Boards is that less than half survived the cut. About half are rejected out of hand. Half go to the Debt Review Board and of those one-half or one-quarter of the total may stay on the farm.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is 60 per cent in Alberta.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I stress "may" because very few of them get written and signed agreements. Sixty per cent may have gone through the process but they do not have their farm saved yet, Sir.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
They have not saved their farm yet, Sir. I point to the testimony by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture in the committee this morning. They said that so far in Ontario there have been 425 applications received in front of the Debt Review Boards, of those 193 actually were reviewed, that after seven months, and of those, two succeeded in getting signed agreements. So we know where two farm families are in Ontario having gone through the debt review process.
The farmers in difficulty are estimated by Agriculture Canada to have about $10 billion in debt at risk. In Ontario it amounts to $2 billion. The sad fact is that as these farms become more and more at risk, the value of the farm assets that Canadian farmers are working with is declining quite rapidly. There is no clear formula, as you might imagine, but basically once you get into a down slide in price for the basic commodity, grains in this case, when you have a price decline of something like 50 per cent, which we have faced for all grains, the price of land will drop even more than 50 per cent. The rents simply cannot sustain those prices.
I made a series of calls around my riding, speaking with municipal councils and attending annual municipal meetings where farmers come out to discuss farm problems just prior to the spring planting. In areas where production is very high, very good land with good rainfall, the Spalding area in the black soil zone, well-watered, very high-yielding crops, land which has been continuously cropped for eight or 10 years on a cash rental basis, I heard stories where they are having great difficulty finding anyone to look after the land. The landlords have got to the point where they are offering the land if the rent will pay the taxes. People are not jumping to take it up. That is what it has come to and the announcement of an additional 18 per cent decline in the initial wheat price had not been made at that point.
The situation is bad and has triggered a tremendous decline in the value of farm assets. That creates its own set of problems. I submit that the Minister of Agriculture, by pulling off his moratorium, has set to work a whole host of other credit institutions who will take action that I think they were delaying because they were awaiting a signal from the federal agency.
I note that the B.C. Farm Credit Corporation, which is relatively small on a national basis, with only about 2,300 loans, some 488 of which are in arrears for more than two years, has now decided or is expected to announce shortly that it will be lifting the moratorium it had on provincial-based loans. There are 12 immediate candidates for foreclosure, most of them in the Peace River district. The banks in British
April 28, 1987

Columbia, which has a very small agricultural base, are now estimated to hold, according to the B.C. Federation of Agriculture, some 40,000 hectares of British Columbia farmland. For those who think in Imperial, that is 100,000 acres. The FCC is now estimated to hold about 5,000 hectares, and with the lifting of this moratorium the B.C. Federation of Agriculture estimates that the FCC will be holding in excess of 35,000 hectares very quickly in the Province of British Columbia. Again, most of that is in the Peace River block.
Those are the kinds of things which have been triggered by what the Government's Ministers tell us were very simple and rather tame announcements. Those kinds of tame announcements put farm families out of business, under stress, trigger an even higher rate of suicide, and create distress and destruction, financial, economic, and social, throughout the farming community. That is the kind of announcement that only a Minister of Agriculture who was totally insensitive to the real situation could have made. I deplore it and find it very difficult to understand. Knowing him as a person, I thought he was in tune with what is going on in agriculture, but he seems to have totally missed the mark on this one.
We regret as well that no announcements have been made or no indication has been forthcoming from the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) as to what levels of assistance are forthcoming in the 1987-88 crop year. That is something we as New Democrats are looking for, but farmers represented by the Saskatchewan Pool and others, various federations of agriculture, and the National Farmers Union as well, have all called for more clear programs and clear intentions on the part of the Government.
You see, the problem is farmers' memories go back quite a ways. People my age and older hark back to the Diefenbaker Government which came out with an acreage payment under circumstances not unlike this in the 1960s. That was a very welcome program. I have to give the Progressive Conservative Government of that day great credit for having initiated the program. I also note with some awe that it managed to sell that $200 an acre maximum payment for two years before another payment was made, at which time there happened to be an election going on. They are starting to ask themselves whether this is not another of the same kind of political ploy.
Everyone, even four-year old kids on the Prairies, knows that the $1 billion came because Grant Devine was having trouble getting re-elected last fall. They noted that the pay-out did not come until the next calendar year which, I suppose, was to be expected, so they got through 1986 and 1987. The payment was broken into two pieces to spread it over a longer period of time.
With the signals they are getting from the two Ministers they are starting to think that some of the same shenanigans are at work here because it looks as though these payments will be stretched out as long as possible in order to keep everyone on tenterhooks and to keep it as a political issue
before the electorate in the west. The Government is hoping it will result in its re-election.
I want to remind the Progressive Conservatives who sit across from me that it did not work for John Diefenbaker. The last acreage payment did not get him re-elected. I submit that unless the Government is honest and straightforward with Canadian farmers now, it will not work this time either. There are no political brownie points to be earned for withholding this announcement. Make it now as the farmers and farm organizations are expecting and give some necessary underpinning to the incomes of Canadian farmers which, by the way, are being maintained almost totally by federal programs. A good many of those programs were in place and would be operating regardless of which Party were in Government.
The net income of farmers in the coming year will be between $3 billion and $4 billion. According to the figures of the Minister, the Government will be pumping slightly more than $4 billion into the farming industry. We do not hear members of the Government talking about the fact that they have almost made farmers public servants or making comparisons with Russia, but if our Party was in Government I am sure they would be taking those kinds of shots at us. The net income of Canada's farmers in the last couple of years has come almost exclusively from the Government. That is deplorable. It is time there were some international agreements to change that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Tell us what to do.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: If the Minister will listen, I will point out that we cannot realistically reach such international agreements within three to five years. Therefore, this sort of pay-out will have to continue and be made on a regularized basis with the announcement being made at the same time as the wheat price announcements so that people will have some idea of what they are facing. That is our policy.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the early part of the speech of the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), he made reference to the initial payments being a reduction in price of 18 per cent. Western farmers understand that that is not the price but simply an advance received when grain is delivered to the elevator on the price to be received later There are headlines all across the country stating that wheat prices are down 18 per cent. This frightens bankers and all other people who deal with farmers. By repeating it here in the House tonight the Member is unwittingly attacking the Canadian Wheat Board.
If he read the Canadian Wheat Board Act carefully he would recognize, as very few farmers do, that the Minister has literally no power under this Act.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: This is no time to brag about it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The Act makes it very clear that the setting of the initial price is the responsibility of the Wheat Board. It is an indication to farmers of what the directors of the Wheat

April 28, 1987
Board think the price will be for the coming crop year. The crop year lasts for another year and a half as far as payments are concerned.
I want to emphasize to all good Canadians that Members of Parliament, and particularly members of the Government, cannot make any comments about the Wheat Board which would attack its independence under this Act.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Who's doing that?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
This Act was set up to make it clear to the country that the marketing of grain was turned over to an independent board which was to do the best job possible for the farmer.
The directors of the Wheat Board have tried desperately over the years to set an initial payment which they know is less than what the actual price will be. They are human beings and sometimes make mistakes, but sometimes they are right. Last year was a bad year for them. There is always pressure from farmers to get the initial payment out as fast as possible. That is a natural thing for them to push for and Governments are guilty of it too. However, the fact remains, as the directors of the Wheat Board know, that if that price is set too high, as it was last year, the Government will stand good for it but the responsibility essentially falls on the Wheat Board.
When Members attack the Wheat Board for making an initial payment which is too low, they are attacking in advance because they will not know what the price will be until the crop year is over.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Who's attacking them?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I would like to suggest that the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) would be well advised to listen because I will come to him later.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I've been listening to you for 20 years.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I have been trying my level best to impress upon the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, who is a fair person and a credit to the House, that by joining in this media misconception that the initial price is the price, he is unwittingly harming the farmers. I think that farmers in general understand that this is an advance payment.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is not. It's the price on delivery.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
It's the price on delivery to the elevator and is backed up by the Government with a floor price because the Governor in Council has to agree. By saying the things he has the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre is adding a load on the back of the Wheat Board which it does not deserve. They are trying to be responsible. They remember when the Wheat Pool set the initial price in the days when the pools did the selling. They set the price at $i a bushel and, through no fault of the pool, the world price collapsed to 32 cents. The Manitoba Pool, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and the Alberta Wheat Pool were all bankrupt.
The Bennett Government stepped in and bailed them out to keep them from going bankrupt. To this day the pools have not sold a bushel of wheat in spite of the fact that this was their purpose and they have a licence to do so. It is true, however, that they formed a group with the United Grain Growers approximately 15 years ago.
The fact is that we in the House of Commons, in our attempt to help the farmer, should not be creating a conception that the Wheat Board made a mistake by setting those prices too low.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Nobody said that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I think the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. Benjamin) knows that several papers have mentioned the price being down 18 per cent. It was also mentioned today and tonight by the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: No he didn't.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Are you saying that I am a liar, Sir?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I can't do that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Anyone who has the reputation of being known as "Mr. Suck and Blow" hardly calls me a liar.
The point I am making is that we must relate the facts as best we can so that a proper decision can be made. The main fact facing the farmer today is the high interest rates with which he must deal.
The Opposition can be very constructive on this point. They must remember that when the Farm Credit Corporation Act was implemented in 1959, the Government provided a statutory ceiling of 5 per cent for interest rates. Some of us in the House will remember when the NDP-Liberal alliance allowed the Liberal Government to remove that statutory provision and raise the interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation. The farmers will never forgive the NDP for joining with the Liberals in that initiative, simply to oppose the Conservatives who were in opposition. We are paying a heavy price for the love affair that existed then.
As a result of the New Democratic Party's dissatisfaction and perhaps dislike for us, its alliance with the Liberals ultimately worked against the interests of western Canadians. Our Government faced many problems during that 1957-1962 period, yet we tried hard to implement our five-point national policy program which is still in place today. I feel strongly about this debate because our Government is trying just as hard to honour that fundamental agricultural policy that we put in place between 1957 and 1962.
When 1 was in opposition many years ago, I was very much concerned about the Farm Credit Corporation drifting from its original purpose. However, no one listened to me because I was in opposition. The Farm Credit Corporation is now paying a
April 28, 1987

heavy price as a result of the decisions by the bureaucrats who make the policy here in Ottawa.
In 1963, the Pearson administration established an agricultural task force whose members included the brightest agricultural and economic people of this country. That task force examined the past and considered the future, and reported in 1968-69. It predicted that there would only be a need for one-third of the farmers in Canada since we would only be selling three hundred million bushels a year by 1980. It recommended that young people be discouraged from farming and the acreage of farm land be cut in half in the west in three years. This was known in part of the west as the LIFT Program, lower inventory for tomorrow. However, the program turned out to be "lower income for tomorrow".
Although 87 per cent of the farmers were opposed to that program, they had to become involved because they did not have the reserves to survive through the year. Those memories will die hard in the west, and to this day they will hold to account those who supported that program.
I must give credit to the NDP that it was smart enough to dissociate itself from the LIFT Program and work for the farmers in opposing it. In the debate that took place between 1968 and 1972, the program was reversed so that I believe every seat in Saskatchewan became Conservative as a result of that debate.
My request of Hon. Members tonight is not to be so eager to shine in the House by reading these headlines in the paper about prices going down 18 per cent when only the advance payment has gone down.
I am saddened by the negative attitude from all Parties in the House toward the problems facing Canada. Therefore, I want to finish my remarks with a positive suggestion.
Let us consider, leaving the interest rate problem aside for the moment, how we can increase the price. When the Americans dropped their loan price last year, the natural response in Canada was to drop it as well. Furthermore, the Wheat Board sets its price as a result of a knee-jerk response to what is taking place in Kansas City and Chicago. But how do our customers react?
While the Americans dropped their price of grain and compensated their farmers at the same time, our customers did not take the bait of lower prices to buy American grain. Not only did the Russians and the Chinese refuse to buy from the Americans, they are asking us for more grain and pleading with us not to go out of production.
Economists tell us that the greater production of grains in the world is being equalled or surpassed by the number of people eating more bread grain than rice. This phenomenon has spread to Asia and North Africa so that no matter how much more the Chinese increase their production, they do not provide the type of wheat that their people want. They want fresh Canadian grain, and fortunately, there are innovative
Canadians using Canadian know-how to increase the production of grain. It is Canadian expertise that has sold our grain around the world, and that is why our customers still want us as a steady supplier.
In closing I wish to say that while there is an impression that there is a surplus of grain in the world, there is no surplus of good Canadian grain. The fact is that we are moving as much grain as the railroads can carry. We have to improve the railroads and bring them to top efficiency. There is hope for the future. A positive suggestion would be to take a look at a bonus payment on wheat which does not cost the Government of Canada a cent. Let us follow the American custom on protein bonuses. I think that is 6 per cent, and for everything above that the farmer gets 70 cents to 90 cents. Let us adopt a practical solution. Let us ask the advisory board of the Wheat Board. We cannot give advice because that would be interfering. We do occasionally, but we are not supposed to do so. Let us ask the advisory board, which is elected, give it all the facts as to how we can set up a system where there is a ceiling of 5 per cent and 10 cents for every percentage point above that. Therefore, if the farmer grows 14 per cent protein, he receives 90 cents a bushel extra, and our customers will buy that because they are accepting that principle from the United States.
They want us to stay in production so they have to help us to keep us there. Conservatives will buy that, I believe. I think we should start to talk to members of the advisory board publicly and ask them to make this proposal to the Wheat Board. They have the right as elected representatives of the people of the west to advise the Wheat Board. Let them advise the Wheat Board. They should not shy away from their responsibilities because they are responsible to the people.
In conclusion, I believe all Canadians should unite on a positive approach to remedying this problem in all agricultural sectors, but at the particular moment it is needed in the grain and oil seeds sector.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past three or four months there have been in this House three or four opposition days dealing with the problems of western Canada. There have been two or three emergency debates. The purpose of each debate was to try to draw attention in the forum of this country to the growing and accelerating difficulties being faced by farm communities in the west. Each time the answer from the government benches has been the same. It is not a problem. Do not take it seriously. They bob, they weave, they duck, they hide. They dig back into the vaults of history to try to find someone else to blame. The clear answer is that they do not want to govern. They do not know how to govern and, in fact, the people do not want them to govern any more, as we can clearly see from the polls. They are afraid to face up to their responsibilities. They are afraid to come to grips with contemporary issues and answers.

April 28, 1987
What do they do instead? They do as did the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) who digs back in the old files when he was a member of the Opposition and pulls out the old arguments and the old hoary tales of wrongdoing. It has never dawned on that poor soul that he is a member of the Government, that he is going into a caucus tomorrow where he has Ministers in front of him who are derelict in their responsibilities in dealing with the farm issue. He is much happier looking back in his old files and digging out the old arguments because it has never dawned on him that one of the clear responsibilities of a Member of Parliament on the government side is to try to persuade his own Government to accept the responsibility and requirement to take action on real problems.
Like a lot of Canadians I was a little intrigued and somewhat curious when I read the story about the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), having to build a large closet for his 84 pairs of shoes. I wondered what someone could possibly need all those shoes for. Well, we discovered the answer tonight. I think every Conservative Member of Parliament must have a huge closet full of shoes because they are all up on their tippytoes dancing around the issues so hard that they wear out their shoes quickly. We do not have a Government, we have a ballet company. What all Members of the Government are doing is jumping around on their tippytoes trying to evade the questions. They pirouette, turn, and do all the kinds of gymnastics they can possibly do in order to evade coming to grips with an issue that goes to the very deep and fundamental roots of the western Canadian economy and western Canadian society. That is what this emergency debate is all about.
I find it exceedingly interesting that the message finally seems to be getting through. A report on the National News tonight is that the Tories are in disarray, that they are in mass confusion. So what is their answer? They are going to send the Prime Minister out west. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the westerners will say: "don't send the PM, send cash instead". That is what they want. They do not want any more of the Prime Minister's blarney. They do not want him dancing around. They do not want an extra plane so he can carry his famous shoe collection with him. They simply want some assistance. All they want from the Government is some small sign that it understands what is going on.
Members of the Government love to get up and say: "We are farmers. We really know what is going on". Some of them may be good farmers but they are a lousy Government. They are lousy policy makers and lousy administrators when it comes to finding the kind of answers that will cut into the heart of the problem. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), quite correctly pointed out that for 19 months we had a moratorium on FCC loans. Surely one would think that in that 19 month period someone over there might have had the wit to come up with some answer to deal with debt restructuring. Farm organizations have done it.
The Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin asks where the policies are. There are many of them out there. We put some forward which the Hon. Member for Algoma presented. There was the world stability program put forward by the Wheat Pool. The policies are there, but the government Members must be
incapable of reading, comprehending or responding because there has been no attempt during the 19-month period to find an answer that will allow the responsibilities to be shared between the farmers, the banks and the Government, the Government representing society and the banks carrying the private loans and the farmers themselves. We are saying that everyone must take a fair share of responsibility. They must come together. However, the Government has not even brought the major players to the game to the table to find an answer. It has not even had the capacity as a Government to bring together the major participants in this issue, the federal and provincial Governments, the farm organizations and the banks.
When we asked today in the House of Commons if it would not be important to bring together the banks to talk about this issue because they carry 60 per cent of the debt, the Minister asked: "Why would we do that? Why would we talk to the banks?" We know why the Government should talk to the banks. It is because every banker tonight is looking at the statement issued on Monday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and is saying: "Well, if the Government can foreclose, so can we". They will begin to look at all their outstanding loans.
When farmers begin walking in and asking for their production loans, looking for the credit for the forthcoming crop year, Mr. Speaker, how do you think those banks will respond when the Government of Canada, in a disgraceful and despicable way, has said: "We are cancelling the moratorium. Instead we are going to let the grinding machinery of the FCC churn farm communities into bits and pieces"?
It is an open invitation to the banks and other credit operations to do exactly the same thing. What stops them now? What possible compunction would they have when the federal Government, which is presumably there to defend the farmer's interests-because it is a public interest organization, or at least it used to be-is acting in the crassest and most vulgar way possible? Yet the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board asks: "Why would I talk to the banks?" Is this something that does not involve them? Are they such generous, open-minded and charitable organizations?
The naivety and simplicity of thought which has been brought to this problem is mind-boggling. It would almost be laughable if the situation were not so serious. That is perhaps the worst condemnation that can be made. We have some jokes at the expense of all those Conservative Members who will not be here the next time around because, in western Canada, they have dropped 20 per cent to 25 per cent in the polls. They should ask themselves why. The reason is that the very people who elected them in 1984 no longer trust them, believe in them or have confidence in them.
One of their members had some courage. I refer to the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) who stood
April 28, 1987

up and publicly said that the Government does not understand western Canada, is not responding to its needs and does not know how to cope with the problems. What did that Hon. Member receive as a reward for his honesty? He was chopped. He was sent off the team. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who has suffered incredible types of transgressions, could not abide 24 hours of honesty from a member of his own caucus. It was a matter of shooting the messenger because he did not like the message.
If Members opposite will not even listen to one of their own members who are prepared to say those things, and they will not listen to the people of western Canada who are saying those things, then to whom will they listen? At what point in time do we simply say: "For God's sake, go. We have had enough. You no longer understand what is going on. You have been blinded by your own sense of omnipotence that was passed to you in 1984, but it is no longer possible for you to come to grips with real issues in a real way"?
I wish to speak to the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin because he was so happy to say that he would read the promises that came from other Members. What I found particularly amusing was that the Hon. Member decided he would use the Winnipeg Free Press editorial page, not the news page but the editorial page, as his source of wisdom. That shows the bankruptcy of the Conservative benches. Conservative Members now rely upon the editorial page of the Winnipeg Free Press as their source of wisdom. Let us just follow that Hon. Member's logic through for a moment. He begged the indulgence of the House to listen to him. I would like to quote from the April 23 editorial of the Winnipeg Free Press which states:
Prime Minister Brian Mulroney is inviting the smaller Canadian provinces to
Meech Lake next week to enshrine their powerlessness in the Constitution.
It goes on to state:
-the effect of his proposals will be to entrench even further the powers of
Central Canada and to block any hopes of achieving the reforms sought by
other regions.
Considering that the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin has placed such great faith in the editorials of the Winnipeg Free Press I ask him if he agrees with this editorial which states that his Government is now engaged in a process that will denude even further the powers of the western provinces and ignore the types of claims for reform coming from the Premier of his own province. If the editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press is so convincing to the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin maybe he will get up in his caucus tomorrow morning and read this editorial to his Prime Minister and tell him that perhaps he is making a mistake in his approach to constitutional reform. I give this advice to the Hon. Member: Do not necessarily rely upon the editorials of the Winnipeg Free Press. Listen to the people. What they are saying is that the Government does not know what it is doing.
Let us talk about all the wonderful promises that the Tories made. My goodness, Mr. Speaker, how proud they were at the great Prince Albert meeting when they launched their
promises. They promised to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to offer agri-bonds. Do you see an agri-bond around, Mr. Speaker? I am looking under my desk and I do not see an agribond there. Are there any agri-bonds in Canada? No. I ask the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin to show me his agri-bonds. I ask him to show me his solution to that problem. I guess that is a promise that the Government has not got around to fulfilling yet.
Here is another interesting promise. Catch this one, Mr. Speaker. The Conservatives promised that they would expand agricultural research and development by providing greater assistance to agricultural colleges. In 1985 agricultural research had a budget of $263 million. In the Estimates for 1987 the figure stands at $221 million. I know that Tory mathematics have a curious way of flip-flopping. But I think that even the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin, even that Member who reads Winnipeg Free Press editorials and believes them, might be able to figure out that that is a reduction in agricultural research and development, not greater assistance. He might be able to figure out as well that when we are trying to meet toughened international competition, when we need to develop new crop strains and new products and value-added, where we will find this is in the type of research being done in the agricultural colleges. I ask the Hon. Member to explain to me and to western Canadians why his great Government that cares about agriculture so much has cut $50 million from agricultural research and development. I ask the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin to explain that small inconsistency in the promises.
I could go on and talk about a great many of the other great promises that have not been developed by this great defender of the Government.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that what the Government is carrying out is a camouflage operation. Let us talk for a moment about what the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) says with great frequency and in great seriousness. He says that his Government is doing all it can on the international front. He says that they are working diligently to bring to the attention of the world agricultural problems. Let us look at that proposition for a moment. Let us look at the proposition as to why the Government of Canada as yet has not put forward as yet its proposals on agricultural negotiation, even though it has had an invitation for over two months from GATT to do so.
A decision was made in Uruguay last fall and the GATT organization issued an invitation as late as last February for participating countries to put forward what their negotiating positions should be, what their priorities would be in agriculture and what they are prepared to deal with in terms of bargaining. If the Government of Canada is so active to show leadership and if it is so prepared to try to give direction, why has it yet been unable to find the wit or ability to put together

April 28, 1987
its proposals to show where we want to go in order to give a message to the rest of the world?
We met with members of the Congressional Agricultural Committee yesterday. We read in the U.S. press that those great friends of the Prime Minister, Mr. Reagan and all the rest of them with whom he has jaw-boned time and time again, the very week we are debating this resolution are putting proposals forward to the U.S. Congress to expand substantially the Export Enhancement Act to apply to all countries and to change the U.S. Farm Bill and the U.S. Trade Bill to give even further powers on agriculture to force us out of the market. If that is the result of the Prime Minister's jaw-boning, then God help us in all of the other negotiations that he is carrying out. I say that because we are getting the reverse of what we want. That is the end result of his great efforts. It is a failure to provide specific proposals and an encouragement to his allies, the Reagan administration in the United States, to include in the new Trade Bill incredibly damaging measures dealing with agriculture and the expansion of the Export Enhancement Act. After all those discussions and negotiations what does our friend, the U.S. President, want to do? He wants to drive it even harder into Canadian agriculture.
One has to ask oneself from time to time what the Government is trying to do. We recognize full well that the drop in international price is a decision being taken in Washington and other places. One of the reasons why this resolution says that we need an immediate announcement for a regular form of income support, a deficiency payment, for western agriculture is that until we get that kind of clear signal we will not let our farmers be pushed out of business by the Americans or the Europeans. Until we get that signal, we will keep on pushing.
While it is essential to provide the necessary cash support to keep our farmers in business, it is also essential that we provide a clear signal to the international marauders and pirates in agricultural trade that we will not be cowed and intimidated by them.
We need an immediate announcement now so that our farmers will be able to obtain whatever credit is necessary in order to continue operating over the next crop year. In order to get the necessary moneys, the lending institutions need this kind of guarantee. As well, it will provide a strong and uncertain message to the Americans and the Europeans that we are not about to be backed off.
The Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board has said that he wants to have a strong international bargaining position, and the best way for him to achieve that is to rise in this House and announce a support system for the western grain producers for the next year, the year after that, and for however long prices are continued to be ratcheted down.
We have to send a strong signal to our competitors in the world markets that we are not going to be put out of business.
Such an announcement by the Minister would go a long way toward convincing these international pirates that it is time they backed off from this craziness and insanity in which they are engaging.

speechtext: What is your policy?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

The Hon. Member wants to know what our policy is. I have just outlined what our policy is. What I have outlined is an important policy to adopt. A second policy direction to take is to embark on the kind of debt restructuring that we have talked about. Our farmers need that kind of major assistance.
The Minister rose in his place and said: "Well, we are only going to crunch 50 people a month". It will be a game of Russian roulette. No one will know which 50 will be chosen. I suppose they will put all of the names in the hat and pull out 50. We will have 6,000 farmers who are more than two years in arrears all living in terror. They will not know from month to month whose name will be chosen from the hat. What a peculiar way of twisting the knife in the backs of these farmers!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It will be a knock on the door.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is, that particular system has nothing whatever to do with the problem. The problem, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma, has said, is the incredible uncertainty which these farmers face. They are living in a state of never knowing exactly what is going to happen, or to whom.
What we have here is a failure of public policy. What we have here is a failure to put in place a farm policy that is relevant to the conditions we face.
All of the attempts by the Progressive Conservative Members in pulling out the old files and rehashing the old arguments will do nothing to assist in the crisis that our farmers are now facing.
If the members of this Government wish to redeem themselves in the eyes of westerners, they had better not send the Prime Minister out to do another song and dance number in those ballet slippers of his; rather, they need to show that they are prepared to come to grips with the conditions as they exist now, to deal with the problem as it is now.
If they do that, western farmers may have their faith restored in what we in this House of Commons can do, and what this Government can do.

The Grits have a solid policy, Turner said recently. It's just that they haven't
"correlated, co-ordinated, communicated, repeated and honed the message."
Well, of course, that is absolutely accurate, because they have nothing to correlate, they have nothing to co-ordinate, they have nothing to communicate. speechtext:
The Hon. Member speaks best from his seat, Mr. Speaker.
In 1987, the rate on farm improvement loans stands at 10.25 per cent; in 1981, the rate was 23.75 per cent.
We now have a Senator travelling around western Canada in his air-conditioned Suburban, pulling a trailer. He is travelling the highways and byways, saying how terrible the conditions are in the agricultural sector.
I can tell you about the disasters that were inflicted upon agriculture when the Liberals formed the Government. This particular individual was the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board in the last Liberal Government, and he did nothing. Now we have "blazing" Hazen Argue going around the countryside trying to drum up political support on the backs of the farmers. He is trying to use the farmers, who are in serious trouble, as a means by which to drum up political support. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, he is not gaining much support, and he certainly is not gaining any credibility for the Liberal Party.
Here we have a communique headed: "Western Liberal Caucus Releases Report on Western Economy". This is the official policy, Mr. Speaker, that was issued by the western Liberal caucus on the western economy, not the policies that are put forth during these emergency debates. And what are they going to do? Well, they propose that a federal-provincial conference on economic union "be convened as the first step in developing an economic blueprint for the West." The communique goes on to say:
The conference would establish policy priorities for each of the major regions
and sectors of the economy including education and research and

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
As the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle- Moose Mountain pointed out, in effect the New Democrats have really been deliberately or unwittingly attacking the Wheat Board. The Wheat Board makes the recommendation for the establishment of the prices. To do otherwise would be certainly in violation of the spirit, if not the intent, of the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
They are asking for a further $1 billion pay-out. However, I should like to refer to the January 8, 1987 edition of The Ottawa Citizen which quoted the NFU president as follows:
I know the Government believes it's proceeding in the right direction with its
$1 billion grain program, but we need a program that actually deals with the
real problems we're having, not one that throws x amount of dollars at us.
These people across the way are asking for more money without really looking at the root causes. I will get to the root causes very shortly.
I should like to make another point by referring to the October 30, 1986 edition of The Ottawa Citizen, which reads as follows:
A past-president of the Canadian Grains Council. .. told delegates that the
federal $46.6 million Rural Transition Assistance Program designed to help
April 28, 1987

farmers forced off the land is an example of government policy that honestly
looks at the problem of debt-burdened farmers.
Those are the kinds of things that clearly reflect that the policies of the Government are on the right track. There is no question about that.
The Opposition is now charging that thousands of farmers will be put off the land as a result of the actions which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced on April 27. That is absolutely false. It is malicious and it is misleading. If Hon. Members had had the courtesy of at least reading the news release and listening to the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), they would have a clear idea of why this action has been taken.
The moratorium was really beginning to create two classes of farmers in financial difficulty-the FCC farmers who were not facing foreclosure and therefore not applying for assistance through the debt review process, and the non-FCC borrowers who through the debt review process have access to an impartial review of their financial situation.
When the moratorium was put in place, it was put in place until such time as other programs such as the Rural Transition Assistance Program, farm debt review boards, commodity based loans, and shared risk loans, were put in place.
As has been indicated, every farmer who is in difficulty with farm credit will be dealt with on a personal basis, and arrangements will be worked out in a satisfactory manner. This action is not to force farmers off the land. This action is to help keep farmers on the land and to help establish a viable farm unit. That is the point which has been clearly lost, deliberately or perhaps unwittingly; I am not sure.
Our record in agriculture as a Government is clear. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has not, is not, and will not abandon or ignore the farmers of Canada. We recognize, as do all Members, I am sure, that there are some very serious problems particularly in the grains and oil seeds industry. There are difficulties caused by actions beyond our control, but we have responded on several fronts.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry talked about the international front. A year ago, before the Prime Minister left for the Tokyo Summit, he met with the agricultural community and was successful, with the support of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), in bringing agriculture to the top of the agenda at that summit.
Since then there were multilateral trade meetings in Uruguay. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) met with the Fair Traders group in New Zealand where she outlined five basic principles. Perhaps I should put them on record. They read:
Agriculture policies should be designed so as not to adversely affect
international trade.
To this end progressively over time:
(1)	agriculture policies must become more price responsive;
(2)	support should be provided for farmers not farming;
(3)	countries should freeze and seek to reduce governmental assistance measures that artificially distort world prices;
(4)	countries should not introduce new import barriers not mandated by existing legislation;
(5)	these basic principles must be implemented collectively.
Essentially those principles were accepted. Out of that meeting has been arranged a further meeting of the Cairns group which will take place here in Ottawa between May 21 and May 23.
At the present time the Minister for International Trade is in Japan furthering this campaign. I am pleased to report that momentum is building to deal with the crisis in agricultural trade caused by huge export subsidies. It is the only long-term realistic solution, and I think progress is clearly being made.
I should like to refer to the Sunday, April 26 edition of The Edmonton Journal which reads:
Canada, strongly supported by Australia, has championed the cause of
countries that have seen their agricultural trade suffer largely due to a farm
subsidy battle between the United States and the European Community.
I think that is pretty clear evidence that we are on the right track, and we are making progress.
That is what Mr. Fang believes in. That is what Mr. Turner of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool believes in. That is what Mr. Simpson or the editorial staff of The Globe and Mail believe in. That is what Darryl Kraft, the head of the University of Manitoba believes in. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry knows him. However, he has suggested that that is the right long-term course of action. That will provide the long-term solution.
What do we do in the meantime? We have addressed the input cost question. I just referred to the massive reduction in interest rates, which has been the result of good financial management by the Government. Every time the interest rate goes down by one percentage point, the farmers of Canada save between $130 million and $140 million. If we look at it, it has dropped at least 5.5 percentage points since we assumed office. That is a savings on an annualized basis of something between $600 million and $700 million.
Interest rates are the lowest in 14 years. FCC rates are the lowest in eight years. We removed all fuel taxes, 33.75 cents per gallon.
Those people over there did nothing. They put on fuel taxes. Farm fuel is now nine cents to ten cents per litre in Alberta, that is, 40 cents per gallon.
Do Hon. Members know what it was in February, 1984? Farm fuel was $1.45 per gallon or over a dollar per gallon more than it is today. There were 60 cents worth of taxes on that fuel thanks to the NEP. There were taxes on ammonia of something like $70 per tonne. Freight rates have been reduced.

In terms of direct support, Mr. Speaker, something in the order of $3.5 billion will be flowing into the agricultural industry, primarily to the western Canadian economy this year. That is an increase of 58 per cent over last year. When you look at last year's 1986 realized net farm income, it was up 20 per cent over 1985. The 1987 projections are that it will be about the same with the support. As a matter of fact, the Alberta Wheat Pool budget says that 1986 total realized net farm income in Alberta was $788 billion, a remarkable 45 per cent over the 1985 level. April 28, 1987
