speechtext:
Let me expand on what the Deputy Prime Minister calls a joke and what the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board calls a joke. My grandfather settled in southern Saskatchewan. His sons and daughters built and expanded that farm. Their sons and daughters built and expanded that farm. Today they are uncertain whether they will be able to continue because of the inaction, in part of this Government. They feel this Government has turned its back on them. The Government has said, "We are no longer interested in a family farm that for three generations has struggled on the plains of southern Saskatchewan".
Let me tell you something else. This past month I have toured my constituency and I have attended three auction
sales, all ranches that have been forced out of business. They can no longer continue. On one ranch, the Bar P Ranch, the rancher's health has broken. He had run the ranch for two generations. He has a stress-related health problem because he simply cannot continue with this impossible 200 head cow operation. He can no longer continue and he is selling out. That was one auction sale, Mr. Speaker. I saw men who have worked 20 hours a day for their entire life, rough, tough cow men, standing there with their eyes bleary because they know that it is not the Cartwright family or the Brown family who own the ranch lands but the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank of Canada, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. The banks are taking over the country. The banks are taking over the ranch lands of central British Columbia. Today when the questions were put-listen, is the Minister now prepared to meet with the bankers to see what kind of a situation we can arrange? The Minister said he was not prepared to do that and was not even interested. It is time we had a Government in place that put farmers rather than bankers first. That is not what we are experiencing at the moment.
One might ask why the Minister would say that. I remember when the Hon. Member for Lethbridge (Mr. Thacker) was on this side of the House. For two or three years before the last election, he kept rising to say that when his Party governed, there would be agri-bonds, agri-bonds would save the day and enable the farmers to continue. April 28, 1987
but they will go in. Farmers are a resilient group, always have been and will continue to be in the future.

The Government will support our agricultural industry as it has in the past and will in the future. Mr. Speaker, the evening is now getting late and there are still several Members who wish to speak on this emergency debate on the subject of the crisis on the farm front today which was forced on the House by the New Democratic Party. This crisis has not developed only in the last few weeks or months. Over the last several years we have seen the financial position of the farmers of Canada deteriorating, at first slowly and, in more recent times, rather quickly.
I should begin this evening by stating that in this debate I will speak primarily about farmers in my constituency in central Canada. However, farmers right across the country are suffering today as a result of poorly thought out government programs, world market forces, and the inability of successive Governments to respond to those world market forces.
I recall talking, not long ago, to a Conservative Member of Parliament from Westminster who was visiting Ottawa. 1 asked him why the British farmer today is doing quite well relative to the situation which had obtained in the United Kingdom prior to its entry into the EEC. He said that the British farmer is better off today than it was at that time because the Government made a conscious philosophical decision to preserve British farms. It was a Government's conscious, philosophical decision rather than an economic one. It was a commitment that farms in the United Kingdom were worth preserving.
After hearing him say that, I could not help but think that the major problem in this country is that we do not have a Government in Ottawa, nor did we have one prior to 1984, which was consciously prepared to make the philosophical decision that the family farm was worth preserving. Unless and until we have a national farm policy, the basic premise of which is that the family farm is a viable, worthwhile economic union and that the rural way of life must be preserved, we will not be able to tackle the day-to-day financial and economic
problems which plague that sector of the economy. Once the basic philosophic decision is made, the solutions will begin to flow from that basic decision. The fact that we have not yet arrived at that point is what is so deplorable about the reason behind this debate tonight.
I am convinced that if we had a rational national farm policy in this country to preserve the family farm, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) would not have announced the lifting of the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loan repayments a few days ago. It would have been logically contrary to a national farm policy because he would have realized that lifting that moratorium would injure perhaps anywhere from 50 farms a month to 600 or 6,000 farms a year.

This evening we are not just debating a financial crisis on the farm front. We may very well be debating the end of the family farm as an institution in this country. I am not suggesting that farmers will go into bankruptcy in the near future. I am saying that this might very well be a watershed week in the history of family farming in this country.
From now on, an increasing number of farmers will be of the belief that Ottawa does not care and is casting them adrift at the darkest moment of their economic crisis. They will believe that Ottawa is telling them that they must pay up or go out of business.

I want to tell the Minister about some of their major concerns. I am not only talking about the lifting of a moratorium on debt, which is a major critical issue at this time, but there are many very difficult, complex problems facing the farm community today not just in southern Ontario or my riding of Brant, but right across the country. In that list we have, for example-and this will come as no surprise to the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board-low commodity prices, high production costs, debt, land values, depreciation or erosion, short term aid, long term solutions and the lack of them, marketing, free trade and political will.
April 28, 1987

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Cost of machinery.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The farmers could pay for Massey Ferguson combines when farmers were making a decent living. They could afford those combines. They cannot afford them today because they are not making any money. That is one problem.
With respect to low commodity prices, and virtually everyone tonight has mentioned this as a major problem, obviously there has to be some kind of guaranteed assistance in the short term. The American Farm Bill is helping its farmers. The EEC is subsidizing its farmers. Are we going to sit back and let our farmers go out of business because the Conservative Government is opposed to some kind of subsidization which is guaranteed to farmers for, say, two, three or four years, not just every six months or from seeding to harvest?
We should be telling the farmers that we are going to guarantee them a reasonable return on their investment and hard work for the next five years, if need be, in order to give them a breathing space so that they can plan ahead instead of thinking: "Well, this may help me this growing year, but God knows where I will be next year".
With respect to high production costs, farmers in my riding today are receiving less today for a bushel of corn than they were in, I believe, 1975 or 1977. Yet their production costs go up every year. I may be wrong but 1 think they are something like seven-fold higher than they were in 1975. That is a lot. It may be five-fold, but the point is that production costs have gone up immensely and prices have gone down. I would like to know what small city industrialist who employs perhaps 15 or 20 people would stay in business under those conditions. But a business in the city can perhaps get out of one line and move into another line which is more productive. What can a farmer do? Can he give up the rural life, give up his traditions?
I talked to young farmers in my constituency and they feel embarrassed. I am sure that is true across the country. Our farmers are among the best trained farmers in the world. We have a sign on a farm gate in my constituency which says "Century farm". It was a project, I believe, of one of the young farm organizations in Ontario. Young farmers feel personally ashamed that they are getting deeper and deeper into debt and can see nothing but bankruptcy at the end, when their grandfather, greatgrandfather, and in some cases their great greatgrandfather, going back to the 1840s and 1850s, first started farming on that parcel of land. It is easy for us to say that they should not feel personally guilty but they do. That is what young farmers are like.
It would be different if the situation were as it was in the late 1950s when a lot of farmers refused to modernize, to study and to improve their ability to farm. But today some of the best farmers are going bankrupt. Is it true in city industry that the best industries are going under? I do not think so. I think the industries which are going under in our cities today,
certainly in southern Ontario where the urban economy is basically booming in the so-called "golden horseshoe", are seen as very poor businessmen, incompetent in many cases. But in farming it is the best farmers who are going deeper into debt and are staring bankruptcy in the face.
The other problem, of course, is debt, and that is what this debate is all about. I would like to ask the Minister, who is here, why, in God's name, did the Government decide at the end of last week to lift the moratorium? Why now? Was it pressure from the banks so that they could then go into lockstep right behind? Was it to give them further justification to pull the rug out from under their debtors?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: What has that got to do with the banks? It has nothing to do with the banks.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The farmers are beginning to wonder whether or not the Government was pressured by the banks into making this move.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It has nothing to do with the banks whatsoever.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Well, many farmers are beginning to doubt that. Many farmers are saying that perhaps the Government knuckled under to the banks and made the first move. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is saying he is not getting his message across. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) is saying that one of the reasons the Government is doing so poorly in the polls is that it is not selling its programs to the people. It is not informing the people. Perhaps the Government had better start doing that because the farmers in my constituency, generally speaking, are saying to me it is the banks which are probably pushing the Government into lifting the moratorium. If the banks are not, the Minister had better go down there and tell those farmers the true story.
I find it depressingly agonizing to participate in this kind of debate. I have been involved in debates like this before in this House, in my constituency and in other parts of Canada. We are dealing with some of the best farmers in the world. I am not exaggerating when I say that the suicide rate is 12 times the national rate by occupation. Something is obviously wrong. The incidence of nervous breakdowns, mental illness and emotional stress is highest amongst farmers, farmers' wives and their children. Something has to be done and it has to be done soon.
Let me end by simply saying that the solution to preserving the family farm in this country is not to fund its demise. It is not to pass on money to farmers so that they can get out of farming. My God, how hypocritical can a policy be? It is argued on the one hand that we want to preserve the family farm and on the other hand the Government is prepared to give them money to get out of farming. That is the national disgrace which we are debating tonight.

I make no apology for speaking here tonight because Quebecers, even if many of us have now become urbanized, do not have to go back very far in their history to discover a past that is firmly rooted in the rural communities of their province.

I for one could claim to be a Montrealer, that is true. However, my grandfather and all of my uncles and cousins in Two Mountains are all farmers. It is for that reason I want to have my remarks on the record, even if they are brief.
I made some notes while one of my colleagues was speaking.
I wish to request in the strongest possible terms that the Government give a commitment now to save the family farm and the entire rural life of the country.
The lifting of the moratorium on loan repayments announced by the Government and the fact that it will now start foreclosing on thousands of farm loans causes great distress. There is no doubt about that. We have to understand the family concept. We have to understand what it means for someone who, suddenly, because of outside forces, finds himself in an immense difficulty. I do not necessarily blame the Government for this. I think it is the duty of all Canadians to follow closely the events that are taking place.
As a Canadian I do not apologize for taking the floor at this time. As I said in French, I am not an expert on the western grain economy. However, I want to have the same version in both languages. It is too easy to go from one to the other and not to say exactly the same thing.
People will probably say that here I go again on my Canadian trip. However, to me, that is the price that we pay when we are Canadians. Sometimes it is the Maritimes that suffer. When that happens western Canadians have to show generosity. Sometimes it is central Canada that is freezing. It is not good for Canada to hear people from western Canada say: "Let them freeze in the East". When the West is suffering it is not in the good interests of Canada to say: "I am from Quebec and $1 billion last year is too much and maybe another billion this year is too much". That limits the scope of what Canada should be for all of us.
We are all in this boat as one, supporting each other. That is the strength of Canada. That is why many of my colleagues and I said during the famous debate that took place some years ago in the Province of Quebec when some Quebecers wanted to pursue their future in another way, probably by moving out of Canada and having their own country, that the beauty of Canada, with a small population of 25 million, is in helping each other. We must understand that when there is a rough time in one part of Canada we should all be interested in the good of each other. It is late, I realize that, and when it gets to be this time my English leaves me, but

-in French, I would like to state that we must understand there is now a tremendous tragedy in western Canada. And I know Quebecers ask that question often enough. I see my

esteemed colleague, the new Member, and he knows there is often a tendency to say in Quebec: The Canadian Government always looks after western farmers, which always find themselves in a tight spot, and it always gives them a lot of money. But it must be added that the money that comes back to Canada brings a lot to Canadians from coast-to-coast. And this is why I believe we should unite in these difficult moments.

We have in these difficult times to get together and sacrifice. Some people in one part of Canada have to sacrifice so that other people in the rest of Canada can survive. Of course it will be an immense tragedy for someone like me who is still very attached to the rural farming area.
I do not know if I said it in French or English but it is well known in Quebec that my family comes from rural places in Quebec. I am very proud of that. I do not see why people should not repeat such a thing in public. I have learned a lot about the attachment to the earth and the values that one sometimes finds more in rural communities than in urban communities. Of course the Government will have to find the money to carry out its decision. In finding the money it will help our rural communities to survive. It will keep what is so precious in Canada. I do not see that because I am from Montreal I should remain silent. I do not see why I should not show to the rest of Canada my attachment to rural communities and to the fact that it is a duty of all Canadians to support each other.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that it does indeed add a very important element to the debate because, setting aside all partisanship, many federal Liberals are at the present time travelling throughout Quebec, Ontario and the Maritime provinces saying that the Progressive Conservative government is doing nothing for Canadian agriculture. I am not the one saying this, Mr. Speaker. The Liberals are. Is this partisanship or an objective debate? I cannot believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Member for Saint-Denis would say such things. If we want to talk about statistics, we could talk objectively about interest rates. In 1984, when we came to power, interest rates were in the 16 to 22 percent range. Today, they stand at 10 per cent. Yet Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) accused the Government a while ago of failing to take concrete action. Mr. Speaker, interest rates have fallen from 16.75 per cent to 10 per cent, from 22 per cent to 10 per cent! The interest rate on loans is now 6 per cent! These are concrete actions on the part of the Prograssive Conservative government since coming to power in 1984. Mr. Speaker, to maintain that the Liberals and New Democrats will support the government motion in favour of agriculture-when in fact the Liberals and New Democrats opposed the introduction of the capital gains exemption. They claimed that it would only help the rich. They said that it would not help Canadian farmers. That's funny, because I represent a rural riding. I have travelled throughout my riding and I have met with farmers. They have told me that the elimination of the capital gains tax has allowed the family farms to survive to this day, because parents are not forced to sell at two, three or four times the price because of the tax. Now they get a capital gains exemption. Mr. Speaker, this is one concrete step we have taken to help agriculture. We have indeed taken action since 1984.
I could also speak objectively about our electoral platform. Some opposition Members will say that we have not kept any of our promises. Fine. But I remember the commitments we made in 1984. I'm sure the Liberals and New Democrats have them written down in their little books. We spoke of doing away with the capital gains tax. We have followed through on this. We also spoke of formulating a long-term dairy policy. This has also become a reality!
During the 1984 election campaign in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, I remember that the interest rates charged by the Farm Credit Corporation were 16.75 per cent. Farmers were saying to me: "You know, Mr. Champagne, if interest rates were in the 10 per cent range, that would be reasonable. Then we might be able to see the light at the end of the tunnel." In 1984, when the Farm Credit Corporation was charging 16.75 per cent in interest, the provincial Office du credit agricole was charging only 8.5 per cent. There was a difference of 8 per cent between the two agencies. This means that in 1984, the chances of survival for a young farmer wishing to take up the challenge, to take his rightful place on the Canadian agricultural scene and to assume the social role of economic "developer", worker and taxpayer, were slimmer if he turned to the Farm Credit Corporation for assistance instead of to the Office du credit agricole. Why was that? Because at the time, there was no
mechanism in place to provide for competitive interest rates between the two farm credit agencies. Therefore if two farmers borrowed the same amount, one from the provincial corporation and the other from the FCC, the one borrowing from the province had a better chance of coming out ahead. All the farmer who borrowed from the federal agency had to show for his efforts, in many cases, was a moratorium.
Mr. Speaker, we were not overjoyed about introducing the moratorium. The fact is we realized that there was a debt problem. The problem existed because to a certain extent farmers had not been dealt with in a responsible manner.
When our Government says that it represents fairly effectively the entire agricultural population, it means that it has Members involved in agriculture in almost every province. Although I have a great deal of respect for my colleague from Saint-Denis, he cannot say the same about the former Government which had no more than one or two sitting Members west of Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, what kind of treatment did western farmers receive over the last 10 or 15 years? It is normal for them to get what they rightfuly deserve now. It is normal for us to want to help out our western farmers and grain producers in their time of need. How did we in fact help them, Mr. Speaker? First of all, by instituting payment stabilization mechanisms. The former Government did not feel that such mechanisms were really needed, but we put them in place. We agreed, coast-to-coast, to use a well known expression, that it was important to agriculture to implement such mechanisms. We allocated one billion dollars in aid and we succeeded, Mr. Speaker-as for the New Democrats and the Liberals, I believe I see the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) laughing about the situation. I think that this is shameful indeed since when his Party was in power, he did nothing at all for agriculture. It was our government, Mr. Speaker, that distributed $1 billion equitably between the farmers from the west, the east and the Maritimes. We did this for a reason. We realized that Canadian farmers needed the government's support. During our 1984 election campaign, we gave our firm commitment that we would take action in this area.
Of course the opposition Parties claim that we are not doing enough. But you can never do enough. Mr. Speaker, we have to look at what was done in the past and what is being done today. Some of the expectations of Canadian farmers have been met through the introduction of the 6 per cent loan program, the signing of a long-term dairy policy for farmers in general and the one billion in aid. When the Opposition accuses us of not having done anything-and I am speaking here of those who want to raise this debate beyond the realm of partisanship-it should take a good hard look at what's happening across Canada. However, it should not view the situation across the country from the comfort of an air-conditioned limousine. It should travel to the rural ridings and look at what's happening with farmers. If it is truly objective, it will see that the Progressive Conservative Government has fulfilled about 80 or 90 per cent of its 1984 election promises.

April 28, 1987
I heard members of the New Democratic Party speak of agri-bonds and of the fact that our Government had not introduced any agri-bonds. However, I would like one opposition Member to rise just once and say: "Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Government, through the Farm Credit Corporation, has made it possible for farmers to take out loans at 10 per cent interest, rather than 16.75 per cent". Of course no Opposition member has ever once done this. No, the opposition Members have only risen to protest the lifting of the moratorium. Mr. Speaker, what is even more scandalous is the fact that the New Democrats supported the Liberals in their failure to take steps to formulate a clear, concrete agricultural policy.
It's true, Mr. Speaker. When have we ever seen the New Democrats rise and say to the Liberals: "When your Party was in power, interest rates were too high".

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: They kept them in office!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
That's quite true, Mr. Speaker. I can see that some of the New Democratic Members are amused by this statement, but that's what really happened. Yes, indeed.
As my colleague from Saint-Denis pointed out, when one wants to work for the sake of unity-and I'm excluding my colleague from Saint-Denis here because he is the exception that confirms the rule in many cases-when one wants to establish farm programs and work in a positive way, this does not mean that one must put obstacles in the government's way. It means that one must look at the positive achievements and work to improve, rather than criticize, the situation.
All that we keep hearing in the agriculture committees and in reports everywhere and in the statements by the Opposition on the subject of agriculture, is that the Government has failed to keep its promises.
Our electoral platform, Mr. Speaker, was very simple. It contained 12 promises, more or less, to quote the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis: to provide financial aid to farmers, to renew their confidence, to establish the marketing boards of their choice, to sign a long-term dairy policy, to reduce the rates charged by the Farm Credit Corporation, to introduce a capital gains exemption, to have grain stabilization payments more in tune with reality and to deal equitably with the agricultural community as a whole. We have fulfilled our promises, Mr. Speaker. Why then does the Opposition continue to criticize us, why did it insist on holding an emergency debate to discuss the plight of farmers and why is it trying to make the Government out to be the villain?
Mr. Speaker, the opposition Parties must be very well aware of the fact that the current problem is the result of a trade war between the European Economic Community and the United States.
Canada, despite its efforts and the funds allocated to agriculture, does not have the power to control the United States and the European Economic Community or to demand that they act as it would like. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that we are being unfair in telling Canadians that the Government is irresponsible. When has any government, with the exception of ours, taken such a radical stand and provided one billion in aid to grain farmers? The Government took such action because it realized full well that farmers were experiencing difficulty on international markets.
The Government was acting in a responsible, moral manner toward farmers. In providing this aid, the Government was acknowledging its economic responsibility and its economic priorities and was admitting that Canadian agriculture, not simply agriculture in Ontario, Quebec or the Maritime Provinces, is the cornerstone of healthy, future growth and development. It was acknowledging the expectations of Canadians wishing to make farming their livelihood.
Never once did the Government claim to have resolved all of the country's agricultural problems.
We are continuing to work in this area. For the first time ever, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) met with his 10 provincial counterparts to negotiate a national agricultural policy. They continue to meet regularly and are scheduled to get together this summer in Quebec City. Together, they have given a new thrust and impetus to farming in Canada. They are trying to avoid what happened in the past when the federal Government disregarded the wishes and demands of the provinces.
Thanks to our innate knowledge, we believe we are doing what is right for agriculture in Canada. We have seen, Mr. Speaker, the effects of a $200 billion deficit in the agricultural sector and what happens with interest payments when this deficit must be reimbursed. Funds cannot be used effectively for agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, when the Liberal Government completely disregarded the demands of the provinces and sought only to create a climate of confrontation within a federalist context that clearly made no sense, it caused serious harm to agriculture. The impact of this confrontation will be felt by future generations.
Do the New Democrats and the Liberals object to our adopting a conciliatory approach with the provinces? Do the New Democrats and the Liberals object to our consulting with our provincial counterparts to ensure that agriculture remains the cornerstone of economic development? That's what I've been hearing all evening from the Opposition, nothing more than recriminations based 90 per cent of the time on partisan feelings. The 10 per cent exclusion is for my colleague from Saint-Denis.
April 28, 1987

Mr. Speaker, it is highly unusual that I have not heard one opposition Member say this evening that the government has done at least something good. I can say one thing, Mr. Speaker.
As a responsible Member and as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, I can say that since 1984, our Government has worked to rebuild the agricultural sector. This task cannot be accomplished alone. It will require the concerted efforts of many parties. This means that meetings will be held and concessions will be made. Policy discussions concerning agriculture will take place with each province. Our Government will not indulge in navel gazing, as most of my Opposition colleagues who feel they are very knowledgeable about this issue are prone to doing. Mr. Speaker, we have seen what innate knowledge can accomplish. If the Opposition accuses us of not keeping our election promises, we can find a great deal to say about the broken promises of the former Government. And we could also say the same about certain provincial NDP Governments.
If we want to raise the level of this debate beyond the realm of partisanship, we must recognize, firstly, that Canadian farmers are in trouble, and secondly, that the Government has taken steps and will continue to take steps to turn the situation economic problems by instituting certain structures and mechanisms.
In all honesty, Mr. Speaker, when I see the Opposition criticize our Government for giving $1 billion to Canadian farmers to help them out, when I see the Opposition criticize our Government for providing a 6 per cent loan system- something which has never been seen before-when I see the Opposition protest shared-cost interest rates, when I see the Opposition criticize the drop in interest rates, the introduction of the capital gains exemption and efforts to formulate national agricultural policies with our provincial colleagues, I ask myself, Mr. Speaker, who is acting in the most responsible fashion, the Opposition or the Government. The Opposition only indulges in negativism. The Government, n the other hand, is showing its willingness to implement a policy that will save our agricultural industry, not in the short term but in the long term.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join in the emergency debate at this early morning hour, at least it is in Ottawa, which has been requested by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). There is obviously no doubt that agriculture, particularly western agriculture, is facing a crisis in many ways similar to that faced in the time of the Great Depression. There are similar as well as different aspects to the crisis that confronts agriculture today, and I agree that there are no simple, easy solutions. It is a very complex age with new developments occurring on the political
front, on the economic front and on the technological front which increase the uncertainty in agriculture today.
As I said, there are no simple, easy solutions. We have to deal with the economic problem that exists in the trade war between the European countries and the U.S.A. where billions of dollars from the public treasuries of Europe and the United States are being used to support their respective farmers. This has been explained by Members on all sides of the House. The Canadian farmer, in essence, is out there alone. He is suffering because he does not have the type of protection given to the European and the American farmer. There is talk about the uncertainty being brought about by technological changes, changes in genetic engineering and hydroponics which can change the face of agriculture in a very short period of time. These are some of the long-term uncertainties that farmers, particularly western Canadian farmers, face.
It is true that this Government has spent more on agriculture than any previous Government. There is no doubt of that. Given the magnitude of the crisis it would not really have mattered whether we had a Liberal Government, a New Democratic Party Government or a Conservative Government, because any responsible federal Government today would have had to have spent the amount of money that has been spent supporting the grain producers of Canada. Not to have done so would have created such a crisis that we would have had a worse situation made so much worse. No responsible elected Government could have withstood the political uproar that that would have created.
I agree that this Government has spent more than any previous Government on support for agriculture. However, we must ask if it has been adequate. Given the support the European and American farmers face, have we provided enough protection for our farmers to ensure that they will survive at least on a minimal level? To that question, the answer must be a resounding no. The policies have not been adequate. They have not provided the support that is necessary to enable the family farm to continue to be a viable economic operation.
Let us look at some of the figures dealing with farm bankruptcies. The evidence before the Agriculture Committee on March 24 dealt with farms with sales of over $20,000. We learned that 8 per cent of those farms are basically insolvent. That amounts to roughly 13,680 farms. Evidence also showed that 23 per cent had major cash flow problems. That amounts to around 53,000 farms across Canada.
Thousands of farms on the verge of bankruptcy are ready to go down the tubes. The policies of the Government have not been adequate. They have not prevented that crisis. They have not provided the security that would assure those farmers that they will not go into receivership. That is the simple truth of the matter.

April 28, 1987
A sense of betrayal is felt in many rural areas across Canada and I would say particularly in western Canada. For many, many years, western Canadian farmers have very consistently voted Conservative. They have continued to return Conservative Members of Parliament to Ottawa year after year. Of the 14 Members of Parliament who come from my home province, there are only five New Democrats. There is a sense of anger and betrayal in western Canada. Because western Canadians have voted Conservative in so many elections, they had the sense that a Conservative Government in Ottawa would at least be sympathetic to and would understand the needs and problems they face.
When I return to the rural parts of my constituency, the message I get is one of anger and disappointment. They are angry and disappointed because the Government has not been adequately addressing their needs and concerns. They feel that they are on the edge of going bankrupt and they have no confidence that the Government is aware of their situation or, more important, has any coherent plan in mind to prevent them from going into bankruptcy.
We in the House of Commons have asked time and time again for the Government to make a public statement as to its intentions. Farming in and of itself is a very risky business. There are a great many uncertainties including the weather, the market, costs and the grasshoppers. A farmer runs a gambit of gambles. One of the other gambles is what the government policy will be. Farmers are making business decisions about what to plant and how much to plant and they recognize it is a gamble because they do not know what the government policy will be. They do have the sense that in the end, the Government will have to provide some program of deficiency-type payments but they do not know upon what basis it will be provided. They want to act in an economically rational and sane way but they cannot because there is this other uncertainty, the uncertainty about the programs.
We in the House of Commons have been rising day after day trying to get from the Government some indication of its thinking. Does it have a coherent policy in mind? I have a terrible suspicion, and I pray that I am wrong, that the Government really does not have a coherent policy in mind. This is inexcusable because everyone knew that the trade war between the Europeans and the Americans would occur. When the U.S. Farm Bill was before the American legislators and when it was passed, we knew what the results would be. There was a lot of lead time that could be used to begin to get some sense of the problem for Canadian farmers and to begin to devise some mechanism that would afford some protection for Canadian farmers.
The first time we got to hear about a program was, I believe, a day or two after the Speech from the Throne was read in the fall of last year. In the speech itself, there was no mention of a specific program. In fact, there was very little mention of
agriculture. When this was raised in the House, the Government tried to justify it by saying that this was the first time agriculture was mentioned on the first page of a Throne Speech. Well, big deal. Obviously that would not wash on the Prairies.
At that time, there was an election occurring in Saskatchewan. When the Speech from the Throne was brought down, the Deputy Premier of Saskatchewan was in Ottawa trying to ensure that there would be something there for Canadian farmers because Mr. Devine's Conservative Government was in serious trouble back in Saskatchewan. Well, there was nothing in the speech so the Deputy Premier of Saskatchewan, the Premier of Saskatchewan and a fair number of Saskatchewan cabinet Ministers started phoning. They phoned senior cabinet Ministers from Saskatchewan and I am sure they phoned the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). They did get something. When the Prime Minister spoke, inserted in his speech was the promise of $1 billion.
Then we in the House tried to get some idea of what this $ 1 billion was all about. Day in and day out, we asked if this was new money and what the thinking behind it was. It became apparent that the announcement of the $1 billion did not reflect something that had been thought through, something that had required some intelligence to determine how the Government would tackle the problem. It became obvious that it was a political response, not a response to the crisis facing farmers today, not a response to the wars between the Europeans and the Americans-

April 28, 1987

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, you are being challenged with this point of order. Second, had the Hon. Member been listening to my remarks when I quoted the number of farms and farm families on the verge of bankruptcy, he would not come into this House and say there is no crisis. Third, I was trying to explain to the Hon. Member why there are many farmers in my constituency who are wondering what to seed and how much to seed. They are wondering right now, tonight, and it is an emergency for them.
It may not be an emergency for the Hon. Member of the government Party. That is his problem, but if he wants to understand the emergency nature of the crisis, I invite him to come to Fort Qu'Appelle, Qu'Appelle, Edenwold or Balgonie and talk to some of the rural members of those communities. In that way he will get some appreciation of the crisis which exists for some of the people whom I represent.
While giving credit to the Government for bringing in its $1 billion support program, I was trying to point out that this program was not a result of planning, thinking, anticipating and intelligence, but was a response to a political problem which existed for the Conservative Party in Saskatchewan. This became typified when a reporter from the Star Phoenix overheard the Premier of Saskatchewan, in the middle of the campaign in a small motel room in the wee hours of the morning, phoning senior cabinet Ministers in Ottawa and saying there was going to be hell to pay unless the feds came through with some package.
That is the story behind the so-called billion-dollar deal. The Government is trying to stretch that out as far as possible. It is trying to get maximum political results from minimum public involvement, effort and assistance. That is what it is all about. It is the barest of minimum and is not enough to cover our farmers who are totally exposed. That is the message we are trying to send to the Government. It is a message the Government is determined not to hear.
We have heard government Members in the House tonight dancing around the basic issues. They listed all the sins of the Liberals and the Liberals have many sins. It is all summed up in my mind and, I think, in the minds of most western Canadian farmers, in that one simple statement by former Prime Minister Trudeau: "Why should I sell your wheat?" The arrogance and the lack of understanding of what the country is all about is exhibited in that one quote. It says volumes. That one sentence will condemn the Liberal Party in western Canada for years and years to come.
The people of western Canada expected better from this Government and they did not get it. That is the cause of the sadness, frustration and anger which exists in western Canada today. That is why there are political movements beginning in western Canada which are thinking in terms of separation. They believe that the people they supported year in and year out in election after election have forsaken them now that they
are in Government. Significant numbers of western Canadians are now talking in terms of western separation.
Our frustration in the west is due to the fact that when times were good we paid our share. When the Liberals were in Government they made resource grabs. They tried to grab the potash in Saskatchewan. To set the record straight, we never supported the National Energy Program. The Conservatives continued to tell that lie. If they would go back to the voting record they would see that it is Goebbels propaganda of repeating a lie to insist that we supported the National Energy Program.
The National Energy Program took about $25 billion out of the west. We in the West say that the $1 billion that the Government has spent on farm assistance is the first billion dollars and there are $24 billion more to go. That is the position of the west and I have a lot of sympathy for that.
The economy and well-being of hundreds of thousands of farmers in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba is at stake. From a federal Government we expect responsibility and the assurance that it will stand by us to see us through these difficult times and will not sell us down the river. Unfortunately, the Government has not yet given that message.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the good fortune to leave the city this morning and fly to the great Province of British Columbia and meet with a number of leaders of farm organizations. I participated in the opening ceremonies of a world-class research centre which was designed, sponsored and built by Agriculture Canada. I refer, of course, to the opening of the Summerland Station. I am happy that I arrived back here tonight in time to have an opportunity to listen to some of the debate in the House. I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate regardless of the hour.
Mr. Speaker, I have been in this House for 15 years and I believe I have participated, almost without exception, in all of the opposition days in this House. I have never heard so many false statements coming from the other side; I have never heard so much untruth coming from the other side; I have never heard so many extreme statements coming from the other side and, indeed, so much hypocrisy, as I have heard within the last hour or hour and a half that I have been back in the House.
To stand up and say that the Government has done absolutely nothing for Canadian agriculture is absolutely false. It is untrue.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Nobody said that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Although I was not here, many of my colleagues were who are knowledgeable on agriculture and understand and have a full appreciation of the situation. Many of them are farmers, which makes a big difference. I do not see too many farmers on the other side, particularly on the Official Opposition benches. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I do not see anyone sitting on the benches of the Official Opposition. To be accurate, I do

April 28, 1987
now see the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) in his seat, but I do not believe the Hon. Member is a farmer.
I do want to give some credit to the NDP Members, particularly the last speaker. I must admit that many of his comments were very sensible and I listened to the Hon. Member very closely.
However, I have notes on certain comments which were made. It was said that the Government has done absolutely nothing for Canadian agriculture and that is not true. We made 16 campaign commitments to which I guess I will have to refer again. I am sure previous speakers, particularly those on this side of the House, have utilized this opportunity to set the record straight. We have to keep doing it over and over again. The fact of the matter is that we campaigned across this country and made some 16 commitments. To date we have fulfilled 14 of those commitments and we are going to fulfil all of them. We are going to deliver on all of our promises, certainly well before the end of our mandate.
In addition to that we have to date taken some 414 agricultural initiatives. That is more than one initiative every other working day since we were sworn into office. We have delivered more than $6 billion, most of which went into the hands of Canadian farmers.
1 can remember being the Opposition dairy critic and then the Opposition agricultural critic and I remember many farm organizations coming to the capital and saying that if we have the opportunity of getting into Government, and they certainly hoped we would, if you have one thing to do for us would you do something about capital gains. Shortly after we were sworn in, in fact in the first Budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) delivered on that campaign commitment.
I can recall a number of people meeting with us and asking us to do something about farm input costs. Would we give some serious consideration to a rebate of the excise taxes on farm fuels. Obviously because of the priority we place on agriculture we responded to that request. In doing so we effectively eliminated all federal sales and excise taxes on farm fuels. That represents a saving to Canadian farmers of about $200 million.
On a subject which is fairly close to my own heart, that of the dairy industry, I can remember dairy farmers coming to Ottawa year after year since about 1970 asking the federal Government to deliver a long-term dairy policy. We responded, made the campaign commitment, and in January of last year this Government provided a long-term dairy policy. We made a long-term commitment of five years and $1.5 billion. Another request made of us was to amend the Advance Payments for Crops legislation. We did that and doubled the payments. We were requested to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act. We responded and did so, and I am going to say something more about that. I am sure my colleague, the
Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) had something to say about that earlier.
For over a decade the provinces and meat producers in this country have been working together to try and put together a tripartite stabilization program for red meat. The previous Government was never able to negotiate successfully with the provinces or the producers. Indeed, it was unable to amend the Act and provide the legislative framework for tripartite stabilization. We were able to negotiate with the provinces and the producers, amend the Act, and deliver on another campaign commitment.
The list goes on. I am not going to use all my time to list all of the campaign commitments, but I thought it was appropriate to read into the record some of the major requests made to us by farm organizations and I think it was appropriate to remind people that this Government has responded. I am sure that with the help of the Parliamentary Library the record would show that the Government has delivered on more campaign commitments than any other Government in the history of the country. I am sure that if you look at our record, not only legislatively but also on delivery of badly needed financial support, it will show that this Government has responded to a greater extent than any other Government in the history of Canada.
When this Government was sworn into office, the budget to operate Agriculture Canada and pay for support programs required about $1.2 billion. Now here we are not even half way through this year and the commitments we have made amount to over $4 billion. In addition, we continue to work with farm leaders. We met them on March 5 and we will meet them again in the first week of June. We will continue to work with them to work out some new support program. I have heard some Members say that we should make some commitment about the kind of program we will have. We should make some commitment as to the extent we will be able to finance that program. What will be the distribution formula?
I would just remind Members of the fact that in our meeting of March 5 with 55 farm leaders, representing 35 farm organizations, we issued a joint press statement to the effect that farmers should make the decision themselves. Farmers must read market signals and I know their difficulty. However, they are in a far better position than you and I or all of the bureaucrats in Ottawa and in all the provinces, as well as all the politicians, to read the signals of the market-place.
We could put all these so-called great minds together but invariably we would not be in a position to read market signals with the accuracy that farmers and farm organizations can for themselves. That was precisely why we came out of that meeting with a press release. I do not have it with me, but I have read it into the record a couple of times and I would remind Hon. Members, particularly those across the way, that this was not a press release written by the Minister of Agriculture or his bureaucrats. This was not a press release by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board.
April 28, 1987

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It was written by your guys.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Algoma was not there. He speaks with the same uninformed voice on this issue as he does on most occasions in the House. No question about it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Most of them felt used so I would not bring up that argument, John.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
There is no question about the fact that there is a very clear message that we should not be making statements of this kind at this time.
1 have complimented the Member who spoke previously but he made a few comments that were not quite correct. He indicated that when the Government made the commitment to support Canadian farmers we arrived at a billion-dollar figure. He gave some political reason for why we arrived at that figure. Of course, he is wrong.
I cannot say when the Saskatchewan election took place, but I can say that we were meeting with farm leaders at the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) initiative and as a result of his leadership. It was at his request that the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and myself, as well as the Parliamentary Secretary, the Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), convened a meeting of farm leaders in Vancouver before he left for the Tokyo summit. The Hon. Member for Algoma speaks from his seat, but he was not there.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: You were not here when I spoke.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Perhaps that is a good thing. The fact is that we were meeting with farm leaders throughout the late spring and early summer and were working with farm leaders throughout the season. Indeed, we had come to the conclusion that it would require at least a billion dollars and we then continued working with them to devise some fair and equitable form of distributing that $1 billion.
We should not be critical of farm leaders but should compliment them. When we met in Ottawa at the Sir John Carling Building, many people thought that it would be impossible for 25 or 30 farm leaders to sit down with us to work out some type of program that would be fair and equitable, with a fair and equitable distribution formula. That can only be achieved by working together, and as a result of the leadership of the farm leaders involved in those meetings we were able to form the program. We were able to develop a formula that was fair and equitable.
If we look at that formula and consider a typical grain farm in Saskatchewan with the cropping pattern that the individual uses, and put that through the Special Canadian Grains Program formula, we will find that it triggers out about $9,300. If we look at southwestern Ontario and consider a typical farmer and his farm's cropping pattern, we will see that
it will trigger almost identical to what the typical farm could receive in western Canada.
Let me indicate that we are basically in the same position this year as we were last year. It is not appropriate for us, at this time, to indicate the degree of support that will be required. It is not possible to indicate at this time our financial ability as a Government to respond.
However, the commitment was made in the Speech from the Throne that the Government will spare no effort. Furthermore, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in his February 18 Budget, extended a mandate to the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board and myself to reconvene those meetings. We reconvened the meetings and held the first one on March 5.
I have made reference to the statement that was issued and there may be some question about it. However, I will stand by that statement and I am sure, if you want to check with the farmers who participated at that meeting, the vast majority of them stand by that statement. I have talked with many of them since then and, indeed, they still stand by that statement. We will be meeting with them in June and will continue to work with them to develop some type of program.
There has been a fair amount of time and comment, perhaps quite properly, on why the Government made a decision to lift the moratorium. I remind the House that there is no question that the phase-out is very much controlled.
While I placed that moratorium on farm foreclosures, I must remind the House that the foreclosures only applied to FCC clients. The Minister of Agriculture has no authority to place that moratorium on clients other than FCC clients.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Yes, you have the authority.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says that I do. I do not. I took that initiative at the time for good reason. If I had the opportunity to do it again I am sure I would introduce it. I indicated when I placed this moratorium in September, 1985, that there were a number of things that we as a Government wanted to do. The first was to respond to the interest rate conversion program. We did that with an $80 million commitment, bringing down the 5,600 FCC clients from 16.75 per cent to 12.75 per cent.
I said that I wanted to introduce the shared risk mortgage. We introduced that.
I indicated that we wanted to introduce the commodity-based loan. We have introduced the commodity-based loan.
I indicated that we wanted to bring forward the Farm Debt Review legislation which, indeed, we put into place. I said that we wanted to establish Farm Debt Review Boards in all the provinces. They have been established in all the provinces.
I indicated that we wanted to let these review boards have an opportunity for some experience in order that they could be established and functioning. That has happened and they have been doing an excellent job. While some people are critical of

April 28, 1987
the legislation, there is no question in my mind as I continue to consult with the rank and file of the farm population that that legislation is right.
I am also satisfied that the farm debt review process is proper and that they are doing an excellent job, considering the very difficult cases that the Farm Debt Review Board must deal with.
I see that you are giving me a signal, Mr. Speaker. I have not really begun.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to allow the Minister to continue?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I thank Hon. Members for the courtesy. I will try not to take too long.
I also indicated that we wanted to develop the Canadian rural transition program.
The Government has been forced to break new ground on just about every occasion in the last year and one-half. Any Government can enlarge, enrich or expand existing programs with very little difficulty, providing the financial resources are available. Although we have had the financial resources, the challenge is writing new legislation, developing new programs and new schemes. While this can be done, we must have the will of the Government and the co-operation of the Canadian farm population. We have had that will and that co-operation as well.
I suspect that those who are critical of the performance of the Farm Debt Review Boards have not taken the time to research and consider these questions on a case-by-case basis. I invite them to do so.
I also ask them to consider the question of the moratorium. I will always have to live with the question of whether it was the right decision for me to place that moratorium on FCC foreclosures in September, 1985. Has it been helpful or harmful to those people who have been held in that moratorium net? I can say that in some cases of which I am aware we might have been better off not to have placed that moratorium initially, or, perhaps certain people would have been better off financially if we had removed the moratorium earlier. I am sure that reasoning will make sense to Members if they consider that for some time.
If we look at the people who are in serious financial trouble we would probably find there is some exaggeration in these numbers. I think people have a tendency to make extreme statements.
The FCC does have a higher percentage of high risk cases. How did that come about? It came about very simply because the previous Government did not make sufficient funds available to the Farm Credit Corporation.
Second, the previous Government directed the Farm Credit Corporation, quite contrary to its mandate, to become a lender of last resort. When that direction is given, then the corporation has to assume, not by choice but rather by necessity, a far larger percentage and number of high risk cases. That is why the traditional -lending institutions have a figure of probably 4 per cent, 5 per cent, 6 per cent or seven per cent in very serious trouble, and if we look at the Farm Credit Corporation we find these figures much much higher.
Hon. Members opposite are critical of the performance of the Farm Debt Review Boards which, incidentally, have about a 55 per cent success rate across the country, about a 66 per cent success rate in the Province of Ontario and about a 65 per cent success rate in the Province of Alberta. If we look at those individuals who are in trouble on an almost case by case basis, we find almost without exception they go back to the mid 1970s. What happened in the mid 1970s? The so-called experts around the world looked into the late 1970s, the 1980s and beyond, and sent out signals. The signals were very dangerous, very inaccurate and wrong. They have caused a great deal of difficulty to many people who are in the farming business today.
The experts indicated that farmers should expand their operations. They should not bother renovating a barn, they should bulldoze it down and build a new one. They advised not to borrow $25,000 to renovate something, but just tear it down and they would be happy to lend the farmer $100,000 or a quarter of a million dollars.
Farmers were told to buy more land, that they were not going to have any difficulty at all because interest rates were going to remain stable. Well, the experts were wrong. They said the inflation rate was going to remain stable. They were wrong. They said farm input costs were going to remain stable, but they were wrong. They said that we would be going through a time right now of record high commodity prices and they were dead wrong there. They said as well that we would be going through a time of world shortages in commodities and we have gone through a period of world surpluses.
We have heard the predictions and encouragement of the previous Government. I can go back into Hansard and dig out speeches of my predecessor who travelled the country sending messages to young Canadian farmers to go out and produce to beat the band because the future was theirs and would be secure. Of course, we have now found out that all of those things have turned out to be wrong.
Upon examination we find there was another factor. One of those conditions which the experts said would not happen, which did happen, was probably the major contributing factor to the farmers' downfall and to their difficulty, and that was the interest rate increases. A lot of people really could be in a much better position today had they had not been caught up in the interest rate increases which occurred in 1981 and 1982. During that period of time interest rates increased from 9 per cent and 10 per cent up to 25 per cent, 26 per cent and 27 per cent. Anyone who operates a farm or business will
April 28, 1987

automatically and immediately recognize the damaging effects interest rate increases of that kind have.
Members of the Official Opposition in particular are indicating to us that we have not done enough for agriculture, yet we have increased our Budget from $1 billion to $2 billion to $3 billion to $4 billion. I do not know what more will be required, but because of the priority the Government places on agriculture, we have been with Canadian farmers in the past and we are going to be with them in the future.
We have seen tonight the hypocrisy of the Liberal Members of Parliament who have made critical comment about the Special Canadian Grains Program. That $1 billion was the single largest payment to Canadian farmers by any Government in the history of the country. A billion dollars is a tremendous amount of money.
What was the added input costs to Canadian farmers because of interest rates increasing from 9 per cent to 24 per cent or 25 per cent? The fact is that an added input cost of about $2 billion was extended by the previous Government in allowing interest rates to run from 9 per cent to 24 per cent and doing almost nothing about it. There was one measure, the Special Farm Assistance Program, which assisted about 1,900 people. The interesting fact about that was the added cost of that program was carried on the backs of other Canadian farmers. There is an input cost which exceeds by quite a lot the harmful effect on Canadian grain prices as a result of the U.S. Farm Bill, the Export Enhancement Program and the trade war between the United States and the EEC.
I would like to conclude by setting the record straight with respect to the lifting of the moratorium. I made some earlier comments about it and 1 could still talk for quite a while and give a number of experiences with respect to it. However, I am not going to take the time of the House to do so. Some people, again the uninformed-the uninterested I suppose-have indicated that the Farm Credit Corporation will be going in and seizing farms left, right and centre. All Hon. Members, if they want to be honest with themselves, know full well that I have always been complimentary and will continue to be complimentary to the Farm Credit Corporation. It has served Canadian farmers extremely well over the last 55, 56 and 57 years. I was complimentary of the Farm Credit Corporation when I sat across the House and I will continue to be supportive of that corporation.
Canadian farmers know that the Farm Credit Corporation is more understanding, and more sympathetic in dealing with their cases than any other lending institution in the country, and it is going to continue to be that way. The Farm Credit Corporation, by lifting the moratorium, will not be going out seizing farms and putting farmers off their land. That is not its task. That is not what it wants to do. Its philosophy is the same as the Government's philosophy. We are going to do everything possible to keep farmers on the land and in the business of producing food. There is no question about that. So let us put aside that inaccuracy.
The Canadian farming population have enough difficulty as it is. They do not need to read statements to the effect that the Farm Credit Corporation is going to go out and seize farms and put massive numbers of farmers off the land. They do not need that. It is not going to happen. The corporation does not want to put large acreages of land onto the market-place for very obvious reasons. Everything that can be done to reach agreements will be done.
The Farm Credit Corporation will be going out and sitting down on a one-to-one basis with every individual who has been affected and held by the moratorium. Again, every effort will be made to reach an agreement, to reach a settlement. We will look at the utilization of longer term leases than we have been able to sign up to this point in time. We believe that under the Act we can sign a lease for five years. That is not bad, but it is not long enough, and for very obvious reasons. We know that.
We know as well that it might be possible for us to extend the five-year lease to perhaps seven or 10 years. We believe that we can do that through the Order in Council process. If we can use the Order in Council process to provide a longer term lease, then we will do it. Do Hon. Members know why? Because we want to keep people on the land. We do not want to put them off it. We will be looking at every opportunity, at utilizing everything that we have-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: How come they're still going off the land?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The Hon. Member raises a legitimate question. He asks why some are still going off the land. It is very obvious that it is the same with the speculative number that is used as far as those people who are held by the moratorium are concerned. When we start to negotiate with them we know already that during that period of time a large number of clients have come forward on a voluntary basis. In some cases settlements have been reached. We know that some of them will come forward on a voluntary basis to indicate to us that they have had an opportunity to assess their situations, that they have had an opportunity to look at their futures and they have determined that it would be better for them to go. In fact, some of them have told me that they might have been better off had they gone earlier on their own. That is why I raise the question with respect to whether or not the moratorium has been helpful or harmful.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: They had no choice.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
But that process will only allow the corporation to deal with upwards to 50 cases-I say upwards, Mr. Speaker, to 50 cases per month on a national basis. That is not 50 cases in Alberta or 50 cases in Ontario. It is 50 cases on a national basis per month. They will then have communication on a regular basis, whether it be weekly or monthly, with the farm debt review boards in each province.
There will be some cases in which the corporation will recognize that a settlement can be reached if these people are

April 28, 1987
referred to the farm debt review boards. Thus they will be referred to the farm debt review boards. Other settlements will be more difficult to reach. Then, there will be others which, obviously, will have to be referred to the review boards by the Farm Credit Corporation. The Farm Credit Corporation is the same as any other lending institution.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That's the problem.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is bound by the Act. It is bound by the farm debt review legislation. Therefore it will not be seizing lands. There will not be a large number of farmers losing their farms.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The banks will do it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The other important thing to remember about this is the fact that when a farm debt review board in a province believes it has an adequate number of cases with which to deal it will then signal the Farm Credit Corporation that no further action be taken until such time as it has adequate time to deal with the cases with which it has to deal.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sorry to interrupt the Hon. Minister. I appreciate all the matters he is going into. Will he permit a question?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Absolutely.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. gentleman this. Is it not correct that it is not the FCC that seizes the land, it is the lender of first resort, the banks, through which the FCC guarantees loans and it is the banks that end up as the holders of the land and not the FCC?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has asked a legitimate question. The danger is in generalizing. If I were to give the Hon. Member a general answer it would be no. However, it would carry with it some inaccuracy because in some cases the action of the farm debt review board is not the decision of the FCC. It holds a secondary position, shall I say, and the primary client or creditor is the bank. So of course the bank would be the one that would petition it. Regardless of whether it is the bank petitioning or if it is the FCC petitioning there is still that process.
I could go on for quite some time, Mr. Speaker, but I know that there are a large number of Members on this side of the House in particular who wish to participate in the debate.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: We want to hear them.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I thought that it would be advisable to concentrate on some of the larger measures we have taken. This Government has done more for Canadian agriculture than has any other Government in the history of the country. I wanted to point to some of the reasons why we have some very serious financial positions in the farm community today. I wanted to give some clarification as far as the moratorium is concerned.
I could take a considerable amount of time to indicate where the real problem lies and where the Government has really concentrated its efforts. I could indicate where the Government and, in particular, the Prime Minister have played a leading role in the international forum with respect to bringing this problem to the attention of world leaders. I could also mention the new round of multilateral trade negotiations. The Prime Minister has been successful in placing agriculture on the agenda and some real progress has been made in terms of bringing about an earlier resolution.
I ask Members opposite to examine the record. I ask them to look at the make-up and the composition of the caucus which speaks for itself. I ask Hon. Members opposite to look at the composition of Cabinet and the statements that have been made. If Hon. Members were to check the record they would find that this is the first time in the history of the country in which the Prime Minister has referred to the plight of the Canadian farmer and the subject of agriculture more frequently than any other Prime Minister in our history. There is no question about that.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
We have been supportive of Canadian agriculture in the past. Our mandate is clear. Our schedule is clear, as is our timetable. We will continue to work with farm leaders. At the appropriate time we will make announcements. But it is inappropriate at this point in time to indicate exactly what the financial support will be. It is certainly inappropriate at this time to indicate what type of repayment or formula of distribution will be required.
As I talk to Canadian farmers they are quite appreciative of what we have done. They recognize that the Government recognizes the industry. They know that the Government places a priority on their industry. We have been helpful in the past and we are with them today. We will have to be with them tomorrow and into the future particularly when we consider some of the grain and oil seed sectors. Those problems will not go away tomorrow. They will be there tomorrow and for quite some time. Because of the priorities we have we will continue to hold them in the same priority as we have held them in the past. We will be there with them in the future.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!
