speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to follow at 1.30 in the morning the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and to see the tremendous support that agriculture has here in the House of Commons. While this debate may have its downside at 1.30 in the morning, I want to assure the constituents of Assiniboia, all the western Canadian farmers and all farmers across Canada that there has never been stronger representation in the House of Commons for farmers than what we have witnessed here today.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
April 28, 1987

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The leadership that has been given by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), by the Minister of Agriculture and by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) has never been equalled before in this country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Is that the Anvil chorus or the Greek chorus?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That is the truth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That was just a warming up exercise.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is the Hallelujah chorus.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I should like to speak for a moment about the questions put forward by the Opposition this evening. There is a major problem in the way in which the NDP and the Liberals have put forward this debate.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: There is a major problem with the NDP!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: In bringing forward the debate in the way they have, the Liberals and the NDP are challenging the Canadian Wheat Board and the decision made and supported by farm groups, thus undermining the Canadian Wheat Board.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Shame!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I wish to read to the House some of the things that the farm groups have said. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), just a few minutes ago, reiterated the support that the Government has had from various farm groups across the country.
I quote from the Winnipeg Free Press, as follows:
Canada cannot possibly match the power of the treasuries of either the U.S. or
the EEC. The government would have made a bad choice had it announced
initial grain prices that were unrealistic and had dealt with the resultant deficit
after the fact.
Neither the NDP nor the Liberals recognize where the problem comes from.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Sure we do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The problem stems from the U.S. and EEC agricultural subsidies.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: And what are you doing to protect our agricultural sector?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: In introducing these subsidies, neither the EEC nor the U.S. has looked into the future. Well, we have a Government in Canada that is looking into the future. In so doing, we have come to the conclusion that the answer rests in an international solution.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That takes three to five years, if we are lucky. What are you going to do tomorrow?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
It is obvious to me that the Opposition, in wanting to intervene on the initial prices of grain as set by the Canadian Wheat Board, is not looking for a long-term solution to the problems in the market-place.
For the benefit of the Opposition, I want to read-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Why don't you tell us what SaskPool is saying.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
If the Opposition would just listen for a moment, I can tell them what the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has to say. I quote Garf Stevenson, President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, as reported in the Western Producer of April 23, 1987:
-the Pool agrees with the government's decision to set initial prices to reflect world prices.
That is what SaskPool is saying. That is one of the largest, if not the largest, farm groups in western Canada.
Next, let me tell you what the Alberta Wheat Pool is saying. I quote:
-the Wheat Pool is all in favour of the Wheat Board setting an initial price that reflects real market conditions.
That is the Alberta Wheat Pool. Next, let me quote what the Cattlemen's Association is saying. Again, I quote from the Western Producer of April 23, 1987:
Chris Mills, policy adviser to the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, said the CCA agrees with the grain groups that initial prices should be set realistically to provide "one clear signal'' what world prices are and to avoid distorting domestic feed grain prices.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: A tough cookie!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I could go on and on. We have the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association saying the same thing: They support it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: An arm of the Tory Party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: In fact, I have not been able to find a farm group that does not support this policy. We have heard all night that the farm groups do not support the position the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is putting forward, the position that the Minister of Agriculture is putting forward, the position the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) is putting forward on this subject, both in Question Period and over the last week.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. I am wondering whether the Hon. Member will permit a question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has quoted Garf Stevenson, the President of SaskPool. Does he agree with the request in Mr. Stevenson's letter that the Government

April 28, 1987
provide, on an urgent basis, substantial deficiency payments for the 1987-88 crop year?
Since he is quoting Mr. Stevenson with regard to the setting of initial prices, perhaps he can tell us whether or not he agrees with the request in this letter from Mr. Stevenson to the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Certainly, we have no problem with that kind of request. The Minister of Agriculture has made that very clear. He has said that he was at a meeting less than a month ago at which Mr. Garf Stevenson was in attendance- and indeed, 1 was at that meeting. At that meeting, it was indicated, very clearly, that the Government had already set in motion a request to the farm groups for advice along these lines.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: This is a letter dated April 28, 1987.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Are you agreeing with the request set out in this letter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member must understand that it is a process of seeding and harvesting. We are dealing with a crop year now that will not end until July 31, 1988. The farmers will receive, this week, a payment from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, amounting, in the case of the average farm of two sections in Saskatchewan, or Manitoba, or Alberta, to something in the order of $14,000. In less than a month from now, the farmers will receive, by way of a deficiency payment, up to $25,000, and that payment will be relative to the crop year ending July 31, 1987.
I think there has to be a clear understanding as to what it is we are talking about. It is clear that the farm groups understand it. And so, yes, a letter from Mr. Stevenson looking forward to the future is quite proper. But for the Opposition to make the accusation in this House that this Government has not been dealing with the situation is uncalled for.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is outrageous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is totally uncalled for. I am sure the farmers recognize this. Farmers are very knowledgeable when it comes to agricultural issues. They realize the importance of the situation and appreciate the problems they face.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Stevenson's request is set out in this letter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
No one here would deny that the agricultural sector is facing problems, and will continue to face problems; but we, as a Government, are dealing with those problems, and we have a record of dealing with them.
As we look to the future, the agricultural community can have confidence in the direction that this Government will take on its behalf.
I wish to get back to the point I was making about the setting of the initial prices for grain. This Government has taken the position that we will support the farmer in place of
supporting the commodity-something which can only distort the international market-place. I think that is very clear.
The Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board has provided leadership in this area internationally, as has the Prime Minister.
The Minister of Agriculture spoke about the meeting held in Vancouver attended by some 30-odd members of the agricultural community, a meeting was held before the Prime Minister attended the Tokyo Conference.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That was after the smoke and mirror show here in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I was at that meeting personally, and it was very interesting to see both the interest of the Prime Minister and the response of the farm groups to the Prime Minister in terms of what could be done internationally.
There has been a great deal of co-operation on the part of the farm groups, on the part of the Prime Minister, on behalf of the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, and on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture and the Government in general, and that kind of co-operation has resulted in Canada providing leadership in the international arena toward finding a solution to these problems.
If anyone has a quick formula to solve these problems, we would certainly be open to hearing it. Canada will be providing leadership in this area. No other country is in a better position than Canada to provide the necessary leadership.
Canada recognizes that one of its great building blocks has been and will continue to be agriculture. The Government sees the importance of that building block. We intend to build upon it.
There is no question that we face difficult times. The initial price certainly was a disappointment. We on this side of the House do not like the word "subsidy". We are not particularly elated by the fact that we have to bring in subsidies, but at this point in time there is no other choice but to subsidize farmers.
What about the Farm Credit Corporation? I should like to refer to my own riding. Many farmers facing difficulties have been in my own livingroom. It is to the credit of the FCC that I have seen more flexibility on the part of that corporation in the last few months-and I see several Hon. Members nodding their heads-than I have ever seen before.
The Minister of Agriculture just made statements in the House about the fact that the review process is a move to help farmers. A number of us met with the committee chairmen who attended before the standing committee. They put forward the difficult situations faced by farmers in all provinces. A past Member of the House of Commons, Doug Neil, is serving the committee from the Province of Saskatchewan very well. He gave an excellent presentation to the standing committee on the work being done in Saskatchewan
April 28, 1987

which faces one of the more difficult situations in terms of bankruptcies. The flexibility on the part of the FCC is a credit to that organization.
What was the cause of the problem? I should like to deal with it. The basic cause of farm bankruptcies goes back to one thing-high interest rates. I am talking about interest rates of 22 per cent, 23 per cent, and 24 per cent. We had those kinds of interest rates three years running. If we take 20 per cent interest rates and multiply them over three years, we find 60 per cent of the principal debt of the farmers involved. Farmer after farmer has said to me as a Member of Parliament-and I am sure others have experienced it in their ridings-that his problems began with 20 per cent interest rates. They ask why the then Government of Canada did not do something about them.
I can recall the situation after we were elected in 1984. Day after day we heard the following cry: "Get interest rates down". Do Hon. Members know that they are down by 10 per cent to 12 per cent? I do not hear Hon. Members opposite giving any credit to the Government in this regard. There is a lack of vision on the part of the Opposition. It does not seek a solution.
The Liberals failed farmers drastically. That is one basic reason farmers in western Canada have very little confidence in the Liberal Party.
Let us look at the record of the Government. It was a difficult time to represent the Government as chairman of the task force on drought in western Canada. In my riding, especially in the Bengough and Swift Current areas, that drought went on for about three years. However, it was not until the Conservative Government was elected in 1984 that something was done. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board said that something had to be done. The Government set up a committee. We went to Bengough, Saskatchewan where there were 1,500 farmers. Hon. Members probably remember seeing it on television. One farmer was going to kick us all the way to Ottawa and back. They wanted an instant solution. We were saying that we wanted to hear from farm groups and from farmers. We were asking for just a few days.
The Government responded to the drought. Certainly some farmers were not satisfied. There was an odd problem here and an odd problem there. Few things in life are perfect. For the most part farmers in southern Saskatchewan, southern Alberta, southern Manitoba, the Peace River area, and wherever else there was drought were satisfied with the way in which the Government treated them.
There is a parallel situation now with the deficiency payments. The Opposition is asking us to do something quickly. It is asking us to respond momentarily, before we have had a chance to hear from farm groups or to move in a seasonal way.
I am going to close off now because I have covered the ground. I could tell the House about our record again and
again. We will put our record up against the record of the other Parties in the House. We are proud of what we have done. We have not done enough. More must be done. Agriculture is important. However, when it is done, it will be this Government that will do it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent an urban constituency, but I do not hesitate to participate in the debate because many of the people I represent are railway workers, farm machinery industry workers, oil workers, truck drivers, and dairy workers. They know from experience that their welfare depends upon a prosperous agricultural industry.
When farmers suffer, they suffer. If there is a drought or a flood, there are no crops. If the price farmers receive for their crops is not enough for them to make a living, then my constituents suffer.
What is happening to farmers? They are efficient producers. They are as efficient as any in the world. We must ask ourselves why they are in trouble. It is not because they have failed. They are in trouble because of the tremendous subsidies which the United States Government pays to its farmers and which the Governments of countries belonging to the European Economic Community pay to their farmers.
The Government is on the right track when it tries to persuade the American Government and the Governments of the countries belonging to the European Economic Community to stop the insane levels of subsidy. However, the Government is kidding itself-and it is certainly kidding farmers-if it thinks that the subsidies paid by these Governments will be reduced very much in the next short while.
The farmers of this country are in trouble, Mr. Speaker. No member of the New Democratic Party who has spoken in the debate today has said that the Conservative Government has done nothing to help the grain farmers of western Canada. We know, and the farmers know, that the Government produced a deficiency payment of $1 billion. I do not have time today to debate why the Government produced that payment or whether it was pure coincidence that the Government did that in the midst of a Saskatchewan election, but the Government did produce it. What we say and what the farmers are saying is that that one shot payment is just not enough.
What is the situation of our farmers, Mr. Speaker? Let me quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of a week ago, April 21, dealing with the decision of the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) to reduce the initial payment by 18 per cent. The paper reported that decision as follows: "Prairie grain farmers will receive a record $705 million payment to offset an 18 per cent drop in initial prices, Wheat Board Charlie Mayer announced yesterday. It is the second straight year prices for wheat, oats and barley sold by the Board have

April 28, 1987
dropped. The University of Manitoba agricultural economist Darryl Croft said increased funding will not offset the low prices set by the Board. He said that prices in government funding, while realistic, are disappointing to all farmers who rely on grain sales for their income". I could quote further. Then the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced that he would terminate the moratorium on farm credit foreclosures. The following is the way The Globe and Mail reported that in yesterday's newspaper. I want to quote from part of the The Globe and Mail's report because of the claims of the Minister of Agriculture and of the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) that farmers were satisfied, were happy, with the Government's decision with regard to the reduction in the initial price and with regard to the finishing off of the foreclosure program. Here is what The Globe and Mail reports in yesterday's issue "Garfield Stevenson, President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, said that the termination of the moratorium will cause a further decline in the market value of farm land. It is completely irresponsible and just not acceptable. I thought the Minister had more on the ball than this". I see the Hon. Member for Brandon- Souris (Mr. Clark) here. Then The Globe and Mail also quotes the President of Keystone Agricultural Producers, an organization which represents all the farm producers in Manitoba. This is what The Globe said: "Jack Penner, President of the Manitoba Keystone Agricultural Producers said termination of the farm credit moratorium will make it more difficult for farmers to get loans from banks and other lenders. At this time of year many farmers are trying to borrow money to purchase fuel, seed, fertilizer and chemicals for the coming crop season. A farmer needs a lot more cash at this time of the year than at any other time of the year. This is an extremely unfortunate time".
Maybe Members will say that the two newspapers misquoted or took out of context what the farm leaders said. Let me put on the record part of a letter sent yesterday which was addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) by the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Mr. Stevenson. "The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool believes that the rural way of life and related service industries are in jeopardy. We specifically recommend (1) that programs be immediately developed through federal and provincial co-operation to keep families on their farms in productive capacities. (2) that early consideration be given to the acute need for a substantial deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year. (3) that the Government continue its efforts to restore sanity in the international grain market".
Let me go back for a second to what farmers are saying about deficiency payments. They say that they want early consideration. They want a substantial deficiency payment not for last year's crop year but for the 1987-88 crop year.
Last week the President of Keystone Agricultural Producers, Mr. Jack Penner, a good friend of the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board, wrote to the Prime Minister. Here is part of what he wrote: "On behalf of grain producers in
Manitoba, we call on your Government to announce as soon as possible an intention to introduce a similar program for the 1987-88 crop year with support levels at least equivalent to those under the 1986 program. We feel strongly that any such additional program should be based simply on acreages to keep the production neutral. The farm financial crisis is so serious that we feel action must be taken prior to the end of April to assure grain farmers in the business community that the federal Government is supportive".
He goes on to say, "A second important step should be a bold new initiative through the Farm Credit Corporation to save thousands of commercial farms from insolvency. In addition to new loan funds at affordable rates, the FCC should become a full service lender to the farm community. This we feel will provide the assurances required now by the farm community in times when other lending institutions are threatening to withdraw services".
I find it very strange that when Members on this side of the House raise these kinds of questions and make these kinds of suggestions we are told that we are being alarmist and that we are making the situation worse. We are told that farmers are satisfied, that they are quite happy with the Government. I happen to believe that when the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool speaks, when the head of Keystone Agricultural Producers speaks, they know what their farmers need. Obviously we can see just by reading from those two letters that they are far from satisfied with what this Government has done. We are always accused of being wild-eyed radicals and the things that we say are said for partisan advantage.

That is the situation which is facing farmers, particularly in western Canada. What goes along with those economic difficulties are tremendous psychological and emotional problems. subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to join in this debate which focuses on a very important problem facing our economy at this time. I would be remiss if I did not compliment the Hon. Member who just spoke, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), for a very reasonable and responsible contribution to the debate.
I think it is important that Canadians be reminded again of the crisis that is facing Canadian grain producers. It is important also that Canadians understand that the mover of the motion which brought about this debate and his Party do not have a monopoly on concern for the farm community or for Canadian agriculture. The fact is that this Government, in spite of the legacy of past debt which hampers it, has made an unprecedented response to agriculture and particularly to the hard-pressed grains sector.
I believe prairie grain farmers understand very well that the problems they face are caused by factors that lie beyond our borders. The disastrous grain trade war that is going on between the European Economic Community and the United States, both economic superpowers which are determined to retain and enhance their share of the world grain export market no matter the cost, is such a factor.
Both the common market and the Americans are subsidizing their farmers considerably on wheat production and then dumping that production on the world market at virtually any price through export enhancement programs. In the result, Canada, which is heavily export dependent, in fact exporting 80 per cent of its wheat production, and with a population of 25 million, is facing unfair competition from the EEC which has a population base of 330 million and exports perhaps 20 per cent of its production. Of course, the Americans have a population base of some 250 million and an enormously larger treasury. Obviously it is extremely difficult for Canada to match the treasuries of western Europe and the U.S.
Canadian farmers know this. I believe the great majority of them feel the response of this Government has been fair and reasonable. However, I have a fear that there may be some misunderstanding in some of the urban areas of Canada. I hear rumblings of disquiet over what some urban dwellers
appear to perceive as very handsome payments being made to the farm community. There are stories in the press that the average amount of government payments to farmers is in the area of $25,000 to $30,000 in cash each year. One hears mutterings of discontent about this from those in urban areas who do not understand the importance of the agricultural sector to this country.
I think it is extremely important that in this debate we outline again the seriousness of the plight facing grain farmers. As a Member from Saskatchewan I would like to give some figures. They will relate solely to the Province of Saskatchewan. This information has been given to me by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and Statistics Canada.
Total farm receipts in the 1986 calendar year, crop, livestock and other, was in the area of $4.1 billion. Operating expenses were $2.8 billion, depreciation $674 million, leaving a net realized farm income of some $636 million, down 9 per cent from 1985. At first blush, $636 million in net income might sound pretty good, but the fact is that this is divided up among approximately 66,000 farmers in Saskatchewan. The average net income in 1986 per farm was in the area of $9,600, representing a return on capital and a payment for labour. Out of that sum obviously the farm family must not only meet its everyday living expenses such as food, clothing, heat, utilities and so on, but also pay the principal on loan payments. By way of comparison, the minimum wage in Saskatchewan at $4.50 an hour, based on a 40-hour week, returned some $960, obviously without the kind of intensive capital investment that the average farmer has made.
I should point out that these revenue figures include contributions from the federal Government of considerable magnitude. In 1986 there was crop drought assistance of $71 million, under federal-provincial crop insurance some $120 million, the federal farm fuel tax rebates accounted for another $43 million, and the western grain stabilization accounted for $450 million.
The fact is that without these federal programs farm income in Saskatchewan for 1986 would have been a negative figure. Projections for 1987 point to gross farm receipts of $4.2 billion, operating expenses of $2.7 billion, depreciation of $678 million, leaving net realized income of $849 million or around $12,500 per farm. That is up 33 per cent from 1986. Federal government payments contributing to this gross farm income in Saskatchewan for 1987 include $415 million under the special grains program, roughly $50 million in fuel rebates, and $382 million being Saskatchewan's share of the interim western grain stabilization payment, and those cheques are now in the mail with more to come. By June the federal contribution to the Saskatchewan grain sector will be in excess of $850 million. That equals the entire projected net income in farming in Saskatchewan for 1987.
While this is going on the equity position is eroding. In 1984 the average capital investment was some $460 an acre. The average farm size in Saskatchewan is around 1,000 acres. There is an average capital investment of $460,000 in land,
April 28, 1987

machinery and equipment. I know that some may find these figures rather tiresome but I think it is important at some stage in this rather lengthy debate that up-to-date figures go into the record in order to try and illustrate the impact of government assistance in turning around, indeed in keeping afloat the farm sector in Canada at this time.
The latest figures for 1985 indicate an erosion of equity as capital investment dropped to $420 an acre as a result of falling land prices. Undoubtedly the 1986 figures, when they are available, will indicate a further diminution of land values and a further erosion of equity. That represents a brief summary of farm income and equity positions in Saskatchewan. It is an indication of the importance of the federal response.
The mover of this debate cited lower grain prices, the lifting of the FCC moratorium, and the matter of deficiency payments for the next crop year as reasons for the debate. We all know that the initial price for No. 1 wheat in 1985-86 was $4.35 a bushel. It fell in the current year to $3.54 a bushel, and for the next crop year, 1987-88, it will drop to $2.99 a bushel. Canadian farmers also know, as do opposition Members, that this disastrous decline was caused by the subsidy war originating beyond our borders.
In order for Canada to retain its traditional share of the world export market it is necessary that the Canadian Wheat Board lower its prices in order to meet world competition. That is the reality. The Canadian Wheat Board has its sensors in the market-place and recommends to the federal Government what the initial payment should be. Farmers know that quite clearly and I think opposition Members should understand it as well. One would hope they are not questioning the integrity of the Canadian Wheat Board in that regard.
Opposition Members lament the lifting of the FCC moratorium which has been in place for some 19 months. The fact is that the employees of the Farm Credit Corporation, and I am not talking about head office people in Ottawa but the people who work in the field and deal every day with farmers in Saskatchewan, tell me that of the farmers who are experiencing difficulty in making their payments, the good operators come in ahead of time. If they are having difficulty making payments, they come in and talk to their counsellors and discuss the problems and find ways to overcome the difficulties. The FCC counsellors also say, unfortunately, that there is a small minority of borrowers in difficulty who tend not to co-operate, who tend to avoid the situation. They have to be called in or badgered and some suggest they hide behind the moratorium.
What the FCC people tell me is that the moratorium might as well be lifted because it is not going to make any difference at all insofar as a responsible and co-operative farmer is concerned. There are ways of assisting those people and they are being used at the present time and will continue to be used. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) indicated earlier in this debate the possibility of some further initiatives and alternatives.
The FCC field people do make the suggestion that perhaps the commodity-based loan criteria of equity might be changed somewhat in order that existing FCC clients whose equity has eroded might still be able to qualify for a commodity-based loan. I think it is a sensible suggestion and I urge the Minister of Agriculture to seriously consider the proposal.
The Opposition is asking for assurance of a deficiency payment for the next crop year which begins August 1, 1987, and ends July 31, 1988. We are 15 months away from the end of that crop year. One might ask whether they do this in order to gain some political points, whether they would expect the Government to do this without knowing all of the factors; the size and quality of the crop, world prices in the future, and conditions in other countries.
They ask this with the full knowledge that $705 million in interim payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Act is already in the mail and the fact that there will be another $700 million paid to Canadian grain and oilseed producers in the next month under the final instalment of the Special Grains Assistance Program. They know, too, that last fall the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a commitment in the Throne Speech that the Government would spare no efforts in protecting the interests of Canadian farmers and that that commitment was followed up with a $1 billion Canada Grains Assistance Program.
Actions speak louder than words. I believe that most western farmers know that the Government is solidly behind them, not with the empty rhetoric which characterized the previous Government, but with action, programs and cash.
I would be less than honest if I did not indicate that I was somewhat disgusted by the antics of some members of the Liberal Party earlier this evening. I find repugnant their smug response that somehow it is the fault of the Government that world grain prices have dropped and their temerity in suggesting that the Government is insensitive to the Canadian grain sector.
This comes from a Liberal Party which brought capital gains to western agriculture in 1971 and initiated the infamous LIFT program which brought 23 per cent floating interest rates to Canadian agriculture in the early 1980s which amounted to a time capsule, a delayed reaction which is being released even at this time. Interest rates were the root cause of the debt problems of many Canadian farmers.
The Leader of that Liberal Government said, "Why should I sell your wheat?" During the good years in this country that Party not only failed to balance the books but in fact went head over heels in debt for magnificent and outstanding programs such as Katimavik. In the good times the Liberal Party saddled the nation with a debt of such magnitude that the interest charges on it now consume virtually one-third of federal Government revenue.

April 28, 1987
This massive debt servicing requirement makes it extremely difficult for the Government to be able to respond to the urgent needs of Canadian agriculture without running up the deficit further, increasing inflationary pressures, and putting upward pressure on interest rates which can only harm the farm community. That, I think, represents the Liberal legacy. What do they offer today? A 17-page report, Directions for the West, which the Winnipeg Free Press quite properly describes as "pathetic and empty".
I want to touch briefly on some of the initiatives which the Government has taken with regard to Canadian agriculture, some large and some small, which I believe indicate that the Government has paid attention to prairie grain farmers, initiatives which contradict in a very real and concrete way the allegations put forward by the mover of this debate.
For all practical purposes the Government got rid of capital gains immediately upon taking office, the fulfillment of a campaign commitment made when land prices were higher. The Government instituted a program of farm fuel tax rebates which, in effect, has eliminated federal taxes on farm fuels. It changed federal-provincial crop insurance to increase coverage without premium increase.
It amended the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act to tidy it up and eliminate the need for the landlord's signature to be obtained in order that a tenant can secure cash advances. It amended the Western Grain Stabilization Act to provide for timely interim payments each spring in time for seeding. These were sizeable payments; $580 million in 1986 and $705 million this spring.
The Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) today, or I guess I should say yesterday, in Question Period noted that the Western Grain Stabilization Fund is presently in deficit. It has been exhausted and in view of the fact that the accumulated past contributions by both the Government and producers have run out, the fund will have to be replenished with new money. This may well be the time to open up the Act to enable the approximately 17 per cent of western producers who are not part of that program to enter. I believe the Minister indicated that he is certainly prepared to examine that situation.
There is the situation of the No. 5 Durum which a number of producers on the Prairies have and, unfortunately, cannot get rid of other than by mixing with hay for animal feed. In the circumstances they have a crop and therefore cannot secure crop insurance. They cannot contribute to western grain stabilization because they have not sold the product. I wonder, as do producers, whether there is some mechanism by which contributions to the Western Grain Stabilization Program might be made in such circumstances. That is the type of problem which all Members in this House, regardless of their partisan stripe, ought to try to address themselves to for the benefit of agriculture generally.
The Government supported Canadian cattlemen in their successful countervail application against European Economic
Community beef. It instituted Debt Review Boards which I believe are generally working well. It instituted the commodity-based loan program, an innovative and experimental approach to existing Farm Credit Corporation mortgage clients. As I mentioned earlier, I think there may be room there to ask for consideration of changing the equity requirements.
I should compliment the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) who noted an ill-conceived heavy equipment overallowance special audit being performed by the bureaucrats, a program which threatened the farm community with the spectre of field auditors from Revenue Canada examining every single machine deal which has taken place in the last four or five years and trying to substitute their idea of the fair market value of that piece of equipment for that fairly arrived at in the market-place between the dealer and the farmer.
After reviewing that situation in detail and noting that farmers are already subject to the same kind of audit procedures as is every other taxpayer, the Minister believed that there was indeed no need for a special over-allowance program targeted at the farm community. As a result, he has responded to the representations of Members on all sides of this House and cancelled the program.
For years we witnessed the almost annual shutdown in the flow of grain from the farm gate to the ports through stoppages at Vancouver and Thunder Bay. There is presently a Private Member's Bill, Bill C-244, coming before this House, the intent of which is to substitute a process of binding conciliation for the strike or lock-out mechanism. 1 urge Members of this House to support that Bill.
The Western Canadian Wheat Growers and United Grain Growers have already indicated support. Perhaps the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which is, quite properly, quick to ask for assistance for farmers, might consider publicly getting behind such a Bill which would help to maintain Canada's reputation as a dependable supplier of quality wheat and would also enable farmers to avoid those inevitable demurrage charges which result from these stoppages. Certainly many pool members individually want this legislation and I suggest that if the NDP are genuine about wanting to help the farm community they will get behind an initiative of this nature.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that interest rates generally are down 4 per cent as a result of the prudent approach of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), as a result of downsizing of Government which, incidentally, has been battled every step of the way by the Opposition in this House, in spite of low world oil, grain, potash and uranium prices owing to factors beyond our borders, and in spite of the monumental deficit build-up of the past.
Against all odds the Minister of Finance has been able to find ways to service that awful debt, to help out the agriculture and energy sectors, and still reduce the growth in the deficit. The result of that is 700,000 new jobs and 500,000 people in the workforce.
April 28, 1987

Clearly, the answer to the problems here is $6 wheat and the solution lies internationally, beyond our borders. In the meantime, producers can rest assured that the commitment in last year's Throne Speech that the Government will spare no effort to assist the farm community during these difficult times will be met. There is no question that western farmers and all Canadian farmers will know, in terms of actual cash received, and action rather than words, that the Government will live up to its commitment.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

That is all right, they were like that then.
There are not many of us left here, but I am one of those who had to suffer through operation LIFT at the hands of the Liberal Party and Otto Lang. I saw the abandonment of 3,000 miles of railway track in the prairie provinces at the hands of Otto Lang and the Liberals.
When they introduced the Grain Stabilization Bill, I can modestly say that I helped four farmers take the Liberal Government to court where we won the case and $100 million. The ultimate irony is when we consider who led the fight and introduced the Bill to get rid of the statutory grain rates. It was the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), who had the unmitigated gall to get up and cry about the high cost of production for farmers. If he had at least the courtesy to blush, 1 would have accepted his conversion on the road to his own Damascus. However, he did not have the courtesy to do so.
As well, there is a Senator travelling around southern Saskatchewan on a mission called "Journey for Justice". In October, 1983, we had a reception here to deal with retaining the Crow's Nest Pass rate for grain producers. Three hundred farmers from Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba gathered in the Railway Committee Room and asked the Hon. Senator if he would resign from the Senate if the Bill to eliminate the statutory grain rate was passed. The Senator left the meeting. I do not believe we need to hear any more from Liberals because they are the ones who are responsible for this dilemma.
I want to deal with the Party that is perpetuating the sins of omission and commission. Since Confederation, grain producers have only wanted what they believe is rightfully theirs, which is a price for their product which provides a return for their cost of production and their cost of living. They have never asked for more than that.
Grain producers have never been able to set their own price for their production yet a union member can bargain for his wages in an attempt to meet his cost of living. If he is not satisfied he can go on strike.
Professionals can set their fees to recover their costs and maintain their standard of living, as can Members of Parliament. However, as soon as a farmer asks for a return that meets his cost of production and provides a half decent living the Government decides to lift the moratorium on his mortgage. The concern is not that the Government will seize the land of one farmer or 500 farmers, but that it is prepared to lift a moratorium on their mortgages at the FCC. It means that the Government does not give a damn.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
It means that it is not prepared to provide the same standard of living for agricultural producers as it is prepared to provide for every other sector of our economy that can set its price and recover its cost or shut down.
Agriculture is so fundamental to our country that it cannot shut down.
There has been much said in the press about the fact that Mexico, Poland and Brazil owe the banks of Europe and North America tens of billions of dollars. There is a consortium of eight banks-six American and two Canadian-which are owed $6 billion by Poland, Mexico and other countries. Furthermore, a consortium of six airlines in North America owe those banks $6 billion.
One does not often read amusing stories in the financial pages of The Globe and Mail, but I was amused to read the interview with the vice-president of the Chase Manhattan Bank, the spokesman for this consortium of banks. When we apply this reasoning to the Farm Credit Corporation, we see that the land stays, the bank stays, but the farmers must leave. There is something fundamentally wrong in a system that allows us to bail out other countries, airlines, railroads, automobile companies by writing down their debts and writing off interest charges but when it comes to farmers-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: And we can pay the Crow's Nest Pass rate to the railroads under the direction of the NDP.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
My hon. friend should either sit down or fall down.
I find that double standard unsupportable and I think my hon. friends opposite will agree that there is a double standard. The land stays there, the banks stay there, and the farmers have to leave. Every civilization going back to the Babylonian

April 28, 1987
destroyed itself when it destroyed its agricultural community, and that is what we are in the process of doing.
The Government talks about lifting a moratorium and tells us it will not review more than 50 farmers a month. Is that not nice of the Government? It could review 100 farmers a month or 500 farmers. After all, there are upwards of 7,000 in them in hock up to their eyeballs. But it was very nice of the Government to say it would only do 50 farmers a month. I thought that was sort of half decent. Fifty farmers a month is only 600 a year. If we give this Government another couple of years, that will only be 1,200 or 1,300 more farmers who have been called up on the carpet.
Why does this Government not say to the farmers: "You cannot possibly pay the principal and interest on the loan on your land and machinery, therefore, we will cancel the mortgage. You get the land. You pay a lease fee which covers the minimum interest charges and land taxes and it is yours"? It stays in the family. It does not go to anyone else. Banks do not know how to run farms. Why does the Government not do that? I hesitate to mention the word but 1 have to bring it up again, it is called "banking land". It is called a "land bank". It is the means to preserve our rural communities and family farms. It is not just farmers, it is every bulk dealer, corner grocery store, postmaster, local school, curling rink, you name it, in every province of this country, which is at stake. So it ain't just wheat and it ain't just farmers.
The Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) talked about initial prices. I want to remind you gentlemen, when he accuses us of attacking the Canadian Wheat Board, that he is the man, as Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board in 1960 who removed feed grains from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. He was the one who started the attack on orderly marketing in the Canadian Wheat Board, and that was endorsed and continued by the Liberal Party when it took over, which means there ain't no difference. Let us bring interest charges under the Farm Credit Corporation at or below the bank rate. Let us not only put in place a moratorium, let us say to all the family farmers in this country-

Mr. Speaker, could I have another half hour to teach these dummies something? In the dirty thirties the Tories were in power followed by the Liberals. But it was the CCF who had to bail out Saskatchewan. They told us that money did not grow on gooseberry bushes. Who was it that victimized farmers with seed grain debts, relief debts and property tax debts in the dirty thirties and early forties? It took a war and a CCF Government to clear that situation up. But we declared a moratorium. We cancelled those bloody debts. We told the banks to go to hell. We brought in a farm security Act which did not allow anyone to take a home quarter of land and a farmer's home away from him.
I want to tell my hon. friend opposite that he should get the courage and the intestinal fortitude, to put it nicely, to say to the financial institutions, including a government financial institution, that no longer will we allow our agricultural producers to receive less than their costs of production. That has to be a minimum goal of any Government of any political stripe. If that means higher costs for consumers it means that we will offset it for old age pensioners and the poor in other ways. And the rest of us can darn well pay our share of the costs of that agricultural production. We must stop preventing the one and only sector-although I guess we could add the fishermen to that-in all our economy from receiving a price that covers its costs of production.

not a hell of a lot to brag about. It has done better than the Liberals. The Government is like the two guys out fishing. The boat tipped over and one of them hollered: "Help, I can't swim". The other one said: "This is no time to brag about it".

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in this debate after the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). When he started his comments, the Hon. Member told us that he had been both amazed and disappointed when listening to the speeches made here in the House this evening. Mr. Speaker, I was expecting a Member with the extensive experience of the Hon. Member for Regina West to produce a truly excellent speech. Unfortunately, we were treated to a flood of verbiage totally devoid of ideas, something the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is particularly good at. Mr. Speaker, it takes incredible nerve to ask for an emergency debate on the situation of western grain producers. Nerve, however, is something of which the Hon. Member for Regina West and his seatmate from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) have an abundant supply. Mr. Speaker, this is not an emergency because many western grain producers are in intensive care and others are enjoying extended care. With the kind of policies we had for the past 20 years, certain producers went from emergency to intensive care, others to extended care, some years ago, nevertheless, our socialist friends have changed the words to their tune and now keep repeating this Government is not doing enough.
Mr. Speaker, whatever we do, it will never be enough, and there are producers, not only in western Canada but across this country, who have gone from the emergency stage to the terminal phase. Their financial health has deteriorated to the point where treatment would be to no avail. They are doomed. The tragic part is that we got into this situation as a result of the socialists being hand-in-glove with the Liberals. Mr. Speaker, this crowd of unfrocked capitalists never had to manage a single dollar of taxpayers' money and never will. They will never have a chance to run this country. The closest the Hon. Member for Regina West has come to a western farmer is in his air-conditioned Cadillac with the windows rolled up tight. That close.

April 28, 1987

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have not paid for my last car, let alone drive a Cadillac. I am a socialist from Saskatchewan. I do not have a Cadillac and I have never had one.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those unfrocked capitalists, as I said before, probably leave their Cadillacs in Ottawa when they go out west. And if they don't have a Cadillac, they borrow or rent one.
Mr. Speaker, our socialist friends can go on with their campaigns to win members. They were campaigning all over the country, not just in Western Canada but also in Quebec: operation charm. Well, moral victories will be about as close as they will get to power. Between elections, their operation charm, led by the kind of leader they have now, a leader who-
Mr. Speaker, when one has no responsibility for running the country, no administrative concerns, one can afford to make promises and bend socialist principles so far as to promise the capitalist banks will be making the same enormous profits they are making now. The banks are making these profits because our unfrocked capitalists, our Sunday socialists supported the Liberals for so many years. Mr. Speaker, you will never see one of these socialists rise in the House to support one of the Conservative Government's policies. Never! That is because their support comes from the west. There are no Liberals in the west. There are Conservatives. So how can we logically expect our Sunday socialists to support a good policy introduced by the Conservative Government?
Mr. Speaker, they can go on harping on the fact that it is not enough, but that is not going to stop us from trying to correct 20 years of irresponsible administration by a Liberal Party supported by its socialist bedfellows. Mr. Speaker, that is not going to stop us from fulfilling our election promises. It will not prevent us from further developing our agricultural industry and trying to keep it on a sound basis, to improve the situation and do everything we can to help those who are in financial difficulty today.
Earlier I was listening to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) giving us a lecture. Mr. Speaker, 1 shall refrain. I will not bore you with another lecture. You have had enough tonight. It is past three o'clock in the morning. The Hon. Member recalled the case of the young farmer who had taken over the family farm from his father with a great deal of courage and goodwill and enthusiasm, and who was now facing tremendous financial problems. The Hon. Member was trying to impress western farmers with his knowledge of a situation that they know a lot more about than do our socialist friends.
But, Mr. Speaker, sitting here I found it hard to imagine that the accomplice of the Liberals would even dare before the House-indeed, Mr. Speaker, this is not a theater because, if a hockey game had been scheduled for this evening in western
Canada, would our socialist friends have asked for an emergency debate? No way! But you know that the Edmonton Oilers have defeated the Winnipeg Jets. So, considering that Eastern and Central Canada had something to watch, like hockey games, they thought they would simply have to perform for their electors and others they are trying to woo. And they have managed to do just that.
Still, Mr. Speaker, I thought it was my responsibility to remind them that these sittings are doing them good only in between election campaigns. It will probably give them a roller-coaster image in public polls, but it will not lead them to power.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, because I know that many of my colleagues also have interesting comments to make, certainly more so than what we have heard so far from our colleagues opposite, I should like to remind our Liberal friends that the commitments of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) are quite different from those of their former Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, who once told western grain producers: I am not going to sell your wheat.
Now then, Mr. Speaker, a Prime Minister who dares mouth such inanities has little in common with a man who had the courage to put on the economic summit agenda a topic like the economic problems facing farm producers, as Prime Minister Mulroney did in Tokyo.
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank you for giving me this opportunity to set the record straight in the House. We simply could not sit still after listening to some of their remarks, there has to be a limit somewhere. I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that our socialists friends, this tiny group of unfrocked capitalists, have almost gone too far this evening.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie).

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: He is not a farmer, but he will do the best he can.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should begin by first addressing what has been said in jest by the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) about my not being a farmer. In many of the exchanges in the House, both in Question Period and in debate, I have been disturbed by the presumption-and I understand it to a degree because I think it is a natural tendency-that people who are not farmers by vocation or by occupation somehow have some diminished right to speak about agriculture. Today during Question Period certain members of the Opposition had a few remarks to make about my Leader in respect of the fact that he was not a farmer. I have seen that in the House since I came here in 1979. I want to say that I reject that.
April 28, 1987

1 respect the knowledge which farmers have by virtue of the fact that they are farmers. Therefore, obviously they have a unique and important perspective on any debate when it comes to agriculture. Elowever, the fact of the matter is that this is the House of Commons, this is Parliament. All of us are charged with the responsibility of being as informed, as reasonable, and as intelligent as we can about all issues before Parliament.
What would happen if we restricted a transportation debate to those people only who have had experience in the railways? What would happen if we restricted a health care debate to only people who were formerly nurses or doctors before coming to the EEouse of Commons? I use these as examples. In that event surely we would not be able to do our jobs properly.
I simply ask Hon. Members, some of whom are farmers and some who are not, to respect the fact that even though some of us may not be farmers we have taken an interest in agriculture. In my own case-and I am not the agriculture critic or anything like that-I have taken an interest in agricultural matters, particularly from an environmental point of view, for many years.
I think these perspectives must be thrown into the mix whenever we are debating something. I hope that will be respected by Hon. Members.
I do not come from an agricultural family although my grandfather was a homesteader in Saskatchewan. We are not primarily a farm family; we are primarily a railroad family. When Members talk about the railways, I do not get up and say that because they do not have any carmen, machinists, switchmen, or hogheads in their families they do not have any right to comment on matters pertaining to railways. I think the same respect should be shown when it comes to other matters.
We all know that it is late. We have had some sharp exchanges tonight. We have also had what one might call, in a more negative way, partisan debate. Surely we all agree that it falls to the Opposition by virtue of the procedures of the House, not by virtue of anything else, to call for emergency motions. Obviously the Government does not call for an emergency debate; it is the Opposition which does that.
1 hope it would be fair to say that all of us recognize that there is a crisis, indeed an emergency, in the agricultural sector. If it is not an emergency, it is at least a continuing crisis. Even though we may disagree with each other strongly, I think it is very useful for the House of Commons and for Members of Parliament to have it out about the issue, so to speak. The only problem I have with that is that there is a tendency in which we all engage-and I am not pointing fingers here, except to point fingers at all of us including myself-to want to ridicule the arguments of others or to have a laugh at some of the claims or policies espoused by various Members.
However, I hope we can all agree on two things, the first one being that there is a crisis. The Government itself acknowledges that. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) acknowledges it when he rightly claims that he is trying to put this matter on the agenda of various international meetings, both bilateral and multilateral ones. The Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), and others acknowledge that we have a crisis. They may not agree with our analysis of the emergency or crisis, but they agree that there is a crisis. Certainly that should be common currency in the debate before us.
The other thing upon which we could agree is our mutual desire and commitment to solve the crisis or to reach some kind of solution however we might disagree about the solution.
I begin by saying that I do not doubt the commitment of many members of the government Party to trying to find a solution to the crisis now facing us in respect of agriculture. I do not think that we should get into impugning the motives of each other in respect of the particular crisis. I think we should have a real debate, and we have had some of that tonight.
That is what the House of Commons is for. I make a plea for Parliament being what Parliament should be, that is, a place where people of differing views who represent the people of Canada get together and debate, albeit in a lively fashion, but in a serious fashion, what might be some of the solutions to the serious problems faced by the country. One of the most serious problems which the country is facing is indeed the crisis in the agricultural sector.
I sometimes sense a problem, and I hope I will have the time to get into it. I hesitate to say it to a certain extent. There are two sides in this House and there are really only two sides to the debate, that is, that of the Conservatives and that of the New Democrats, because the Liberals went home a long time ago. They do not really care about western Canada or about the agricultural sector. I think it is fair to say that both the Conservatives and the New Democrats care in their own particular ways about the future of western Canada, even though we disagree sometimes with each other.
The one Liberal Member who has been here all night has just wandered back into the House. However, I think it is fair to say that we might both be open to the accusation that we are two sides of the same coin. We might be open to the accusation that the argument we carry on with each other about agriculture is within the limits of a certain understanding of agriculture and of Canada's place in the global agricultural economy that has grown up over the last 40 years, a place which many Canadians take for granted and regard as simply a fact of life.
I do not have the answers to the questions, but I hope I might be able to ask some of the right questions. I think that is what Canadians will be looking for, particularly farmers. I do not think farmers are particularly impressed by either side or by both sides of the House getting up and saying what they would do for farmers or what they have done for farmers. I

think farmers and Canadians in general are looking, when it comes to agriculture and a lot of other questions, for who is asking the right questions. The Hon. Member raises an old favourite of his concerning property rights. He continues to ignore the fact that during the Constitution debate one of the main obstacles to entrenching property rights in the Constitution was the provinces of Canada, most of which had progressive Governments at that time. I do not make any apologies for the fact that the New Democratic Party at that time was opposed to the entrenchment of property rights because it is quite illusory for the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) to imagine that property rights have only to do with the rights of individual farmers. Property rights could well have to do with the rights of banks and multinational corporations and could well have to do with the rights of a great many other institutions which make claims about their property which are at odds with either the environmental, the social or the longterm well-being of either society as a whole or of regions of this country. 1 can imagine a great many situations in which the property rights of large and powerful institutions like the banks would be at odds with policies that various Governments might want to adopt from time to time for the very purpose of preserving individual ownership of land.
I ask the Hon. Member to consider that, but to note that one likes a certain degree of predictability in political debate. Tell us more about the small "c" conservative business. It seems to me that one of the ironies of Progressive Conservatives, politics in this day and age is that although certain values are espoused, and presumably authentically espoused, about the preservation of the family farm, of traditional values, of smaller communities, a rural way of life and all these sorts of things, one has to ask whether or not those are the primary, the fundamental values of the Progressive Conservative Party. When a Progressive Conservative
April 28, 1987

Government has to choose between intervening in the marketplace in order to preserve the economic and social structures and so nurture and enhance those values or of allowing the market-place to take its full effect, a certain kind of conceptual paralysis takes over Conservatives at that point. They are unwilling to do so, and I think this is part of the debate that is going on here tonight.
It is not a question of the internal commitment, at the feeling level, of Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament to preserving the family farm or preserving the rural way of life; it is a question of whether or not they have the capability, ideologically or philosophically, if you like, to imagine acceptable solutions to those problems. I would contend as a New Democrat that most of the solutions to these problems- and I do not pretend to know all of them but in my judgment, whether Progressive Conservatives want to hear it or not-will be interventionist in nature. They will require more than simply standing back from trends in the international marketplace and simply trying to put out brush fires here and there or throwing a billion dollars here or having a program there. Part of what is involved will be the kind of intervention, the kind of reshaping of our agricultural economy, to preserve those values and to preserve the family farm, that most Progressive Conservatives will find unacceptable. That is the problem. Otherwise, it seems to me that what we are facing is a situation in which we will literally, over the course of time- perhaps not in the lifetime of very few people in this Parliament

have a return to a kind of feudalism where one of the very foundations on which this country was built, which was the widespread individual ownership of land, will have disappeared.
What I cannot understand for the life of me is why certain members of the Progressive Conservative Party cannot see the danger to the very things which I believe they genuinely cherish in not resisting trends which now exist in the agricultural market-place. I cannot for the life of me understand that.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the environment. In Canada, there is a tendency to see environmental problems as being primarily problems of trans-boundary air pollution, acid rain emissions either coming from the United States or from our own smelters and hydro plants or water pollution. Globally, one of the more pressing environmental problems is the disappearance of productive arable land. We have not faced up to that question here in Canada because I think many Canadians have been under the illusion for years that unlike other parts of the world, we live in a boundless environment, we can do what we want when we want and to the extent that we want with our environment.
When I was growing up and going to elementary school in the 1950s and early 1960s, the impression that was created among young Canadians was that Canada was a land of boundless resources and that the future lay in exploiting those resources to the fullest. We were given the impression that there really was no end to the exploitation of our natural resources. One of those resources is the soil of western Canada. We heard western Canada called the bread-basket of the world and so it was.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It still is.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

So it is and so it could remain. However, it will have to be that bread-basket in a changing world.
When I grew up, the world was full of countries that were unable to feed themselves. This provided a demand for Canadian grain, a demand that in many respects does not exist any longer. It is not that the world does not need Canadian grain any longer, as the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) mentioned. Our grain economy has been based on providing grain to countries able to pay enough for grain that the production of it was made sustainable in Canada. We may be moving into a different era now, not only with respect to costs of production but also because most of the people in the world who need food cannot pay for it. There, of course, I am alluding to the question of world hunger. I do not propose to try to deal with that tonight but I think it is something that should be on our minds when dealing with grain production.
I wanted to touch on the question of soil erosion. I would call the attention of the House to the report on soil conservation prepared by the Standing Committees on Agriculture, and Fisheries and Oceans for the Senate of Canada.

You can rest assured that I will not read the whole report since the Pages have gone home for the night and I do not have a glass of water. Reading from the beginning of the summary, the report indicates the following:
Soil erosion may well be the most underrated yet most damaging natural resource problem of the 80s. Must we wait for crisis conditions before action is taken to safeguard our scarce and dwindling soil resource base?
There the report quotes the Soil Conservation Society of America, Ontario Chapter. I see Hon. Members are trying to bring my speech to a close. I will say what I have to say and then Hon. Members will have their chances as well.
We have been literally mining our soil. We have been treating it not as the renewable resource it should be but as if it were a gold mine or a nickel mine. We are taking away from it as much as we possibly can, as quickly as we possibly can, without having regard for the future. In doing so, we have developed attitudes toward production that have resulted in other environmentally destructive tendencies.
As the environment critic for the federal NDP, one of the things that has come to my attention has been the extent to which, by virtue of the system that is in place now, farmers are pressured into putting as much land into production as possible. This is a concern shared by groups like Ducks Unlimited, for instance, hardly a socialist organization. Not only is this pressure put on farmers but another pressure is put on the habitat of waterfowl through the environment. All I am saying is that everything is connected to everything else.
When we consider the economics of agriculture or for that matter the economics of anything else, we do not take into consideration the fact that we have to do more and more in order to get the same result. Input costs are going up astronomically, not only for agriculture but for forestry. We have to go farther and farther to get to the mature trees. The same is true of the fisheries and of many of our natural resources because we have not managed those resources properly.
It is the environmental dimension of the agricultural crisis that all of us should be able to jointly address. Perhaps in addressing that we could find some common ground, some way of asking ourselves the difficult questions that must be asked if we are to have sustainable agriculture well into the 21st century. We should not be faced with history's judgment that we left our children with a disaster in western Canada and that is precisely what is in danger of happening if we do not smarten up.
The summary of the report on soil conservation to which I referred earlier reads in part as follows:
The Committee found that much of the problem lies with the great pressures being placed on our agricultural sector. Canadian farmers have been asked to demand the last ounce of productivity from our soils-largely because of economic necessity, international prices and technological progress.
As well, both old and new agricultural practices have contributed to the problem.
Old practices and technologies such as summerfallowing and the use of mouldboard plows contribute to salinity and erosion in certain parts of the country.
New practices and technology, such as the use of monoculture and large, heavy machinery contribute to loss of organic matter, soil compaction and erosion.
It then concludes by saying that over the years the priority put on production has taken its toll on soil quality.
There are many other criticisms contained in this report which has received a lot less attention than it should have. We do a lot of talking, and I am as guilty as anyone else, about high profile environmental matters like acid rain, but in the meantime our soil is disappearing. According to this report that is not an environmental problem which can be rehabilitated. Once it is gone, it is gone.
I ask Hon. Members to think about the ways in which we have externalized the cost of the way we do certain things in our economy. We now have to pick up a lot of the costs of the way we do things. The fact is the costs, which have been externalized and not taken into account because we have regarded soil and air and water as free commodities which we did not have to take into account in the way we accounted for our economic activity, we now have to take into account. We now have to ask, what is the cost of replacing fertile soil? What is the cost of good clean air? What is the cost of having potable water? What is the cost of doing all these things?

farmers in western Canada. The headline reads: "Manitoba Farm Budget Swamped by Saskatchewan and Alberta". For those Canadians who do not know it, Manitoba has an NDP Government. The Opposition has accused us of doing so little for farmers, of not addressing the issue of farmers at all.

The NDP Opposition suggests that the Conservative Government does not do enough but the fact is that it has done more for agriculture than any other Government in the history of Canada. It makes them absolutely sick to hear that hon. gentleman talk about how he and his Party are going to help farmers in western Canada. They do not believe him. They would like to believe him but they have been led down the garden path for 22 years, and there are Members in the New Democratic Party who have followed the principle of the Liberal Party of helping western farmers.
I will tell you a very sad story, Mr. Speaker. My dad was a devout and very strong Liberal for many years mainly because when he immigrated to this country there was a Liberal Government in power. He associated his ability to immigrate and start a life in Canada with the Government in power in 1926. He changed his mind when we had the likes of Pierre Elliott Trudeau and the Liberal administration, of which a good number are still here.
