speechtext:
The Member can name a lot more than 1 can because I am a new Member of Parliament. My father changed his mind about what a Liberal Government can do for western farmers in general. He had no use for them any more because not only did that arrogant group not give a darn about us, but they told us so. They literally told us exactly that.
As long as I am a Member of Parliament there is not a western Canadian who will ever forget what the Liberal Party did to us, whether with regard to interest rates or its attitude about selling our grain. As a matter of fact, the Liberal Party could hardly elect one Member of Parliament and now that the Government has done so much for agriculture all across Canada it is pretending, through the Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), to now have all the solutions for us. It is true that there is an emergency on hand, prices are going down and there are real problems. However, that Party will never be a Government with representatives from every province who understand farming. A Liberal Government will never be in that situation again because farmers do not forget.
April 28, 1987

Many Members who do not represent farming areas may believe farmers are not intelligent. I suggest any Member who rises to speak on this issue better know something about farming because farmers will not be fooled by those drugstore cowboys we have heard tonight. I do not take this issue very lightly and anyone in the Opposition who wishes to speak better know something about farming because, quite frankly, my constituents do not want to hear their rhetoric, garbage and promises.
During the Easter break I met with farmers. Some Hon. Members may be shocked to learn that not only do farmers not like subsidies, they hate them. In fact, many farmers in my area refer to the Special Canadian Grains Program as a kind of welfare payment. They will accept it because it helps them to buy grain, fertilizer, and pay for the gas in their tractors to seed their crops, but they have never received such a payment in the history of this country. They are grateful.
I challenge Members opposite, especially the New Democratic Party who proposed the motion, to suggest that the Government has not done enough. I challenge them to reflect on what has been said in this debate.
The only New Democratic Government in this country, in Manitoba, does not care. I will stay to the end of this debate and if I hear a member from that Party defend this motion, every person in my riding will hear about it because I will tell them personally that the idiots who are giving us this rhetoric are not farmers.
The New Democratic Party accomplished something tonight. They provoked the Government into telling Canadians what has happened in the last two and one-half years. Canadian farmers have never had such a direct input into this Chamber as they have had under this Government. The opposition Parties have demonstrated that they play an important part in this Chamber by allowing us to explain that.
I want to draw the attention of the House to a magazine article in a periodical that one can hardly consider a farming magazine. It is Maclean's magazine. Of course, the main story in Maclean's this week concerns Dome. I will not deal with that issue now because the NDP will suggest that we borrow, loan or give money as a Canadian solution to buy Dome. I presume the NDP can find money under shoe boxes to pay for these solutions. Farmers pay taxes as well, but how do New Democrats know that farmers want to buy Dome Petroleum? That may be another of their suggestions, considering the ridiculous proposals they have made already.
In any event, page 10 of Maclean's magazine contains a photo of our good looking Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). I have heard that members of both opposition Parties actually believe the Minister is doing a favourable job for Canadian farmers. He is a farmer and, in this photograph, he is farming and actually holding a grease gun. I wonder if anybody in the Liberal Party knows what a
grease gun is, but I know that there are some members in the New Democratic Party who know what grease is.
I am proud that we have a man representing the Wheat Board who understands the grain industry. If the New Democrats were ever the Government, I would not doubt that they would make the Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board. Incidentally, at one time he belonged to the Young Conservatives. He admitted that.
Mir. Blaikie: Youthful folly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am also very pleased that you found there was an emergency which permitted us to stay up all night, it now being 4.15 a.m. You found an emergency yesterday and I hope you can find an emergency tomorrow so we can come back here again and again because there is a record of this Government which needs to be shown to the country.
This Parliament is built for the Opposition. The national media queue in only to Question Period, which is designed for the Opposition and which we, when we were the Opposition used very effectively. It does, however, have the effect over time of giving a false impression which people will pick up and the effect of these debates is to give us a chance to even the score, so to speak. Over the course of last night and this morning we have been able to show what a truly wonderful record the Cabinet, under the able leadership of the Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, has put in place and I would like to talk about that in terms of my own riding.
I know my riding very well. I have been here for eight years. I have many, many good friends out there. In 1984 when we had barely come to power, the livestock industry was in serious trouble, and the Prime Minister was there. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) was there and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) was there.
We in Alberta have great pride in our Deputy Prime Minister who has served Alberta and this country so well and who is still here at 4.15 in the morning. The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) are here. These are Ministers of the Crown and they have stayed here throughout the night. I do not ever remember that occurring when we were in opposition and the Liberal Government was in power. There was never a Minister of the Crown who would stay on. I remember one
April 28, 1987

time speaking at 6.30 in the morning in an all-night debate and there was not a Minister of the Crown in the House.
In 1985 my constituency got into a serious drought problem. The highest payments went to my riding. The farmers in Pincher Creek and down through Cardston had the highest per acre payment of this entire country. Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board were there when I, as the Member of Parliament for Lethbridge-Foothills, told them that we had serious problems and needed their help. The Cabinet was there and the Progressive Conservative Party was there and we received the highest per acre payment in the entire country.
Again in 1986, through no fault of any individual farmer, but because of subsidies caused by socialist Governments and other Governments in Europe which built up over the years, we got into serious problems. The Americans then took them on nose to nose and we had that enormous battle between these economic super powers. We now have serious problems, and they are affecting my riding. Again, when we came as Members of Parliament to Cabinet and said we needed help, they were there. Prime Minister Brian Mulroney was there when he was needed and the Deputy Prime Minister was there, not only for the $1 billion, but for a stabilization program which has been richer than any program in the entire history of this nation.
Then we put in sound agricultural policies like tripartite stabilization where we have a producer who has to make a premium payment, a provincial Government, because agriculture is a concurrent jurisdiction in this country, and the federal Government. That is the way to set up a program which will last for years and years. This Government was there.
In my riding I have some 600 plus sugar-beet growers. There were some 600 in Manitoba and some in the Province of Quebec. They were in deep trouble and in fact in 1985 we did not produce any sugar-beets in Alberta. But I went as a Member of Parliament and said we needed help for the sugar-beet industry. We initiated a program through the officials in Lethbridge, brought the farmers down and talked to Conservative Members of Parliament from every province, and the Progressive Conservative Party was there, the Cabinet was there.
For 20 years, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) should understand, sugar-beets were a designated commodity under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. That meant that every year members of the industry had to come to Ottawa and get on their knees to beg the Minister of Agriculture for help. It was a yearly, fragile situation. Within two years-

What about Manitoba that is controlled by a socialist Government? subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

For years these scientists have been doing vital research on viruses. They have been working with very dangerous animal viruses which, if allowed to escape, could cause havoc in the livestock population, let alone in the human population which lives in the vicinity of the Institute. For years and years the Liberal Party delayed the construction of the station. Every year I would come before the committee considering the Estimates and ask the Minister when we would get the building. I would talk to officials in order to keep the pressure on. It was promised every election. And after every election its construction was delayed.
Our Party formed the Government in 1984. Because of the enormous national debt and the deficit there had to be all sorts of cut-backs. But not to the Animal Diseases Research Institute in Lethbridge-Foothills. So my people in Lethbridge-Foothills know-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Brian needed a shoe cupboard and he got it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Waterton National Park is a site that we hold out as Canadians to attract tourists from around the world. It has a main street which is in an absolute shambles, a disgrace to a nation such as Canada. We could never get it changed. It is now being redone. subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Tell us how your farmers are suffering.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
There is a coal town in the Crowsnest Pass which is in very deep trouble because for years and years the Liberals would not do anything about coal. Within months of being in power we had a joint federal-provincial task force put in place. There is a very distinct possibility that we can export more coal to Ontario. In spite of the federal Liberals we may have a better chance with the provincial Liberals since they seem to be talking sensibly about the subject.
There is also a Community Futures program. Tonight the Minister signed a document for the Crowsnest Pass to become a Community Futures town, which will give it hope. We have an enormous infrastructure of towns, houses, water facilities and sewage facilities, schools and churches, but it is a one-industry town. Like 800 others it is in very deep trouble. It now has a chance under the Community Futures program.
I could go on and on and talk to you, Mr. Speaker, about the advance payments that were doubled by our Minister of Agriculture. I could also speak about the Western Grain Stabilization Act which has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into western Canada.that would not have been poured into it under the Liberal regime because we changed the statute. Under the former Minister of Agriculture, Eugene
Whelan, the Liberals averaged about one agricultural Bill a year. We have had well over 10 Bills go through all totalled, which affect agriculture in major ways.
I would now like to refer to cash advances which are simple measures which could have been taken years and years ago but were not. Which Party doubled cash advances? It was the Conservative Party under the present Prime Minister. Which Party changed the Western Grain Transportation Act? It was the Conservative Party under the present Prime Minister.
Let me delve into the other Parties. What does the New Democratic Party have to say about agriculture? I want to read some of the Party's resolutions on agriculture. Mr. Speaker, I want you to ignore its position on NATO which would totally abandon our allies. The NDP wants to pull us out of NATO.
I want Your Honour to forget the Party's position on NORAD. It would isolate Canada so that we would lose our freedom far faster by being outside NORAD than by being in it.
I want you to forget the Party's insult to President Reagan, Mr. Speaker, who was here as a representative of the people of America and as our invited guest. Members of the New Democratic Party did not have the courtesy even to hear him out. That was a very real error of judgment on their part. What it shows, and it comes out on occasion, is what they would be like in power. It shows a lack of tolerance and a lack of respect. That is what we would get if that Party were ever to form the Government.
I do not want you to speak, Mr. Speaker, on the justice question. I have been a member of the Justice Committee for some four or five years now. I have sat in committee when members of the NDP have put forward motions which would have had the effect of legalizing anal intercourse between boys 14 to 18 years of age. That is what the NDP stand for. It is the Conservative Government that defeated those motions which would have legalized anal intercourse between boys 14 to 18 years of age. This is what Canadians need to hear because that Party is so sanctimonious.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) talked about his Leader. Members of his Party have said some very unkind things about the Prime Minister, things that are not fair at all. What is fair about the Leader of the NDP is that he refused to take a reduction in salary. The Leader of our Party, the Prime Minister, took a reduction in his salary. We threw out the same challenge to the Leader of the NDP. We said: "Okay, if you want to help ordinary Canadians then reduce your salary by 15 per cent". He refused.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That is not true, and you know it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I have seen that gentleman day after day leave the Chamber in his lovely fur hat and his lovely fur coat, with a big cigar, and get into a limousine and drive off. He refused to take any drop in income. How does that help the old
April 28, 1987

people of Canada? Our Prime Minister led by taking a drop in his income.
Let us not talk about that. Let us talk about what the NDP plans for farming. The way one can find out what a Party wants to do is by going to the resolutions that are on its books. We have all of the resolutions.
I wish to read for Members the NDP resolutions on farming. First, I will refer to something under the subtitle "Process of Planning". That sums up the NDP-the process of planning-since every socialist nation in the world believes in central planning. They believe that a small group can make decisions that will affect the masses, and the masses have to accept those decisions; and if the masses do not like the decision, then the system becomes more and more oppressive, and on it goes, as will become apparent when I read to you what the NDP has to say about farming.
Under the subtitle "The Process of Planning" they have an omnibus resolution on the future of the family farm. They recommend the "establishment of industrial plants to be cooperatively or publicly owned for the processing of food and the manufacture of farm supply items in the region of production".
There it is, Mr. Speaker: There is the nationalization; there is your Canagrex, plus.
And I can go on. The resolution goes on to state that related industries and services "should be encouraged through industrial estates and planned communities".
The NDP philosophy calls for collective estates and planned communities.
This is their resolution, Mr. Speaker. I would like to have them rise in this place and tell us-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: You will find that type of planning in every major city in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It goes on and on. If this is not the policy of the NDP, I invite them to rise in this place and say so.

speechtext: It is not terribly radical. Everybody has been doing it for some time.

speechtext:
If the policy of the NDP is not that well represented by the resolutions it has passed, what is that policy?

That is the policy of the New Democratic Party. Why is it that the members of that Party are not telling people about that policy?

speechtext: It is not-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport

speechtext:
When I tell my constituents about these policies, the immediate response is: "My God, I had no idea they stood for that type of thing. I didn't realize that they stand for abortion on demand". And that is right up to the day before the child is born. That is the NDP policy, and it is done through the injection of a saline solution into the amniotic fluid which burns the skin off the foetus.
That is the reality of the NDP policy. Once abortion is removed from the Criminal Code, that is what we are faced with; and that is what we are now telling people.
There was a time when the New Democratic Party could be ignored as a lunatic fringe. Now that it is up in the polls, people are starting to look at it, and we now have to tell people exactly what it stands for.
We can no longer afford to be smug about the New Democratic Party. It is a Party that is coming down in the polls, and it is going to come down real hard.
The proposals contained in this NDP resolution are tantamount to the state takeover of agriculture, with farmers taking their marching orders from Ottawa. We all know what that is like. I can remember the LIFT Program, where we were taking our orders from Ottawa.
For example, under this resolution, government bureaucrats would decide what equipment a farmer could buy, as they, to quote the resolution, "regulate the distribution, sale and servicing of farm machinery to promote standardization".
There it is again, Mr. Speaker: The NDP wants everybody to be exactly the same. They would not want to see private ownership of property for fear that someone might get ahead in this world.
I have had enough, Mr. Speaker, of the NDP. I cannot take it any more. But what about the Grits? They, too, have a resolution on agriculture. This is a resolution that is hot off the press, having come out only a couple of weeks ago.
The Liberals conducted a study on the western Canadian economy, coming out with some proposals-proposals which the media has had a fine time with, and quite properly so. Everybody sees these proposals for what they really are.
For the agriculture sector, here is what the Liberals say:
It is vital that the Canadian government take action that gives a clear message to both Canadian farmers and to the farmers and agricultural industries of other countries of the world that Canada is committed to remaining in the business of farming.
That is exactly what the Progressive Conservative Government has done.
In making this statement, what are the Liberals talking about? Are they talking about market share?
The paper goes on:
The Western Caucus recommends that the federal government consider efforts to rationalize our many and diverse federal and provincial agricultural programs so that our scarce resources can be put to maximum use-

April 28, 1987
In this proposal, Mr. Speaker, they use the word "rationalize"-and we all know what that means. It means "to cut back". According to Webster's, "rationalize" means to provide plausible but untrue reasons for conduct. That is the Liberal Party of Canada. That is the misinformation and false material that they have been putting out for years and years.
But what is it they are going to rationalize? Which programs will they cut out? Will they cut out the Western Grain Stabilization Act? Will they cut out the Agricultural Stabilization Act? Are they going to cut out crop insurance, the dairy policy, the marketing products boards?
These are all "safety net" programs serving western Canada, and indeed all of Canada, in a very fine way; and yet, the Liberal Party is going to "rationalize" them. It is going to take these programs away.
Are they going to take away the Farm Fuels Tax Relief Program? Are they going to take away the capital gains exemption? They certainly will. Every farmer in this country, every small business person in this country needs to understand that the moment a Liberal or NDP Government is elected, they will lose their capital gains exemption.
This very thing happened in Ontario. The first thing the Liberal Government did in Ontario was to take away the capital gains exemption, thus taking away one of the fundamental rights of the citizens of this country.
Because of the policy of the Progressive Conservative Government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Mul-roney, every citizen of Canada has the opportunity to amass $500,000 in capital exempt of taxation.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, let me say that I appreciate the opportunity, at 4.27 in the morning, to join in the debate that faces the grain farmers of our country, and particularly those in western Canada.
We have heard a great deal of nonsense from the last two Progressive Conservative speakers, who chose to talk about the crisis primarily by attacking us and the Liberals as being opposed to considering what actually needs to be done for the farmers of Canada.
I suspect that the farmers of Canada will see through that kind of guff, turfing Progressive Conservatives out at the next opportunity, as the public opinion polls across Canada suggest will happen.
There is certainly a crisis in agriculture in Canada, and that becomes apparent in an overwhelming way when one tours any of the agricultural parts of our country. I had the opportunity to spend the last week of February in southern Manitoba. In fact, I started out in the riding of the Member responsible for the Wheat Board, the riding of Portage-Marquette, and went south and west from there.
I very quickly discovered the sense that farmers have of no one dealing very effectively with the problems that they face in the production of grains. Our farmers are looking about desperately for answers. Instead of being used for partisan gain, the farmers of Canada want their Members of Parliament to consider real solutions to their problems, thus enabling them to carry on their operations.
The Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) wondered about the amount of experience in farming that might exist within the New Democratic Party caucus. I say, with pride, that I grew up on a Manitoba farm. Before going off to the University of Manitoba, I lived on a mixed farm in southern Manitoba. I know what it is like to work the grease gun, to drive a tractor, to care for pigs, and to do the various things that are required in a farming operation. 1 have to admit, of course, that it has been years since I have had the pleasure of working on a farm and experiencing first-hand what is involved. To be away from the farm is not necessarily to be removed from the problems, the challenges, and the recognition of the importance of agriculture and the need to come to grips with the situation facing us today.
We in Thunder Bay have a very large interest in prairie agriculture. We move more than half of the grain grown on the Prairies year by year, or at least we want to move more than half of it. We have 1,200 workers-and not many years ago we used to have 1,800 workers-moving from 20 million to 25 million tonnes of grain each season. We have our own interest in agriculture and our own reason to be concerned about the situation facing us now.
April 28, 1987

The Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake had something to say about the contrasting record of the prairie provinces in dealing with the farm situation facing them. It is worth recognizing that the Province of Manitoba has a much smaller farming area than is true in Saskatchewan and Alberta. That would immediately suggest that expenditures on agriculture would be a smaller proportion of the budget in Manitoba than is true of the two provinces to the west.
However, it is worth recognizing that in the Province of Saskatchewan the Conservative Government became involved in one of the most incredible pieces of buying itself power which we have seen in a long time. The loans offered to Saskatchewan farmers before the last provincial election amounted to well over $1 billion in total. They went to farmers whether or not they needed them.
It is a scandal of the program that farmers took the money and put it in the bank in order to earn interest on it. They knew that they would have to pay less interest than the bank was paying. They used taxpayers' money to give themselves a bit more of a cushion.
In some cases farmers who have been at it for a long time do not have the burden of interest which oppresses so many of the younger ones. For farmers in reasonable circumstances, this was a nice addition to their incomes.
I was in Saskatchewan a few weeks ago. I was told that one of the results was-and it was on the front pages of the newspapers-that communities and cities in Saskatchewan were facing cut-backs in provincial government expenditures. Of course the consequence was incredible unrest among the people of Saskatchewan in its cities, towns, and perhaps country areas.
In fact, I was told that the Conservative Government in Saskatchewan was hesitating to recall the Legislature because of the reaction to what it was doing as a result of its incredible deficit. Thanks to the farm program, a total of $1.2 billion or more had been added to the deficit. That Conservative Government faced the possibility that as many as half a dozen MLAs might cross to the opposition benches to sit as independents. In such circumstances the Government would lose the majority which it had just spent an incredible amount of taxpayers' dollars trying to win.
That kind of politics or that kind of assistance to agriculture is incredible. Farmers cannot have any respect for it. It is simply incredible that an agricultural economist, as Premier of a province, could indulge in that kind of political adventurism with the resources of a province. It is just an indication which matches the kind of partisanship we have seen in the last two Conservative speeches. They are prepared to do anything in order to maintain power and, in the process, achieve only a short-term answer to the difficulties facing us.
When I was in Manitoba in the last week of February I was struck by the fact that there is a diversity in the experience of farmers. For example, there are those involved in the dairy industry who are not doing all that badly. There are those
farmers who have been able to take advantage of supply management arrangements as a result of thinking ahead and the kind of planning which New Democrats, in the resolutions in our policy book, have put forward over the years. Those farmers find themselves able to carry on.
In dealing with the crisis facing us in agriculture these days, it seems to me that the beginning of wisdom is to recognize the need to consider the possibilities of supply management in other sectors of agriculture beyond dairy, egg and poultry production and so on where we have seen successful application of marketing boards in various provinces.
It is not easy to consider supply management for grain production when the grain growing areas of the Canadian west have flourished in many years on the basis of production for world markets. Considering the possibility of managing the world's supply as Canadian Governments have done for many years in the past through international wheat agreements seems almost impossible these days. There is no point in wasting breath on partisan rhetoric when the first problem faces us.
Subsidization of production in the United States and in Europe-in fact it is in many countries of the world-has created a situation of over-supply and has driven down prices to such an extent that prairie farmers who have gloried in growing grain for the markets of the world find themselves unable to sell their products at any kind of remunerative price.
I must confess that in visiting with farmers in Manitoba in February and talking with them about their situations these circumstances were driven home to me particularly. No matter what crop one took, if it was a grain crop designed or destined for large commercial markets, the prices farmers expected to receive for production were driven home. Of course the announcement this week of 18 per cent less than the level of last year only underscored the urgency of the situation. The distressing or profoundly shocking reality of the industry was that for crop after crop one could look at the value of output per acre and discover that it would not match the cost of production, the cost of various inputs, particularly the fuel, chemicals, and fertilizers required in order to produce grain on the basis that farmers presently produce it.
I talked with one large commercial farmer in Winkler who showed me the calculations he had made in the days before I was there. In crop after crop he expected that, on the basis of a good yield and at the prices one could expect at that point, he would be losing from $15 to $50 per acre.
That of course is the brute reality which has had the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) calling upon the Government, almost day by day, to make clear to farmers what it would do to ensure that they can cover the costs of production in this season and be assured of it at the time they made their decisions to seed.

April 28, 1987
If one faces that kind of situation, what is the logical thing to do? It would be not to grow anything. When a grain farmer can plan reasonably in February, 1987 to make a profit only on the certified seed business-and of course there is a small number of farmers who are able to do that-we recognize how serious is this crisis. It is a crisis which has resulted from the grotesque subsidization policies of the United States and in other countries as well. That is at the root of the difficulty. Clearly having international discussions with the various Governments concerned to cut back on these things to do the rationalizing which the Hon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills (Mr. Thacker) was disparaging a few minutes ago when he was looking at one of our resolutions, to come to some kind of reason in these areas, surely it is a kind of lunacy to disparage it when that is exactly what is required. It will not be easy to do that. There is always the possibility in the present circumstances that the grain which Canadian farmers want to produce will not be saleable in these next years because it is not actually needed on the world markets, almost aside from the policies of the United States, the European Economic Community and other countries.
1 hesitate a bit to say that because there is by no means an end to starvation on the globe. Rather the contrary. The debt situation in which various countries find themselves is such that they do not have the resources these days to buy food. Of course what we find in many cases is the production of cash crops in these countries for export in a desperate desire to earn the foreign exchange they need to meet the interest payments on the borrowing which they did in years past. Those activities require rationalization.
What we need is to come to grips with the international debt crisis facing us these days. It was made so much worse by the interest rate depression of the early 1980s which loaded countries down as it loaded Canadian farmers down with the enormous debt. We need to recognize that we are sliding toward depression rather than moving to prosperity. That requires intelligent thought, not partisan wrangling of the sort we have had here this morning.
If it becomes clear that prairie farmers can grow far more than we are going to be able to sell this year over the next five or 10 years-I should not try to add up the years into the future because it becomes too difficult to know those things- but if it is not possible to sell anything like the kind of output we can achieve, then what are we going to do about it? What are the possibilities that we can deal with the human dimensions, the environmental dimensions, the economic social dimensions of the problems that face us? What are the possibilities that we can come up with means to enable older farmers whose expectation just a few years ago was that their pension would be drawn from the sale of their lands? That is why we New Democrats are determined to maintain the capital gains exemption for the family farm, because it is exactly that. It is a source of the farmer's retirement income so
he can sell his farm and buy a new one or do whatever he will with the money that results from the sale.
What if it is not possible for an older farmer to do that any longer? I met farmers in Manitoba who were desperately anxious about that happening to them. What are we going to do about younger farmers, the people who entered the industry in the last few years, those who were encouraged by professors and faculties of agriculture in various places, such as the University of Manitoba, to do it big, who had bank managers encouraging them to load up with debt and to go with the most advanced kind of agriculture which is incredibly capitalintensive, who then found the Bank of Canada following faithfully behind the Federal Reserve Board of the United States? The Canadian Government allowed the Farm Credit Corporation to do the same thing. The Liberal Government did nothing to reduce the impact on farmers of loading them down with incredible burdens of debt. What are we going to do when these young farmers find themselves faced with a Government allowing the Farm Credit Corporation to lift a moratorium on foreclosures?
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) may do his best to minimize the number of farmers who are affected. My God, what will these young farmers do when they find themselves faced with banks and the Farm Credit Corporations approaching them? I got one sense of the desperation, the change in mentality. Conservative Members of Parliament may still think they know what is going around them in the prairie provinces. Farmers are prepared, in Manitoba at least, to think about the possibility of land banking arrangements of various sorts that they would not have thought of a few years ago because they face the possibility now of farming bank land and not owning the land any longer. In those circumstances what is one going to do about that situation?
These Conservative MPs may still think they know what is going around them in the prairie provinces. What are the possibilities of using various pro agricultural programs which the federal and provincial Governments have? What are the possibilities of taking the crop insurance schemes, the western grain stabilization arrangements, the special grains programs as an instance of what the Government can do as a kind of one-shot special program? The farmers are desperately anxious these days that it might be pretty close to a one shot arrangement. The politics of it will force the Government into doing something similar, I am sure, for the next crop year, but how long will it be before the farmers know what that action is?
What are the possibilities that these various arrangements could be integrated into a plan that would not necessarily cost any more than is presently the case but that could be operated on the basis of a crop insurance and a price assurance scheme?
What are the possibilities that through the offices already existing for crop insurance we add to the activity there and to the arrangements without necessarily adding very much to the cost in order to provide the farmer with protection both against natural disasters, which will occur some of the time, and
April 28, 1987

against the consequences of the kind of price decline we have these days?
Across the West a great deal of thought has been given to these plans. The great grain growing Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, even more than Manitoba, are areas in which Governments and farmers and their organizations are wrestling with these questions. Instead of serving up all the partisan guff we have had last night and this morning, why is the Government not considering the possibility of doing something in the way of long-term planning, if you will? If planning is a dirty word, come up with some other word that assures farmers that their needs will be met.
I want to say in addition that the speech made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), in which he talked about environmental concerns seems to me immediately relevant when I note that the Agricultural Institute of Canada in a presentation it made to all three of the federal caucuses here in Ottawa not very long ago declared the need for an effective strategy to halt and reverse the long-term effects of soil degradation. It recognized that although many current practices are effective in controlling soil degradation, they are frequently uneconomical in the short term. This means that innovative soil and crop management practices combining soil conservation measures with sound economics must be developed, and the performance of these must be monitored beyond the first few years. That surely points to another of the directions in which we should be going.
Surely if the soil itself is in question, the basis for agriculture in the long term is also profoundly in question. What we want to do is to consider the possibility that we might bring our supply down to a level which would match the market in Canada and abroad while at the same time we provide farmers with the financial resources required in order to allow this land to be restored.
I want to suggest seriously the reduction of acreage in order to reduce production with the intention of renewing the soil, taking land that is being cropped year after year with the use of chemicals, the summer following having been abandoned. We should consider ways in which that soil could restore itself over several years perhaps but be out of production in the process of restoring itself. Surely in the present circumstances that is the kind of thing that should be done. We might remember that it was in the "dirty thirties" of the Great Depression and drought experience of the 1930s that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was passed and the Canadian Government began to provide resources for that.

I would suggest that that instance from half a century ago is one that we might well keep in mind today as we recognize what the agrologists are telling us, which is that we need to deal with soil degradation. Surely taking land out of production in order to bring us closer to producing a crop that can meet Canadian needs and find sales abroad, combined with a crop-insurance and a price-assurance scheme, would provide a long-term plan for agriculture. The farmers are desperate for that sort of a plan.
I was struck by the urgency of one of the constituents of the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board who swept the Liberal proposals off the table with the back of his hand. He recognized that the Special Grains Program was something more than a mandate though it had not been as carefully targeted and well carried out as it might have been. He said that we need progressive planning for agriculture. On the basis of what I have heard tonight, we are not getting that planning from Conservative Members. I urge the Government to take up the thoughts that I have put forward, though they are hardly original to me. I have listened to farmers carefully, talked with them about the situation and recognized the good sense of what they were saying.
Let us get together with the provinces. Let us realize that we need a long-term plan for agriculture and let us get it by doing something. The Minister responsible for the Wheat Board is himself a farmer in Manitoba. Surely Members like that have the sense to know that this must be done. I hope he has the clout in Cabinet required to move the Government toward just that kind of future for grain growers, a future that might match the reasonable prosperity farmers in various other sectors have experienced thanks to the supply management programs worked out over the years by marketing boards.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise this morning at three minutes after 5 a.m. to add my words to this debate that has been going on since early last evening. I would first like to comment on some of the speeches that have been made and particularly on the speech made by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme).
The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis is a very experienced parliamentarian and certainly speaks very eloquently in both official languages. I thought he made a very reasoned presentation, pointing out the difficulty facing Government when dealing with this crisis in agriculture. He pointed out that regardless of the Party in power, it is a very large problem and one that will cause a good deal of difficulty for a Government.
I thought the reasoned approach the Hon. Member took and the way he expressed his feelings did him credit as a parliamentarian. That type of debate is more needed more often

April 28, 1987
than debate containing the rhetoric in which we often engage and the interchange back and forth across the Chamber. Tonight, though, I thought that some of the very friendly interchange that went on across the floor added greatly to the debate.
The problem with which we are faced has been highlighted many times, not only in this Chamber but certainly around the country. The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) who just spoke made mention of the fact that he was in southern Manitoba last week in the riding of the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. I myself have had meetings in my riding,
I recently attended a meeting that dealt with a railway problem and the problem of wheat prices and farm financing came up at that time. I heard about the crisis, the extreme interest rates some people are paying and the cost of servicing those debts. I heard of the difficulties that are being caused by the cost price squeeze in which agriculture is involved.
The problem has been highlighted over and over again. It is generally agreed that this problem began in the early 1980s with the high interest rates of the time. Last week, while I was driving to my constituency office in Moose Jaw, I happened to be listening to a CBC radio program on which a group of farmers from Manitoba were discussing their spring planting plans and the financial situations on their farms which varied from small farms to very large farms. As I recall, the largest farm had 2,500 seeded acres. The only farm that was not in extreme financial stress was the small farm because it had absolutely no debt. This farm was owned by a lady and the land was farmed by her son. She made mention of the fact that they were in no difficulty because they had no debt load. The actual cash cost of operation was the only cost they had to bear. They did not have a big mortgage to service.
One of the other farmers had a large mortgage to service and he made mention of the fact that his troubles began in the early 1980s with the high interest rates. That is a story that is very familiar to me. I often hear it from constituents of mine and from other Members who relate stories their constituents have told them. The problem is the inability of producers to service their debts based on today's costs, the cost price squeeze.
Many of us came through the high-interest years. 1 am a farmer and I still operate a grain farm in Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact, I was on my tractor on Monday getting ready to plant the 1987 crop.
Another fallacy that is being promoted by the media, by some agricultural groups and certainly by some opposition Members is that land will lie idle this year. I can assure the House that in the area of Saskatchewan with which I am familiar, the south central portion of Saskatchewan more commonly known as the federal constituency of Moose Jaw, I do not know of one acre that will not be planted this year.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Good land.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
My colleague, the Hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark), has mentioned that it is good land and it is. He knows that very well. I am sure he has some real estate in that area. It is a great part of Saskatchewan and the land there is very, very productive. It is farmed by people who for the most part are second or third-generation farmers whose ancestors came from overseas, as did mine. My grandfather came to Regina in 1901 and farmed in that area. My father farmed there all his life and I am now farming some of the land my father farmed. The land means something to me. I feel great compassion when constituents relate the difficulties they are having servicing their debts.
It is often said that these farmers must make management decisions. That may be so, but they make those decisions after consultation with bank managers, farm credit field men or people who counsel them to buy land. Often they make the decision on the basis of interest rates that were reasonable at the time but later almost doubled. A lot of farm mortgages that I am aware of went from 12 per cent to 18 per cent, 19 per cent and 20 per cent. An operation that was viable at 12 per cent simply is not viable at 20 per cent. There is absolutely no way you can service that debt.
You really cannot say that the producer made the management decision. He made the decision at 12 per cent, but he certainly did not anticipate interest rates getting to the level they did. He was probably told by a bank or some other financial institution that he probably did not have to worry about interest rates getting to that level.
When we talk about this production problem we have, I want to point out that my area of Saskatchewan has very, very productive land. With any kind of break at all in the weather, with some rain, and we do not need a lot if we get it at the right time, we produce abundant yields. We must export about 90 per cent of our production. For us export is a necessity and a very large part of our operation. The European Economic Community has an over-production of only about 20 per cent. That means mountains of butter and grain and beef and all those other commodities, but it is only a 20 per cent problem for them. The Americans also consume much more of their produce than we do. They do not have the same problem. The Americans and the EEC are both determined to bring the other to its knees. They are going to have this shoot-out in the international market-place and we are caught in the middle. We know that we simply do not have the treasury to fight this subsidy battle. There is just no way we can take them on. Our treasury will not stand it.
Having said that, we have to put something in place and we have done several things. The most recent thing we did, I guess, was put in place the special Canadian grains program. We put $1 billion into the farm economy. That money went to grain producers. It was certainly a big help, and that commitment was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). We are not going to abandon agriculture this year. We did not
April 28, 1987

abandon it last year. We changed the western grain stabilization process over the last two years and made record pay-outs.
One of the most important things we have done is to get the major world grain exporters to sit down at the table and discuss the subsidy problem. We had the chairman and two other Members of the British House of Commons Standing Committee on Agriculture here last fall and they appeared before our Standing Committee on Agriculture. They admitted that the subsidy war had to end. Even in Europe they were not going to be able to keep up the subsidy forever. The problem there is that it is part of their social policy. Some members of the EEC are involved in elections each year. If there was even a hint of the farm subsidy program being cut back or dropped, Governments would fall.
We are all political people in this House, I presume. We know that in order to accomplish programs, you must remain in power. That is the number one rule. So, to get them dealing with this problem will take some negotiations at a very high level, and I think it is to the credit of our Prime Minister and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) that these discussions have been initiated. They are dealing with the problem at the highest level in the GATT negotiations.
We have kept up our grain markets. Certainly we have had to meet the competition. That is the reality of the day. Anyone who is an agriculture producer in Canada today must certainly be aware of the uncertainty in the international market-place. I spoke to many of my constituents before the last initial price of grain was announced. They were anticipating a decrease. Everyone felt it had to come. There had to be a decrease in the price to meet world competition today. However, they also stress the need for a special Canadian grains program this year. Certainly I have voiced that concern to the Ministers at our agriculture and national caucuses. Other Members have as well. We are well aware of the necessity to put in place a special Canadian grains program again this year.
We are told that farmers are going to get anywhere from $25,000 to $35,000 this year in direct government subsidies. Granted that is not enough, but think of the stress there would be if we did not put that money in place. We are never going to be able to put out enough money that people would finally say yes, it is enough. However, within the fiscal restraints placed upon us we must look after our agricultural producers. Agriculture is the front line in any country, and having an adequate food supply is necessary.
We also know that the high quality wheat we produce sells very well year in and year out. Through the Canadian Wheat Board we have gained a far larger share of the world market than other countries. At the Agriculture Outlook Conference last year here in Ottawa we had a professor from a U.S. university who mentioned the fact that although the Americans had much more grain, it was of a lower quality and was not selling as well as ours. He said in a tight market situation we are actually gaining a much larger share because of the high quality grain we produce. He commended us for stressing
high quality and remaining competitive by producing that high quality. Both Americans and the EEC are producing varieties of grain which produce more bushels, although of a lower quality, in order to get the maximum subsidy. We have maintained a consistent quality in our hard red wheats and that is something we are going to continue. The high-protein wheat is in great demand. It is selling well and commanding a premium price in a tight world market. We have to continue with that.
We have done several things, one of the really important ones being the lowering of the price of fuel. The average farm in Saskatchewan is 1,000 to 1,200 acres. The reduction we brought about in the price of fuel means that on a 1,200-acre farm the saving amounts to $5,000. That amount in today's tight economy is a lot. That is one of the very real things we have done. The lower interest rates we have today represent a considerable saving to agricultural producers. There is hardly a farmer today who does not have to get an operating loan some time during the year.
People tell me that they never used to have to be concerned with operating loans but that now, because of increasing costs, some time during the year they need to have operating money. They have to go to the bank first thing in the spring and arrange for operating money to plant the crops. The special Canada Grains Program which is coming out, the Western Grain Stabilization Program, and the fact that we are moving grain at record levels this year will assist producers greatly in dealing with those costs.
The Minister responsible for the Wheat Board recently returned from a trip to the Soviet Union. While there he made some excellent contacts with the Russians, resulting in the firming up of some of the long-term sales agreements we have. We have some long-term sales agreements with Brazil as well. We amended the Western Grain Transportation Act. The projected rate would have been $11 per tonne under the formula which was in place when the Liberals were in power. We have reduced that to an average rate of $6 per tonne.
I would like to quote the responses of some farm papers to some of the programs which were announced by the federal Government. The Manitoba Co-operator of May, 1986, commented on the farm package which was announced by the Prime Minister. It said:
It is a far cry from former Liberal Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau who told prairie grain growers: "Why should I sell your wheat?" ... It is also unlikely Trudeau would have vowed to bring up agricultural problems at the economic summit or talked about the need for government action on them.
I believe that represents a very solid endorsement from a newspaper with a rural voice.
Ray Guay, commenting on the rural transition program said:
In short, the program is pure common sense and will help only those who have no choice but to leave the farm.

April 28, 1987
Barry Wilson was quoted in The Western Producer, another rural newspaper.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to begin with a few complimentary words for the Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) who made a very straightforward and sincere speech. He is obviously quite well informed about conditions in the Saskatchewan economy. Two key points which were stressed by the Member deserve to be emphasized.
The first is that the 12 per cent management decision which gets translated to a 20 per cent interest rate situation is an extremely difficult situation for any farmer to face. That is something which the House has not yet sufficiently addressed in order to reverse that situation and make it possible for good farmers who made a correct management decision at the 12 per cent interest level to get back to the point where they can once more make decisions without the huge debt overhang which the change to 20 per cent eventually brought about.
The second point which the Hon. Member made was what he called the international shoot-out which is taking place in the grain trade. There is absolutely no doubt that such a situation exists. However, the Member went on to say that our treasury obviously cannot' afford to respond to that. My comment in response is that this country, this treasury, and this society cannot afford not to respond to that situation. If
we fail to make sufficient response to that international shootout there will be a great many family farms going down the drain, a great many people badly hurt, and our economy, which depends on good solid economic conditions in the farm sector, will be in much worse shape.
This is not only a western problem. I am not trying to suggest that it is not a western problem. Western farmers are facing immense difficulties. However, I want to make it clear that in Essex County in southwestern Ontario farmers are feeling precisely the same kinds of economic stress, the same kinds of pressures, and the same sense of frustration and fear as is being felt throughout western Canada. We conducted a survey of farm families within my constituency, concentrating on farm women in particular. I have 200 or 300 of the survey results in the House this morning in which the responses are consistent.
One family says that they feel very much under pressure and that it is the financial crunch which is causing that sense of stress. When they were asked what issues are of most concern to them as part of the farming community, they responded that they wanted to make a decent living to survive. That answer was given by a farm family from Pointe aux Roches.
Another farm family from Stoney Point responded that the issue of most concern was the price of produce and a need for low interest rates.
The response from Maidstone suggested that the main issue was crop prices, the price of machinery repair, and fair marketing boards. The response from Wheatley asked for adequate income. That family states: "We have sold one-third of our operation just to remain solvent".
A response from Tilbury states that the price of our crops, bank interest rates, keeping input costs down of fertilizers, sprays and fuel were the main issues.
Another response from Wheatley states better prices and lower interest rates. A response from Comber is for better pricing on grains, fairer taxes for farmers, and better farm insurance rates.
Another response from Comber identifies commodity pricing, better marketing of crops and so on as primary issues. I could go on to list a whole set of responses to the surveys, but these responses form a clear picture of serious impending disaster which faces a great part of our farm community in Essex County.
Earlier this year in Essex County we conducted a farm forum to give farmers and farm organizations across the county an opportunity to speak both with our provincial and federal agricultural and trade representatives. There were 16 organizations from the whole breadth of commodity groups speaking to us. These groups included the National Farmers Union, the Essex County Federation of Agriculture and groups of farm women.
April 28, 1987

The message which they placed before us was one of extreme urgency. First, they felt that the deficiency payment which had been made especially by the Government-the so-called $1 billion which the Member who just spoke suggested had done so much to solve the distress in the farm community-had simply not been nearly enough to try to meet the debt pressure, price pressure and cost of production pressure which farms in my community experience.
Soybean producers in particular suggested that the way in which that pay-out had been calculated, crop by crop, had not been sufficiently thought through to be fair to soybean producers, compared to those who were producing other commodities. They also expressed a tremendous concern about what would happen to them, their marketing boards, and their protection from low cost imports from the United States under a potential free trade arrangement with that country.
They stressed that help was very badly needed with respect to the debt crisis and that the Debt Review Boards which had been set up simply did not have enough power to be able to reach real solutions which would put them in a position to survive satisfactorily as effective farmers.
As part of that, they felt that more financing was required for the Farm Credit Corporation. They also stressed to us that it was necessary to have improved marketing structures for farm commodities and thereby gain improved pricing levels for crops across the board in this country.
Finally, they stressed to us that one of the promises which the Conservative Party made in the last campaign, to improve significantly the operation of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act to permit farm loss deductions from off-farm earnings, had not been carried through. They stated that it was crucial that this be done if farmers in Essex County were going to survive. We are facing a serious crisis that affects not only the west but Ontario as well. It is a crisis that is sure to continue.
On Monday, we had a meeting with a group of U.S. Congressmen, primarily from western states, who stressed very strongly to us that the U.S. Farm Bill will not disappear and that the Americans would not back away from the extremely high levels of subsidy they have been providing their farmers.
They stated that from their perspective the shoot-out in the international grain trade will continue and the assistance they are providing to American farmers, which is having such a devastating effect on prices for Canadian farmers, will continue to be a reality.
I do not question the sincerity of many government spokes-people who are trying to develop a response, but so far it has simply been inadequate. As the Ontario Federation of Agriculture told us just yesterday morning, with respect to Debt Review Boards, there are simply not enough enforcement mechanisms to permit the debt review process, first, to establish a clear-cut agreement in the case of a farmer who faces high debt, and second, to turn to the courts if necessary to ensure that some kind of debt relief is achieved for that farmer.
There is simply not enough done with respect to fighting back with financial help to farmers in the face of the tremendous grain war which continues. It has not worked in the past sufficiently; at least that is the very strong message I receive from my farming community, and it is certainly not working so far as the future is concerned in that there has been no commitment made to this point. There has not even been an inference that deficiency payments, which are so crucial for this coming crop year, will again be made available by the Government.
With respect to input costs, we have not seen any action taken seriously to bring down the cost of inputs, especially fertilizers, which for many of the farmers in my community are a key part of their costs.
My farming families also look at free trade not as something that is going to assist them but as something which is a very serious threat to their future livelihood both because of the import competition which they will face from the United States and because they see it as a very serious threat to the future of their marketing board structures where these have been established.
Finally, we have to say that there has been a great deal of talk with respect to the problems of the international grain trade. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) have talked a great deal about it. The Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) has also talked about it a great deal. Despite this, there has not been a single concrete step taken actually to do something about the serious problems of the international grain trade.
The story we heard in Uruguay at the GATT meetings that took place there was that our Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board had not pushed forcefully to try to get immediate and strong changes to improve the situation in the international grain trade. So I have to ask how much of the talk which is taking place is simply for rhetorical purposes and how much is a serious hard hitting effort to try to save Canadian farmers from the crunch they are facing?
When I think of the future, and as the farmers in my community think of the future, we look for action, and action of a definite and immediate character. We look for action first to establish orderly marketing arrangements for a much wider range of commodities. Second, we look for action with respect to giving much more strength and effectiveness to debt review boards. Third, we look for action to cut back the costs of inputs and, fourth, we look for action with respect to trying to reduce the threats which are coming from that international grain shoot-out which is taking place. Those are the challenges which face the Government. I have to say, looking at it from the perspective of my farming community, that the challenges have not been met. They are challenges which have to be met not just for the sake of farmers in Essex County, not just for the sake of farmers across Canada, but for the sake of a sound
