subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be here this morning to take part in this debate. I think I can indicate to the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) that we do take this debate in a serious manner. I think the fact that there are those of us here on the government side representing agriculture in such numbers indicates that we do have a commitment and concern.
I see it is about 16 minutes to six o'clock, which would be 15 minutes to four o'clock in Alberta, and that is about the time a lot of our people are getting up to go out on the land to do a lot of things. I have never gotten up in the House at this time of the day to do anything but I have done some strange things at this time in the morning. I have been in the livestock business and agriculture all of my adult life. I got into the cattle business when I was 18 years old, buying some cattle in the fall and seeing the price of that livestock cut in half with foot and mouth disease in February of the following year.
I listened to the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) indicate the background of his family as they moved west. A lot of us, I think, came from a similar background. My family went west in 1883 with the railway. They took out a homestead and developed a horse ranch. After the country was settled my family turned primarily to livestock production. Horses were needed in those early days as settlers came in to develop western Canada. Everyone needed a team and a saddle horse. We ran a lot of horses then and I still maintain the brand which was used in the early 1880s on our horses. We still run cattle with the same brand.
I have two sons at home who, if things are going well, should be getting ready to continue seeding again this morning. I have two sons who are producing grain and livestock on some of the same land their great great grandfather developed before the turn of the century. 1 think it goes to show that with good animal husbandry and a commitment to agriculture, we can ensure that another 100 years from now other generations will be making use of the same land which is so important to the development of agriculture.
I do agree with some of the comments made by Members of the New Democratic Party on soil degradation. It is important and we should look into it. But I get a little nervous at times when, after agreeing with Members of the NDP, they come back and say something which makes it very difficult to agree.
Speaking at this time of day, one thing I can tell, Mr. Speaker, and I do not know if it is appropriate in the House of Commons, but in the livestock business, a number of things work out better in the early morning. I spent 11 years breeding cattle artificially. I found that cows were more romantic at this time of day. It was easier to pick up a cow that was in heat. The other thing is that if one is moving cattle any distance this is the best time of day to do it. The sun will just be coming up and it will still be cool. The flies will not be too bad.
I found that I could move a little bull a lot further this time of day. I do not know whether it works the same in the House or not. In listening to speeches tonight I think it has become obvious in some cases that that may in fact be true.
I can sympathize with a great many of those people we are talking about tonight, those people who are in agriculture and who are in debt. As I indicated earlier, I have been in it all my life. I could also tell Hon. Members that I have probably been in debt most of that time as well. Most of us in agriculture have never been out of debt. We are either using operating capital or we are expanding. It has been difficult, I know, and I have met a great many of those farmers who will eventually meet with our farm debt review panels. The difficulties they face are as a result of a number of things, certainly the result of what we see happening on the world market.
A great many problems in the country would go away with $6 wheat and $25 oil, problems created outside Canada, but also problems to which the Government has attempted to react in both of these areas. More measures have been taken in these areas. I think people in western Canada will appreciate, knowing the difficulties they are in at the present time, that the Government has tried to do its utmost to bring forward programs which, in some cases, have been emergency programs. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) talked about the drought program in particular. These are programs which respond to matters about which we cannot make forecasts.
Those of us who have been in agriculture, and this is where I probably take exception to some of the comments made by members of the New Democratic Party, realize that there are no guarantees. I guess we are in agriculture to do the best we can to make a living, to try to do what is best in the region in which we live to take advantage of the climate and soil conditions to produce livestock, grain, hogs, whatever it may be, and to make the best use of it. But nobody ever said that there was a guarantee because you wanted to be a farmer.
I think we have seen that in the business sector. People in other areas have come to realize that we do take some risks. It is risk-takers who developed the country. If there had not been people willing to go west in the early 1880s when the country was developed, people willing to take risks without any of the guarantees that we seem to need in place today, then this country would never have developed into the type of land about which we, as Canadians, can be proud.
I am sure that a great many things can go wrong when one is in the agricultural sector. Some 20 years ago this month we had a severe storm in southern Alberta. I am sure some Members will remember the spring of 1967 when feed was airlifted by helicopter into the Foothills. I recall it very vividly. We were almost through calving at that time. The weather was not that cold and we had about a foot and a half of heavy wet snow. The sun was high, as it is at this time of year. In my case the sun happened to come out, which reflected on the snow. I
April 28, 1987

had Hereford cattle. The udders of the cows were sunburned and before the situation was over we had lost 75 cows. Those are the types of things that can happen. Good management could not have made any difference in that situation.
I think a great many people who were hurt, certainly more than I was at the time, felt it was part of the risk one takes in being in the real world of business. I do not think anyone ran to Government for help. They tried to do the best they could. But we are in a different situation now. Certainly, much of it is caused by the financial crisis in which we have found ourselves. Almost all of us in agriculture are still paying off the debt from the times when interest rates were as high as 23 per cent and 24 per cent. I had cattle in the feedlot. A feed bill which had to be paid regardless of the interest rate came in every month. I am still paying that debt, as I am sure many people are.
The ones who are having the difficulty, and I have met with them as I said earlier, are a great many young farmers who have come into my constituency office. It is the young farmers who got into agriculture in the late 1970s who have been hurt. Other established farmers, probably through good management, saw their way clear to be able to expand and did go out and use money that was expensive at the time to buy land that was extremely expensive. I think Hon. Members will realize that the price of land from Valuation Day went up dramatically from 1971. In some cases it went up five and six times as much as it had been when we valued that land for tax purposes in 1971. If there was someone here to recall it from the Official Opposition they would remember what happened when capital gains came in. Capital gains did a number of things. I can tell Hon. Members that it did a number on agriculture. What it did was help to escalate the price of land.
When credit was relatively easy to obtain and a piece of land came up for sale, the person selling the land, after consulting with his accountant, felt that whatever he needed out of it he needed after the capital gains tax was paid. So that was added on. It was added on again and again and again. The land in parts of southern Alberta that was valued at $12,000 a quarter, by the late 1970s, by 1978, was hitting around $40,000 and peaked at about $75,000 to $80,000. That was about the top. It is on its way back down now. At that price, with high interest rates, there is nothing that one can produce in agriculture that would sustain it. I am surprised that the situation went on for as long as it did before we reached a point of collapse. I suppose some people who are in this serious financial situation could have survived, but a great many of them were very badly hurt.
I think that those people who have complained about the $500,000 capital gains exemption should sit and listen to some of the people who tried to sell out prior to the exemption being put in place. There were elderly people who wanted to sell out and transfer their land to the next generation. However, because of taxes, because of some of the debt load they were carrying, there was very little left by the time they liquidated the farm and paid off the debt that most farms carry, as well
as the capital gains. So it certainly had an effect on agriculture.
The fact is that the capital gains exemption has been put in place for all Canadians. It should be an incentive to Canadians to work to invest. There is something about having initiative. I do not think initiative is a dirty word on this side of the House. I do not think guts or backbone are, either. I think it takes people who are willing to get out and work. If one does and if one is successful then probably one should have the right to enjoy some of the rewards of that success.
I think those are the things to which Canadians can look forward. We have gone through numerous programs, and a great many other Members have commented on the programs that the Government has put in place. I have listened to members of the Opposition who have criticized most of the areas in which we brought in programs.
I went to the presentation that was made in the case of the Liberals, something called "Directions for the West". It was put out by the Liberal western caucus. I believe there were two Members of the Commons and about 10 or 11 from the other place who went out and held a series of hearings and came up with a long list. It is a good page long and the last page summarizes some of the problems. I think we are all aware of these problems. Some of the recommendations have already been commented upon. I would hope that they would not bring forward a program similar to the LIFT program they put in place in 1971, the full name of that program being Lower Inventory For Tomorrow.
I had a permit book at that time, and still do. Some aerial photographs were taken of my land, and I received a letter from Winnipeg stating that my permit book did not match with the expert analysis done as a result of the aerial photographs that were taken. I was asked to make the necessary corrections in my permit book. They had inadvertently included some of my neighbour's land and some land that had been used to raise horses.
That program was brought in as the answer to some problems that existed at that time. Certainly, it created additional problems. It did not do anything for the agricultural sector-other than perhaps leading to a change of Ministers.
The Liberal policy paper talks about ensuring that "returns from grain production in the new crop year will at least equal the level of the 1986-87 crop year".
It asks that we make initial payments at some level that has nothing whatsoever to do with the market-place, and nothing to do with reality, thus depriving those in agriculture of some indication of the direction in which things are going. We need only look to Europe to realize the problems that can result from such an approach.
If you have $6 a bushel wheat, $7 a bushel wheat, $8 a bushel wheat, people are going to grow it until it literally buries them-and that is exactly what has happened.

April 28, 1987
There seems to be a real problem in having the public understand what we are talking about when we speak of initial payments, final payments, stabilization payments, and deficiency payments. The public does not seem to realize that, in most cases, these payments represent the moneys due to the farmers for the products sold.
Certainly, the market price has to be there to indicate the reality of the market. Looking back to last year and what happened to barley, of the $203 million deficit that we saw, $179 million was attributable to the problems in marketing barley.
That meant that livestock producers in Canada were paying 75 cents a bushel more to use Canadian barley to feed Canadian livestock in Canada than we were selling that barley for on world markets.
This is the type of thing that we have to be very careful of. It is fortunate that the livestock situation turned around. Elad our livestock producers been losing money in addition to paying that premium for barley, we would have heard a lot more from that sector.
The Liberal policy paper also speaks of maintaining the current freeze on grain freight rates charged to farmers.
Had we continued with the Liberal structure, those rates would now be somewhere around $11 a tonne.
Another proposal is to reduce farm input costs "through methods that include measures to deal with high chemical prices". What did the Liberals do in this regard? They switched to the metric system of measurement for chemical containers, with the result that we never knew the precise price or rate of application.
The last of the five proposals is as follows:
-in view of the worsening farm debt crisis, to provide greater assistance to preserve the family farm as the primary means of production and a vital part of rural Canadian life.
These are the recommendations flowing from the Liberal task force on the western Canadian economy. Those constitute the total sum and substance of what came out of that tour across western Canada.
Let me quote again from the Winnipeg Free Press of April 11, 1987, as follows:
The 17-page report is an empty document offering ringing declarations of discredited party policy, outright distortions of economic reality and not a single firm proposal which would make any significant difference to the economy of Western Canada.
The Liberal Party was in power for a great many years and had the opportunity to bring in all kinds of programs, and yet its members rise in this Chamber and criticize whatever this Government brings forward.
As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) indicated earlier in this debate, this Government, in the last two and one half years, has brought in more programs for the agricultural sector than any past Government.
Let me now turn to the New Democratic Party. I have here a resolution reference, a document published last fall outlining a number of resolutions that that Party has in place-and I gather that they are current today. Under the subtitle "The Process of Planning" we have an omnibus resolution on the future of the family farm, recommending the "establishment of industrial plants to be co-operatively or publicly owned for the processing of food and the manufacture of farm supply items in the region of production".
The resolution goes on to say:
This industrialization in rural Canada would provide new employment and enable those who migrate out of farming to find alternative jobs within the region.
This Government has come up with the Rural Transition Program. It is not something that is intended to move people out of agriculture; rather, it is intended to give those in our agricultural sector the same opportunities that are taken for granted by people in other sectors of the Canadian economy. That is its only purpose.
Certainly, with funding of $46 million, it is not a rich enough program to cause people to flock out of agriculture. But for those who do-and there will always be people getting out of agriculture-the program is there to provide some assistance.
And why shouldn't the self-employed in agriculture have the same benefits that others in this country have taken for granted for years?
I see that my time is drawing to a close, Mr. Speaker. In the remaining time, I should like to highlight one or two other items arising from the resolutions of the New Democratic Party. Under the same subtitle, we have the following:
It might be necessary as well to take into public ownership some existing farm supply retail operations, farm machinery assembly plants, meat-packing and canneries.
1 can assure Hon. Members right now that as long as I am in the livestock business, I will be very reluctant to ever take a product that I have produced to a government-operated packing plant.
The same resolution goes on to recommend limits on farm sizes. It is the policy of the New Democratic Party to establish a public commission to determine a formula for a farm unit size on a unit basis.

April 28, 1987

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I can say that I am happy about debating at this hour of the day, though I must commend the Minister for his presence throughout this long debate. I hope that his presence means that this Government will take further action in alleviating the problems facing the agricultural sector.
Obviously, the Government does deserve some credit for the increased support that has been forthcoming for the agricultural sector, and particularly for the grain farmers of western Canada.
However, as one considers the over-all situation, what stands out is the crisis in the farming sector of western Canada. While there has been help, it has not been sufficient or adequate to give farmers the security they need in order to continue their struggle to survive and to continue their efforts at planting and producing crops.
I just wanted to ensure that I put forward at least my understanding of what is going on. To put it quite simply, while farmers are receiving some increased aid, what they need at the moment is to know whether or not they will be receiving a deficiency payment for the crop they will seed this spring. I know that my colleague will correct me if I am wrong, given that he is a farmer. Farmers need to know that because they need to know how their books will balance at harvest time. If everything goes well-and of course the weather is beyond their control-and they have a good harvest, they need to know whether they will make a profit on it or whether they will suffer a loss. Farmers need to know whether they will have incomes as a result of their efforts so that they can decide whether or not to seed.
Of course it is not a viable alternative to say that given the fall in prices the odds are that they will lose money on their crops. Over the last few years farmers have been struggling to
keep their operations going. They need an assured income so that they can continue to hang in.
We all know-and I am sure farmers know it better than any of us-the international context in which grain farming in western Canada exists today. The fact is that there is a trade war between American farmers and their Government and European farmers and their Governments. These powerful and large Governments are pouring billions of dollars in subsidies into their farming sectors which put at risk our entire grain industry. One of the first aspects of the grain trade at which we must look is the whole question of international trade. The Government has undertaken an initiative in what they call free trade. It has sought to negotiate an agreement with the United States. While Mr. Reisman is meeting with Mr. Murphy, what is going on in reality is that the American Government is grossly oversubsidizing its grain industry, which is threatening the very existence of Canadian grain farming. The American Government is threatening the way of life in western Canada, and the Government blindly proceeds with its trade initiatives and says that it will negotiate a trade agreement with its American friends.
Given the present action of the Americans with regard to grain and what it is doing to the grain sector in western Canada, with friends like that, who needs enemies? The Government is blithely going ahead and promising prosperity as a result of a trade agreement with the United States.
If we were to have some confidence in the capacity of the Government to address vital issues affecting Canadians, such as the whole question of international trade, particularly in grain, and therefore the survival of grain farming and the western Canadian economy, we would want to see some results in terms of the present actions of the Government.

In fact, it leaves us with a sense of worry, because it looks as if the Government believed in the tooth fairy, that if it could only sign an agreement with the Americans everything would be okay. Obviously, in the present case we are not just talking about a market, we are talking about the American and the European Governments that have intervened in the grain market and have subsidized their farmers. We have an international trade war going on and that is why our farmers are suffering.
When farmers are suffering so greatly, it is time for the Government to step in and take action. The individual farmer cannot defend himself or herself in the present circumstance. We do need our elected institutions to provide the basic security that farmers need in order to continue to survive. In a couple of years when this crisis is resolved we should be sure that we have farmers who will be there to grow the grain and take advantage of the international markets, not having been driven out of farming because the Government failed to act and failed to get the message that the whole way of life in western Canada is threatened. It is impossible for farmers to face the present circumstances without solid action by the Government. We wanted this debate so we could get across to the Government that while its increased support for western agriculture is appreciated, the Government has to take another step.
The Government needs now to tell western farmers that they will have a deficiency payment for the present crop to be seeded now so that farmers know, when it comes time to
harvest, that they will make money on the crop. We need that additional security. We in Canada in western liberal democracies have used the Government ever since the 1930s, even since the election of Theodore Roosevelt in the United States, to provide a measure of security for citizens. We would not say to people, "If you haven't got a job or if you don't have unemployment insurance, then we won't give you any social security to enable you to eat". We are not willing to be that harsh to allow the whole of people's existence to depend upon the market. In the same manner in terms of agriculture we need to say that it is the function of Government to provide at least a minimum basis of security.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating that my time is coming to a close. It is a legitimate function of Government to provide a base of security for all Canadians, for western Canadians, for western Canadian farmers, for the grain farmers, and now is the time to do it. Now is the time when the whole way of life in western Canada is under threat. While the Government deserves credit for the action taken so far, it needs to take another step and provide that minimum of security, and it needs to do it now.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin with a personal observation. As I sat here throughout the night, I thought back to my nomination night. Some of my friends in the House were there then. I remember making my acceptance speech at 1 a.m. and thinking that was really quite an incredible time of night to be making such a speech. I see it it is now 6.30 a.m., dawn has arrived in Ottawa, and as others have indicated, the farmers will soon be on the land in the Prairies if indeed they have not worked all night like some of us have.
I also want to note with approval that throughout the night we have been honoured with the continuing presence of several cabinet Ministers. My time here is not all that extensive. It is only about three and a half years now. However, I remember other all-night debates and I do not remember Cabinet Ministers being present.
During the course of this evening we have seen the continuing presence of the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski). I hope I have not forgotten anyone. As well, we have had many of our caucus here during the night. Perhaps it is only coincidental but many of those are either farmers or have a continuing interest in agriculture. Let me say at the beginning that I have never pretended to be a farmer as such, but I am proud to say that I grew up on a farm and I continue to own farmland. I think I recognize, therefore, the importance of this debate on the issues before us.
I also want to make it clear that we on the government side recognize the gravity of the problem which exists in the grain and oilseed industry in western Canada. We have recognized

April 28, 1987
and continue to recognize those problems. The proof of that recognition lies in our record to date and the fact that we readily participate in a debate such as this. I for one will agree that the NDP are sincere in sharing that concern as well. I must say that I am disappointed, however, that throughout the last four and a half hours only two Parties have been represented in the House, to the best of my recollection. I think that is unfortunate because it suggests there is not as much interest as there should be.
The Hon. Member who just spoke made reference to two or three points which I would like to refer to. He made reference to the freer trade talks, if I remember correctly, and did so in a critical fashion. 1 have just had the opportunity to look at the Western Producer dated April 23, 1987, and I thought Members might be interested in a story contained therein. The headline reads: "Free trade would help Manitoba hog industry". In light of the fact that both the Hon. Member who just spoke and myself are from the Province of Manitoba I think this is a particularly interesting story.
The story says that an increase in exports is a key to a healthy hog industry. William Boggs, Chairman of the Manitoba Hog Producers' Marketing Board, said Manitoba must export 70 per cent of its present pork production. In order for the industry to grow, export markets must be developed further. That implies freer if not free trade. The U.S. market in particular is important to the province's hog producers. Boggs said that three-quarters of its exports go to the U.S. He said we must keep a door open to U.S. trade. We in Canada must be constantly on top of potential Canada-U.S. trade road-blocks and we must be in a position to remove or, better yet, prevent their formation.
Later on in the same story he said in spite of the fact that some analysts predict gloomy hog prices toward the end of this year, he was more optimistic and still looked for a very positive market in 1987. That forecast is based on the fact that the hog kill in the U.S. is 50,000 head short of what it was a year ago. Hamburger from the dairy herd buy-out will soon be moved off the market and the Americans predict an 8 per cent to 10 per cent decrease in slaughter cattle for later this fall, and that the amount of red meat in cold storage in the U.S., particularly pork, is the lowest it has ever been.
What that story suggests very clearly is the very significant importance of the freer trade talks to at least Manitoba's hog industry. I think you will find if you look at the future of this industry in other parts of the country there are benefits to be derived. I say that because the Party which has proposed the motion this evening has consistently downplayed, criticized and ridiculed the significance of the freer trade talks. I think we on this side have perhaps done ourselves a disservice by not adequately rebuking their criticisms to this point in time.
With respect to the problem which does exist in Canadian agriculture today, there are two or three points which have been made earlier this evening but it is important to reiterate them.
First, as you know, the high interest rates of the 1970s had a devastating impact on a certain group of farmers. That group of farmers are those in their thirties and forties who, through no fault of their own, began farming at a time when inflation was beginning to occur and interest rates were beginning to rise. As a result that group found itself with a very heavy debt load. During the days of rising inflation the significance of that debt load was not as apparent as it would subsequently become.
Unfortunately, in the 1980s a combination of that debt load, deflation, and the trade war currently under way between the EEC and the U.S., put a generation of farmers in a very vulnerable position. For me this was a very tragic situation and one which the Government must continue to address. 1 stress that because I think our record to date is an excellent one, particularly bearing in mind the legacy we inherited some two and a half years ago.
When I speak of that legacy I am referring of course to the size of the national debt and what it means with respect to interest rates. As you know, this Government must spend somewhere around $28 billion or $29 billion on interest alone to service the national debt. That is an incredible sum of money which, if it were available to us, would give us a great deal of latitude to deal with problems, whether they be in agriculture, the forest or fishing industry, or wherever. We do not have that flexibility today, to a large degree because of the debt we inherited from our predecessors.
As to our own particular record, I think there are several points which need to be stressed. The most important thing I want to say at the outset is that I for one am particularly pleased that the Canadian agricultural community is served by two particularly distinguished Ministers. As you may know, I have been a teacher most of my life. I have had a strong interest in Canadian history and I do not recall anywhere in Canadian history, at least in the last 30 years, when Canada has been as well served, and Canadian agriculture has been as well served, as it presently is by the Minister of Agriculture. He is very sensitive to the needs of the community.

It is for

Let me just make a couple of comments about two of the points discussed here in the course of the evening, the question of initial prices and the FCC moratorium. First with respect to the moratorium, it was very clear when that was put in place its purpose was to provide time for certain programs to be developed. The moratorium was never perceived to be, by any spokesman on this side of the House at least, a solution in itself.
Since that time two programs in particular have been developed which have reference for the farmers who would be affected by severe economic conditions. I think particularly of the Farm Debt Review Boards which are now in place in each of the provinces. My understanding is that many of the initial start-up problems have been alleviated. When the chairman of that group appeared recently before the Standing Committee on Agriculture he spoke with confidence about their responsibilities and the future.
I would like to address a few remarks, if I may, to the Rural Transition Program because I think it has been very unfairly criticized by some politicians, some farm organizations and, unfortunately, by the media as well. I happened to be at the press conference where this program was announced. One of the things which disturbed me at that time was that, seemingly out of the woodwork, there arrived at that press conference of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) a number of journalists whom I never see at meetings of the Committee on Agriculture.
Although there are some 350 journalists who work on the Hill, I regret that there are only four or five who, with any consistency, appear at meetings of the Committee on Agriculture. The unfortunate significance of that is that when a major event comes along which does attract the attention of the Gallery at large, it seems to me that many of them come to their responsibilities with an inadequate background which is often reflected in their reporting.
The Rural Transition Program has been badly maligned by its critics. I happen to believe it is long overdue and am very pleased that it is now in place and is able to provide a service to those who wish to participate in it. It provides, albeit perhaps in an inadequate way, the types of opportunities for retraining and financial assistance for relocation if desired which have long been available to other sectors of the economy but have historically been denied to the agricultural community.
Having been involved in education most of my life, I have been aware that many young people have received assistance to achieve upgrading. Older people in urban communities who wish to go back to school have had programs available to them
but these types of programs have consistently and tragically never been available to the farm community. In addition, it has been denied the opportunity of participating in programs such as unemployment insurance.
Transition from rural areas to urban areas is not a new phenomenon. However, when it occurred in the past the people who were compelled to or chose to make that transition, for whatever reason, were denied the basic economic and counselling support programs which were often available to their urban neighbours.
The Rural Transition Program is now providing those services in a small way. I am pleased that in the Province of Manitoba, for example, a major part of this program is being provided by a research team and support program in the City of Brandon. Through fairly constant consultation with them I know that both the dollars and the counselling which is now being provided to the rural community, which was not available previously, are much appreciated and, quite frankly, much needed.
I have heard Members opposite suggest that this program is somehow or other designed to either persuade or force people to move off the land. Nothing could be more ridiculous than that assertion because it implies that you could persuade someone to leave the land for approximately $6,000 per year, which is the type of support of which we are speaking. It is, quite frankly, an insult to the Canadian farming community to imply that they would make decisions about this issue based upon that rather meagre sum of money.
People who are leaving agriculture today deserve the kind of support which the Rural Transition Program is trying to provide. I dare say that we should be doing more to benefit them. For example, one of my criticisms of that program is that it will provide assistance for only one year. As you know, Mr. Speaker, someone who wishes to enter into a university program of more than one year is not eligible to participate in the Rural Transition Program and I think that weakness should be remedied. Another deficiency in the program, as I understand it, is that they cannot participate in part-time programs. I think that is also something which the Government should address.
However, the concept is extremely valuable and has been long overdue. I feel nothing but frustration and anger with regard to those who deliberately misrepresent that program to the public because, in so doing, they are adding to the aggravation felt by those who are compelled to participate in it because it is implying that they are somehow being bought off. As I say, Mr. Speaker, that is both inaccurate and insulting.
It is important to look to the future and I see some signs for positive encouragement. Speaking as an individual Member of Parliament rather than on behalf of the Government per se, I believe that the Government will have to continue to provide assistance in the future comparable to that which it has provided in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I want to echo the sentiments expressed by my hon. friends.
I want to participate in this debate because I am very concerned about the situation facing western agriculture and eastern agriculture not only for the crop year into which we are entering but for the future as well.
This debate was triggered by the Government's decision to lift the moratorium on the FCC loans. We are talking about whether agriculture in western Canada has a future and whether the Government's record will be one of a Government that turned its back on western Canadian agriculture after making many promises when in opposition, and of a government which effectively brought on a situation where western Canadian agriculture was cut to half or one-third of its traditional place in the Canadian economy.
Under current circumstances, the moratorium being lifted on Farm Credit loans is not just a direct threat to some 7,000 farmers who are currently behind in their payments and may now find themselves being foreclosed by the FCC, it is also a signal to every supplier, bank and financial institution that is involved in western agriculture that the Government has lost faith in western farmers.
The Government, through the Farm Credit Corporation, has lost faith and since the FCC is effectively the lead lender in this particular area, the message will be absorbed and acted upon by banks and other financial institutions.
I suspect that as early as yesterday morning when the announcement was made public in the press, people in the boardrooms, the headquarters of Canada's major banks and in the financial institutions in New York, London and Tokyo were asking about the situation with lending to Canada's western agriculture now that it appears the Government is lifting a moratorium that was initially imposed to protect farmers in September, 1985.
The financial institutions will examine the actions of the Government over the succeeding period of some 18 months to
April 28, 1987

see that the Government did make a certain commitment for a while. It has taken initiatives in terms of international trade, through meetings with other countries that are involved. These financial institutions will also note that the Government came through with the Special Canadian Grains Program for the 1986 crop year, albeit possibly because of the Government's hopes of keeping Saskatchewan as a Conservative province at the time of its provincial election.

Let me tell Hon. Members from western Canada that the problems in agriculture are not confined to western Canada. They are also being experienced in eastern Canada.
London, Ontario is the heart of the western Ontario farming belt. I want to tell Hon. Members that land that was being rented for $100 an acre a few years ago is now going begging because farmers cannot afford to farm it themselves and cannot find anyone else to farm it.
I talked to a friend who was farming 450 acres five years ago in the area of London. She is now only farming 85 acres. The reason that she is essentially going into retirement is that she cannot make a dollar from the farm. She pointed out that the input costs have continued to rise, as anyone will know, but that the prices she fetches for her produce goes down. Last year she had a white bean crop which almost failed totally because, after an excellent summer, weather conditions turned against her.
I cite these facts to indicate to Hon. Members opposite that one can be an urban Member, as I am, and still have a good idea of the situation facing farmers in the farm economy. I suggest to Hon. Members from western Canada who were barracking a minute ago that I believe the crisis in western agriculture is a crisis that affects all Canadians, whether they be represented by urban members or rural members. If they try to wrap themselves in the flag and suggest that only they alone are qualified to talk about this issue, they are talking hooey. If they try to wrap themselves in the flag and say that they alone are qualified to talk about this particular issue, then they are talking hooey.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member should know. He would find it on his farm if he looked for it.
We are talking about a very serious situation, and as the finance spokesperson for the New Democratic Party I have been pointing out that we are facing a situation of unreasonable and unjustifiable world competition, and the choice we face in Canada is whether we are prepared to weather this out with our western farmers or whether we are going to have a Government which decides to abandon the western farmers and just simply throw them out to the free market hoping that somehow some will survive. The Farm Credit Corporation figures would indicate those farmers will not survive under those circumstances.

April 28, 1987
The transition program mentioned by the Hon. Member who just spoke is certainly not going to bring them out of that particular situation. It will affect too few. We have to make a choice, and this is what my Leader was saying yesterday when he was asking questions of the Government on this particular issue. Are we as a country prepared to seek to maintain western agriculture during this period of transition or is the Government intent on imposing a short, bitter and devastating shock of readjustment on western farmers which, in the next year and a half, could easily mean 10,000 to 20,000 western farmers forced out of business, hundreds of thousands, if not millions of acres of prairie grain producing land, the most efficient grain producing land in the world, forced into idleness and in many cases forced back into prairie with no agricultural uses at all? These are the choices we are talking about.
I am very concerned as well because I represent urban workers, many working for the Government of Canada and working in high tech industries which serve rural as well as urban uses. It is quite obvious, as my friend the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) indicated as well, that urban workers and the urban economy in Canada are also affected by the crisis which is now taking place in rural Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize how serious the problem is now that the Government has decided to lift the moratorium on FCC foreclosures. The crises affects not only western wheat growers, but also farmers in eastern Canada. The figures of the FCC show that about 8 per cent of Canadian farmers are going through very hard times and are probably bankrupt. In addition, 14 per cent of farmers, or about 42,000, are having serious financial difficulties. As a whole, nearly one third of our farmers are now affected.
In addition, it is quite clear that, while one third of the farmers are directly affected by the financial crisis, the picture is not that good for the rest of them either. In western Canada, farm income will be substantially lower because of the announcement that decrease the prices paid under the Government program will go down by 18 percent, after a 20 per cent decrease last year. The crisis is affecting everyone. This means that even the farmers who are still financially healthy, who have resources, who have finished paying for their land and, who do not have large mortgages or bank loans to reimburse have seen their incomes and profits go down.
As I have just noted in English, the situation in eastern Canada is also difficult. Last weekend, I was in London, Ontario, where I spent some time with a farming friend who worked about 500 acres some five years ago. She told me that people used to pay $100 an acre to lease farmland, but that the land-owners in her region of rich farmlands in south-western Ontario cannot find any farmers willing to lease their land. They have to let it to the farmers free to ensure that someone will work the land and keep it from deteriorating. My friend, who used to work 500 acres, now works only 85. She decided
to reduce her acreage because the rest was not bringing in any profits. The profitability of agriculture is therefore affected in both eastern and western Canada.
The situation in Western Canada is particularly serious. The moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures has just been lifted. This gives a message not only to the farmers who are directly affected, but also to all banking institutions. It is now time to seed for the 1987 crop year. All the farmers who need bank credit to begin their activities in the spring will therefore be affected. All the farms and all the farmers with mortgages or bank loans will be affected because the banks will have to reassess farm credit, especially in western Canada. The banks will consider the fact that the Government has lifted the moratorium and will see in this a very clear message, namely that the Government has decided not to continue to support the farmers until the subsidy war with the United States and the Common Market has been resolved. It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that the agricultural crisis began with the decision of the Common Market to subsidize farming and the decision of the American Government to respond by subsidizing American farmers instead of letting them face this difficult situation by themselves, going as far as subsidizing wheat sales to what President Reagan called the evil empire, the Soviet Union. What can we, in Canada, do in such a case?
On a point of order, I object to the comment of the Hon. Member. I believe that such a comment is out of order and should be withdrawn.

The moratorium was placed on the Farm Credit Corporation because it was given a mandate by the previous Government, which came out of the legislation, and it became a lender of last resort. A great many farmers, because of the disastrous interest rate policies of the previous administration, were caught in the credit squeeze that went on. Some of them got into tight situations.
I want to tell the Hon. Member that I have farmers in my riding and that I have worked with the Farm Credit Corporation. I have always found the corporation to be very helpful. I have always found when I went to the people there with a farmer who was having a problem, and we had to do some work on a loan to redo it, to stretch out the payments, or to refinance it in some way, that they were always there front and centre ready to do it.
The need to put a moratorium on the Farm Credit Corporation was as a result of the legislation under which the Farm Credit Corporation was operating. We brought about the moratorium so that we could put in place farm debt review
boards to assist farmers and so that we could also put in place a transition program to assist farmers. These were the measures which had to be taken so that farmers who were experiencing financial difficulty could sit down and so that we could work with them to help them through a crisis situation.
Let us look at what is happening now that we have the farm debt review boards working, and working well, and now that we have the transition program working, and working well. We had farmers, instead of making the effort, some of them, who were quite able to pay their loans and keep current with the Farm Credit Corporation. But all they did was look over down the road and say: "There is not much need for me to keep myself current because there is a moratorium". What were the banks saying? The banks were saying to farmers in my area: "We are going to cut your loan off because you can now go to the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow because they have a moratorium". That is the type of situation and climate we would have been creating if we had carried the moratorium on any further. The moratorium served its purpose. It allowed us the time to do what we wanted to do. We will now be able to work with those farmers in a sensible way.
I also smiled to myself when I listened to a number of Members of Parliament, particularly from the NDP, since Liberal Members of Parliament were not here past midnight. I have not seen anyone in their benches all night long. There were perhaps three speakers from the Party during the whole debate. I had to smile because about every second Member who stood up talked about the $1 billion or the 5.30 phone call that Premier Grant Devine made to Ottawa seeking help for farmers. I think they missed a very significant point. The very significant point about Grant Devine phoning Ottawa was that there was somebody here in Ottawa to take the call. There was somebody here in Ottawa to take the call and to say: "Yes, we understand that you have a problem; we understand the Province of Manitoba has a problem, and we will do something about it."

speechtext:
The significant thing to bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, is that there was somebody in Ottawa who would answer a call from Grant Devine.
Can you imagine Allan Blakeney calling Pierre Trudeau and asking for some assistance for the agricultural sector in Saskatchewan? Pierre Trudeau's response would probably have been: "Why should I bother helping you? Why should I sell your wheat?"
This is the kind of thing we are talking about.
Can you imagine Peter Lougheed telephoning Ottawa requesting help for the farmers of Alberta?
The whole point is, there is now someone in Ottawa who is there to answer the telephone call when it comes and respond-and I think that is important.
April 28, 1987

We now have a Prime Minister in Ottawa who responds to the concerns of western Canada, and he has made that clear on a number of occasions. Ele made that clear with his actions on the National Energy Program; he has made that clear through the Prince Albert Declaration.
We on this side of the House do not take the position that there are no problems in the agricultural sector. We do not say that we have all of the answers. What we do say is that we have a Government in Ottawa which is going to respond to the regions, and in fact it has responded in an unprecedented way to date.
Without taking into consideration interest rates, we know that farm income in 1987 will surpass the farm income in 1986. We know today that farm incomes for 1987 for grain and oil seeds will exceed farm incomes in 1986.
Given current commodity prices and the situation that exists between the EEC and the U. S., one should consider that a tremendous accomplishment of this Government.
Let's talk about some of the reactions to the Government's record on agriculture.
Prime Minister Mulroney, in April of 1986, announced a farm package. Alex Binkley, as reported in Manitoba Cooperator of May 8, 1986, had this to say about that farm package:
It is a far cry from former Liberal Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, who told Prairie Grain growers: "Why should I sell your wheat?" -It is also unlikely Trudeau would have vowed to bring up agricultural problems at the Economic Summit, or talk about the need for government action on them.
Next we have Barry Wilson of The Western Producer, who had the following to say:
It-marked the first time in at least six years that a Prime Minister devoted a press conference primarily to agricultural issues.
Let's see what they had to say about the Rural Transition Program. Ray Guay of the Saskatoon Star Phoenix, on September 12, 1986, had the following to say:
In short, the program is pure common sense and will help only those who have no choice but to leave the farm.
Gren Winslow, of the Cattlemen Magazine, in August of 1986, had the following to say on the Farm Debt Review Act:
A good idea has come out of Ottawa which deserves support. It's the Farm Debt Review Act. It has merit, not for what it does, but for what it does not do-it does not impose mandatory solutions on negotiations between farmers in financial trouble and their creditors.
These publications, Mr. Speaker, are organs of the farm communities. These are the people who speak for the farmers of western Canada.
On December 4, 1986, we had an editorial in the Manitoba Co-operator on the Western Grain Stabilization Act amendments and the 1986 final payment. I quote from that editorial:
Just when government officials must wonder if they can ever do anything that will please a restless or seemingly unappreciative agricultural community and farm press, along comes an action that warrants curtain call after curtain call. The recent payout from the much-improved Western Grain Stabilization Program is such an action.
That is the view of the Manitoba Co-operative, a publication that has not always been kind to this Government and the actions of this Government.
What has been said about the Special Canadian Grains Program? I quote from the Regina Leader Post of December 10, 1986, as follows:
Farm leaders from across the country have praised the federal Government's decision to provide farmers with $1 billion to offset the impact of an international grain war.
Avery Sahl, First Vice-President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, said: Tm pleased there are no strings attached to the money. It is cash and not a loan and that is good news.'
As I said, that was the view of the Regina Leader Post, as expressed on December 10, 1986.
And what did the Opposition do with respect to this announcement? They spent the time between the Prime Minister's pledge of $1 billion and the Government's delivery of the program unnecessarily scaring farmers.
On countless occasions, thoughtless Members opposite stood in this House and asked if this $1 billion was new money, a loan, or what.
Time and time again the Leader of the New Democratic Party stood in this House and asked: "Is it new money?"
All that the Members opposite were doing through that tactic was to add to the fear and uncertainty on the part of the farming communities of this country.
Let's look at some of the things the New Democratic Party, the Party of the socialists, was perpetrating on the Canadian people.
My colleague from Lethbridge, earlier in this debate-and I think it was around two o'clock this morning-made a couple of points that I should like to reiterate at this point.
One point he made was that traditionally we did not have to worry about the socialists; that we always looked upon them as the "kooky" left. But now that they are up in the polls, they are beginning to think that they can smell substantial successes in an election-and God forbid that they ever form a federal Government.
In the light of the standing of the New Democratic Party in the polls, I think we should make perfectly clear to the Canadian people exactly what it is that these socialists, masquerading as the New Democratic Party, stand for.
The New Democratic Party consider convention and NDP Federal Council resolutions to be binding. Over the years, they have developed an extensive list of resolutions, covering everything from the nationalization of the meat packing industry to legalized prostitution.
And what are some of those resolutions? Last fall, Mr. Speaker, the NDP published a consolidation of those resolutions in a publication entitled Resolutions Reference-and I want to thank my hon. friends for doing that. We are now

April 28, 1987
going to be able to use this published document to show the socialists for what they are.
I have a copy of this publication, and I suggest that all Members of Parliament and all Canadians obtain a copy. They will find it to be an enlightening document.
For those who are seriously thinking of embracing the socialist horde known as the New Democratic Party, this publication should be mandatory reading.
As the Foreword to the book states, this book contains those resolutions passed by New Democrats since 1961 which are still current today, that is, resolutions which have not been overtaken by events or superseded by subsequent resolutions.
Let's look at some of these resolutions. While there are many of them, I want to highlight but a few.
We have a resolution on exchange controls. We all know what exchange controls are.
The NDP realizes that there would be a massive flight of capital from Canada if they were ever elected.
As such, the NDP has a resolution which is still current today. It calls for the NDP to use exchange controls to prevent the flight of capital. What a difference that would be. We have created nearly one million jobs since taking office two years ago because of the attraction Canada has become for investment.
We are a trading nation. We are an international nation. We need capital to develop our resources. We have attracted unprecedented numbers over the last few years and have created jobs. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what would happen if the socialists in the NDP were brought to power and they put on exchange controls? The jobs would go.
Let us look at sexual offences. One NDP resolution, which is still current today, calls for amendments to the Criminal Code which eliminate the definition of crime on the basis of consent in adult sexual activity in Sections Nos. 155, 157, 158.1, 179.1, 180.1(d), and 193 and define such activities as crimes only on the basis of commitment of acts of violence. Unlike those who attend NDP conventions, most Canadians cannot cite the sexual offences provisions of the Criminal Code section by section.
Let me translate it into layman's language. This resolution states that the NDP will legalize prostitution, common bawdy houses, sex in public places, and group sex, provided that everyone consents and provided that there is no violence. What about the neighbours who may not consent to having a brothel next door? Is it not strange that a Party which claims to have principles will sometimes try to hide them?
Let us now look at population growth controls. I am talking about a socialist Party which is parading itself as being an alternative Government or even an alternative Official
Opposition. Some NDP resolutions sound as though they were plagiarized from Mao Tse-Tung's little red book.
One resolution which is still current today states that population growth will be directed toward areas that require more people. Does this mean that the NDP will tell people where they may live? Does it mean that the NDP will solve the problem of regional unemployment through mass migration?
We are talking about resolutions which are current today and have been published by the New Democratic Party. The NDP not only wants to control where Canadians live, but it wants to control what consumer goods they would be allowed to manufacture and purchase.
Another resolution which is still current calls for legislation to define and prohibit the manufacture of socially useless energy consuming devices, for example, electrical gadgetry. What is included in that definition of socially useless electrical gadgetry? Does it include VCRs, electric razors, blow dryers, food processors, dishwashers, and electric lights?
The NDP also has resolutions to look after airport expansion. Its Members do not want any more. They have a shopping list of Crown corporations which is quite extensive.
Turning to the area of farm planning, one of its resolutions indicates that it might be necessary, as well, to take into public ownership some existing farm supply retail operations, farm machinery assembly plants, meat packing plants, and canneries.
I know that my time is coming to an end, but there are just two more resolutions to which I want to refer. They are very important because we are talking about agriculture. One resolution recommends limits on farm sizes. The NDP wants the establishment of a public commission to determine a formula for farm unit size on a regional basis. The commission's findings would be subject to local approval. Can we imagine that?
The very last one is a current resolution which is still on the books of the NDP. It indicates that farm income would be negotiated directly with farmers on an industry-wide level and would be based on costs of production, family need, and the productive potential of various farming operations in relation to what was produced. It is to be negotiated. Will it be negotiated in the way industrial unions negotiate? How do farmers shut down their operations for six months? It blows the mind. Truly it is what socialists stand for. Canadians should recognize this debate for what it really is-headline grabbing by the socialists in the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, never in my wildest imagination did I think that I would be speaking in the House at 7.35 a.m. I have been here since eight o'clock last night. It is amazing. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) said to me: "Walter, stick around. This will be interesting".
It has not only been interesting but very revealing. I suppose in some ways we should thank the NDP for this debate. The
April 28, 1987

Conservatives have capitalized on this opportunity to expose the socialists and their policies. Farmers will not be fooled.
If efficiency and competitiveness could guarantee a fair return, Canadian farmers would not have as many problems as they have today. There are no better, more efficient or more competitive grain farmers in the world. We have good land and a good grain growing climate. Canadian farmers produce quality products. However, those things do not count as they used to in the world market-place.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting for-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Order, please. We have listened to Members for 12 hours. Could we listen to a few more.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that some of these Members have just come into the Chamber.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: There are five Tories in the House.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Should I count them for you?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: One, two, three, four, five.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Count the ones in the back too.
We must recognize the reality of subsidies. Only a few countries have treasuries rich enough to meet that of the United States. Canada cannot possibly meet it. Everyone who thinks otherwise should consider the facts for a moment. Farmers do not want subsidies. They want a fair price and a stable market.
Let us look at the happenings in the European Common Market. About two-thirds of its budget is spent on agriculture. The common agricultural policy of the community is providing $33 billion Canadian in farm expenditures. European farmers are now receiving about $480 per tonne for Durum wheat, compared with Canada's 1987-88 initial price of $110. Their farmers are receiving $285 per tonne for barley, compared with Canada's initial price of $60 in the next crop year.
Because of these heavy subsidies, the European Common Market has moved from a net importer of 24 million tonnes of grain 10 years ago to being the third largest exporter today behind the United States and Canada. That is what we are up against.
The U.S., with a huge treasury, has a five-year Farm Bill. For the 1986 fiscal year alone, the Bill will provide in the neighbourhood of $35 billion in direct farm program payments. In addition, the United States is targeting markets with heavy export subsidies under its export enhancement program. Those are the stakes in the subsidy war. Canadian farmers are victims of this war.
Subsidies and surpluses have combined to push world grain prices to ridiculously low figures. Often they do not even cover
the farmer's cost of production. Western Canada is being particularly hard hit because that is where most of the grain is produced. A number of farmers are suffering the consequences and the economies of the many rural communities in the west are feeling the impact. That is why this Government has taken the unprecedented action to provide direct assistance to grain farmers during these difficult times.
Actions within our boundaries are not enough. Canada is a major grain exporter. Grain producers derive the great majority of their farm income receipts from exports. The reality is that we face an international problem that will require an international solution. I just want to point out that the federal Government has placed a very high priority on seeking fairness in the world agricultural trade. It is this Government's objective to establish fair international rules of trade in agriculture for all countries to follow.
Let us talk about the Government's action on the international solution. Canada has placed agriculture on the GATT agenda. Canada has organized meetings of the producing countries. That is positive. That is leadership; yes, leadership that was provided by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), by our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), by our Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer).
As a former director of a large grain company, a farmer-owned company, I was pleased to see the statements concerning initial prices by the United Grain Growers and the prairie pools. What did they say, Mr. Speaker? These companies, speaking on behalf of their farmer members, indicated their support of the Canadian Wheat Board's setting of initial prices that reflect world market prices. I think that is very important. I was surprised that some of the Members opposite are questioning the Canadian Wheat Board's decision. Initial prices have to reflect the world market-place. That is a sound decision. We have to come to grips with reality.
These are difficult times for grain farmers. During the few months that I have been in Ottawa, I have listened to Hon. Members in the Opposition state the problem over and over. I did not come to Ottawa to have the problem restated for me. As a grain farmer, an agri-businessman and a former director of a farm organization, I know the situation. I am pleased to be a member of this Government, a Government that is addressing the situation, a Government that is showing leadership. When was the last time that a Canadian Government paid $1.3 billion to the farmers? I ask the question, Mr. Speaker. When was the last time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Never.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
That is right. Never in the history of Canada has any government ever made those kinds of commitments to farmers. I want to indicate to you that farmers will plant their crops this spring. I am amazed at the negative attitude that exists on the part of some of the Members. Do they not have any future? Do they not see a future in Canada? I do and I know the farmers do. We have heard all this doom and gloom about the family farm, how it is

April 28, 1987
going to disappear and all that sort of thing. But let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that my parents came to this country and it as the land of opportunity. We have a family farm. That family farm will continue to exist, along with the other family farms, because we are resourceful, innovative and we will survive. More than that, I know that all Canadians want to see agriculture prosper.
In conclusion, may I say that here in Canada it is my belief that we have demonstrated that this country can produce quality grain. We have maintained our share of the world markets. Agriculture is important to the economy of Canada. It means employment and food. Farmers know only too well that this Government is committed to agriculture. A strong viable farm industry is in the interests of all Canadians. Our Government has provided assistance to farmers when it was needed in the past and I know that we will provide that kind of assistance again so that agriculture will be viable.

speechtext:
It is not unusual for farmers, like the Hon. Member who just spoke, or the Members from this side who have been taking part in this debate, to be up all evening. I have been up many evenings seeding my crop. 1 have been up many evenings taking off my crop, as have other colleagues. I have been in and out of a nice warm bed at calving time.
I think the Liberal Party put up three speakers. I see that a Liberal Member is present now. I hope he said goodbye to his teddy bear and rushed over to the House at the call. It is nice to see him here.
There has been much debate this evening and I would like to pay a compliment to two Hon. Members of the Opposition who took part in this debate. When Hansard is reviewed sometime tomorrow or later today, Hon. Members and Canadians in general should read the speech delivered by the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) on behalf of the New Democratic Party and the speech delivered by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) on behalf of the Liberal Party. One would find in those speeches that the concern for western
agriculture and agriculture in general can be very well expressed by Hon. Members who may not be as closely associated with the agricultural industry as some of us are.
The Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) mentioned earlier that the Government does not set the initial price of wheat. The Government seeks advice from the Canadian Wheat Board and accepts, rejects or compromises on that advice when necessary in establishing the initial payments farmers receive for grain. Members of the NDP have long espoused support for the Canadian Wheat Board. Today, speaker after speaker condemned the initial prices set by the Canadian Wheat Board as being too low, not just this year but last year as well.
I find it strange that members of the NDP have been leaderless throughout this debate. The Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) was much more concerned about the shareholders of TransCanada PipeLines and Bell Canada during yesterday's debate.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

I would suggest that the Hon. Member take his time. I presume that the debate will go on and in all likelihood, other people will enter into it.
I would like to take a minute to talk about the contribution the Government made to agriculture and particularly to the grains and oil-seeds industry during the last crop year. The Canadian people have supported the grains and oil-seeds industry in western Canada to the tune of $27,000 per commercial farm. That was a commitment made by the Government, but it has been supported by the taxpayers of Canada.
In my Province of Saskatchewan, net farm income will increase by 34 per cent this year. Why will it increase? A couple of reasons are quite apparent. The Special Grains Program was delivered. I remember when that program was announced. I remember that the Leader of the New Democratic Party in Saskatchewan said that it was a charade, it would not be new money, it would be a loan, it was flim-flam. I remember the Liberals here in Ottawa-we do not have too many Liberals in Saskatchewan-saying, as did the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), that the money would have to be repaid and would come from existing programs. His Leader said the same thing.
We now have proof to the contrary. In the Province of Saskatchewan, the Special Grains Program delivered $415 million while the anticipated net farm income before that program was about $425 million. That one government
April 28, 1987

program doubled the net farm income in the Province of Saskatchewan.
Let us take a moment to look ahead. Totalling the production of wheat, feed grains and oil-seeds with what could possibly be $4 million of support in this crop year could amount to an assistance package to the producers of $2.50 per bushel, and Hon. Members will be able to check this at the conclusion of the year.
I made a comment earlier about $4 billion. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), the spokesperson for the New Democratic Party, concluded his remarks by saying that about $4 billion will be paid and that that was terrible because the net farm income of farmers in western Canada would come almost totally from Government. He said that that made farmers public servants. Then in the same breath he told us to put in more money-

The Liberal Member who has now arrived said, "With due consideration".
Of the three members of the Liberal Party who spoke, I paid a compliment to the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis, but I would like to mention now the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who was a Minister of the Crown in the last administration. He condemned this Government for not doing enough. Hon. Members opposite said that last year grain prices were reduced by close to 20 per cent and this year wheat prices by 15 per cent, with the total close to 18 per cent. Compare that with 1981 to 1983 when the Liberal Government was in power. At that time, there was a decrease of 48 per cent, but what did the Government do? That decrease was the largest since 1938. It brought the value of grain down to 1938-dollars. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry railed and condemned this Government, but what did his Government do? It did nothing.
Senator "Blazin" Hazen from the other place is travelling across southern Canada with his whiskers, his big hat and his pointy-toed shoes. He is saying: "We want justice". Where was
he? He was a member of the Cabinet of the Liberal Government. Not only that, he was the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. In 1983 did he do anything? No. Did he go to Cabinet? We are not sure because we do not know if he was allowed to go to Cabinet. It is sometimes alleged that he attended Cabinet but we never saw anything that would make us believe he was there.
In 1981 the prime rate in Canada was 22.75 per cent. Now, in 1987, it is 9.25 per cent. When the Liberals were in power with their high interest rate policies in 1981, FCC loans were at 16.75 per cent. Today FCC farm loans are at an eight-year low at 10 per cent. Farm improvement loans were 23.75 per cent in 1981. Today they are at 10.25 per cent. Yet the Liberals have the audacity to condemn the Prime Minister and this Government for not doing enough for western farmers. They did absolutely nothing. They did not even have the courtesy to recognize that there was a problem.
Let us look at subsidies in the U.S. and the EEC. The Americans subsidize agriculture to the extent of $3 billion a month. The EEC is spending $6 billion on storage alone. We cannot compete with that, but if we could, would it be right? The Americans took on the EEC and what happened to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Argentina? What happened to our producers? If Canada joined in this madness what would happen to Australia, New Zealand and Argentina? If Australia joined in this madness what would happen? It is sheer lunacy to enter into this form of competition. As much as it is needed at this time Canada cannot afford it and it is not the way to solve the problem.
I want to talk briefly about some statements made yesterday and early today. First let us talk a little bit about the removal of the moratorium as a sign of confidence. I hear the NDP and Liberals laugh and snicker. Yet it is a sign of confidence because this Government and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) have put in place programs which will allow the removal of that moratorium. It is a sign of confidence because we started with interest rate write downs, we put farm debt review boards in place, shared risk mortgages in place, commodity-based mortgages in place, and a rural transition program in place.
I heard members from the NDP say the rural transition program is wrong. If that is so, then it must be wrong to have unemployment insurance. With that attitude the NDP must believe that unemployment insurance is wrong for the workers that they claim support them. They must believe it is wrong if they condemn the rural transition program.
This Government and the people of Canada contributed to agriculture in the form of the special grains program. We put money at the disposal of western farmers and agriculture in general.

April 28, 1987
Instead of supporting that, instead of building confidence and making the financial institutions believe that this is going to work, what did the NDP and the Liberals do? They spread gloom and doom. They dragged down that confidence. They refused to assist and buoy up the farmers. Farmers are by nature confident people. We put a crop in the ground in the spring and we know we are going to be taking it off in the fall. We get calves in the spring and we know those calves are going to be worth money in the fall. We have confidence.
Yet what do the Liberals and NDP do? Because we have removed the FCC moratorium, because we have confidence that we have programs in place to keep farmers on the land, they send signals of doom and gloom. I heard the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), whose only concern and knowledge about agriculture is that as long as Safeway is open he is sure it is in good shape, say that this is a bad signal to the financial institutions. The bad signal is being sent by the NDP and the Liberals. They have negative thoughts.

I may be jumping to conclusions but I cannot find any other reason for that happening.
I would like to say in conclusion that I compliment the NDP for allowing government Members to take part in this debate in order to clearly enunciate the actions taken by the Prime Minister and his Government, and the support the people of Canada have given the grains and oilseeds industry in this country.
