speechtext:
The Hon. House Leader of the NDP is an outstanding member of this House and will be given opportunities to make more speeches, and I will listen to him with respect as I always do. I know he will want to do the same for members of the Government as they address some pretty fundamental issues.
I indicated that this is a question of attitude. It is very much a question of attitude. We indicated to western Canada very clearly in the campaign that we would get rid of FIRA. We said that we would get rid of the NEP. We said we would implement the Prince Albert declaration designed to be of assistance to western agriculture, western energy, and western Canada in general.
We said we would deal with the question of interest rates. Lowering interest rates is not just an abstract theory. For every percentage point they are lowered farmers pay approximately $150 million less to the banks. We have lowered them between 4 per cent and 5 per cent which results in $600 million to $700 million that farmers are not paying to the banks but using to reinvest in their own farms.
We said that we would deal with a capital gains exemption for the family farm. We said we would get rid of the tax on
farm fuels. We have done this. We made a series of commitments to western Canada and we have honoured them because by building a stronger base for western Canada we are contributing to Canadian unity.

Mr. Speaker, francophone or anglophone, Conservative or New Democrat, we must all face up to the regional realities of this country. Western Canada is going through difficult times. It is true that certain regions of Canada-for instance, Ontario, Manitoba, some regions of Greater Montreal-are experiencing a rather significant economic recovery. We have serious problems in western Canada, in Alberta, in the interior of British Columbia, in Saskatchewan, and our fellow Canadians in these provinces quite properly expect national assistance from the federal Government.

I am here to say on behalf of all Canadians that this is not something for which western Canadians or farmers are asking. This is something which Canada must respond to in the interests of not only fairness to western Canada, but to our own citizenship and the building of a stronger united Canada.

I apologize. I referred to him as Alvin only because that is the way the country has known him and loved him. It was a great privilege for me to work with him 25 years ago as a private secretary, to have travelled with the Minister of Agriculture to every village and town in western Canada and to have seen first hand the tremendous strength of western agriculture and the tremendous commitment of farmers; their devotion to family and their devotion to hard work.
An extraordinary situation has developed in Canada. It is not to be blamed on political Parties, but it is here. Farmers in Canada in general, but western Canada in a special way because of the nature of the territory, have always been told that if they work hard and make sacrifices they will increase their productivity, contribute to the national wealth, and will be rewarded. Western farmers have devoted their lives to making Canada a richer and better place. They have increased their productivity and have been penalized for it. That is wrong and must be reversed. Farmers must receive a greater degree of fairness.

The matter of the climate in which this is dealt with is also important because it has been placed in the context of western Canada. I doubt if there has ever been a federation within which there has not been regional strains and tensions. It is the duty of federal politicians, not to exacerbate those strains and tensions but to try to reduce them, to try to

April 28, 1987
harmonize the interests of the people of Saskatchewan with those of the people of Nova Scotia.

The interests of Matane with the interests of the residents of Esterhazy in Saskatchewan.

The beauty of Fort St. John, British Columbia, must be brought into harmony with the interests of Port-au-Basque, Newfoundland. That is the obligation of federal Members of Parliament and that is what we are here for. That as well requires a degree of fairness in representation.
This is indeed a country of regions. Thousands of miles of geography are bound together by a small population base essentially in the south. There are indeed discernible regions with different interests. This is a vital part of our citizenship. We have to respond to it not in a parochial way but in a recognition that these regions make our national strength when brought together by a national Parliament.
Let us examine those from western Canada who sit on this side of the House. The trade issue, which is the top issue in Canada today, is being handled by a person from British Columbia.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle), the Deputy Prime Minister and Government House Leader (Mr. Mazankowski), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) are representatives from western Canada in the Government of Canada. I invite Hon. Members to objectively analyse this and compare it with other administrations. I believe they will come to the conclusion that never, since this Parliament was founded, has western Canada been more powerfully represented in the Government of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Not only are the internal workings of government important, all of us must realize that we have a role to play and a place of strength and importance in the national Government. This translates as well into a number of different instruments. We are all familiar with how the House and, in many ways, how the Government works.
For example, it is important to mention that there are very powerful visible committees of Cabinet. The Government Operations Committee of Cabinet, which is so important, is chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister, who is from Alberta. The Foreign Policy and Defence Committee, which is second
most important, is chaired by a member of the Government from Alberta. The committee on social policy, which is responsible for all social policy spending by the Government of Canada, is chaired by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is from Manitoba. The committee dealing with economic expenditures is chaired by the Member from Quebec.
I suggest it is an indication of the tremendous respect for regional realities and the tremendous role that western Canada plays and must play in the heart of the decision-making process in Canada. I made a commitment to the people of western Canada that these things would happen, and that, most of all, western Canada would be brought back to the centre of the decision-making process in Ottawa from which it had been estranged for 20 years. I stand in the House today to tell you that western Canada is very much playing a leadership role in the decision-making process in Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The issue today is not about partisanship. On a question involving agriculture, alienation and concern, the issue is about human beings. Today it involves farmers, their spouses and their families. I believe it is a great tribute to the House that we are all here doing our best to try to improve the lot of farmers.
Regretfully, I doubt very much that our great newspapers will reflect the prominence that this issue should have. The subject of this debate on western agriculture and agriculture generally should be on the front page of every newspaper, English and French, from St. John's to Vancouver. I doubt we will see it, but I say to those responsible for establishing the priorities in the media that this is an opportunity for them to prove their involvement in the true national priorities. If ever there was a question that should be dominating the front pages of the eastern press, it is the problems of western agriculture. I invite them to get with it, deal with an urgent and important issue, and give it the publicity that it deserves so that all Canadians can be aware of this dilemma.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Later, we can see what those front pages reflect, but I say with sadness that I doubt very much if this tremendous priority that is shared by all Members of the House will find that kind of reflection.
The issue today deals with a number of vital areas that go to the heart of federalism. These areas include the perception of estrangement by western Canada, the question of agriculture and the implicit question of transportation. Also inherent in this issue is the question of protectionism internationally and our role internationally.
I cannot imagine anything more important for an easterner-someone from Toronto, Peterborough, Halifax, or St. John's-than to understand this clear sense of frustration of western Canada. They are crying out, asking Canadians to try
April 28, 1987

to understand, not that they are dissatisfied with their Canadian citizenship, but that there is a sense of delaissement and that western Canadians are not receiving the priority for their concern that western Canadians are being hit with a double whammy in declining energy prices and commodity prices in agriculture.
May 1 say in tribute to all Members that the House of Commons has responded very nobly to that concern and will continue to do so. It is important that all Canadians, from Vancouver to St. John's, English and French, understand the cri de coeur of western Canadians. By our actions in government and in the House of Commons we are trying to signal to western Canada, as we would to any other region, that without fairness and a sense of justice and a perceptible feeling that indeed this is a reasonable country, we have failed western Canadians and all Canadians in our duties as national parliamentarians. That is a duty which we never lose. Today we are talking about the lives and welfare of people who work the soil and contribute to our national well-being and are going through extremely difficult times.
I know that statistics have been mentioned throughout the debate last night, and arguments have been made back and forth. May I touch on one aspect of our attempt as a Government to resolve the international grain subsidy wars which, in many ways, are at the heart of the problems facing our producers today.
No one is scott-free. In this business no one is perfect and no one is without the stain of sin. However, these subsidies, particularly those that have emanated recently from the United States and the European Community, which can only be characterized as a trade war, have driven down world prices and have distorted both production and marketing patterns. This war is having disastrous implications for traditional exporting nations such as Canada and Australia.
As I indicated a year ago, my Government is not prepared to stand idly by while Canadian farmers go down the tubes through no fault of their own. I recognize that when we responded with a billion dollars for western grain farmers that inadvertently we were contributing, not to the immediate resolution to the problem, but perhaps in some way to at least getting Canada a position at the table so we could tell the others that in the name of God we cannot let our farmers go down the tube while they are fighting wars. But if the war continues we will all lose.
Canada's treasury is not large enough to compete with the Europeans and the United States while they wage this fratricidal war that can only doom Canadian farmers. That is why I know Members of Parliament recognize the importance of government programs and of bilateral arrangements with provinces. Indeed, that is what we did.
I make no apologies for having authorized the emission of $1 billion in cheques to western farmers last October. It was the right thing to do. Western Canadian farmers were hurting; we received the request and we responded affirmatively. It was the
right and proper step for the Parliament of Canada to take. However, it does not solve the problem.
The alternative is more billions and more billions of dollars. When this is added to the burden of debt we inherited, there is an increase in interest rates which are then passed on to the farmers who are placed on the treadmill to oblivion from which we, as parliamentarians, must try to remove them.
If there is one issue that should not be partisan, it is an approach to international commodity difficulties on behalf of farmers.
As an initial step, Canada chose to make agriculture its top priority at the annual economic summit of industrialized nations in Tokyo last year. That marked the first time in the history of economic summits that any country had made agriculture a priority. Before leaving for the summit, I, along with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), and the distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs met with farm leaders. We got them together in Vancouver and discussed Canada's strategy for the summit. The summit was an effective step forward in our efforts to get agriculture on the GATT agenda.
Following the Tokyo Summit, Canada organized a meeting with the five major wheat exporters in Whistler under the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board. A second meeting was held in San Diego. These meetings have increased mutual understanding about agricultural trade and have strengthened our collective resolve to restore fairness to the world grain trade.
Another of the key steps involved a group, a very important group we have come to refer to as the Cairns Group, 14 countries including Canada, all of which consider themselves fair traders in agriculture. By co-operating, these countries are aiming to balance the power of the European community, the United States and Japan. We do not have to go much further than a trip which is taking place this week between two economic super powers to see the debilitating impacts of protectionism even against a power like Japan.
Where the United States reacts, rightly or wrongly, against an economic power like Japan, one can see the incredible effects not only economically for those two countries but the powerfully negative impacts on currency transactions around the world and the way in which that ultimately impacts, strange to say, on the guy who always gets it in the chin, the Canadian farmer. All of these variables cannot be seen in isolation. Currency transactions in Tokyo, economic summits in Punta del Este all impact on the Canadian prairies and those who make the Canadian prairies grow, namely, the farmers.
This interlock of interest, I think, is shared in the House of Commons by Members of all Parties because if there were an easy and one-shot solution, I think Members would have

April 28, 1987
shared it with all of us a long time ago. So we got together for the first time in Cairns, Australia, last August and our representative was the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board. There we agreed on a common approach for agriculture which could be taken to Uruguay at the launching of a new round of multilateral trade negotiations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. These negotiations, which are now under way, will seek agreement on new rules governing international trade. There is no miracle or overnight solution, but the fundamental building blocks are in place for a sane resolution of a complex and tragic problem.
The co-operation and solidarity of the Cairns Group was a major factor in the eventual success at the GATT launching. We obtained agreement for a very explicit reference to trade in agricultural products which has never happened before, a fact the House Leader of the New Democratic Party, who knows a lot about this, will confirm. Year after year the Europeans tried to avoid the inclusion of this kind of discussion. Members of the Common Market, for reasons we can well understand, tried to avoid Canada's insistence on bringing this matter forward simply because of the very structure of their own agricultural basis and the enormous and overwhelming subsidies which are paid to European farmers, which then engender the kind of reaction in the United States which impacts so negatively on our own producers. So we obtained that agreement for a very explicit reference to trade in agricultural products. It called for talks aimed at establishing greater discipline on the use of all direct and indirect subsidies in agriculture with a view to achieving more open and fairer trade.
It is predicated on a simple proposition as far as Canadians are concerned. We believe that Canadian farmers, if uninhibited and unfettered, are tremendous producers who can compete with anyone in the world. It is only when they are crushed by subsidies coming at them from the competition that they cannot compete, and this is designed to free up the entrepreneurial genius of the Canadian farmer so he can compete and build a stronger Canada through his own efforts.
Following the Uruguay round, I personally met again with farm leaders and other Ministers to keep them abreast of our efforts, our imperfect efforts, because this is a long and difficult struggle. It has been a year of hard work and of building bridges with other countries. I think I can tell the House with a modest degree of satisfaction that our efforts on behalf of agriculture are beginning to pay off. But it is far from over. Now that agriculture is on the GATT agenda, Canada is continuing to push for an agreement that would establish fair rules governing world agricultural trade.
The Cairns Group will meet again next month, this time in Canada, down the street, and 1 invite Members of any political Party, when the representatives of the Cairns Group are here, to please take the time to visit with them. Please take the time to share your views and the views of your Parties with the international representatives who, at our request will be meeting down the street here in Ottawa prior to the Venice
Summit so that we can have the kind of common front and approach which Canadian farmers expect from responsible parliamentarians. I assure all Hon. Members of the full cooperation of the Government in their efforts to participate in this process.
On another front, when the President of the United States came to Ottawa earlier this month we discussed at very great length two things; first, the choice we were given last year. Canada was given, as all the participants were, one item which could be raised at the industrialized summit. As Prime Minister of Canada, I chose to raise the issue of western agriculture at the summit. We made the first case which has been made for agriculture in those terms at the industrialized summit and at my meetings with President Reagan here.
Because of the tremendous impact, obviously, that the United States has on this kind of venture, I worked closely, as did the Secretary of State for External Affairs, with Mr. Shultz in seeking joint approaches, this time in Venice, so that measures we initiated last year in Vancouver and carried to Tokyo could now be brought to some degree of fruition with the support of the United States of America and other industrialized countries which surely must have come to that conclusion when we were telling them last year, that this was lunacy. The $24 billion and $25 billion worth of subsidies going to the agricultural producers in the United States would cripple not only people in Australia but throughout western Canada, would imbalance traditional markets, would be unfair, debilitating and would have the kinds of anti-free trade implications that we are all trying to resist. I think it has dawned on all of the others that perhaps that was right and perhaps it is time for us to come together in a sense of maturity and reasonableness to protect people in all countries.
I preach for my own parish. I have no hesitation in saying it. When I go there, I defend the interests of Canadian farmers. But I think the interests of Canadian farmers are defended fairly. Western and European farmers find solace in that because their interests are being fairly represented by their leaders, as are the interests of the United States farmers.
So it is a complex and a socially challenging issue.
The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) met last week with the Trade Ministers of Japan, the United States and the European community. It was their first meeting since the launch of the Uruguay round. Our Minister stressed that agricultural issues are at the top of our agenda for the summit in Venice and for the GATT. She told them that for the Government of Canada no issue is more important than agriculture. I think all Hon. Members would agree-because we are pleased when a Canadian succeeds in representing our interests so vigorously-that the Minister scored a victory for Canada by getting their commitment for the first time that this matter be properly discussed as an agenda item at the OECD meeting in Paris next month.
April 28, 1987

So the work and the pressure continue. Sanity will not be restored to world agricultural trade overnight. We recognize that. It is a long and a difficult process. No one invented this problem yesterday. The problem was some time in coming. It has been exacerbated by nationalistic impulses in other countries. It has had very grave and serious consequences for western producers. It is something that I think the farmer more quickly than anyone else understands-there is no quick fix. It will not be resolved satisfactorily overnight.
However, I think Canadian farmers will watch the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada to measure the seriousness of our commitment and the logic of the steps we have taken. Farmers are saying: "Do not give us a quick fix that is not going to work in six months. We know there are grave international implications. We know that they can only be solved in co-operation with the summit countries and with the GATT. We want the Parliament of Canada and the Government of Canada to work in harmony with their trading partners to ensure that this trade war stops and that Canadian farmers get every reasonable opportunity for fairness and prosperity".

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, internationally our principles state that the agricultural policy should be designed so as not to adversely affect in any way international trade. To this end, and progressively over time, agricultural policies must become more price responsive. Support for agriculture should avoid production incentives, namely, support should be for farmers and not necessarily for any specific kind of farming. Farmers are the key.
Individuals, human beings are what this debate and what this commitment are all about. Countries should seek to reduce governmental assistance measures that artificially distort world prices and contribute to an accelerated trade war. Countries should not introduce new import barriers that are not mandated by existing legislation. These basic principles must be implemented collectively so that the United States, the Community, Canada, Australia and the Cairns Group can respond in a timely and effective manner.

Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of all farmers in Quebec, Ontario, the Maritimes and western Canada, I think this was an excellent opportunity for parliamentarians of all political factions to air their views on the agricultural sector which is so important, so vital with respect to the future of Canada. We have a serious and even a moral obligation towards our agricultural community. For decades now this community has been making a generous contribution to the national wellbeing, and now as parliamentarians we have an opportunity to respond directly to the concerns of both this community and the individuals who belong to it.

That is what it is about. In my judgment the debate is about finding long-term solutions to very complex problems that escape the simple writing of a cheque yesterday. I say without the slightest fear of contradiction by anybody that the influence, the real influence, in the decision-making process by western Canadians that I have talked about-I see my friend from Winnipeg has just come in.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. With that slight altercation behind us, I shall now get on with the substance of the debate.
I was about to say that the Prime Minister spoke at some length, as it is entirely appropriate for him to do, and during the course of his remarks he made the point that when a western Premier calls and demonstrates a real need in respect of particular problems in the west, he, the Prime Minister, responds. Well, Mr. Speaker, during the course of his 30 or 35 minute speech, the Prime Minister talked in generalities. He did not give a single new response.
1 say to the Prime Minister, if the situation was bad last fall, when the Prime Minister did respond, in the middle of a Saskatchewan election, to a call, the situation in western Canada is worse today, and now is the time that action is required; now is the time that the Prime Minister should be responding.
Let me take a moment to deal with that situation. We are having this debate by virtue of a motion brought by a Member of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), who himself is a farmer. He is one who recognizes the absolute necessity for the Government of Canada to respond, not simply in the long term-and I will come back to that in a moment-but in the short term to the very serious crisis that is taking place today in western Canada.
In that context, I want to say that it was interesting to again hear the Prime Minister talking about the long term. As the Leader of a Party that has always believed in planning, I can tell you that when one hears a Progressive Conservative talking about the long term-and with your background, Mr. Speaker, you will appreciate what I am about to say-one can be very sure that he is not prepared to do anything about the short term. The only time Progressive Conservatives are interested in the long term view, Mr. Speaker, is when they have nothing to offer in the short term.
The situation in western Canada is indeed serious. I had the occasion to attend a meeting last night at which various farm groups from southern Ontario expressed their concerns and apprehension about a free trade agreement being entered into with the United States with nothing being done about the need of farmers to have effective marketing boards.
It was pointed out at that meeting that somewhere between 23 per cent and 25 per cent of Canadian farmers are on the

April 28, 1987
point of bankruptcy, or are at least in a very precarious financial situation-and that applies to farmers in all agricultural sectors: grain producers, corn producers, hog producers, dairy farmers, and so on. While the costs of production have been on the increase, commodity prices have been on the decline.
I say again to the Prime Minister: If the situation was bad last fall, it certainly has worsened since that time; and we recently had the announcement that grain producers are going to suffer another 18 per cent drop in prices. So, if action was needed in the context of a Saskatchewan election-or, to put it bluntly, to buy votes-now action is needed to save farms all across Canada.
In this context I wish to say something about two immediate areas where we thought action could have been forthcoming, two areas that we in this Party asked questions about in Question Period yesterday and to which we received no answers; two areas that we kept front and centre in the contributions made by the members of the New Democratic Party in this very important debate.
The first one was the credit position of farmers. As the House knows, the Government, with what seemed to be calculated insensitivity, announced that on Friday the moratorium on farm foreclosures will be lifted. When the moratorium was put on some 19 months ago, it was said by the Government at that time that there were good reasons for it.
Indeed there were good reasons for putting a moratorium on foreclosures. Farmers were in the midst of a crisis over which they had no control. The vast majority of farmers who then found and now find themselves in difficulty are not in this position because they were incompetent or did not know what they were doing. It is because they were caught in an international crisis in part and a domestic crisis in part, the general nature over which they have no control. For the men and women, whether they are industrial workers, miners, or agricultural workers, in this kind of situation, a Government with any sensitivity should rapidly move in, bail them out, and protect them in the short run. That is what is needed now.
However, the point is that when the moratorium was put on some 700 farmers specifically, at that time, were on the verge of losing their farms. It was a serious situation, so action was taken. Now when the situation has not become better but has become worse, and when there are about 6,000 farmers in the same position as the 700 were in 19 months ago, does the Government say that logic should compel us to extend the moratorium? By no means should it be forever because farmers are self-respecting and, as Canadians in other walks of life, they want to make their contributions and to ensure that they have responsibility over their farming operations. They want to live up to those responsibilities, so they do not want an indefinite extension. If there was a crisis when there were 700 farms on the verge of bankruptcy, surely when that number has now risen to 6,000 we should be announcing an indefinite
extension of the moratorium until farmers are out of the crisis, not lifting it on Friday.
I do not need to remind the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that not long after he came to office certain banks at the other end of the economic ledger required in his judgment immediate bail-outs. They got billions of dollars. That decision was made over a week-end. I say to the Prime Minister that many more Canadians, specifically Canadian farmers, are being threatened at this time. If he could take that action for the banks, surely he should be taking it in the interests of prairie producers.
We will continue to press right up until Friday for the Government to rethink its decision to put an end to the moratorium. It must think about the serious situation of farm families and the importance of a farm family as a continuing and crucial element to the social fabric of the country. It should think about those farmers, think about those families, and announce by Friday a change in its decision to lift the moratorium on foreclosures. That is one specific with which the Prime Minister could have dealt today. He could have come into this important debate and said, "Yes, there has been some reconsideration and we are going to change that". However, he did not do that.
I should like to refer to the second area. If anything is perhaps more serious-and certainly it is equally serious-it is the income position of farmers who are rising this morning across the country as we sit here. With the time difference between here and the Prairies, they are up now and are seeding. They are making crucial decisions about the income fate of their families for the coming year because they are putting in their present crops.
What the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) did yesterday frankly surprised me. I have respect for the attitude of that Minister. I think he takes his responsibilities most seriously. I do not agree at all with the policies he is implementing right now.
When he responded to questions which I put to him yesterday he left the impression that there was something off about my question. Well, I do not think there was. I did not pretend then-and I do not pretend now-to have the same detailed knowledge of agriculture as the Minister of State for the Wheat Board who happens to be a farmer. I respect that there are certain things in this area, to say the least, on which he has more detailed knowledge than I have.
I asked the following question yesterday on behalf of grain producers who were making decisions now, and on behalf of my colleagues in the NDP who know the details of agriculture, would the Government of Canada be prepared to guarantee farmers who are currently seeding that when they look at the final results of their crops in terms of net income it will be no lower than it was for last year's crop? The question was relevant, and I ought to have received the answer that the Government of Canada would guarantee that the income would not go any lower. Again I ask the Prime Minister that
April 28, 1987

question. We will get back to it in Question Period today. He could have dealt with it.
The Government of Canada should recognize that grain producers had a 20 per cent drop last year. The announcement indicates that they can expect another 18 per cent drop unless they receive a deficiency payment. We are saying that a deficiency payment should be announced to ensure that farmers working out there and putting in new crops as we are debating today will not have a drop in income which will take them below what they got last year. That is the point.
I say to the Prime Minister quite seriously that we agree that long-term solutions are needed. We agree that action must be taken through GATT. We agree that all pressures ought to be put on the European Community to stop its counter-productive, massive subsidy program which has been equalled and exceeded in good measure by the United States. With these massive subsidies by these two large economic entities in the world-the European Community on the one hand and the United States of America on the other-we cannot compete over the period of a decade. Canadian farmers do not want that. Canadian farmers can produce competitively and they have shown it. They are the best in the world in the grain sector if the competition is fair.
We agree that steps should be taken at the international level to get the EEC and the United States to live up to their own rhetoric. The rhetoric, particularly in the case of the United States, is to put an end to these kinds of subsidies. If the Americans are going to preach to others abroad, they should start practising it at home.
Indeed there are long-run steps which must be taken. I could talk about other measures such as stabilization of income programs for our producers as well as certain international steps. However, I want to return to the emergency.
By definition, the emergency concerns steps which should be taken now. We cannot stand back and watch our grain producers getting some S3 per bushel, which is well below what it costs them to produce. We cannot tolerate depression level prices. We cannot stand back and watch 23 per cent to 25 per cent of our farmers being on the verge of bankruptcy. We cannot stand back and watch a moratorium, which was appropriately put on farm foreclosures 19 months ago, being lifted on Friday.
We want the Government of Canada to live up to its short-run obligations as well as its long-run obligations. This means that the Government must come to the aid of Canada's prairie producers now, at a time when there is not an ongoing provincial election and when the need is much greater than it was last fall when there was one.
I would conclude by saying that from now until Friday, we are going to keep the heat on. We are going to get the Government to realize what it must do about the moratorium on foreclosures. We will put the pressure on the Government
.S'. O. 29
so it will announce an appropriate deficiency payment for farmers who need it and deserve it.

Mr. Speaker, this morning we heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) say that his Government would be prepared to respond to a call from the farmers of Canada. Before this debate began and, indeed, during its currency, the Prime Minister received an urgent wire in the form of a telecopied letter from Garf Stevenson, President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, relating to this emergency debate on, as he puts it in his letter, the farm economic crisis. Though there was no response made by the Prime Minister this morning to this particularly urgent call, Mr. Stevenson did call upon the Prime Minister to bring to mind the fact that the rural way of life and related service industries are in jeopardy. Mr. Stevenson said the following:
The pool asks that all Members of Parliament recognize the very critical
economic situation confronting Western Canadian families and communities.
This crisis has far-reaching social and economic implications for the national
economy, as well as for the West.
Then the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool set forth what he believes would be a minimum program including joint federal and provincial co-operation to keep families on their farms in productive capacities, early consideration to be given to an acute need for a substantial deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year and the continuation of the federal Government's efforts to restore sanity in the international grain market.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), and myself held a joint press conference in Winnipeg and Ottawa last week dealing with this very issue. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), spent a good deal of the Easter break dealing with this issue. Last week, for the thirty-second time since the election, I as Leader of the Opposition travelled to western Canada, not only to meet the commodity crisis in wider terms but to again respond directly to the agricultural crisis.
We are desperately concerned. We are dealing not only with a cyclical crisis affecting part of our economy, we are dealing with the survival of the family farm, we are dealing with the survival of a way of life in rural communities and we are dealing with something that is now beginning to affect the infrastructure and tax base of all of western Canada. It is affecting the survival of rural municipalities in the western provinces. We have a major situation on our hands, a situation that is not cyclical but is structural. If the Government of Canada does not respond in urgent and immediate terms, we risk sacrificing an entire way of life.
The Prime Minister spent some time dealing with the international grain crisis and describing in rather vague terms what the Government was doing to try to bring together the major producing powers in an attempt to restore some sanity to international grain markets. That was just one of the items mentioned by Mr. Stevenson in his urgent letter to the Prime Minister of last night. What the Prime Minister did not say is

April 28, 1987
what the Government will do by way of an urgent and immediate response.
We on this side of the House believe that we need now an announcement of a deficiency payment sufficient to restore this year's prices to last year's initial prices and to guarantee to Canadian farmers at least the same returns as they received last year. That is number one. Second, we believe that not only must this cash flow be maintained and maintained so that farmers know when to seed, what to seed and whether to seed, we also believe that the growing credit crunch and avalanche of debt, punishing Canadian farmers, should be resolved soon and in some meaningful way.
Yesterday during Question Period we said that we could not understand the cruel, insensitive timing of the lifting of the moratorium on farm debt by the Farm Credit Corporation. One week after the initial grain prices were lowered by 18 per cent, the Government lifted the moratorium and threw the 6,000 farmers who were at risk into immediate jeopardy. That we cannot understand and we want a rationalization of it.
1 have studied recent interest rates applicable to prime, efficient farmers. On 15 or 20-year mortgages the interest rate under the Farm Credit Corporation, which is supposed to be a preferential rate, is 11 per cent.

It is 11 per cent and longterm, 15 per cent to 20 per cent. I could say that the Hon. Member from Mississauga is a short-term operator. He ought to look at the long-term rates. I have them right here.
Subtracting the current rate of inflation, which is running at approximately 4 per cent-and here I am sure I will again get some gratuitous advice from Mississauga-from the 11 per cent, the real rate of interest faced by farmers under the preferential status of the Farm Credit Corporation is 7 per cent. That is higher than the rate farmers had to pay during the height of the recession in 1981-82 when in effective terms they were paying a real rate of 1.5 per cent. Now they are paying 7 per cent.
Western farmers are in deep trouble and the response of the Government is totally inadequate. Initial prices for grain as announced by the Wheat Board last week have been cut by 18 per cent over last year's prices. Last year initial prices were down by 20 per cent over the year before. In 1984-85, the price per tonne for No. 1 wheat was $170. In 1986-87, that price was reduced to $130 per tonne. This year, under the initial prices just announced by the Wheat Board, No. 1 wheat is down to $110 per tonne. In three years the initial price has gone from $170 per tonne to $110 per tonne. That is lower than the cost of production.
Last year the Government could say that it was eating into the profit margins of farmers. Most farmers could not even meet the cost of production last year, but this year it is certain that even the most efficient farmer who is all paid up and has his family working with him will not be able to meet the cost
of production. I challenge the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board to argue that point.
A couple of years ago, in 1984-85, No. 1 barley was $125 per tonne. Last year, 1986-87, it was down to $80 per tonne. In 1987-88, this year, under the initial prices just announced, it is down to $60 a tonne.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: No deficiency payment.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
And no deficiency payment. Farmers have a decision to make. They have to decide what to seed, when to seed and whether to seed. The Government has made no commitment to the farmer at this time when the farmer needs answers. The farmers need answers and they need them now, not next July or next October.
It seems that the only time western farmers see any activity on the part of the federal Government is when a provincial election threatens a sitting provincial Government.

At the minimum, we want the Government to guarantee to farmers that the return for this year's crop will be at least the same as last year's levels. We must tell farmers they will get the support they need and deserve and we must send a strong signal to rural Canada and the agricultural industry that we as a nation are in the grain business to stay.

I think we must also send a strong signal to the United States and the European Community indicating that we will not let our farmers continue to be the victims of our officially low grain prices, provoked by a treasury war between Europe and the United States which has prompted an artificial surplus and has lowered prices throughout the world.
As I said to the President of the United States when he was in this country three weeks ago, the U.S. Farm Bill, with its export subsidies, is killing the Canadian farmer. I was bitterly disappointed when the President spoke in this Chamber to hear not one word on agriculture, not one word in response to the Canadian farmers' plight, not one word to indicate he would attempt to rationalize the North American market, not one word in response to what I hoped the Prime Minister said to him in those private meetings that there must be some rationalization of the North American and world grain situation. If the American Congress continues to artificially ratchet down grain prices by way of subsidy, our grain producers are going to be driven off the land and we are going to be a different kind of country. Yet there was no public response to that by the President of the U.S.
Farmers are not asking for hand-outs. They are asking only for what is rightfully theirs, a fair price for their grain and fair market conditions. This is not just a cyclical economic crisis. It is taking its toll in human terms. Farms are facing bankruptcy.
April 28, 1987

The psychological pressures on farm families, the concern about whether children will stay on the farm, is forcing family breakups. A whole way of life is being threatened.
I have said that the only way western Canada seems to be able to get assistance these days from the Government is through threats. The fear of an election loss in Saskatchewan last year brought aid to farmers last fall. A threat from Premier Getty to split the Alberta Tory Party finally brought some help to the oil industry. Farmers are getting ready to seed their 1987 crop. They have tough decisions to make and they need answers from the Government and they need them now.
I want to conclude as I began by saying that we in the Opposition call upon the Government to do two things immediately: Announce a deficiency payment sufficient to raise the return this year to farmers equal to last year's return, and do it now so that farmers have some assurance that when they seed they will have a return that will cover at least the cost of production. Second, we call for a rationalization of farm debt and a revocation of the decision of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to lift the FCC moratorium.
I end where I began by reciting the urgent letter telecopied to the Prime Minister from Garf Stevenson last night during the course of this debate. If he has not already seen it, he will find it in his files. On behalf of western farmers Mr. Stevenson calls upon the Prime Minister directly for immediate action. Fie wants joint programs to keep the family farm alive. He referred to the deficiency payment. He wants restoration of sanity in the international grain market and I would add, as well, the rationalization of farm credit to assuage the overwhelming avalanche of debt which is absolutely crushing the family farm in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is amazing to see the change which has come over the NDP and the Liberals during the last few days.
I would like to deal with some of the things which are the cause of farmers being in the position they are in today. A lot of it is because of policies put forward by the Liberal Party and supported by the NDP. I am not talking with the wind like some members of the Opposition. I spent four days of last week visiting farms and towns in my constituency. I know what farmers are saying.
Farmers are not crying crisis as the Opposition is today. Sure there is a crisis. They know the Government will come through at a proper time and in a proper way. That is the message the farmers are sending. They are not worried as they were a few years ago. They can recall that in 1979 we had good prices. Inflation was driving the price of food up. Things were good on the farm. Young farmers said here is our chance to expand. We will buy more land and so they did. They
expanded their holdings so they could make a greater contribution to Canada. Then what happened? The situation changed entirely.

I apologize for being at the wrong seat. I thought there was something funny over here, but I did not realize it was me.
As I was saying, prices started to change and interest rates went up and up and up. We pleaded with the Liberal Party to do something about interest rates. They went up to 22 per cent. That is the main cause of farmers being in trouble today. The international situation is certainly serious, but not as serious as the problem caused by the increase in interest rates which was permitted by the Liberal Party and not opposed by the NDP.
Many young people have already lost their farms. They were losing their farms during the Liberal Government; but what did the Liberals do? Not a thing. They let interest rates rise and rise and rise. Now they are crying the blues. Now they are suddenly interested in the western farmer and farmers in general. I say "suddenly".
Sometimes when we asked the Liberal Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, when he would do something, he would say "soon". His only reply was "soon". Well, "soon" never came. There were more than 1,400 farmers in this country who went bankrupt during the term of the Liberal Government because they did nothing about interest rates. They may have short memories but farmers do not. Neither do Members on this side of the House. We pleaded with the Liberals to change that policy but nothing was done.
Today there are still farmers who are stuck with interest rates from that time. This Government is doing something about it. We are going to the banks and asking why they set interest rates at 14 per cent, 15 per cent and 18 per cent today when the prime rate is below 10 per cent? That should be changed. We are doing our utmost to have that changed. However, it is not the Government, it is the banks who have a lot to do with it.
The problem lies with the Bank Act passed by the Liberal Government. Our banks should have a mandate that when interest rates drop from as high as 22 per cent and 23 per cent to below 10 per cent, there must be a corresponding change in mortgages which were taken out during that time. Otherwise

April 28, 1987
there is simply a massive amount of money going to the banks which is unearned and unnecessary. The banks have to keep going, but they have to be realistic as well.
What is one of the main causes of many farmers being on the verge of losing their farms, or in fact losing their farms? The international situation is only a small part of it. The main cause was the interest rates permitted by the Liberal Government during that time. They are still stuck with those rates and we are feeling the aftermath now. So is the farming community. It is the aftermath of the Liberal Government.
The same thing applies to the energy situation. What is the problem there? Again it is the aftermath of the National Energy Program. That is what ruined the energy situation in Alberta.
It was a deliberate attempt to destroy the energy industry in the Province of Alberta and, to a lesser extent, in the Province of Saskatchewan. The Liberals can talk all they want today but they cannot change that. They did their utmost to get every rig possible out of Alberta. There was a line-up of rigs leaving the country because of the national energy policy. Today we are suffering the aftermath of the Liberal administration and no one can deny that.
The Member who was the Minister of Energy in the Liberal administration said there is more drilling going on today than there was last year. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills (Mr. Thacker) had shown pictures of rigs lined up at the border leaving the country along with the expertise and their capital.
It is no wonder that western Canada is in a depression today. It is a created depression almost as bad as that imposed upon Ukrainian people years ago. I have read the history of how Ukrainian people had to submit to giving two-thirds, 75 per cent or 90 per cent of their production to the communist regime. Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian people died, not because the land did not produce, but because food was taken right off their tables for taxation. It is a blight on the history of the world that that was ever permitted.
That is almost comparable to the depression created by the Liberal Party with the national energy policy. It affected every farm. One of the main causes was the increase in fuel costs because of the national energy policy and the massive taxation imposed upon the people. It is comparable to what the Communists did in Ukraine during the 1930s when people died right and left because of a lack of food.
The same thing happened in Alberta as a result of the national energy policy. I saw the effects on our towns and villages, our merchants, and even on our churches. Everyone felt the depression which was created by the national energy policy deliberately to hurt one part of the country.
They now stand up and ask what the Government is doing for western Canada. They cry because the Premier of Saskatchewan phoned in the middle of the night. Well, the
Premier of Saskatchewan was so concerned that he was up in the middle of the night worrying about what could be done to help the farmers of western Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Members can smile all they like but the western farmers did not smile because that policy resulted in scores of them losing their homes and farms. One of the major reasons that scores of them are on the verge of bankruptcy today is the high interest rates which were supported by the Liberal regime which did nothing about it. It is not the international market which is causing them to lose their farms today. The international market will have an effect from now on and I will deal with that in a moment, but let us not kid ourselves. The Liberals and the NDP are not pulling the wool over my eyes or over the eyes of the farmers of Canada.
Farmers know that the main cause was the national energy policy and the high interest rates during the Liberal regime. I ask any Member on that side of the House to prove that that is not so. That is a proven fact which has been notarized by many, many people.
I have sat in farm homes with people who are today still paying 15 and 18 per cent interest. When a man on the farm weeps, you know there is something wrong. The whole family was crying because the bank was going to take over their farm, not because of anything the present Government did, but because of the interest rates which were permitted to be charged during 1981, 1982 and 1983.
I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) in this Government to plead with the banks and he did that. One fine young third or fourth generation farmer in my constituency saw the opportunity to expand his holdings in 1979, thereby making a better contribution to his country and providing a better living for his family. He bought more land. How was he to know that the Liberal Government would permit interest rates to go up to 22 per cent? The bank then said it would take his farm because he could not make his payments. What farmer can make payments with a 22 per cent interest rate? What business in Canada can stand up under an interest charge of 22 per cent? It is impossible.
I lived through the depression years. I was teaching during the hungry thirties and saw an insurance company remove a farmer from his farm. I went to the company and said, "This man has farmed here all his life". They said, "He owes money and if he cannot pay it, off he goes". Other farmers pleaded but nothing happened.
April 28, 1987

I will tell you the story of that farmer. His wife had TB. There was no medicare, no free medicine for tuberculosis in those days. The most important thing for him was to save his wife, so he borrowed the money to send his wife to the best doctors he could find. He borrowed the money when wheat was selling for about $2 per bushel. He expected to repay bushel for bushel plus a little more for interest charges. His wife passed away. The insurance company then said that he was way behind in his payments. How could he make the payments when the price of wheat had dropped to 19 cents a bushel and the price of eggs had dropped to six cents a dozen? This was in 1934 and the insurance company would not even listen. It said, "Off he goes."
That farmer pulled a granary which was on skids to another piece of land which another farmer said he could farm for him because he was being treated shabbily. That farmer lost his farm through no fault of his own. There was no compassion or consideration. The company even threatened to take him to court for moving the granary which was on skids.
I have seen many such things during my lifetime. I have recently been in farm homes where the same thing is happening. The high interest rates which prevailed in 1981, 1982 and 1983 are now catching up to farmers just as the interest rates of 1918 and 1919 caught up with the farmer of whom I just spoke. At that time scores of people were moved off their farms. In 1935 a moratorium was put on by the Government of Alberta, supported by the Government of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. After 1936 we were able to save hundreds of farms in Alberta.
However, the moratorium had some bad effects. Farmers in my riding tell me today to be cautious with moratoriums because they suffered for many years as a result of the moratoriums imposed by the Government in 1937 and 1938.
The farmers said that without credit they cannot operate and want us to proceed carefully when using moratoriums. There are better ways to deal with the issue because moratoriums hurt farmers who are able to get credit and need it to operate. We must be careful that we do not adversely affect the farms that are not in trouble. While there is some merit to moratoriums, I have suggested to the Government that it proceed cautiously. Not all the farmers in my riding want moratoriums to be extended, and many of them are completely against a moratorium because it ruins their credit.
Our Government realizes the necessity of moratoriums and the Minister of Agriculture has extended moratoriums on FCC a number of times. However, if we follow the Opposition's suggestion and impose too many moratoriums, many farms that are solvent could go on the rocks. We want to save the farms that are already suffering, we do not want more farms sent down the drain.
In 1937 we established Debtors Assistance Boards which were able to bring together the principal lenders and the
borrowers. Those boards were given the power by legislation at that time to roll back the interest rates because they were completely unfair.
The Minister of Agriculture has established boards that will be able to allow both sides to meet. These boards do not yet have the power to force back mortgage interest rates, which may become necessary if the financial institutions and insurance companies insist on retaining interest rates of 15 per cent to 20 per cent that were in effect between 1981 and 1983. The farmer, or anyone else, cannot make ends meet at such interest rates, no matter what the Government does. The farmers who are experiencing difficulty today are those who tried to expand their holdings during better economic times in 1979 and 1980. They had no idea that interest rates would jump so dramatically, which is one of the major causes of farmers losing their homes today. They have not been able to catch up to those interest rates and are therefore losing their farms.
The Minister of Agriculture is considering what should be done. It may be necessary to amend the Bank Act, which I support if it can be done. I believe the banks should receive a fair rate to which they are entitled for repayment of their loans, but they have no right to expand their financial holdings by ruining farmers in this country.
We must help the farmers who are still paying interest rates of 17 per cent. If the financial institutions refuse to take action, I hope the Government will do so.
You are signalling that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker, but I have much more to put on the record. I listened to Opposition speeches. I am amazed how they have suddenly realized what is happening in the agricultural industry, as if a great light suddenly shone upon them. I wish they had come to that realization between 1982 and early 1984 because today we are suffering from the agricultural policies that were enacted during that time.
The agricultural community is receiving help from the Government. The crop year does not begin until July 1. The farmers I have visited are not worried about the seeding because S700 million will go to them very soon. That money was authorized by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). They are men of compassion and understanding. I sometimes get nauseous when I hear Members opposite talking about the problems of farmers when I realize what they did only three or four years ago. Furthermore, some of them do not know the front end of a hog from the back of a cow, yet they stand up to plead for the farmers. They should have given them more consideration when they were in power because now we are suffering the aftermath of what they created.
We will correct the situation, but it will take time. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board are anxious to pull the

April 28, 1987
country together and help every farmer. That is what we are determined to do.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been sitting all night, and the debate may go on for a couple of hours, to discuss the crisis situation in our agricultural industry, especially in western Canada. However, the situation is not unique to that part of the country because the same problems exist elsewhere in Canada, and in fact in the very province and riding which I represent.
Before I continue my speech today, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few moments to speak on behalf, I hope, of all Members of this House and thank our parliamentary staff which has had to work all night.

Sometimes some of us tend to forget about the people who assist us in doing our job here on Parliament Hill. This morning, when I came to the House at approximately 7 a.m. and took the familiar mini bus that brings us here, I was talking to the driver who informed me that he had been working since two o'clock yesterday afternoon.
Indeed, the people who work for us and spend those kinds of hours, whether they work for us as messengers, bus drivers, clerks at the Table, interpreters, or camera personnel, certainly deserve special recognition on a day like this, when we have subjected them to a very tough time. I certainly hope that the Speaker will issue the appropriate thank you on behalf of all of us to the staff who serve us so well.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian farmers have suffered two major setbacks in the last few days. First, we heard about the lifting of the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loans, and second, the Government, or should I say the Canadian Wheat Board, announced that initial payments for this year will be 18 per cent lower than last year. The impact of this price drop will
be particularly severe if we consider the fact that the situation in the industry was not very good to start with.

How did we get into this situation? I listened to speeches by Members opposite. The Prime Minister and other Members have alluded to some of the issues. There is one essential point that I believe has not been raised yet. First, we should remember that the current crisis in the prices of commodities is due to the U.S. Farm Bill. There is no point in calling it anything else. That is in fact the cause of the difficulty we are in.
Some people will say that the U.S. Farm Bill was implemented in order to react against similar legislation initiated by the European Economic Community. That is at least partially accurate, but not totally. There is some measure of accuracy to that suggestion. However, we should remember that the effect we are seeing now in this country directly results from an initiative of the United States Congress, signed by the President in December of 1985, known as the United States Food Security Act, 1985, commonly referred to as the U.S. Farm Bill.
That Bill was debated for months in front of the U.S. Congress. From April 22 to April 24, 1986, a delegation of Members of this House went to Washington in order to be briefed on the U.S. Farm Bill and to find out just what effect it would have on Canadian agriculture. We listened to presentation after presentation describing to us the ill effects this legislation would have on Canadian farmers.
First Bank Agri Services, a division of Bank of Montreal, published a document in February of 1986. It was a document prepared for them by Chase Econometrics and in it we were given the effects of the U.S. Farm Bill. The predictions at that time of Chase Econometrics for the Bank of Montreal were that in 1986 the price of wheat could vary between $2.40 and $2.70. In 1987 it could vary between $2.28 and $2.85. In 1988, it could vary between $2.17 and $2.71. In 1989 it could vary between $2.06 and $2.57, and in 1990, it could vary between $1.95 and $2.44. You have obviously noticed, Mr. Speaker, the dire predictions here and the direction in which the prices will be going, according to Chase Econometrics for the Bank of Montreal.
Knowing that this would be the effect of the U.S. Farm Bill on Canadian agriculture, I have to ask a question of the Government. Where was the Government at the time that Bill was going through the U.S. Congress? We have an embassy in Washington, as we all know. I was at the Canadian Embassy and in view of the deplorable effects of this Bill I asked who we hired to lobby Congress and why were they not more successful in providing some relief for Canada. The answer was that no lobbyist was hired to try and defeat or modify the Bill or convince the U.S. Congress to do something with that legislation.
April 28, 1987

The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) talked about the fact that commodity prices are low because of the previous Government. That is utter nonsense. I do not pretend that everything was perfect under the previous Government but at least this Member of Parliament, coming from the region he does, should know better.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sure the Hon. Member wants to be accurate. I never at any time said that commodity prices were low because of the previous Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
