speechtext: The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
We will review Hansard later, Mr. Speaker. I definitely recall hearing the Hon. Member telling us that the agricultural prices to which farmers are subjected today, and the agricultural crisis, are because of low commodity prices and he said that was caused by the previous Government, and even accused the previous Government of doing things which were similar to what the U.S.S.R. did in Ukraine some 50 years ago. I remember hearing the Hon. Member saying that. He should not have made those remarks. They were totally inappropriate, but were nevertheless made by him. He should apologize for them to everyone, including the Ukrainian-Canadian community, for uttering such nonsense.
1 would like to raise with you, Mr. Speaker, other effects of the U.S. Farm Bill. First, there is a law in the United States which has $70 billion worth of subsidies designed largely to displace other world markets. We are "other world markets" because we sell our products on the world market as well.
According to the United States, and this is information they gave to me in Washington-I am reading from notes I took there-in 1980 the United States decided to boycott sales of wheat to the Soviet Union. It did that for the specific reason that the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan. Because the United States cut off sales to the U.S.S.R. it resulted in a large surplus of wheat at that time. The Americans said that the other countries took advantage of them. They expanded their own markets and the U.S. even accused Canada of having done that.
That is totally ridiculous. Obviously, someone should be straightening that out in Washington. The Americans said they had to do something. They said that Argentina, Brazil, Canada and Australia expanded their markets at the expense of the United States. They said that prior to the embargo they had 32 per cent of world wheat sales but that had now gone down considerably and that the 49 million tonnes they produced in 1982 was now in great measure surplus rather than used for foreign sales. The Americans also said that there is another cause of all this.
At the same time this phenomenon of the Afghanistan boycott was proceeding, there was another situation. Many countries in the Far East, for instance, became largely selfsufficient so that has caused the surpluses we have today.
What is the American solution? They will embark on this program and depress prices until the others are out of business. The Americans were quite candid about that.
Do the others get discouraged with their own subsidies, particularly the EEC? I do not pretend to know Europe as well as perhaps some, but a number of us have ancestors who came from Europe. We know that Europe suffered greatly during the Second World War from hunger, and to believe that the Europeans are going to stop producing because they have to inject too many subsidies is not to remember history very well. There is a will in Europe to be self-sufficient in food which is quite powerful. In my view it is a great deal more powerful than the Americans believe it to be. The subsidies in western Europe will continue, contrary to what the Americans believe.
We now have large U.S. subsidies which will continue on until 1990 since the U.S. Farm Bill will be in effect for five years. There are EEC subsidies which will not stop for reasons which I described earlier. Canada is stuck in between with only two choices. The first choice is to convince everyone else to reduce their subsidies, particularly the United States. The second choice is to increase our subsidies to the level of theirs so that our farmers can exist. There are no other choices. We cannot enlarge the planet in order to find new markets. We cannot do that. What we have to do at this point is to convince the Americans to cut it out.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) went to great pains complimenting and congratulating himself, forgetting of course to mention that at the Shamrock Summit of 1986, though we all received glossy pictures of the Prime Minister and fancy booklets, there was no mention of agriculture. Four months after the U.S. President had signed into law the U.S. Farm Bill the Prime Minister in the booklets, leaflets and information kits concerning important issues to be discussed in Washington, failed even to mention the U.S. Farm Bill.
He now has the unmitigated gall to stand here in the House, chastise everyone else, saying that some opposition Members did not speak, when we sat down to let him speak early this morning out of courtesy-not to him but to the office which he holds. He then has the nerve to make remarks such as he did earlier today in the House.
The Prime Minister should get a little bit more serious about this issue. It is important to western Canada. It is important as well to regions such as the one which I represent, which is largely agricultural but in a very different part of the country.
The Prime Minister said that he talked recently to President Reagan about this very important issue that he described. He forgot to tell us that there is talk of increasing the export subsidy under the U.S. Farm Bill. There is talk now of increasing it, after the President left here. That is what the U.S. is now planning to do.

April 28, 1987

The Prime Minister also referred to GATT and spoke in glowing terms about the steps he had taken in this respect, but unfortunately, he forgot to mention that the documents requested by GATT two months ago, on the specific position Canada was taking, have yet, as far as I know, to reach GATT. And this is about the very subject we spent the night discussing in the Elouse. I think the Prime Minister would be well advised to go back to his office, instead of putting on another pair of Guccis, and to act on GATT's request and provide the necessary documents so that we can put an end to this subsidy war through multilateral negotiations.
The Canadian farmer is no longer competing with the American farmer. Efe is competing with the U.S. Government. How is he ever going to win, Mr. Speaker? Nobody in Canada can win this fight. The Canadian farmer is not begging for subsidies, he seeks justice and, if he is to compete against the American Government, is it not normal that he should expect some kind of assistance from the Government of Canada. The Government of the United States is certainly not going to hand money over to farm producers in this country. Will Canadian farmers have to apply for foreign aid? How can they rely on the Prime Minister to get what they need? Members opposite were telling us earlier that the season has just opened, that perhaps we will hear better news later on. Mr. Speaker, we simply cannot seed retroactively, we have to do it right now if we want a harvest this fall. A farmer cannot wait for subsidies at a later date and then decide that he should have seeded two months earlier. The farmer needs this information, and he needs it now.
I urge the Members of this House to continue to raise these important issues today for as long as it takes to convince the Conservative Government to do something. True enough, subsidies were made available last year, Mr. Speaker, but this happens to be the worst agricultural crisis ever in this country, and it calls for whatever action is required on the part of the Government. The Government would not be doing our farmers a service nor showing how generous it can be with them, because anyone producing food does so for the good of all Canadians and not only for those who are directly involved in the agricultural sector. Therefore it is the duty of the Prime Minister, the duty of the Government, and the duty of all Members of this House to make a positive contribution to ensure a sound agricultural economy.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to have an opportunity to speak on this very important issue. I have a very personal feeling about entering into this debate since I was born and raised on a farm and have farmed, as have my father and my grandfather. In fact, my great grandfather came from England to Ontario and broke the land. I feel something very different than I have ever felt before in the House of Commons when I hear the rhetoric from academe and Bay Street about farming.
Farming is very different from any other profession. I do not know who can really feel it better than someone who has been there. Farmers think long and hard about things. They do not make a lot of rash decisions. They also have some interest in their fellow man and they would probably listen instead of milling around behind me. I listened with interest as the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was talking. I did not see one farmer elected to the Official Opposition sitting in the House today. I say to them, do not beat up politics and get into long-winded rhetoric when you are dealing with such important people.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Say that to the Prime Minister of all people.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Farmers sitting here this morning would probably not make the type of interjection that I just heard from behind me.
I want to tell Hon. Members, because I feel very personally about this matter, that as a boy we did not have a lot. My father took over the farm from my grandfather; through some adversity it carried a great amount of debt. When my mother and father got married they had two old cows and a debt-ridden farm. They did not ask for a whole lot from the Government. They put their heads down and went to work. I would like some of the people who have talked so much today experience that. As kids we did not have anything. We had hand-me-down clothes. I had to milk cows by hand in the summer when the perspiration would roll right from the top of my head to the bottom of my feet; my head was up against one old hot cow with another behind me. By this time we had at least 10 or 12 milking cows. I am glad that I had those experiences. We have at least 20 farmers sitting on the Government benches today, each of whom has I am sure, at least as much farming experience as have I. As such, we have a good understanding of what is needed to address the serious problems facing the agricultural sector in Canada today.
It is with reluctance that the various farm groups approach governments for assistance. In cases where assistance is forthcoming they want it developed with some thought and understanding. They want input from the very learned and qualified groups within Canada, as was the case with the recent grain subsidies.
Just this past weekend I had a discussion with my brother, the full time operator of our farming operation. It is an operation that is not making huge amounts of money. However, that does not cause me to come into this Chamber and fly into a rage against the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), as has happened during the course of this debate.
Both the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) are farmers, and as such have a good understanding of what is required. Certainly, they know more than those who have practised their professions on Bay Street, none of whom have ever had to milk a cow or lift a sheaf of wheat. These people
April 28, 1987

did not have to get mired and dirty in order to make a living. In order for the children of farm families to attend university the family itself had to work that much harder.
I am very concerned about the way in which this whole question is being approached. I am sure that my neighbours in the Sarnia-Lambton area are chuckling at the kind of rhetoric we have been hearing during the course of this debate, particularly from people who have little or no understanding of the problems of the farming community and the way in which they should be addressed. We need a thoughtful approach to these problems, with important input from the farm groups and organizations that exist in this country.
In 1981, the prime rate was at 22.75 per cent. Farmers today are still trying to get out from under the debts incurred during that period. Where were these people then? This is a point raised by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), an individual who has lived with the problems of the farming community longer than I. He was no doubt appealing for a saner approach to interest rates in those days. Today, an FCC five-year loan is at the rate of 10 per cent.
As we went into the 1984 campaign, as a farmer I was certainly impressed by the 16 point agricultural policy developed by the Progressive Conservative Party. I am sure my colleague from Bow River was instrumental in the development of that policy as, no doubt, was the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, and others.
That policy came out of a conference held in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, and became known as the Prince Albert Declaration. The Progressive Conservative Party in that policy said it would remove the capital gains tax for farmers. Since forming the Government, we have provided for the accumulation of $500,000 exempt of taxes. We said that we would remove the sales tax on farm fuels. Of course, we have done that. We said we would change the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Again, that certainly has been done. We said we would change the Western Grain Transportation Act to remove the volume cap and freeze the rate. Again, that was done. Going into the 1984 election campaign the Progressive Conservative Party promised to increase sales and extend our markets for grains. Certainly that has been done. We said that we would bring forth a red meat stabilization program, which we did. We say that we would allow dual labelling, and we have. As well, we have acted to reduce the flow of subsidized beef from the EEC. We said that we would establish Farm Debit Review Boards. We have done so.
I am proud of this Government, a Government that put together that Prince Albert Declaration and in fact followed through on it.
We have heard a lot of rhetoric and yelling about how the western farmers feel. In that regard, let me quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of Thursday, December 18, 1986. The article is headed: "Pool praises PM." It states:
The Alberta Wheat Pool has praised the government of Prime Minister Brian Mulroney for his handling of problems in the agricultural industry-
It is really quite an extraordinary hard time in agriculture right now and we feel that so far the present government has responded well.
Certainly the score card, according to the Winnipeg Free Press-a very important newspaper when it comes to the agricultural sector-comes down in favour of this Government. That is an article that was written at the time the deficiency payment was made.
Next I have a publication entitled: Wheat Pool "budget". Under the heading "Farm Income Record in 1986" we have the following:
Alberta Agriculture estimates that 1986 total realized net farm income in Alberta was $788 million, the highest level on record, and a remarkable 45 per cent over the 1985 level.
The record was achieved because of lower operating expenses, a healthier livestock sector and substantial government program payments.
Payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Plan, crop insurance and other programs accounted for an estimated 17 per cent of total farm cash receipts in 1986.
That is not to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a problem, and one which we need to address, in western Canada and in Canada generally in connection with grain sales. I do wish to emphasize, however, that this is a Government that has shown the way. It is addressing the situation in a very forthright and planned manner.
I know that our farmers do not have the same confidence in the opposition Parties, the members of which have given us so much rhetoric since the start of this debate.
In that connection, I should like to quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of April 11, 1987. The headline is: "No hope from the Liberals".
The article states, in part:
Even the western members of the caucus remain sadly out of touch-
The 17-page report is an empty document offering ringing declarations of discredited party policy, outright distortions of economic reality and not a single firm proposal which would make any significant difference in the economy of Western Canada.
It goes on to say:
Most of the actual proposals of the task force are so vague as to be meaningless.
Then it went on to indicate:
On agriculture, the task force boldly recommends that "income support measures such as the Alberta Liberal Party's suggestion for a negative income tax for farmers should be examined more closely".
It continued:
Significantly missing from the group are two other elected Liberals: Manitoba Liberal Leader Sharon Carstairs and John Turner, Member of Parliament for Vancouver Quadra and Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada. Both should consider themselves lucky to be out of it.
That certainly reflects some thoughts from western Canada on the vague, quickly thrown together, wild promises in connection with agriculture.

April 28, 1987
We have a Government with many actual working farmers who know what it is to have callouses on their hands. They are part and parcel of the way in which we think a government should address the problem.
I should like to refer to the document entitled "Directions for the West-Proposals for the Western Canadian Economy". This Liberal proposal was immediately dismissed by the Winnipeg Free Press as an empty document.
Who are these experts on western Canada? Is it the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy)? I do not know how many cows he has milked or how many sheaves of grain he has stooked. I do not know how understanding he is.
Let us reflect upon what has happened in terms of federal support for agriculture in western Canada since 1983. According to the graph which I have before me, it would be about $300,000 million. In 1984, when the Conservative Government came into play, it shows that federal support of agriculture went up to $1 billion. In 1985 it was about $1.7 billion. In 1986 it was about $2.2 billion. For 1987 the forecast is in the area of $3.2 billion.
I think farmers in western Canada understand a Government which is moving toward assisting in a thought provoking, organized manner, not flailing about with rhetoric. I think that is very important to my farming colleagues across Canada, especially those in western Canada-and we grow a lot of grain in Ontario-in this depressed price time, the result of large amounts of subsidies by the United States and the European Economic Community. They are depressing the prices and we are caught in the middle. It is something which we must address in an organized way.
At the same time it is important that we remember that the Government has brought forward over 400 separate initiatives providing $5.76 billion to the benefit of Canadian agriculture, in sharp contrast to what the previous Liberal administration did. Farmers in Lambton County must chuckle a lot about the statements of Hon. Members on the opposition side as they reflect on what they did. Of course the NDP could not do anything because it has never been in Government. 1 am sure those farmers remember what the Liberals did not do when they were in Government.
On the grains and oil seeds side, a $1 billion payment has provided and will continue to provide a needed boost to cash flow. There have been a number of other issues including new grain deals, advance payments for crops, the record interim payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Act, cash advances for unharvested grain, and amendments to the Western Grain Transportation Act. The producer freight rate was maintained. There is a new domestic feed policy, and commodity based mortgages were introduced. Farm debt review boards were put in place. There was the Canadian Rural Transition Program, and of course, reduced interest rates.
I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker. I will probably not have time to deal with all the initiatives we have introduced as a
government. Of course the farm fuel tax relief was introduced. We also assisted specialty groups. Our long-term dairy policy was lauded and appreciated by that industry.
As a farmer who has deep roots, serious concerns, and an understanding of the industry, I ask the Government to move toward addressing the international pricing situation of grain farmers with a lot of thought, sincere study, and certainly the help of the farming community and its important organizations.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in the debate, and I want to say a word of appreciation to the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) for having initiated it.
The Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James) who just spoke complained about what he called opposition rhetoric. I do not think that the people in western Canada see it in quite that way. They recognize that we have identified very clearly the crisis facing farmers in western Canada and that we are asking the Government to do something about it.
I also heard the Hon. Member read a list of things which the Government has done. Our Party is in full accord with some of those things. We appreciate that those measures have been taken. However, right now we are facing a crisis which demands further immediate action to save the family farm economy of western Canada. It is not good enough for the Conservatives to say that they have done thus and so and the following. They must address the present crisis. They cannot live on the basis of what they did a few months ago. That is not good enough. That will not help the people facing the crisis today.
Also the Hon. Member seemed to suggest that there was something wrong because some of the Members who have spoken were not farmers themselves. He suggested that if academics or business people became involved in the debate, somehow it reflected wrong priorities.
I recall a story which was told by Bill Irvine, a pioneer member of the CCF. I think he was first elected as a member of the Labour Party back in the 1920s. When he and some of his fellow members from western Canada came to Ottawa, they were looking to address some of the urgent issues facing western Canada at that time. The first issue with which they became involved related to Cape Breton coal miners. It was a real eye-opener. He represented western interests. He was very concerned about the needs of western Canada. However, when he came here he had to be concerned about the crying needs of Cape Breton coal miners. It gave him a new vision of what Canada was all about.
I think Hon. Members of the House recognize that, whether we come from a farm in western Canada, a fishing community in British Columbia, or an auto manufacturing town in Ontario. I think we are all concerned with the over-all economy of the country. The fact that we do not come from one particular occupation should not prevent us from being
April 28, 1987

able to speak when a crisis threatens a particular sector of the economy.
The emergency today has been very clearly outlined by our Party. It has three basic components. Of course the first is that initial grain prices announced by the Canadian Wheat Board are down 18 per cent on average from what they were last year, and they were already down 20 per cent from what they were the year before. This results in the lowest initial prices in 15 years and creates a real problem for farmers as they plan their crops for the coming season.
The second part of the crisis is the fact that on Monday of this week, the Government announced that it was lifting the moratorium on the Farm Credit Corporation loans. If the first of those can be said to be due to international markets, and we certainly recognize that international markets are important and that the price of grain is determined on international markets, the second of those is the direct responsibility of the Government. The Government chose the worst possible time, both financially and psychologically, to take that kind of action. It completely undercuts the confidence not only of farmers in their own abilities but it also undercuts the confidence of the financial community in the farmers to whom they will be extending credit. They see that the Government itself is not standing behind farmers.
When the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) spoke, he said that the problem relates back to the high interest rates that were a result of the previous Government. I remember when the Bank Bill was introduced by the previous Government. At that time, the New Democratic Party introduced amendments that we hoped would help to bring this matter under control. The Conservative Party supported the Government rather than the progressive amendments that would have done something about high interest rates. It is a little late for the Hon. Member for Bow River to complain about high interest rates.
The Hon. Member said that they might have to bring back the Bank Act and take a look at it. It comes up for review every 10 years. We hope that this time, Conservative Members might take a little more progressive approach to the Bank Act than they have so far. Every relationship I have seen between the Conservative Party and the Canadian banks does not give me very much hope and I do not think it gives the farmers of Canada very much hope either. I doubt the Hon. Member himself has much hope since, knowing his background, I believe that he does not have any great love for the banks.
The final part of this crisis is the refusal of the Government to guarantee that prices paid to farmers this year will be no less than what they were last year. If there was such a guarantee, the farming community would at least know that there would be a floor beneath which it would not have to sink. The Hon. Member for Bow River said that the Government will come through at the proper time and in the proper way. This is the proper time. Farmers are facing the crisis now.
They have to make decisions about their crops now. They face this huge question mark now.
We heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) speak for 35 minutes. It had been hoped that intervening as he did in such an emergency debate, he would have had something to say. It was hoped that he would have announced the reconsideration of the decision to lift the moratorium on FCC loans or that he had decided to institute deficiency payments. That would have given a real sense of hope and confidence to the farmers. Instead, we listened to 35 minutes of diatribe against the Opposition and then a long list of some of the things the Government has already done. We heard the suggestion that this was an international problem that had to be solved on the international stage. We agree that international efforts are required to solve this problem but it also requires some immediate short-term action that will help farmers right now.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) said that the lifting of the moratorium was an expression of confidence in the farmers and accused us of not having any confidence in them because we wanted to see that moratorium kept in place. What nonsense. It is as though a swimmer had decided to swim across a lake, a storm comes up and the driver of the boat that had been guiding the swimmer suddenly says that he is confident that the swimmer could make it to the other side of the lake and then takes off and leaves the swimmer by himself. That kind of confidence is not really very helpful. We need the kind of confidence that stays with the farmer, the kind of confidence that tells the farmer that we believe he can make it and we will stay with him every step of the way until he does make it. That is the kind of confidence the Government should be showing in farmers rather than the kind that abandons them. I say to the Hon. Member for Bow River that now is the proper time for the Government to be taking some action.
The House of Commons often suffers from a degree of unreality. I suppose that is perhaps inevitable in this kind of a deliberative chamber but in order to help us keep in contact with the reality that is facing Canadians from coast to coast, we are given good travel budgets, phone privileges, mailing privileges and constituency office budgets. That should help us keep in touch with what our constituents are thinking.
I know my colleagues from Saskatchewan and Manitoba have been bringing the needs of the western economy and prairie farmers before the House because of the representations they have heard from their constituents. I presume that at least some Conservative Members have been availing themselves of the resources available to them to hear what their constituents have to say about the real problems they face. I presume they even try to raise some of these issues in caucus. Why has the Government not acted? Why has the Government chosen this particular time to lift the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loans? Why has the Government refused to give the kind of guarantee to farmers that would enable them to go ahead and plant with hope and the confidence that they will be around next year at this time?

April 28, 1987
As I was preparing for this debate, it occurred to me that it has been exactly 49 years since my own family left a farm in Saskatchewan. My father had spent 22 years of his young manhood on that farm and my mother had spent nine years there. They literally had to walk away because of a combination of poor crops caused by rust, dust, grasshoppers and Russian thistles, low prices and a Government that either did not care or could not help. They literally walked away with nothing but a few possessions. Today's details are different but the basic issue is the same. The family farm is threatened and the whole economy of the prairie provinces is under threat.
Just three or four years ago, one of my brothers-in-law who was a farmer in southern Alberta faced this same situation. Because of over-expansion, high interest rates and low commodity prices, he found that he had to sell a family farm and go into another business. Of course, he was not unique nor was my father. I represent a riding in British Columbia in which there are hundreds of retired prairie farmers. Some of them retired after good years, some, like my father, got out because they were literally forced out by poor crops and worse prices.
We face a very serious situation. The Government is refusing to take action to address it. The Government is relying on the fact that it did some things in accordance with its election promises but it is not meeting this current crisis. That is what we must emphasize over and over again. In this respect, the Government is following the same line it is taking with other primary producers.
We have seen the bungling on the softwood lumber issue. The Government was completely incapable of standing up for the interests of Canadian lumber producers. As a result we now have a 15 per cent tax on softwood lumber products. That can perhaps be managed by some producers when markets are buoyant, but it will decimate the interest once there is a bit of slack in the market.
In the same way we have seen the Government's refusal to really come to grips with the needs of the fishing industry. We have a decline in our small craft harbours program. Officials have come before the committee and testified that in order to meet the needs of small craft harbours they need literally millions of dollars. Some $127 million a year is needed and they are getting less than $50 million, we are going to have to shut down small craft harbours across Canada because the Government is not taking seriously the need to maintain an infrastructure for one of Canada's primary resources.
We have seen the back down by the Government in its dealings with France over St. Pierre and Miquelon, refusing to stand up for the needs of Canadian fishermen. We have seen the destruction of habitat while the Government brings in what it calls a no net loss habitat policy which allows fishery habitat to be traded off to other industries. The result is the destruction of valuable fish habitat. We have seen the postponement of promises to create a salmonoid enhancement program.
We see one area after another where the Government is abandoning the primary resources of our country. The latest issue of course is the sell-out of Dome. We are no longer going to maintain any kind of Canadian ownership or control of that very important company. We have to ask why. What are the Government's priorities? Of the 137,000 jobs created last year all but 5,000 were in the Province of Ontario. We certainly have nothing against Ontario. That province needed 132,000 jobs. More power to them. Yet we need jobs in British Columbia. They need jobs in western and Atlantic Canada and in Quebec. Why do we not have policies that would help the economy right across the country?
Getting back to the issue at hand, we need a commitment by this Government to keep the family farm as a workable, economic unit. The land will not go away. Even if some of the people currently farming that land go bankrupt and are forced off the land, even if commodity prices are depressed, at some future time the land will be important and someone somewhere will be interested in farming it. However, unless the Government takes action now the people who are going to be farming it will not be the family farmer. It will not be the people who have invested their lives, the welfare of their families, their savings, their energy, their hopes and their initiatives into building up a farm. They have seen all that destroyed by a combination of international commodity prices and a noncaring Government. It will not be those people on the land.
What we are asking as a Party is that the Government should take action. It should recognize the situation of Canadian farmers, see it as an emergency. Now is the time when the Government should be taking action, not six months from now. Give farmers a chance now so they can plan their crops properly.
It is interesting that some of my colleagues have already pointed to the element of stress in the life of Canadian farmers. They pointed out that the picture of an idyllic life on the farm is completely false. Growing food, they conclude, is one of Canada's most stressful occupations. The stress is chronic and dangerous. The Western Report of January 12, 1987, says that the study revealed that stress symptoms such as headaches, marital problems and irritability were three or four times more prevalent in the average farmer than in an RCMP officer three days after being involved in a shooting.
What is more, the stress on the policeman is transitory, a one-time event, but for farmers the stress just goes on and on. We are talking about stress on our primary producers, the people we require to produce food not only for Canada but for other parts of the world. These are the people we look to to earn primary income for Canada. We are abandoning them in a time of difficulty. They are always under some stress. Now they are under particular stress and we are abandoning them.
For our part we call at the very least for an immediate government commitment to provide grain farmers with a guarantee that total grain receipts for crop being planted now, the 1987-88 crop year, equal those of the 1986-87 year. The Government should not lift the FCC moratorium until it
April 28, 1987

announces a deficiency program for the upcoming crop year and addresses the broad question of Canadian farm debt, which is about $25 billion across Canada.
I urge the Government to recognize the seriousness of the situation we face now. It is not a question of rhetoric. It is an emergency out there on the farm. It is not good enough to simply reiterate what has already been done. Let us have some action now.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased you were able to recognize me today because I think this debate, more than any of the debates we have had recently, clearly demonstrates what our Government has done, is doing, and intends to do in comparison to what some speakers on the other side have had to say.
I would like to first address a couple of the issues raised earlier in the debate by the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broad-bent) and the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). The Leader of the NDP complained about the Government bailing out the banks. He said that Government had $1 billion for the banks but nothing for the farmers. I would like him to know that we did not bail out any banks at all. Those banks are gone. They are dead. They are in receivership. The people we reimbursed were the people in western Canada who had money in those banks and organizations such as municipalities, school boards, credit unions, the City of Grande Prairie, hospital boards, co-ops and farm businesses. These were the kind of people who needed support.
We recognized that the economy was in a sensitive situation. The western economy could not stand the blow of losing $1 billion. We came to the aid of the west when it was needed because those organizations and groups depend for their revenue on people who pay property taxes, farmers and others. That is their only source of revenue. We recognized that so we supported them and the farmers. The Leader of the New Democratic Party should recognize and understand that. The fact that he does not clearly demonstrates that he does not understand the west or farmers, and probably never will.
I will say a little more about the Leader of the Opposition. If there was ever a speech from Bay Street, we heard it this morning. He told us something about nominal interest rates and real interest rates, trying to suggest that the interest rates of today are somehow higher than the interest rates of 20 per cent, 25 per cent, and 30 per cent which we had three and four years ago when the Liberals were in office. He made some kind of argument on inflation, nominal interest rates and real interest rates.
The fact is that while you can listen to some ivory tower economist or Bay Street lawyer, to the farmer "interest rates" means what he pays out in cash. To the farmer cash is cash and money is money. If your payments are half today what they were five years ago that is all that matters. Frankly, it does not matter one bit to the farmer whether some Bay Street lawyer or ivory tower economist from the New Democratic
Party tries to tell us that interest rates of 10 per cent or 12 per cent are really higher than interest rates of 23 per cent because the farmer knows better.
This debate demonstrates the kinds of people there are in the two Parties. Part of the problem with the Liberal Party is that they do not have any members who understand farmers and the west. They never have. The problem with the Liberal Party is that they cannot assemble enough members of their caucus who know something about agriculture to have a game of checkers.
A Member has just handed me some figures on interest rates and I will read them into the record before I go on. The prime rate today is 9.25 per cent, the FCC rate is 10 per cent, and the Farm Improvements Loan Act rate is 10.25 per cent. In 1981, when the former Government was in office the prime rate was 22.75 per cent, we had a 20-year FCC rate of 16.75 and the Farm Improvements Loan Act rate was 23.75. That is more than double what they are now. Where were Hazen Argue and the Leader of the Opposition then? Well, we know where the Leader of the Opposition was. He was on Bay Street. He was the one collecting these interest rates.
I want to talk about farming and agriculture in the west. We have heard from many Members on our side today, from farmers and Members from agricultural ridings. I happen to represent a city riding, but I can remember my roots. I can tell you a little about my roots to illustrate that while some of us may represent people in cities today we know what it is like to live on the farm.
I spent my first 17 years growing up in a place called Bruce. Those of you who read Quorum may have noticed an article a couple of weeks ago about a visit paid there by Don Mazan-kowski, the Member of Parliament for that area, as well as John Wise. They addressed a group of 300 farmers in a little community of only 75 people. The commitment of the Government is illustrated when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) is prepared to meet with people in such a small community and tell them about the Government.
During the 17 years that I spent there my father was a machine dealer, a hog buyer and a cattle buyer. We did a little farming as well. I shovelled my share of fertilizer and grain and some of that other stuff, too, at least enough of it to give me some experience in how to handle some of the things which the Opposition throws at us from time to time.
For your benefit, Mr. Speaker, I would indicate that I got to know the present Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), the Member of Parliament who represents the area where I grew up, a long time ago. I met his wife even earlier than that. She was the nurse in the delivery room when I was born.
I was in Prince Albert just about three years ago in early July when the Conservative Party, then the Opposition, unveiled its program for western agriculture and western farmers. There were 53 or 54 items in that program. I was in Camrose last week in the riding of a prominent western

April 28, 1987
Member, the chairman of the Alberta caucus, Arnold Malone. There were many farmers there. I was reviewing that program and saw that 44 of those 53 points have been addressed in the time since we have been in office. The other nine are currently at some stage of development.
The Government has always been aware of the needs of farmers and agriculture. We have a long history of involvement. The importance of maintaining a strong and dynamic agri-food industry has always been well understood by my Party. Indeed many, perhaps the majority, of agricultural institutions which all farmers and all Members of this House will be familiar with were brought forward by Conservative Governments, including that of Mr. Diefenbaker. The Canadian Wheat Board, the Farm Credit Corporation, crop insurance, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, ARDA, and the PFRA are primary examples of our concern for Canadian agriculture.
I want to make it clear, however, that these institutions and organizations and legislation are only support mechanisms. They were never intended to interfere with farmers' personal freedom and responsibility for their own success.
Any farmer is aware of the harsh realities of agricultural life. He knows that farmers have to be careful, have to be frugal, and have to work hard and live within their means because of the narrow margins, the traditionally poor returns on capital, and the terrible risks which farmers face both through natural hazards and market risks. The market-place is no less threatening to farmers than flood or drought or frost.
Each farmer must take primary responsibility for coping as best as he can with these hazards. Farmers understand that there is no escape from these harsh realities and no excuse for bad management. In short, they must carry their own weight, take their own risks, and live with the consequences. Every independent businessman must maintain that sort of attitude toward his or her enterprise.
However, the federal Government recognizes that there are some aspects of agricultural life which are unique; the vulnerability to the weather and to international political and economic forces for example, plus the historically low rate of return on capital, all of which require governments to adopt special programs for farmers. This is not done to guarantee every farmer a living, but to ensure a general environment in which Canadian farmers may prosper and also to ensure that Canadian consumers have a continuing supply of high quality food at reasonable prices, something which is particularly important to Members such as myself who represent urban ridings. In addition, government support to the agriculture industry enhances that industry's contribution to the national economy, for example, its contribution to the balance of trade.
If hard work and farming skills could solve the problem it would be behind us by now. However, farmers know that they have no control over their problems and that is very frustrating for them. The cause, as has been stated here earlier by other speakers, is rooted outside Canada's borders. An international
subsidy war between the Europeans and the United States has pushed world grain prices so far down that farmers today cannot even cover the cost of production.
This is an incredibly costly war. Literally billions and billions of dollars are being spent. Canada's treasury simply cannot compete dollar for dollar. However, we are not backing away from the problem one bit. We are approaching the situation on three fronts. First, we are working hard to maintain our current markets for grain and we are seeking new ones. With aggressive marketing we are stressing Canada's strengths: dependable delivery, reliable supply and, above all, high quality.
Under the leadership of the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), and even in the face of massive export subsidies, this approach has earned Canada a larger world market share for grain. It is expected to increase to 21.5 per cent for 1986-87.
Our second approach is to fight hard at the international level for fairness in world agricultural trade. Canada pushed successfully to put agriculture on the table in the new round of multilateral trade negotiations. Agriculture is our number one priority in the GATT negotiations, in contrast to the former Government that bargained away, neglected, and ignored agriculture in trade negotiations. If it had not done that and had placed agriculture in the priority position that we have, we would not now be facing these problems.
My colleague, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) has met twice with Ministers from the world's leading grain exporting nations. In fact, Canada organized and hosted the first meeting. Canada is also organizing a meeting for late May, which will bring together 14 of the world trade Ministers to deal with the agricultural trade issue. They will consider their collective position to be carried to the Venice Economic Summit of western nations by Prime Minister Mulroney. These initiatives will eventually restore fairness to world grain trade and a realism to world grain prices. But solutions will not come quickly.
That is the reason behind our third approach. We are providing substantial assistance to grain farmers. It is assistance of a size never matched in this country's history.
In the past two years, prairie farmers have received record payments from the Western Grain Stabilization Program and this year's payment will easily set a new record.
We took the initiative to amend the Act so that farmers would receive interim payments in the spring. Those farmers who participate in the program can expect a substantial interim payment to be announced before the end of the month.
In addition, the Special Canadian Grains Program, the billion-dollar package to which has been referred in this debate, was $1 billion in direct cash to grain and oil seed farmers who have been hurt by the international subsidy war.
April 28, 1987

Alberta farmers will get more than $265 million of that amount. So far, we have mailed cheques for $76 million to farmers in Alberta, and the final payment is going out in May.
The program is going well. There are some hitches and some concerns, but we are dealing with them. We will resolve them.
In the meantime, Charlie Mayer and John Wise are continuing to consult with farm organizations-

This morning we heard some examples of what we have done. In the time I have remaining I want to mention one or two of those examples.

I could go on to list 40 or 50 other initiatives we have taken in the last two and one-half years, but I believe that you have signalled that other Members want to speak.
