speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not in the House to hear all of the Hon. Member's speech. I was not referring to him, but to other Members whom I heard during the night and this morning. The message came across quite clear, as it does daily in the House, that they believe we on this side of the House should not become emotional about our agricultural sector because we do not understand it. I suggest that members of the Opposition should check our backgrounds more carefully.
The Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James) said today that he was brought up on a farm, was involved in the agricultural industry and knew a great deal about that industry in Canada. I do not doubt that the Member was very sincere in what he was saying.
However, I want to tell him that I have a similar background. I was born in 1935 in the Province of Prince Edward Island. I grew up on a family farm and probably milked as many cows-by hand-as any Member of Parliament here today. I know a little about the black flies in the summer and cows swishing their tails when we tried to milk them. Of course, those were the days before milking machines; farmers have progressed a great deal since then. In 1935, the year I was born, my father's total income for the year was $366. When he passed away a few years ago, we still had the old receipts, bills and mortgages which were paid by my father, who was trying to hold on to a family farm on a total of $366 a year and raise a family of three as well. He also looked after my grandmother. At that time there were no senior citizens,

April 28, 1987
homes and the grandparents lived with the son and his children. So I know a little bit about hardship and a little bit about agriculture. Indeed, I dabbled in cattle, operating a small beef herd for many years up until the time I was elected to this House in 1980. My son is still operating the family farm which goes back to my grandfather, some 140 years ago. So before we start commenting on whether or not someone is qualified to speak, we should check their background.
I must say that I am very pleased to see lawyers, veterinarians, doctors and former school teachers take part in this debate because I think they also have a deep interest in our agricultural sector. I want to also point out that the debate which has been going on since eight o'clock last night is not just a debate about western farmers. Yes, that is where the crisis is today but I remind all Hon. Members-and they have heard me on the subject many times since I became a Member of Parliament-about the plight of our potato farmers in the Province of Prince Edward Island. For the last three years, up until this year, we have had a crisis situation in our potato industry. This year the price is a little better. Farmers are certainly able to meet their costs and to pay off a few of their debts.
1 just came back from my riding where I talked to a number of farmers. One individual in particular told me that he is going to show a bit of a profit this year and will be able to pay off a few of his bills but his problem is that he is getting himself into a situation where the banks may foreclose on him. They could not do it last year because he was so far in debt. They knew there was nowhere else to go. The problem is, in some cases, when one has a heavy debt load and gets near a point where one's assets cover one's debts, that is when the banks get a little shaky and can foreclose very quickly. We have seen a lot of that in my province over the last four or five years.
This is what is happening in western Canada today, and it is happening not only in western Canada. The lifting of the moratorium on foreclosures by this Government is going to have a tremendous affect on eastern Canada, Ontario and the west, as we mentioned before, because of the decline of world market price for grain. It is down 18 per cent this year and was down 20 per cent last year, that is 38 per cent below what it was in 1985.
There is no question about what is taking place. One does not have to be a Philadelphia lawyer to figure that one out. Whether one is a farmer, a lawyer, an economist or a dentist, it does not make much difference. It is very simple arithmetic and certainly everyone in Canada can understand it. I hope that everyone in Canada does understand the serious situation in western Canada. More than that, I hope the Prime Minister and his Cabinet, his inner circle, will understand. We know there was $1 billion put in place last year to help the grain farmers, particularly those in western Canada. That was appreciated. I think I would be less than honest if I said
anything different. It was a help. However, government Members say to us: "Look what we have done for farmers". That $1 billion was set aside for the farmers, we agree, but why was the $1 billion put in? It was because there was such a serious crisis. If the money had not been put in most of the farmers would have been gone. Any government with any compassion would have done that, and should have done more.
What we are saying in this debate today is that the Government must move and move quickly not only to put in another $1 billion but to ensure that farmers in western Canada and right across the country are able to put in their crops this year and be guaranteed a price no less than last year. That is not much to ask.
I have heard people asking why we are always standing up and fighting in the House of Commons and elsewhere for the farmers. The farming industry is the real base of our economy. Any country in the world which loses its agriculture sector is kaput, as they say in Newfoundland. It is gone. We cannot be held hostage to other countries, if we lose our agricultural industry, because that is when Canadian consumers are going to pay through the nose.
We all know that farm prices are far too low and we do not have to tell the farmers how to produce. Canadian farmers are the most efficient farmers in the world-any statistics will tell you that, Mr. Speaker even with all the obstacles they have to face such as climatic conditions and so on. They are the most productive farmers in the world, but they have to be given some least a return on their investment. If we do not do something immediately and disallow foreclosures on farm properties in Canada, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, we will be in the most serious crisis this country has ever faced. I say that because when a farmer has a large holding of land and goes bankrupt, the price of that property also declines. It affects all the other farmers. Their collateral is gone. That is a very serious situation. It will have a snowball affect. So we must maintain our integrity as a national Government and as Members of Parliament and see this issue very clearly.
I was looking at the May 4 edition of Macleans magazine and came across an article entitled "Down and out on the Farm". This is not news to me, Mr. Speaker. I would just like to quote one paragraph:
Western farmers can recite a litany of economic misery. In Saskatchewan, which relies most heavily on grain farming, total farm debt climbed from $3.4 billion in 1981 to $4.8 billion in 1985. During the same period net farm income dropped to $699 million from $1.1 billion.
In response, the value of land in southeastern Saskatchewan has dropped as much as 40 per cent in the past three years.
That is exactly what I am trying to point out. We have seen it in my province when we used to pay $1,000 per acre for good potato land. Today and last year some of that land was going for less than $400 per acre. But the farmer had worked for 25 and 30 years on that land. He had put in hard work, blood and sweat. His wife and kids also worked on the farm. The family
April 28, 1987

farm is not a one-man operation. Farming involves a whole household. If we lose our family farms, if we allow them to disappear, it will be an extremely sad day for us all.
The Government has to come up with a program. It has to do so immediately. It is not good enough to say that when world prices go up in two or three years' time that we will still have enough farmers to produce grain at a good market price. I am as much for free marketing as anyone but there comes a time when we have to stand up to provide from the Treasury some money to help an industry. We had no problem in this Chamber and the Government had no problem when the banks in western Canada got were in trouble. We were there very quickly to help that situation out, to bail them out.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Bail who out?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Bail out the depositors. Some of these depositors had millions of dollars on deposit . There was no risk at all and they were receiving a high interest rate. The reason they had their money in those banks was because of the high interest rates they were receiving over and above ordinary bank interest rates. That is the same sort of principle as if I were to go to the horse-races tomorrow and bet on a long shot and lose my money. I could take my ticket back to the Government of Canada and say that I took a chance, I lost, now come up with the money. The Government had no problem coming up with solutions to those types of situations. But I can tell Hon. Members that when our primary producers are concerned, whether it be in agriculture or fisheries, we seem to be very slow in acting. That is disgraceful.
I come back again to the $1 billion payment. I recognize that some people say that this $1 billion was paid out on account of the election in Saskatchewan. I do not know. But whatever happened with respect to the $1 billion we are glad. We support that amount of money going to western farmers. What we are saying is that that was not enough. It is not the farmers' fault that the world price of wheat is down as low as it is. It is the fault of the European Economic Community and the fault of subsidization in the United States.
We have to look at these issues in a clear and concise manner. We have to make up our minds, as does the Government, with respect to whether or not we want an agricultural industry in five years' time or three years' time or two years' time or whether we want to see it disappear. I can tell Hon. Members that I have seen in my own province over the years some of the small family farms that disappeared and went into more corporate-type farming operations. It is a sad day when something like that happens, because when they get into trouble the whole community is in trouble. This happens when we get into specialized commodities. At one time we were very general in agriculture. Certainly, in Atlantic Canada in my province we had beef, pork, grain, potatoes and in the wintertime there was the woodlot. There was some diversification. But when we get into specialized farming in just one commodity and the price drops, as it has dropped for wheat, which is also what happened with potatoes, one is left with nothing.
There was nothing to pay off some of one's debts to tide one over.
I know that my time has expired. I am pleased that I had this opportunity to speak out on behalf of farmers as one Member of Parliament among many who understand the agricultural industry and who worked hard at it over the years. I think every one of us in the House of Commons should take a sober second look at what is happening in western Canada today, especially in respect to our agricultural industry. We should once and for all make a commitment here, before this debate is through, that we will support agriculture and maintain the industry. We should commit ourselves to doing our best to create more and better markets. The problem in agriculture today is with respect to the consistency in the market-place. As I said before, there is no problem to produce. The problem is to sell. I fought the Bill which dealt with the demise of Canagrex. It may not have been a panacea for all the ills of the agricultural industry. No one here said it was, at least no one on this side of the House. But anything that helps in creating and developing new markets in agriculture is good. It is good for our agricultural community which is the basis of community life in Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I normally would not be expected to speak on an issue concerning agriculture. Mississauga South is not an agricultural constituency. But I must advise the House that I have been directly and heavily involved in farming for the past 25 years. I am a partner in a very extensive dairy operation, as well as a partner with my son in a fish farm. I have some interests in embryo transfer and the transfer of cattle by air to other parts of the world. That type of activity has made me quite conversant with what is in fact happening in the reality of agriculture.
This debate got off on a very foolish footing. I am surprised it was even brought to the attention of the House. I wish to read into the record an article from the Alberta Wheat Pool magazine dated April 10, 1987. The heading is: "Farm Income Record in 1986". The article states:
Alberta Agriculture estimates that 1986 total realized net farm income in Alberta was $788 million, the highest level on record, and a remarkable 45 per cent over the 1985 level.
The record was achieved because of lower operating expenses, a healthier livestock sector and substantial government program payments.
Payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Plan, crop insurance and other programs accounted for an estimated 17 per cent of total farm cash receipts in 1986.
Payments in the form of farm fuel rebates, and feed grain adjustment payments and other expense reduction programs reduced total operating expenses by an estimated 12.6 per cent.
Total farm cash receipts for 1986 was not significantly different from that in 1985. Lower grain prices were largely offset by higher government subsidies and higher livestock prices. Total crop receipts were down by 7.7 per cent from 1985 and total livestock receipts increased by 6.7 per cent.
Total operating expenses for 1986 declined by 9.8 per cent. This is the lowest level of operating expenses since 1980.
Net farm income in 1986, which includes the value of inventory change, is estimated to have surpassed all previous records. Record total crop production

April 28, 1987
in 1986, following two consecutive years of drought has increased the value of inventory change by an unprecedented $582 million from 1985. This, combined with record program payments, has pushed net farm income to an estimated $1.28 billion compared with $457 million in 1985.
Mr. Speaker, where is the emergency? The Leader of the Opposition, totally non-conversant with what has happened, has indicated that the interest rates for Farm Credit Corporation loans are at an all time high. Let's get the record straight. The interest rate on a five year fixed interest term mortgage is now at 10 per cent, compared to a previous rate of 10.75 per cent; loans under the Shared Risk Mortgage Program dropped 1.25 per cent, to 9.5 per cent; the rate for a 10 year fixed term is 10.75 per cent, a reduction of one quarter of 1 per cent; loans with fixed terms of 15 years or more remain unchanged, at 11 per cent.
Under the Corporations Commodity-Based Loan Program, the interest rate remains at 6 per cent for the fully indexed option, while the rate for the partially indexed option has been reduced to 8.375 per cent from 8.50 per cent. And I could go on and on.
Mr. Speaker, the fact is, this Government has made sure that the interest rates charged to farmers by the Farm Credit Corporation are lower than people pay on their homes, lower than business pays on its activities.
If one can borrow long term money at 10 per cent at a time when the prime rate is at 9.25 per cent, that amounts to decent financing-and that is what has been made possible by this Government.
Let's talk about this Government's spending on western agriculture. When we formed the Government in 1984, the federal Government was assisting agriculture in western Canada to the extent of about SI billion. This year, it is estimated that federal government assistance to western agriculture will amount to more than $3 billion.
It has been said that we are abandoning the farmers. What utter drivel! It is little wonder that we stand in this place today responding to this fool motion, answering this fool's suggestion that there is an emergency.
Yes, there are problems. But, is there an emergency? I say, "no".
We have made sure that the farmers of western Canada have sufficient cash in their hands to plant their crops and to make sure that their bills are paid, they have sufficient cash to run their operations.
It has been said that we should guarantee future prices; that we should intervene in the market-place to guarantee crop prices next fall, next year, the year after and two years down the road.
The farmers today are on their tractors and are planting, and they will be doing so for another month. Assuming they get decent weather and that they are not bothered by hail, drought, flood or insects, they will have a crop; and hopefully
farmers right across the world will have a crop. But that isn't always the case.
While the future market may look glum today, it is a market that can turn around in an instant. We have seen it turn around.
Mr. Speaker, you and I were Members of this House in 1972, when there was a limit on how much grain a farmer could sell. Farmers who had grain but no permit to sell sold it under the table for as little as 50 cents a bushel.
We have been here before. We have seen the prices change rapidly.
Sir, it is about time that we all recognized that the real problem in agriculture, and indeed the real problem in business generally, has been too much government interference. We have guaranteed too many things.
We now have a problem in world grain prices because other Governments have subsidized the production of grains. Because of the over-supply, the market balance has been upset.
You and I both know, Sir, that it is the market-place that determines reality. We can wish to our heart's content that the wheat price be set at $8 a bushel or $9 a bushel. We can wish to our heart's content that Ontario corn would sell for $150 a tonne. But in the end, it is the market-place that will determine the price.
We can sit back and pretend that the cost of production is approximately average right across the country. People talk easily about the cost of production. But what in fact is the cost of production? The cost of production can vary dramatically from farm to farm. There are many factors involved, including the individuals working the land, the make-up of the land, the kind of equipment used, the kind of weather experienced, and so on.
Those are the factors that determine the cost of production. One farmer can make money at $90 a tonne for corn, whereas his neighbour couldn't make money at $120 a tonne for corn. And why is that? One has to look at the cost of production. One has to look at what it costs to produce that crop on the two farms.
The attitude that the Government can come in and guarantee the cost of production is absolute nonsense. It is something that varies from farm to farm, from district to district, from farmer to farmer, from week to week, from year to year. It is absolute nonsense to say otherwise.
Farming is the type of activity where you buy retail and sell wholesale. When a farmer is sitting on his tractor planting a crop, he doesn't know whether or not he will have a harvest in the fall. He doesn't know whether a newly born calf is going to grow; and if it does grow and is bred, he doesn't know whether he is going to end up with a heifer or a bull, and how it is going to grade. There are simply too many variables involved. You put your best efforts forward and you take the risk. The world is full of risk.
April 28, 1987

Let's get down to the real problem that is affecting agriculture right across the country, that being the price of land and what has happened to the price of land in recent times, with the consequent result on net farm equity.
Through the 1970s, the price of agricultural land was bid up far beyond all reality. The Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) cited the case of potato lands in Prince Edward Island being bid up to $ 1,000 an acre. Good potato land near Alliston was bid up to over $3,500 an acre. One wonders why land gets bid up that high. Somewhere along the line, there was a financial system in place that was prepared to put more money into agricultural lands than it should have; and we had people gambling perhaps a bit more than they should have. But that is the way the world goes. People do bid up properties beyond their value. The reality is that the value of the land is only equal to the value of the crops that can be grown on it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Right on!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
It is worth no more than that. The fact that the crop prices do not reach astronomical prices leads to the conclusion that land prices cannot stay astronomically high. That being so, who is going to be hurt?
Well, the land-owners themselves are going to be hurt, the banks are going to be hurt, the Farm Credit Corporation is going to be hurt. Lenders generally are going to be hurt.
That is what the market does on occasion. Somewhere along the line, you have to wash out some of these ridiculously high prices.
To suggest that we could somehow step in and guarantee some of these inflated values is utter and complete nonsense. It wouldn't do anybody any good. As I said, land is worth what one can grow on it and sell. If one has to plant and grow crops of lesser value, then the land is worth less money.

We have had a few things going for us. Interest rates have dropped, which has helped considerably in terms of financing. We cannot control world prices for commodities, and if the prices of land have to drop, then they will have to drop.
We have incorporated farm review boards and have tried to make it easy for people to settle their claims. A number of banks have taken substantially less than 100 cents on the dollar on their mortgages. They have rewritten their mortgages at less than face value and allowed existing good operators to continue to operate their farms and get them back in shape. They have recognized as lenders that they made a mistake.
The Farm Credit Corporation will have to recognize that it has made some mistakes and will have to take substantially less in some cases than the amount on its books.
Co-ops which advanced money that they should not have advanced to customers are going to have to take less than they have on their books. That is the nature of falling land prices.
However, there is sunshine at the end of the rainbow. The sunshine is that young people entering farming will be able to get in at a decent price level again. As well, people will be able to buy machinery at a decent price level again. The marketplace will work the whole issue through. If we sit back and say that we must maintain a moratorium on mortgages forever and ever, we delay facing the realities of the time. Realities of the time not faced today must be faced tomorrow. When we put a moratorium 19 months ago on FCC mortgages, people were facing foreclosures. Those people are still in difficulty, and to that extent it is time that they perhaps looked at and reorganized their affairs and lifestyle. If it means that some people who have borrowed more than they should must find another occupation or be something other than farmers, sometimes that is the way it has to be. There are other people with experience who want to become involved in farming.
I notice you signalling, Mr. Speaker, but let me indicate briefly that I have been involved in financing for a long time. In my years as a lawyer I only issued a writ of foreclosure on three occasions. However, I was involved in repossessions to settle mortgages on houses, farms, and businesses. The best thing we can do for someone is to say: "You are not going to make it. Let's settle it so you can start a new life, have new prosperity, and have the debt taken off your back". To say that to do some foreclosing or do some pressing on debts which cannot be handled is not to understand the reality of financing.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to participate in the debate and to speak in favour of the emergency motion brought forward by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). Both that Hon. Member and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) are agricultural spokespersons and farmers themselves. They have been out there on the Prairies in western Canada with their ear to the ground.
They and most farmers in the country would be somewhat astonished at the chilling remarks just made by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who really sort of summed it up by saying: "Let the market take its toll". The Hon. Member for Mississauga South did not deal with the cash flow issues facing farmers in western Canada. I intend to do that because farmers who are listening and watching in this debate know the agony among themselves as primary producers of what is really going on out there in the west. They trust that the emergency action taken by the New Democratic Party will in some way alert the Government to what they have been saying to us as we travelled throughout western Canada. Many Members, particularly from the government side, who have spoken in this debate talked about their roots in agriculture. The roots in my family go back over 300 years when my forefathers arrived in the Maritimes from Ireland as spud farmers. There are relatives of mine in almost every province and territory in Canada who are involved in agriculture in some way or another.
In my constituency in northwest British Columbia there is a deep and long-standing interest in what happens, not just in

April 28, 1987
agriculture, but certainly in terms of grain. We have one of the most modern, state of the art grain terminals in the world at Prince Rupert. With the upgrading of the CN line, people from Smithers to Prince Rupert are abundantly aware of the importance of the grain trade to our constituency and to farmers right across the Prairies. We see those grain cars coming through every day on their way down to Prince Rupert to service not only the Pacific Rim but other markets of the world.
Within my constituency as well there are hundreds of farmers. Most of them are involved in dairy and beef. There is some limited grain production, but principally in northwest British Columbia they are involved in various mixed operations.
I should like to spend a moment referring to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who spoke in the debate a couple of hours ago. He urged the media to make this issue a front page one from coast to coast in the newspapers and on the radio. Then we heard the remarks of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South who suggested that he was surprised the issue was even brought before the House. We also heard the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Gustafson), who is from the Prairies himself, saying yesterday as the debate began that there was no reason for it. Earlier this morning the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) said that it would be lunacy for any further assistance to be provided to the farmers in the West.
Who is really speaking for the Government? Why does the Prime Minister say that this should be a major number one issue, not just in western Canada but right across the country, upon which the media should be focusing and talking about to farmers, banks, machinery producers, and everyone else? That is what the Prime Minister said, but the majority of other Conservatives who have spoken have said that we should let the market take its toll, let the farmers go down, take away the moratorium, and not provide any floor price in terms of grain for the coming year.
One has to wonder who is really speaking for the Government. Because of the announcement in terms of the lifting of the moratorium-and we saw a 20 per cent price reduction last year-we will see a further 18 per cent drop for the 1987-88 crop year. One thing we know is that the Cabinet in the present leaderless Government has overridden the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). It certainly did not sound like the view they hold as those who are in most direct contact with Canadian farmers.
The Prime Minister now plans to make a grand tour of western Canada for three days to find out what is really going on there. I am sure that as a result of the emergency debate brought forward by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert there will be farmers at every place he touches down, unless he just touches down briefly for quick Conservative meetings where people are rallied in and rallied out and there is no opportunity for western farmers to have their views heard. I am sure
western farmers will try to tell the Prime Minister what they think about what his Party has been saying, that the emergency debate is unnecessary, unwarranted, and so on.
We in the New Democratic Party are calling for a number of things. At the very least, we are calling for an immediate government commitment to provide Canadian grain farmers with the guarantee that total grain receipts for crops being planted in the 1987-88 crop year will equal those of the 198687 crop year. That will cost between $1.5 billion and $2 billion.
We heard the Hon. Member for Mississauga South crowing about the lucrative area of agri-business in which he is involved. He said that he was surprised the issue was being raised and that we should let the market take its toll. There are farm families sitting out there in communities-men, women, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and other relatives-who are capable of calculating with the greatest of care.
We in this House have a responsibility to dispel the myth that is held in many of the urban areas of Canada, on Bay Street and among certain financial groups, that every farmer in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia has a huge farm, a huge bank account, a Winnebago, goes golfing for six months in Florida and keeps his feet up the rest of the year just planting a quick crop in the spring and harvesting it in the fall. That is hardly what actually goes on on the farm. Farmers take great care with everything, Mr. Speaker. At this crucial time they determine what to plant, how much to plant, whether or not to fertilize once or twice, what kind of farm improvements to make, whether to do some fencing somewhere, whether to move some of the grain sheds, what kinds of livestock to have, what kind of machinery could be bought, leased or borrowed.
All of these crucial questions are honed with a sharp pencil day after day in trying to figure out where a few pennies can be saved. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South for the Government says some producers can produce corn on a piece of land for $90 a tonne whereas someone on a farm nearby cannot make money unless he is getting $130 a tonne. We all know that, Mr. Speaker. We are talking about the broad issue of what is happening to the farming community in western Canada. We all know that. Members in this House were not all born yesterday. We have seen the Government increase taxes, increase service fees, increase freight rates, bring in Bills C-18 and C-19 which will see the dismemberment of all kinds of branch lines and add a whole new layering of costs to all kinds of prairie producers.
There are some things the Government has been doing that have been worth while. I am never one in this House not to point out the good things the Government has been doing as well as pointing out what it should be doing and should be addressing itself to.
This Government is working hard on the international front to bring peace to the world grain markets. We know what is
April 28, 1987

happening concerning the subsidization in the European Economic Community to its farmers, and then the rash move by the Republican Government in the United States to bring in the U.S. Farm Bill which provides, in some cases, to some buyers, one bushel free for every three they buy. In some cases it is even more lucrative than that. We know what the impact is on our Canadian farmers.
The sheer illogic of what government Members have been saying has to be pointed out in relation to that. They say, "Now we cannot continue the moratorium. It is creating a credit crisis and so on. Let the market take its toll". This is the same Government that 18 months ago brought it in. Let us take a look at the evidence given by the Farm Credit Corporation on March 27 before this House. With regard to farms with over $20,000 in sales, 8 per cent of those farmers are involved, so of the 171,000, there are 13,680 farmers involved, and 23 per cent of Canadian farmers have major cash flow problems, that is 39,330, for a total of over 53,000 farms in western Canada facing economic difficulties.
The same evidence comes from the Farm Credit Corporation. Six thousand of their borrowers are more than two years in arrears. Twenty per cent are in arrears at some level, 673 farmers were near the foreclosure level 18 months ago when this Conservative Government brought in the moratorium. The situation is worse and it comes up with a totally wrong-headed argument that now all of a sudden a moratorium should not be kept in place. The Government says it will be there forever and ever. What an interesting time it is to pull the plug on the moratorium right at the time when farmers are heading on to their farms to seed and consider what kinds of crops they will be putting into the ground!
We have the statistical information before us, but let us not just think of them as statistics as the government Members seem to want to talk about western farmers. They are men and women out there. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), pointed out the stress level that is found in the agricultural community, not just in the grain sector but in the beef sector, the dairy sector and the fruit sector. Throughout the agricultural sector in this country we are finding stress levels that are being studied by physicians far above those that you find in supposedly high stress occupations. As my colleague pointed out, an RCMP officer three days after being involved in an incident involving a shooting has only the same levels of stress that the average Canadian farmer experiences every day. For the Government to put such chilling remarks onto the record saying that this debate should not be going on, it is not an emergency, let the market-place take its toll, is sheer hypocrisy. It is ludicrous and the Government's arguments in this debate so far have been totally illogical.
The Government should not lift the moratorium until it announces a deficiency program for the upcoming crop year and it addresses the broad question of farm debt, which is about $25 billion across Canada, much of which is still held at
the high interest rates caused by the former Government, a point made by Members on the other side.
Government Members are always asking, "Where are you going to get the money if you need a couple of billion dollars to help the farmers now so you can put a floor back in the system and maintain some kind of reasonable and reliable financing for those farms?" Let us think back to the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) when the Little Egypt Bump came along for the Reichmann brothers in the Gulf deal. He said, "This is terrible". But once the loophole is closed it is closed, but after the cattle have left the barn. They get the billion dollars.
Let us look somewhere else, Mr. Speaker. Let us look at big corporations. There are over $30 billion in back taxes. Why don't we get the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) to collect some of the money owing from big corporations, particularly those which are capable of paying readily and easily right now rather than using their capital to gobble up other smaller companies which are proliferating from one side of Canada to the other? Why not collect some of that back revenue?
An interesting point was made at a convention I attended recently in Vancouver, perhaps one on which a lot of Canadians have not reflected. One gas station attendant working in Red Deer pumping gas pays more tax than any one of the major oil companies in Canada. That is a travesty, Mr. Speaker. Any single farmer in Canada pays more taxes than any of the large banks or any of the large oil companies. One bank teller in Regina pays more tax than any of the banks, including the bank that he or she might be working in. There is money out there that can be brought in to address problems which this House must respond to when emergency situations arise.
We are in a world that was crisis-ridden in terms of the availability of protein in particular, but in terms of grain we have to think about what is going on and think about what the Government is saying. The Prime Minister says, "This is a long-term problem. We have to think about currency decisions made in Punta del Este. We have to think about all these international issues". Of course we do, Mr. Speaker. That is why we were elected here and that is why we have a Government. What the Government is failing to address logically in terms of cabinet decisions is what are the effects in Canada of not addressing the ability of the farmers to remain solvent, not addressing the need for farmers to have a floor price whereby they can have reliable information on cash flow so they will know how much fertilizer they can buy, what they can spend on fuel, what they can spend on clothing for their kids, what they can spend on fencing, what they can spend on everything else on their farm. Instead, they are left in a crisis situation.
Let us look at what the farm leaders are saying. Let us have a look at what Wayne Easter, President of the National Farmers Union had to say yesterday. The Prime Minister says that this should be the major issue in Canada, front page, everywhere, a major issue on radio and television. All of his

April 28, 1987
back-benchers says no, no, no. That is not the case. This is not a big issue. Let the market operate freely. But with what does the Government start this session after Easter? A Bill on hanging. The Government did not start this session dealing with the crisis in agriculture. It started with announcements saying that the moratorium has ended. It is not going to do anything about setting a floor price. As a matter of fact, the Government is going to let it drop another 18 per cent after a 20 per cent drop last year. Here is what the National Farmers Union had to say yesterday as reported in The Globe and Mail:
I just can't understand why he would announce it now, said Wayne Easter, President of the National Farmers Union.
"Normally farmers feel a sense of optimism at this time of year", he said. But this tears the heart out of thousands of farmers".
Mr. Easter noted that the Canadian farm economy has deteriorated steadily since the moratorium was established in 1985.
"I think it's ironic that they are making this announcement on the same day as Parliament opens its debate on capital punishment," Mr. Easter said.
"To lose your farm is the same as capital punishment. When they lose their land, farmers feel that the life has gone out of them."
"Garfield Stevenson, President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, said the termination of the moratorium will cause a further decline in the market value of farmland.
"It's completely irresponsible and just not acceptable," Mr. Stevenson said.
"I thought the Minister had more on the ball than this".
Another spokesperson for farmers, Jack Penner, President of Manitoba-based Keystone Agricultural Producers, said that the termination of the Farm Credit Corporation moratorium will make it more difficult for farmers to get loans from banks and other lenders.
Let us think about what some of the Conservative Members have been saying. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has said that one of the factors involved when farmers are getting credit is the moratorium that is in place. Where do government Members get this airy-fairy idea that everything is just fine in western Canada? Where do they get the idea that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) can come in here and blow hot air about Punta del Este and all of these other matters for 35 minutes without dealing with the reality of what is taking place on the farms? When there is that stress level, that cash flow problem and those family farms in trouble, the Government has to act. To say it will wait a year or two and then see what kind of consolidation of land base there will be is not good enough.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) says that this is great because, as existing farmers are moved off the land, opportunities will open up for young farmers. What hypocrisy. Anyone who has read any of the history of Manitoba, Saskatchewan or British Columbia knows that the overwhelming majority of farms are intergenerational. When generations of farmers are driven off the land, we cannot expect someone to pop freshly on the scene to buy a couple of
sections of land and suddenly get it going as a major grain concern.
Let me touch on a few of the things the Government has done that have been important, but have not fully addressed the issues before us today. The Government has provided assistance to the farm sector, but it is now saying it will do so no longer. It provided assistance during the Saskatchewan election because the Prime Minister was awakened from his sleep, next to his Gucci shoe parlour, at five o'clock in the morning by Grant Devine saying that he would lose the election, he needed some money. The Prime Minister acted quickly then and made a big announcement of $1 billion.
The crisis is exactly the same now. We are facing major losses of markets to the United States because of the crippling effects of the U.S. Farm Bill and what is happening in the European Economic Community. To simply say that we will let as many farms sink as required over the next couple of years and then come forward with help is hypocrisy. The action the Government took to bring in the moratorium absolutely requires it to maintain the moratorium. The Government that gave $1 billion last year under exactly the same circumstances should give the same kind of money and more to the farming community now.
The Government has consulted farm organizations but it clearly has not listened. It has not heard what farmers have been saying. Simply put, what the Government has done to date has helped a little, and it is doing a little on the international front, but the arguments that have been made in this debate over the last 16 hours demonstrate to me and to every farmer in Canada that it is time to throw the bums out. Conservatives are not representing the farm community. Farmers will wake up and realize it the next time an election is called, and I hope that will be very soon.
