speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if it was perceived that it was my intention to cast any aspersions on members of the Opposition, that was not my intention. Indeed, I said that I myself was out of the House to attend to some urgent business in my office. I merely expressed my fear that I may have missed the debate. Obviously other Hon. Members feel the same pressures after a debate of this length.
I want to point out that I represent an area which is heavily dependent on agriculture for its economy; that is the Peace River country of British Columbia. That area has been a very productive wheat and forage-crops-producing sector, but it is an area that is perhaps suffering more than other prairie regions because it is the newest such area. Some of the area is still being developed. That it has not been settled for very long points to the fact that there is a heavier per capita debt load in the area. Of course, farm financing is the root of the crisis we are debating today.
In the 15 years that I have been here, I have experienced nothing that has caused me more anxiety and pain than this situation. I share with my constituents, my friends and my neighbours the suffering that has resulted from this serious problem.
I deal with people who have inherited farms which have been developed over three generations. Many of these farms were paid off at one point and were debt-free. Often, young farmers who had gone to school came home and encouraged their fathers to get into partnership with them, buy equipment
and develop the farms in the modern way. These people then would go to the bank or the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow some money, but they would find after a few years that the roof had collapsed and the land had eroded beneath their new machinery. They would then have to walk away from what their grandfathers had pursued as their first dreams, from a business that had sustained families for a long period of time.
Sir, you cannot explain in words what goes through the minds of these people as they have to make these decisions. All of us deeply sympathize with them. The question is, what can you do about it? What can a Government by itself do about this? In order to answer these questions one has to look at the costs. One has to first understand that agriculture in Canada is an export industry. We are not just feeding our own population. If we were, we would have to decrease our farm output in a major way. We do not have a population base to sustain the farm structure we have in place. Therefore, we are left heavily dependent on foreign trade.
World markets have undergone a critical adjustment in this century. I looked at some statistics the other day and found that at the turn of the century in North America 46 per cent of the people were engaged in the production of food. Today it is less than 4 per cent. Farmers have become more efficient. Research and development has produced better, healthier and faster growing crops. We have improved our market share. We have built on the strength that we have in Canada through improved species to put our land into production and help feed a hungry world.
However, we have become too dependent on world markets and there is nothing we can do about it. We are now in a situation where we are very much dependent on price trends, transportation facilities, climatic conditions, and other similar factors. We are perhaps more dependent than any other country on the policies of other countries and groups of nations who have chosen to pool their agricultural policies to become more efficient and better satisfy their own needs.
What has brought on this present crisis is an agricultural trade war between the European Economic Community and the United States. In attempting to find a long-term solution, as I see it, we should look at what the EEC has done. Certainly it is the cause of the situation we are in right now. Agriculture is perhaps the biggest factor in keeping the EEC together and developing in the way it has in the post-war period. What the EEC leaders said many years ago, as the community came together, is that a farmer ought to be able to earn as much in return on his investment and labour as anyone in any other industry.
There are of course countries that joined the EEC who are as dependent on agriculture as are we in Canada. It would not have been fair if the average income of their citizens was something less than that of the highly industrialized countries like Germany and Austria. So the EEC said it would have to

April 28, 1987
develop a program that would assure the farm-oriented countries an income comparable to that of the industrialized countries.
They immediately discovered that if you passed along the cost of securing such an income for the farmer to the consumers of the EEC, which would be the obvious thing to do, food prices would have to triple. Those prices were already high in Europe. Consumers were already paying in excess of 40 per cent of their disposable income for food. Therefore it was quite obvious that that could not take place. They could not permit the farmer or the farm dependent countries to increase prices to the consumer. There had to be some kind of subsidy.
The conclusion they came to was very simple. Instead of raising food prices to the point where half the population could not afford to eat, they would have to subsidize the farmer to continue producing cheap food and pass the cost through to the rest of society. They then taxed other industries to support the farm economy.
So far so good. If that were the basis on which the Europeans had developed their farm policies, that would have been fine. However, they should have as well brought in some production limitations and supply management. They did not. Because of the farmer's new-found wealth, production went up to the point where they are now heavy competitors in world markets. They compete with Australia, the U.S., the Argentine and Canada in the production of cereal grains. Had they put some limits on their production it would have perhaps worked, but they did not and now they have a serious problem. The EEC finds it very difficult to sustain this kind of policy.
In addition, they have created an even greater problem for Canada, the U.S. and other countries. The U.S., with its 240 million consumers, could afford to take a very aggressive stance against these EEC policies and subsidize their farmers until they were once again competitive. However, there just is not enough money in our treasury for us to compete with those kinds of measures. We are being ground between the U.S. and Europe as a result. We are sitting between those two millstones and desperately looking for ways to bring some sense to the whole situation.
What are the solutions? First, you have to break them down into the long and short terms. We hear the NDP lamenting the fact that we should be spending another $2.5 billion subsidizing our farmers. We should announce deficiency payments for the next crop year so we create some stability. Yesterday they told us we should borrow $5 billion to buy Dome Petroleum to keep it in Canada.
As I hear these things I ask myself where is the money going to come from? What difference does it really make whether a foreign company owns part of our oil patch or a foreign banker owns the whole country? There is no money tree sitting outside this place. You have to borrow the money, you cannot create it. We are being pushed more and more abroad and offshore in our borrowing. So I ask the question, how can you responsibly
mortgage the future of our children by going abroad to foreign bankers and borrowing the money to sustain these programs?
If the farmers need an indication of what they might expect from this Government let them examine the record of the last two years. What have we done? We have tripled the farm support systems that are in place. We are spending in this crop year over $3 billion, which is three times more than the previous Government spent in one year. Let us look at some of those programs. We moved very aggressively to keep the banks honest and to improve the services of the Farm Credit Corporation. We have made deficiency payments of $1 billion for last year's crop. That was not intended to do anything other than permit the farmer to put his crop in the ground this year. Then we will see what happens as we go along. We will see where we are in the fall. We will see if our efforts in the international arena, in GATT, our discussions with the industrial countries, discussions which we introduced, produce any results.
If farmers want an indication of what they might expect at the end of the next crop year they can examine our record. We shall not sit here and preside over the demise of the family farm, nor shall we preside over the demise of the farm economy, because it is part of our culture, part of Canada, part of our history. We shall ensure that it remains that and that farmers will get a fair shake.
However, it is not easy. There are no easy solutions. Perhaps we ought to look, in a global sense, at what the Europeans have done. Perhaps we ought to remind countries like Japan and some of the Asian industrial countries that they, too, have a responsibility to feed the world. They cannot rely on only the food-producing countries to do that and starve in the process. Perhaps we ought to develop a global scheme similar to that which the European Community has within its own borders. We are working toward that. We have introduced that debate in the national forum.
We have made a deficiency payment of $1 billion. There will be a payment made under the stabilization fund, which all comes from the federal Government. There is nothing left in the fund. There have been transportation subsidies, feed grain assistance, and crop insurance. There are freight rate subsidies and interest subsidies. We have also introduced a Farm Debt Review Board.
When the moratorium was put in place we said that it would stay in place until such time as there were checks and balances and another program in place. We have put another program in place and we are told it is working well. In 80 per cent of the cases which are examined a solution is found which is good for the bank, good for the farmer, and fair to the taxpayer.
We are not going to foreclose on 6,000 farms tomorrow morning. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has clearly stated what the policy of the Farm Credit Corporation will be. We have put in place programs which will permit the farmer,
April 28, 1987

when all is said and done, to make the transition to another way of life.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, before the Conservative Government came into power a farmer who lost his farm was not entitled to unemployment insurance or any of the benefits to which every other citizen is entitled. He walked away from the farm. He did not even have his house because that was part of the land on which the bank foreclosed. He walked into the city and stood in the soup line without a place to sleep. That has all changed. Adjustment programs have been put in place for the most extreme cases.
There must be more because the adjustments and prices which we are experiencing are not just temporary. The longterm outlook is not that good. We must develop long-term solutions and find different uses for our grain. In Dawson Creek we are building an ethanol plant, with the help of the federal Government. The province has been generous in helping us promote this concept. When it is in full operation it could potentially use all the grain produced on the B.C. side of the Peace River country. It will be converted to ethanol and, hopefully, be used in motor fuels. That is only one solution to which we could perhaps look in the future.
This is not a simple matter. It is a very serious crisis. All of us on all sides of the House recognize this crisis and we welcome the support of the Official Opposition and the NDP in helping to find a solution. There is no doubt in my mind, Sir, that in the short term we will have to find additional resources through the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, and others, to stave off the most serious of the impacts which we are experiencing. However, in the long term Canada has committed itself to taking the lead, to bringing together the producing countries and discussing this serious global crisis with the other industrial countries. We have introduced this debate in the international community and shall pursue it with great vigour.
As the NDP, in particular, points out, we must send out a signal indicating where our farmers will be at the end of the next crop year and what will happen to the crop they will harvest this fall. I cannot predict that at this point. If they need an indication they should review what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in many meetings with farmers before he travelled to Japan to discuss this matter with the seven industrialized countries. They should review the speech which the Prime Minister made early this morning in the House. They should judge us by our performance over the last two years.
They will find that we will be their friend rather than their competitor. We will ensure that Canada remains a strong producer of agricultural products, that we will continue to play a vital role in maintaining a vibrant farm industry, and that we will continue to preserve the family farm which is so much a part of our culture and history.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you for allowing me to take part in this important debate which concerns a historic crisis affecting our farming industry, perhaps especially in Western Canada.
The attitude of the government Members in this important debate can be summarized quite simply. Most of them claimed to know all about agriculture. They tried to prove it in various ways. Some said that they had lived on a farm for many years. Others told us that they knew about agriculture because they were married to someone from the farming community. They have quoted all kinds of facts to explain that they know all about agricultural issues. They have also told us that they know all about farming because of their large constituency in western Canada. It is indeed a fact that there are many Conservative Members from western Canada.
This automatically tells us what the most important agricultural issue is in the eyes of the government Members.
First, they told us that they knew all about farming, and then they said that they would explain what they have done for farmers. They listed a whole series of initiatives which they judge useful enough and relevant enough to give farmers hope for the future and security. We have been told time and again that this Government is spending one billion dollars to alleviate the dramatic problems of agriculture, especially in western Canada. In spite of the seriousness of the situation, farmers have been told: Do not worry, we shall take care of the problems; the past is a guarantee of the future; we shall be there to help you.
However, Mr. Speaker, in view of the seriousness of the problem facing these people, it is obvious that we need more than vague commitments. We need clear statements, firm commitments and official guarantees. We are now going through a crucial period in terms of our strategy.
The producers need to know in advance what the future holds for them, and they need to know exactly what the commitments of the Government will be. However, the Government has systematically refused to announce its plans and to give any indication that would enable the producers to face a very uncertain future.
It is as if a worker who needs his car to earn his living were to be told: We have repaired your shock absorbers, repainted your car and fixed your rearview mirrors, but we cannot do anything for you if there was a major problem, with the motor, for instance. This is what the producers need, Mr. Speaker, a commitment that the Government will do something about the sources of the problems facing this essential industry.
Faced with that, I conclude that if one is optimistic, one may believe or feel that one might be entitled to another billion dollars, for instance. But it is my view that in any serious analysis, in any intelligent reflection, producers have every reason to be extremely concerned, and for a number of

April 28, 1987
reasons. I listened a few moments ago to the Elon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) when he said: Listen, the situation is serious, I agree, the problem is dramatic, I acknowledge that, but we must be realistic, the market will have to straighten that up, market forces will have to apply. So what need have I to be more explicit? What need have I to give further details-all this means that those who are having difficulties, those who have accumulated significant amounts of debt will be wiped out by market forces, and they will have-I am using his own terms-to change trades, they will have to redeploy, change direction.
There are thousands of farm producers who right now have enjoyed a breathing space because of the moratorium, who sincerely believed remedial action would be taken, they could relax, difficulties could be met, especially financial difficulties. We have that Member here, who has been in this EJouse for a number of years, who supposedly is well placed to know the concerns and the needs, and this is what he has to say: market forces will have to decide; farming is no exception to rule, we must face up to the fact that the weak will go belly up, to the detriment of bigger ones. These are the facts, and that kind of statement in my view deeply concerned western farmers.
We have another farmer, a Quebec Member this time, the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, the Elon. Member for Bellechasse (Mr. Blais) who stated a few months ago: Farm producers in the near future will have to stop being welfare bums. That statement made a lot of noise, because in fact agriculture is a strategic industry in our economy, and it is an industry that had, has and will have to be supported by the Government, for all kinds of reasons, the two major ones being that it is an industry where participants do not have the ability to make fully informed decisions, the required information including two factors, the first of which of course is wheather conditions, the necessity to abide by nature. This in itself is something of basic importance, because farm producers do not have the ability other businessmen have to take enlightened and intelligent decisions based on all the facts. Producers do not have the capacity nor the possibility to predict what Nature holds for them. This is the first aspect.
The second aspect, Mr. Speaker, is the issue of international markets. At present, international markets are all-powerful, deregulating or, to be more accurate, destabilizing prices so that a country such as Canada has to perform in a very difficult and painful environment. For that reason also, Mr. Speaker, producers cannot take enlightened decisions and plan ahead as businessmen do. They cannot go and see their banker and tell him: "Sir, I cannot meet my commitments. On the other hand, I anticipate a fine season and good revenues." This is precisely what a businessman can do. Thanks to some studies which can be made, he can convince the banker or the bank manager to wait, to make him understand what basically makes sense. The producer cannot do so, because as I mentioned it, he cannot control nature, not to mention international markets. Such being the facts, the banker and the financier
is not an ally of the producer but his enemy, because with his conservative mind, the banker will expect the worst. And the worst, given what happened during the past few years, is quite dramatic. And as a result, several farms and facilities are now in very difficult situation.
Throughout that debate, we heard moving testimonies of farmers, of families of producers who are really desperate as there is a very strong possibility that they might lose in the very short term what it had taken them 25, 30, 40 years, and even in some cases, several generations to build.
In view of the attitude of this Government, Mr. Speaker, I think that farmers have every reason to be concerned, to shout aggressively and to demand concrete measures. An in my opinion, the Canadian Government must on the one hand take quick action as I believe it is essential to preserve that part of the market which we could only secure through several generations of work. On the other hand, I also think it is important to fight aggressively, on the international markets of course, while hoping that a relative harmony may be restored at some point. I believe there is a basic need to support producers for reasons which in my opinion are self-evident.
I would be willing to accept a statement like that of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who said: "Market forces should be allowed to work, and those who cannot compete should get out of the business, consider selling their farm and learn another occupation or relocate themselves"; I would be willing to accept that kind of theory if we were talking on an industrial level, if we were dealing with small and medium businesses. However, let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that it is an absolute shame to adopt and spread such a philosophy with respect to the agricultural community. We should understand that the agricultural industry is what enables us to feed our society, what provides us with the most basic commodities, those commodities which are essential to the welfare of society. Just on that account, and just to that end, I believe the Government should take an exceptional, distinctive and specific stand with respect to the agri-food sector. I think it is not decent or acceptable to view the agricultural industry as an ordinary economic activity on the same level as any other economic sector. In this respect, and for those reasons, the Government should have a reassuring, comforting attitude, an attitude which would enable producers, in particular western producers who are faced with a tremendous crisis, to look to the future with a maximum of safeguards. The producers who are now having problems should be able to go to their banker and say: Here are the statements of two senior Ministers of the Conservative Government who have made a firm commitment that, if the international problems are not resolved, they will make whatever decisions are necessary to help us. As I have already said, the Government should urgently announce its intentions so that the producers who are in the most difficult position will not make any hasty decisions in the belief that they cannot get what they need, and systematically abandon their farms.
April 28, 1987

Mr. Speaker, in view of the very vague and confusing commitments made by the Government, I am trying to put myself in the shoes of someone who is affected by the crisis and who wonders: Should I seed, and since the moratorium has now been lifted, should I take the trouble to go to banker and try to get an individual moratorium or to come to some sort of an agreement with him? Should I take all these steps? I have to ask myself these questions. First, it seems that one way to look at the problem is to say that the past is a guarantee of the future. This is a very common attitude which is admittedly acceptable from many aspects. However, if we apply this principle to the present problem, the western producer must still ask himself whether it is worth it to do these things.
Objectively, I believe that he should consider the statement of the Hon. Member for Mississauga who very clearly and honestly said that we have to get rid of the weak and that the market forces must be allowed to take their toll. There have been all sorts of statements to this effect, and we also have to look at the record of this Government after two and a half years.
As far as their achievements are concerned, government Members will naturally tell us, with the Figures to support their claim, that they have made so many promises and kept so many of them. As you know, Mr. Speaker, most of these promises were about minor issues. However, if we examine the basic problems of agriculture in the light of Government achievements, we naturally have to look at Canagrex. What has happened to Canagrex? It has gone down the tubes. What was its main purpose? To use the phrase we have heard in all the speeches, the purpose of Canagrex was to develop and identify external markets, which is a basic problem for Canadian agriculture. What has happened to Canagrex? It has simply been done away with.
When Canadian producers analyze what has happened, they must also consider the position taken by this Government with our American neighbours on the infamous 15 per cent tax on lumber.
As my allotted time is coming to an end, Mr. Speaker, I shall try to quicken the pace as I make my last few points.
We have also seen this Government increase inspection costs in what can only be described as a cruel and savage manner. The Government decided, just like that, to ensure that producers will pay for inspection costs: some $30 million were taken away from our producers' ability to pay, to the detriment of course of the quality of our products which always has been our international hallmark. We had a corporation for marketing, and we had good quality. The corporation was dismantled, then inspection costs were increased by $35 million.
Everyone is also aware, since it is in the news, of this Government's disquieting approach to the important matter of free trade. Everybody is concerned, nobody knows for sure what is the right banner. This is a picture admittedly that is somewhat summary. But, on the other hand, we have this Government's sales attitude, a Government that helps the
banks that do not have to put up with weather, that have control over shocks, that can plan in the light of financial statements, but that lose $1 billion because of very bad decisions. Very rapidly, on its own initiative, the Government decides to pay $1 billion to a few hundred people. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that in the current circumstances that $1 billion would be most useful.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that in the absence of strong actions, in the absence of clear measures, in the absence of self-evident measures, farm producers and especially western producers-although their concern is shared by Quebec producers-are extremely worried, and I think that as politicians, we should also be most worried in the face of such inaction, such totally irresponsible attitude on the part of this Government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to address the subject before the House today. I spent over two years acquiring a wealth of experience in the agricultural industry, and I had the privilege of being raised on a family farm that has been in the same family for over 300 years. I am therefore in a position to appreciate the constraints that have been placed on the agricultural sector over the years.
The Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif), who quoted me earlier, and unfortunately I will have to respond from the television screen, referred to an engine breakdown in Canada's agriculture. My father used to tell me, and I came to realize this myself, that the principle driving force behind our agriculture is often the heart and soul of the farmer. And if anything has been lacking for 20 years in this Chamber and in our Governments, it was that very heart and soul. The previous Government which ran the country for twenty years and allowed interest rates to rise above 20 per cent certainly did not have much soul. They were quick to forget it ever happened.
When the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe quoted me earlier on the subject of farm producers who do not want to go on welfare, I was, as so often, quoted out of context, and if the Hon. Member had taken the trouble to make enquiries and meet with farm producers ... 1 have 1,300 in my own riding, and I'm certainly not ashamed of that. In fact, I am very proud of the farmers in my riding, Mr. Speaker. I met them, and I spoke and still speak for farm producers who want to make a decent living in Canada and be treated as first-class, noi second-class citizens, and that has always been my message, in everything I have said and written. I think the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe should check his sources. These are just a lot of rumours which he took at face value, without checking any further.
Mr. Speaker, never has any Government done as much for Canadian agriculture as this one, and that has been crystal-clear ever since we came to power. When we came to power, Mr. Speaker, the previous Liberal Government had practically broken off every dialogue with the industry, and we know that Canada has 750 agencies involved in the agricultural sector.

April 28, 1987
Under the previous Government, however, and we remember its arrogance, there was practically no discussion or consultation with the agricultural industry. In fact, that Government went on tolerating a system that literally gouged our farmers with interest rates as high as 20 per cent and even 22 per cent and 24 per cent. Our Government restored the country's economy. It was not just a matter of dealing with agriculture but of considering the economy in general in this country. Our Government restored the economy by dealing with fundamentals, with factors that have a major impact on the economy such as the inflation rate, which was brought back to manageable levels, and also and especially interest rates. How can they say we were insensitive, when today interest rates are down to around 10 per cent?
Mr. Speaker, when I was travelling through my great constituency of Bellechasse during the election campaign, interest rates were the main issue raised by farm producers. In that respect, Mr. Speaker, we have fulfilled our mission and we will continue to monitor the situation very closely. How many millions and billions of dollars can this represent? A drop from 20 per cent to 10 per cent in interest rates on billions in mortgages and various kinds of loans made to Canadian agricultural producers. We are talking about billions of dollars, Mr. Speaker, and it was through the measures we took that interest rates were brought down to levels which agricultural producers could live with. The previous Liberal Government had never been unduly concerned about such issues.
For over two years, Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege-I repeat, privilege-to act as Parliamentary Secretary to both Ministers, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). The other privilege I had, Mr. Speaker, was to work for my peers and colleagues as chairman of our Party's agricultural caucus. As a matter of fact, our Party's agricultural caucus alone has more Members than the whole Opposition put together. Never before we took office had a Government spent so much time and energy looking after agricultural interests. The reason is simple: For the first time we had a truly national Government representing all regions of the country, whereas the previous Liberal Government spoke up for central Canada, Ontario and Quebec, completely ignoring the other regions of Canada. It was never in a position to listen to a group of people who, gathered around a table, did represent all regions of Canada. We set things straight. We restored the delicate balance, Mr. Speaker. We are aware of that. Not to mention our many meetings with the leaders of the agricultural community over the past two and a half years. To become familiar with these questions our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself went out to see the leaders of the farm community both at their annual meetings and here on Parliament Hill. Both the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board as well as
our caucus held several meetings with Canadian agricultural leaders to find out just what their problems were and to gain first-hand knowledge of the agricultural situation in Canada.
There is no ready-made solution. Perhaps it was easier in those days when none of the Liberal Members could represent certain regions of the country. The Government could go about its business with its customary arrogance, totally disregarding these regions. But that is not what we did. We would much rather discuss and consult these people right across Canada with a view to finding solutions which did not come easily but which are already giving obvious results. Besides, the national strategy put forward during the meeting of First Ministers who had mandated the Agriculture Minister to develop an agricultural strategy has been fruitful and an unprecedented consensus has already been achieved about that national strategy. Not a word has been said about this today. They tend to forget it. The Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) would rather dream of statements that go back a few years without even checking his sources.
Perhaps we could, Mr. Speaker, if you would let me, although many of my colleagues have already quoted some figures that speak for themselves about the plight of farmers in Canada . . . Mr. Speaker, for the past couple of years, $6 billion have been injected in the farming industry through more than 400 separate initiatives in every agricultural sector. That is a lot of money, Mr. Speaker. That is a lot of money and it shows that we have come seriously to grips with the problems faced by the farming community. More than 400 separate initiatives have been taken in the agricultural sector. What is the Liberal record? Let us go back 20 years in the past. Nothing was done.
Mr. Speaker, for the past two and a half years, our Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board has continuously met with wheat producers and their representatives both here and throughout the world, in spite of the inherent problems of that sector. If you set aside any partisanship in this regard, everybody is aware that international trade of agricultural products is a world-wide problem. We are dealing with surpluses. We are faced with countries like Europe and the United States that subsidize heavily the farming industry. Our Prime Minister and our responsible Ministers have already "rung the bell" about that issue and ensured that it is one of the major concerns during meetings between farmers' representatives and Ministers and leaders of the most industrialized countries.
Also we have made sure-and the Liberals never did it in the past-that for the first time, agriculture would be one of the main items on the agenda of economic discussions and especially during the new round of negotiation of the GATT agreements. That is what we have to do, Mr. Speaker. As a priority we must get all parties to sit around the same table. That is exactly what the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board has done on several occasions. He is constantly
April 28, 1987

travelling the world to try and maintain our share of the markets and we have succeeded repeatedly with several countries, the USSR in particular not so long ago. We are currently negotiating with China and Brazil. Everywhere in the world we are holding on to our share of the market. That was our duty and we defended with the utmost energy our Canadian wheat producers. I have not mentioned yet the money we invested during the last two and a half years.
Let us now talk about farm financing. One of the points I raised during my campaign-another one was interest rates- was the whole question of loans. Farmers were not happy with the loan structure set up by the Farm Credit Corporation. To give you an example, in the whole Province of Quebec, in 1984, there were only 75 loans. It had become laughable. The Farm Credit Corporation was giving out less money than the smallest credit union in my riding of Bellechasse, where there are some 60 municipalities, Mr. Speaker. Consequently, we had to put some life back into the Corporation in order to meet the needs of the Canadian farming community. That is what we did, Mr. Speaker, and I think we did well.
What about the new 10-year loan program of the Farm Credit Corporation, with a financing of $700 million, where payments are based on commodity prices, with a floor rate of 6 per cent. They never mention this program. They never did anything themselves. As for us, over $100 million in loans have already been granted under this program. This has helped to meet a need. The Farm Credit Corporation has already granted six or seven times as many loans as before in Quebec alone. These are the figures. We are therefore meeting the needs of the farmers better than the previous Government had done before the 1984 election. The figures prove it.
What about another initiative, the Farm Debt Review Board? In spite of the concrete action taken by our Government during the last two years and in spite of our lowering the interest rate to about 10 per cent, we found that a number of farm producers had unfortunately not succeeded in recovering from the black period, before our coming to power, or should I say the red period, since they were substantially in the red at the time.
What we have done, Mr. Speaker, is to show some compassion in dealing with the problems of the farm producers who are the most affected by the crisis. This is why we set up the Farm Debt Review Board. Under this compassionate program, local people analyze the files of farm producers and try to find ways to keep them on the farm. We are not trying as you said earlier to get farmers out of farming. That is completely untrue. What we said, and the Opposition should not try to distort our words, was that some farmers cannot remain in business. It would be structurally impossible. We cannot set up individual loan structures for all 280,000 Canadian farmers. We have to set certain standards. However, we have to try to make these standards more flexible. This is what we have done and thousands of farmers have been able to remain on the farm thanks to the Farm Debt Review Board. In some cases, it
may happen that some producers, in spite of that, are forced to get out of agriculture. We are all sorry, but there is no choice.
We also established a program to meet those requirements-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Unemployment insurance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
No! If you had taken the time to read the program we set up, the financial aid program to help make the transition, the relocation, the search for a job and the training of farm producers in other fields. Under your Government, there was no provision at all. Farm producers, being small entrepreneurs, were entitled to none of those programs. We opened the door for them, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration ensured that those programs were made more flexible to meet that need. This is what I call responding adequately to the representations of farm producers. Shared risk mortgage programs-already, a quarter of the FCC current loans are eligible to that program. The $500,000 capital gains program. Yes! They sometimes scoff when we refer to tax reform and ask that such a provision be abolished. But the provision had a direct impact on farm property transfer from father to son, and it enabled many young farmers to get started. It opened the door to young farmers, and this was an urgent request of the farming industry. We responded adequately, Mr. Speaker. There is still more to do. We are aware of it. We established a dairy policy that involves thousands of farm producers, $1,5 billion in that area. This is how we supported farming.
Consultation, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude on this, consultation since we came to office ensured that this Government's Ministers of Agriculture, that is, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board and the Minister of Agriculture proper, met regularly with all their counterparts in Canada to find together solutions to the problems that confront us. I urge opposition Parties, both the Liberals and the New Democratic Party, to help us, to sit down with us to earnestly look for solutions to the problems that confront us and to try and forget their partisan attitudes and their narrowmindedness in order to evaluate situations, and I would say the many benefits we extended to Canadian farm producers.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this special debate. We have a crisis in rural Canada the likes of which we have not seen since the 1930s. Despite that crisis, we have a Government that has announced that, as of tomorrow, the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loan foreclosures is going to end.
Assuming the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loan foreclosures ends, the banks and other lenders will take that as a signal that they can be a lot tougher on farmers who are indebted to them-and that would be like putting a skunk into

April 28, 1987
the hen-house. The banks will be going after the farmers with avengeance.
Mr. Speaker, this Government thought things were so bad a year ago that it put in place a moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loan foreclosures. Yet this year, with crop prices going down another 18 per cent, it proposes to lift the moratorium.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It doesn't make any sense.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of Tory logic we had in the 1930s with R. B. Bennett. That is the kind of logic that led to my grandfather saying that "Tory times are hard times".
In those days, the farmers of this country were forced to remove the motors from their cars and hitch their cars to horses, calling them "Bennett-buggies".
As a result of that kind of logic, this country rejected the Progressive Conservative Party for a couple of generations.
What we are seeing now, Mr. Speaker, is a re-enactment of the 1930s. Crop prices have reached the level they were at in the 1930s, while production costs are at the levels of the 1980s.
Mr. Speaker, as the Member of Parliament for Yorkton- Melville, I shall not sit idly by and watch the Progressive Conservative Government of this country destroy the family farm, destroy a way of life-a way of life that my forebears built in rural Saskatchewan and across this great country of Canada as they pioneered this land.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Government has taken the decision to end the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loan foreclosures. At the same time, it has announced that, on top of a 19 per cent rollback in wheat prices last year, this year the Canadian Wheat Board will be paying 18 per cent less on the wheat crop.
Mr. Speaker, we haven't seen these kinds of prices in rural Canada since the 1930s.
For the last 20 years, the people of western Canada have been looking for some fundamental changes in the way this country is run. What they want is fairness from Ottawa; what they want is equality from Ottawa.
Over the course of the history of this country, western Canadians have voted for a number of different political Parties. In the west, we had the formation of the CCF and the Social Credit Parties. Many western Canadians turned to John Diefenbaker and the Progressive Conservative Party.
After 20 long lean Liberal years in western Canada, the Progressive Conservative Party was elected to office in 1984. People had some hope, some optimism that things would change; that there would be fairness, justice and equity for the people of western Canada.
And, Mr. Speaker, what do we get? We get worse times now than we have had since the 1930s, when another Conservative Prime Minister, R. B. Bennett, was the Prime Minister of Canada, and he shafted the western part of this country during the Great Depression.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Are you being honest?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Let's talk about the 22 per cent interest rates that prevailed during the term of the last Liberal Government.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is great disappointment in western Canada. There is-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: My friend says, "nonsense". One needs only to look at the results of the Pembina by-election in Alberta, a riding that had a Progressive Conservative majority of 30,000 votes reduced to a pathetic 200 votes in the by-election.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It was good enough to win.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
They can be as cynical as they wish, but the people of western Canada are speaking, and they are saying "no" to this Progressive Conservative Government.
In fact, the Minister of Labour for Saskatchewan, a good friend of mine and a Progressive Conservative MLA from Melville, said at the recent Progressive Conservative convention in Yorkton that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) should go to the west and get his shoes dirty. In that way, he might better understand the problems of western Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: He should get his Guccis dirty, you mean.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: He is visiting western Canada next week.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I do not know what happens to Guccis when one wears them into a barnyard, but I wouldn't want to be around afterwards.
Here is a man, who can build a closet for some 84 pairs of Gucci shoes and whose wife can tear up a carpet three or four times, using public money and using money of people who contribute to the Conservative Party of Canada. That is the kind of man who is the Prime Minister of Canada, and that is why people in western Canada are saying no to the Conservative Party.
Let us look at the headline which appeared in this morning's edition of The Globe and Mail'. "Getty to caution leaders on western separatism". Premier Getty, a Conservative in western Canada, has said time and time again in the last few months that we have a Government which is so insensitive to western problems that unfortunately some western Canadians are turning toward separatism.
April 28, 1987

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
They know that. I know that. The man who had the courage to get up in the House of Commons and say that is the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour). He had the courage to get up and say that we have elected a Government which is insensitive to the problems of western Canada and because of that he would wait until the end of June before deciding whether to stay in the Conservative Party.
I know that some long-time distinguished members of the Conservative Party like the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) must be sitting in the back-benches gnashing their teeth and just cursing the insensitivity of the Government across the way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: You should have heard his speech this morning.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is not only Mr. Getty, the Premier of Alberta, who is disappointed with these birds. He said about three weeks ago that he might separate the Alberta Conservative Party from the federal Conservative Party because it is so insensitive. It is not only the Hon. Member for Edmonton- Strathcona. It is also the voters of Pembina, as well as the people of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba who are saying that it is time for a change and time to get rid of the Conservative Party which is destroying the country and western Canadian farms.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: What absolute nonsense.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Tory times are tough times.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: If John Diefenbaker were alive today, John Diefenbaker would be extremely upset and disappointed about how the Conservative Party has strayed from its roots.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: He is turning over in his grave listening to you.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: At one time the Conservative Party was a great nationalist Party. It stood up for a strong Canada.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It still does.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member is now talking about western Canada. I trust that he is not including British Columbia in his harangue at this point in time.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Yorkton- Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has the floor.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: What have they done in British Columbia?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Let's talk about British Columbia.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

They will tell us how the Conservative Party has sold out British Columbia along with its friend, Premier Vander Zalm.
I appeal to my friends in the Conservative Party to wake up. What is happening in prairie Canada is that a way of life is now being threatened like it was in the 1930s.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: I hear a British Columbian talking down to us prairie folk once again. I know I am just a prairie boy and a farm boy. I picked up a copy of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix- and I see the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis) is here-which contained the following headline: "Food bank restricts help to those near Saskatoon". The Saskatoon food bank had so many people coming to it that it had to make a decision that it could only give food to people within the near radius of Saskatoon. This is Canada. This is 1987. This is Canada with its resources, yet we have food banks giving food to people because they cannot get money to buy food and we have a Conservative Government which wanted to change things for people in the west.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I hear the Hon. Member saying: "What absolute nonsense". What nonsense is it that people in Saskatchewan are suffering? What nonsense is it that people in my riding are selling out because we have a federal Government which is providing grain prices for No. 1 wheat at $2.99
per bushel, while the United States has a guarantee of $6.10 Canadian per bushel of wheat? What nonsense!
We have a Government which is not supporting farm prices like the Americans and the EEC, and we have Government Members saying: "What nonsense".
Our farmers want a guarantee from the Government of Canada that as a minimum the final income for farmers next year should not be any lower than their final income last year. That is exactly what farmers want.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I will tell you what else our farmers want, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: They do not want a socialist Government.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I see the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East giving me thumbs down, indicating that farmers do not want that. I will remember that as well as I campaign in his riding in 1989.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: All the MLAs in your riding are Tories now.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The Hon. Member is saying that all the MLAs in my riding are Tories. They were Tories before. That is the biggest thing I had going for me. I have no bigger allies than the Tory MLAs in my riding, because people see them every day and are reminded about the fact that Tory times are tough times. That Party no longer stands for things that John Diefenbaker stood for. The best thing I have going for me is those five Tory MLAs. They will be the biggest asset I will ever have. Those same Tory MLAs are afraid to call the Saskatchewan Legislature into session.
Let us look again at this morning's edition of The Globe and Mail. It must be serious if it makes the eastern press. It indicated that Saskatchewan was warned about spending. The Lieutenant-Governor of Saskatchewan is warning that he will take action because the provincial Government seems to be continuing spending indefinitely without approval from the Legislature. We have a Government in Saskatchewan which is spending money without a budget and without calling the Legislature into session. That has never happened before.
They are afraid to face the people of Saskatchewan. They know that Tory times are tough times. We have a deficit now which is larger than we ever had in the Province of Saskatchewan, because of an irresponsible, insensitive Conservative Government. That is why I say the biggest asset that I have in my riding is five Conservative MLAs because when the next federal campaign comes I am sure even the Liberal Party and the Rhinoceros Party will move ahead of them and be my stiffest opposition.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we want a guarantee that next year's price will not be a dollar lower than this year's price. We also want a guarantee that this Government will
April 28, 1987

come to its senses, and instead of ending the moratorium tomorrow on Farm Credit Corporation loans and throwing over 600 families to the sharks, what 1 want tomorrow is a guarantee that that moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loans will continue. In addition, I want a guarantee to extend the moratorium to the private banks and financial institutions so that they will not be able to go out and take away a farmer's land. I see the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) is smiling in agreement. I am sure he is embarrassed to be a Member of the Conservative Party because he is afraid to get up in this House and speak to the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona and talk about the insensitivity of Gucci boy, the Prime Minister and the problems of western Canada.
The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East was shouting from his seat a few moments ago. He said what about the NDP and the CCF. Back in the 1930s when the Bennett administration drove us to despair and into poverty all across western Canada, when we had Bennett buggies and starvation in western Canada, the Saskatchewan people elected a CCF Government. At that time the banks were foreclosing on thousands of Saskatchewan farmers.
What did the CCF do? The CCF brought in the Homestead Act and said that a bank could not foreclose on the homestead of a farmer and take away the farmhouse and the farm from an ordinary farmer and his family. That is what the CCF did with Tommy Douglas. Who opposed that? Members of the Conservative Party. If Tommy Douglas did that in 1944, if he could bring in a Homestead Act to protect the family farm, the family homestead and protect the home for the kids, the wife, and everything else, why can we not do it in 1987? I ask that question of my friends in the Conservative Party. They are remaining silent now because they know if we did that we would be talking to their friends, the big bankers in this country. Of course that is where they get their campaign funds and when the banker says jump, the Conservative Party asks how high?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Be honest.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Honesty again. Take a look at the reports of the Chief Electoral Officer of this country. Take a look at the reports of where the Conservative Party gets its money. The Party that gets the most money from the banks is the Conservative Party of Canada. If anybody wants to challenge that, please get up and challenge it now.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Then they lend it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
That is why the Conservative Party will not stand up for the farmers. That is why it will not impose a moratorium on the banks taking over farmland and that is why we are having more and more farm suicides, depressions, crises, family problems, drug problems and alcohol problems all across rural Canada. That is why for the first time in the history of Canada we have a national Government that is running not second in the polls but is running third in the polls from one part of this country to the other. That has never
happened before. The people of Canada are rejecting the Conservative Party.
As I say, there are many things we can do. I would like to see the Conservative Party bring down farm input costs. Why doesn't the Government bring in legislation for generic farm chemicals so we can reduce the price of farm chemicals in Canada? Why doesn't the Conservative Government bring down fertilizer prices in Canada?
Why does the Conservative Party sit idly by when the CTC allows the CNR to charge variable rates, and with variable rates in Canada, which is like free trade and deregulation, the CNR and the CPR will play God. They will decide which community pays which rate and the small communities will be wiped out. Where is the Conservative Party when the CTC makes those kinds of decisions? The Conservative Party is silent. It is silent as it stands on the side of the railways, the banks, and on the side of the big private grain exchange.
The time has come in this country when western Canadians should unite in a crusade to demand our fair share of the national economy, a crusade that says Canadian farmers should receive as much as American farmers, a crusade that says American farmers and Canadian farmers should receive no less than what farmers get in the European Common Market. Why do Conservative Party Members rest content when the Canadian farmer receives $3 a bushel for wheat and the American farmer receives $3 a bushel for wheat and the American farmer receives $6.10 a bushel for wheat. I think that is shameful. I think it is disgusting and I appeal to the Prime Minister of Canada to call an election as soon as possible so the people of this country can vote and elect into office for the first time in Canada a people's Party that represents the ordinary average Canadian and make Ed Broadbent the Prime Minister of Canada.

It is a world problem, there is no question about that. Yes, the short-term things must be done and they are being done. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister of State for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the others have discussed that. However, I think it is important that the public understand that there must be some long-term solutions to a problem that is not the fault of farmers or of Canadians. It is a world commodity problem that must be tackled and it takes time. That is why we are now getting it to the top of the agenda. This Government is the first Government that feels that agriculture is so important that it has to be at the top of that agenda when world leaders meet and we are getting it there.

Members of the NDP quote Diefenbaker quite frequently. They like quoting him better than they like quoting Tommy Douglas. I got a chuckle out of the Hon. Member quoting him again today.
Agricultural policies must become more price-responsive. Support for agriculture should avoid production incentives. The support should be for the farmers, not for farming. Countries should freeze and seek to reduce governmental assistance measures that artificially distort world prices, as we are seeing with the European Economic Community's subsidization contest with the United States. Of course, Canadian farmers are being caught in the crossfire. It is very important that agriculture be kept on top of the international agenda. Countries should not introduce new import barriers not mandated by existing legislation. These basic principles should be implemented collectively. 1 do not think they can be implemented separately. Those are the principles on which we are working now.
I can tell Hon. Members that momentum is gathering for these kinds of principles. More and more, the Ministers of Trade and heads of state are realizing that agriculture is the number one problem in the world commodity base today and that something must be done about it.
Because of the momentum that was started when our Prime Minister insisted that agriculture get on the agenda of the Toyko Summit, many more actions have been taken by the Prime Minister, by the Minister for International Trade, by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin), who also played a very important role in Uruguay, as well as by many

April 28, 1987
others in the Government. We are making headway on the international scene and we will come to successful conclusions in the negotiations that are going on now.

I do not think any Government has consulted more with the agricultural industry, has kept them more up to date about it activities, has taken so much of their advice and has worked so hard with them.
Among all the farm groups and farmers I meet the Minister of Agriculture is held in very high regard. The Government fully understands the problems of agriculture, not like Governments of the past. The Government is taking action. There is no sense in me listing that action in my speech, but this action will continue to take place because the Government is sensitive. Well over $1 billion will be in the hands of farmers within the next five weeks because the Government is taking action. That is a very important impetus for the farm community. They know this Government cares for them. That is why they support us and will continue to support us.
Members of the NDP are great; between elections they are on top. You know what we should have in this country for the NDP; we should have elections between elections so then they might win.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

Come election time, when the Canadian people look around and see what this Government has accomplished, they are going to support us. They will support us next time around because they know we are on the right track and we are doing the right thing. That applies especially to agriculture. For once agriculture in this country is at the top of that important pecking order. Previous Governments placed it so far below that it was totally ignored.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Hon. Member which he indicated earlier he would answer. He is correct when he says that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) have raised a question at international meetings concerning the harm done to farmers all around the world by the tremendous subsidies paid by the American, Japanese and EEC Governments to their respective farmers. Those Ministers have suggested that there is movement, that we are going to see action, that we are going to see a reduction in those subsidies.
Will the Hon. Member tell Members of this House and the farmers of this country when the Government thinks those subsidies will be reduced in a real way? Is it five years from now, 10 years from now, 15 years from now? If it is going to take 10 years, a hell of a lot of farmers in this country will no longer be farming.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

I listened patiently to the Hon. Member's question, perhaps he would give me the courtesy of listening to the answer. Be fair about it.
I wish I could say it was going to be next year. I do not know. All I know is that for once at the OECD meetings coming up agriculture is going to be at the top of the agenda for discussion. It never was before. All countries are now beginning to realize the seriousness of the situation and how it is disrupting the agricultural industry right around the world. They want to do something about it. That is important and it gives hope to farmers. At least something is being done. It was ignored before. It is not any more. This Government is leading the charge and I am proud to be a part of this Government.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have heard talk in this House about interest rates and who has done the most for farmers. The debate has been going back and forth across the floor between the NDP and the Conservatives. They are calling each other intolerant. They are so intolerant of each other that they have almost lost track of the issue under discussion. I have heard comments today from speakers blaming-
