subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: -the Liberals for high interest rates in the early 1980s. Today, when we have a grain problem, who is the Conservative Party blaming? They are saying this is not a Canadian problem, it is the fault of someone else outside our country altogether. If they want to be intellectually honest in this debate they will fully appreciate and understand that the high interest rate problem they are always throwing up in this House was an international problem affecting every nation in the industrialized world. That is a fact of life. It is not just a matter of debate and conjecture back and forth across the floor of this House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Tell us how you handled it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I was quite interested in hearing the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) state that the Government was leading the charge on agricultural problems in the world today. We have all heard of the Charge of the Light Brigade. We know what happened to them. The
April 28, 1987

same thing is going to happen to the Government. When a crisis arises it is not what the Government says it is going to do, but how it handles that crisis that will determine how it is perceived by the Canadian people. The Government has been perceived as incapable of handling such crises.
We have seen all these arguments and debates on free trade. At the time we have an American Farm Bill creating problems for Canada the Government does not want to raise any fuss, simply because it does not want to create bad relations with the U.S.
I seem to be making such an effective presentation here in the House that someone is drilling a hole through the wall up there.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Someone is trying to get out.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
If that is a Government ploy I wish it would call off the driller. It is up to Mr. Speaker to protect all Members in this House, their rights and privileges. I would thank him for sending someone to ask that Conservative up there to put his bit and tools in the box until after this debate is over.
It is quite obvious that the Government is on the defensive on this issue. That is why it is so arrogant about other speakers. I was appalled this morning to hear a couple of Members get up and talk about members in the Opposition who have no right and no qualifications to speak in this debate. I would simply like to say to them that there are a few of us who have that right and those qualifications.
I have a very deep and abiding feeling for the agricultural problems of this country and for the grain farmers. I grew up on a farm. I lived on a farm for many years. I taught school in rural areas and lived in farming communities, not just in one location but in a few. I go back to the day when my mother and father hardly had a cent to their name, but their name was good. That is what happens in rural communities. That is what happened in those days. The word of people who owned a farm was good. It was as good as a certified cheque.
I can remember an all-day trip of 25 miles to town. You stopped at every swamp along the way to put water in the radiator. My father and mother, as I say, never had any money but they were very genuine, loving people. It is because we had parents like them that we got a solid footing for the rest of our lives. That comes from farm communities.
I can well remember driving up to a gas station with my father in a Model A Ford, asking to have $1 worth of gas put in the car and charging it. There was no question asked. They simply did it. It was fully understood. A good lesson to be learned in this debate is that a person's name is probably one of the greatest assets one can carry in this life. We are again seeing people who are having trouble getting $ 1 in these times when $1 is not worth very much.
I have stated that I have great feelings for the problems of farmers. There must be some form of debt restructuring worked out. People who have had problems with mortgages in the past, which the Farm Credit Corporation is still holding, should be given the opportunity to repossess their farms and start anew. That is only fair ball. Otherwise, in many of these cases the banks or the Farm Credit Corporation will sell those farms at a loss. Not only will they have lost money on the farm, they will have lost the farmer, who will have lost his livelihood and will have to find another way to make a living.
I can remember very well the days when we drove teams of horses for two, three, or four weeks at a time, from farm to farm, on threshings from early morning until darkness fell at night. Farm women do not and have never received enough credit in this world. When my father and the rest of us were working until dark my mother used to milk every one of the cows by hand, turn the separator, feed the calves, and clean up everything after she had done her own day's work. I say this because 1 do not want to hear remarks from the other side of the House that no one in the Opposition is qualified to talk about farm problems. That is an arrogant attitude that this place would be well rid of.
During this debate on grain in western Canada the farmer's pride is coming to the surface. He believes his credibility is at stake. When farmers cannot make their payments they tend to blame themselves and feel guilty, even though they are living in an environment over which they seem to have no control. That is the time when the sympathy, the empathy, and the understanding of their financial plight must come to the fore.
The credibility of farmers and their desire to continue to farm will affect the entire community in which they live. It will affect the fertilizer dealer, the farm implement dealer and the local garages. The farm economy reaches into almost every facet of our society. It is not strange that that is so today, because that has always been the case extending back to pioneer days. Fish was a major economic item as was timber and agriculture, and western grain in particular. Western grain was the reason for the great boom in railway building across the west. That is the type of thing which is in jeopardy today.
Parliamentarians should have pride in those three major economic factors which have been the foundation of Canada. We should have pride in the people who built up those farms and who have carried them on, in the people who built up the transportation systems to serve them, and, indeed, the people who are trying to sell grain today.
Why are we pussyfooting around with the American Farm Bill rather than saying up front, as the Government should, that it is absolutely bad international relations for Washington to have brought forward the Farm Bill which is highly subsidizing grain and practically putting the Canadian farmer out of business? If one government is going to do that, another government is either stuck with doing the same thing or it will ignore a large sector of its own economy.

April 28, 1987
This is the test of the Government. Will it bring in a plan for debt restructuring for the farmers to try to get them over the hump? Will it then become more aggressive in the international market on their behalf? It is all right to stand up in the House and talk about trade talks and how the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) took his efforts to Tokyo or Uruguay, but that is not much help to the western grain farmer today when the Farm Credit Corporation will have the opportunity to foreclose on Friday of this week, two days hence. Banks will move in too, because they will see this as a cave-in of the Government with regard to supporting the moratorium on mortgages. It is a sad day when the Government has lifted the moratorium on farm mortgages without having anything else in place to support the farmers, anything for them to work toward, anything to give them some hope.
I have here a list of the various grain and seed prices, the cost of production and the return from sales. It is sad that the American Farm Bill is subsidizing American farmers and their grain to try to outdo the European Economic Community, which is itself trying to outdo the Americans. Agriculture is so structured and financed by government in all those countries that the only position the Government of Canada can take is to be prepared to fight the international markets. It must get together with international governments and come to an agreement, because everyone is hurting each other.
This is a time for solid leadership in this country and throughout the world on agricultural problems. We do not need the Charge of the Light Brigade, about which the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) speaks. We need someone sitting at the table with a firm knowledge of the subject and with empathy for the farm community back home which is witnessing tremendously tough times, which is putting in crops, buying fertilizer, and selling the product for far less than the cost of production. The only way the farming community will exist is by being subsidized in the same way as is the European Economic Community and the American farmers.
This is a tough question and the solution is debt restructuring. That is what should be put in place instead of the removal of the moratorium from mortgages with absolutely nothing to prop the farmer up until we get over this international hurdle.
I come back to my original statement that the Government cannot handle these crises in a knee-jerk fashion, as they arise. Governments will be judged on the manner in which they handle each crisis as it arises. The Government has pulled the rug out from under the farmers by telling the Farm Credit Corporation that as of Friday of this week it is free to move into those farms and foreclose on mortgages. Is that the policy of the Government?
During the last election campaign my opponent said that the Conservatives would solve the agricultural problems in Canada in two years. The Conservatives have had almost three years,
yet today we see that the farm community is facing a bigger disaster than ever.
People are not impressed when they see the comparison between past issues and present. They are not impressed by the Government passing the buck or by the Government becoming so intolerant that it cannot conduct a civilized debate.
Let us consider other questions relating to the farm community in this country. Let us consider rural post offices as they concern the farm community. The Government does not want to attack the real problem of economics within the Post Office corporation, so it singles out the small postmasters in the small rural communities where they believe there is no clout to fight back. They will force every mail contract to go up for tender. It does not care whether that mail contractor has been doing an excellent job or whether that mail contractor has excellent relations with the people along the rural route. The Government will bring in someone else unless that person is fortunate enough to retain the contract.
The sad part is that rural mail contractors have only recently reached a price which makes it worthwhile for them to operate a rural service. For years, they worked for nothing. I was one who supported them over the years because those who come from a rural riding know the service that they provide and the necessity of that service.
In order to get the message of the farm community across it is necessary to have television and news media that relate to their problems and understand the real crisis that they face. The recent terrible decision by the CRTC to allow John Bassett and his friends to bring in another major television station into Ottawa must be the most inconsiderate and unworthy decision of intelligent people. It will destroy the advertising market and the income that already exists for the mid-Canada television network that has stations across eastern Ontario, northern Ontario, Pembroke, North Bay, Sudbury, and Timmins. Furthermore, it will be to the detriment of the CJOH Station here in Ottawa because it will remove revenue from it.

I hope that the Government will announce before Friday that it will come in with a debt restructuring program for farmers who are in trouble and thereby show the great empathy which it claims to have for the farm community. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief, and I thank the House for its consideration.
Let me return to the economic problems and whether the Government has enough sympathy to understand the plight of individual farmers. One need only imagine the farmer who is wondering whether he will even put in a crop, knowing full well that if there is no help coming from Ottawa he will be selling his product for less than it is worth, and if he does not go down now he will go down later. What a future!
When we consider the great contribution agriculture has made to Canada and the contribution we have made in research and development to assist other countries in the world, I think it is time that some of that considerate attitude was displayed at home in dealing with our farmers. They not only have to risk the weather, they must risk dealing with the world market.
I mentioned the European Economic Community. Our farmers also must risk the results of the American Farm Bill, as well as the Conservative Government which promised them everything in the last election. Farmers do not know where they stand today, and I call upon the Government to bring forward a constructive plan that will lay the groundwork to save the farm community in this country. I call on the Government to show some of that empathy because it reflects the heart and soul of the pioneering and modern industries that relate to the agricultural community in this country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with interest to the Member for Renfrew-Nipis-sing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) as well as to the Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson). Both of their speeches contained some rather startling facts.
Let me deal with the Member for Egmont. He was a member of the P.E.I. Legislature and subsequently became a Member of the House of Commons. While I give him credit for having taken some interest in agriculture, when he was a member of the governing party in the Province of P.E.I. and the House of Commons, at no time did I hear him speak up for the farmers when the Liberal policy that was in place was to the disadvantage of his constituency.
The Hon. Member for Egmont spoke of corporate land ownership. Corporate land ownership came about because the Government of Canada, particularly under the leadership of the former Minister, the Hon. Eugene Whelan, ignored some of the very basic and historical policies that had kept the family farm in place. He abandoned price stabilization payments. Historically, price stabilization payments were made before planting. That is the request of the NDP and the Liberals at the moment. They say the farmers should get their money beforehand so that they can plant.
However, I never heard any member of the New Democratic Party bemoan the fact that the horticultural industry could not get price stabilization payments before planting. As I made representations in this House on behalf of the potato industry, about which the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) and myself are very basically and critically concerned, there was not a squawk when they could not get the money, if they could get it at all, in time to plant. Why then is the New Democratic Party so concerned at this moment of seeking agricultural support when its policy has not been agricultural at any time in a meaningful way, and when it has never supported anyone but the Liberal Party, whether it be in committee or in the House? The NDP objective has been to keep the Liberal Party in power, not that there should be good government in Canada.
I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as one touches on the truth, the chirping from the NDP begins, the interference, the heckling, because they know they are extremely vulnerable historically as it relates to agriculture. The Member from Vancouver who has not been associated with agriculture, laughs. I think that merely emphasizes the lack of concern and knowledge the bulk of NDP Members have as it relates to agriculture. Certainly, with the exception of two or three, those Members are devoid of good advice and have not acted on behalf of agriculture. In the process of my remarks I will emphasize-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
They cannot stand the truth of the weakness of their historic position and their determined intention to exploit the downtrodden for their vote regardless of what may be the consequence and without having specific suggestions and policy which would correct the position of the downtrodden.
If those Hon. Members want to get down to cold hard facts of policy and become believable, then I think it is time for Canada and this House to pay attention to them. However, in the past they have been grossly supportive of agricultural neglect by the Liberal Party, and only now are they waking up to the fact that historically they have been wrong and they would like to be right for a change.
There was no response from either the Liberal or the New Democratic Party when 10 per cent of all the potato farmers in Carleton-Charlotte and in the constituency of Madawaska- Victoria fell through the economic skimmer. It was then that corporate land holdings began to develop. It became so bad in Prince Edward Island that I believe the Government of P.E.I.

April 28, 1987
passed legislation to prevent corporate acquisition of land. The little family farm could no longer survive under Liberal policy, yet Liberal policy was supported religiously and without concern for the farmer by the Hon. Member for Egmont and received total support from the New Democratic Party.
Where was the Hon. Member for Egmont, for instance, when feed freight assistance became of very little value to Atlantic Canada? Where was the New Democratic Party? Where was the lady from Vancouver at that point in time? Her voice was not heard.
I would like now to raise a few other questions. Where was the New Democratic Party when apple juice flowed into Canada and we became the gateway to the American market for subsidized product by the European Economic Community for shipment to the United States? Not only did the Europeans export a highly subsidized product and destroy the apple juice industry in Canada, but we were the gateway for damages it might do in the United States, supported, of course, by the NDP with no action by the then Liberal Government. Where was the New Democratic Party and where was the Liberal Government, because they then held the seats in the Niagara Peninsula? Where were they when foreign fruit arrived in Canada at less than the cost of containers and packing in Canada? Where were they as a large portion of the Niagara Peninsula and the Okanagan fruit industry were destroyed because of that? Where were the members of the NDP at that point? They were supporting the Liberal Party, which had a policy to have industrial trade and to hell with agriculture.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Who supported the Liberal Party? What are you talking about, supporting the Liberal Party?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Those Hon. Members have now become extremely conscientious in their support of the agricultural community of Canada after ignoring it utterly and completely.
One of the difficulties in Canadian agriculture today was caused by the abandonment of the price stabilization policy which Jimmy Gardiner, who was a good Minister of Agriculture, even if he was a Liberal, conscientiously, assiduously and regularly supported. When that was abandoned, where was the NDP? They paid no attention to the pleas of the Conservative Party on behalf of the fruit and vegetable industry of the Okanagan and the Niagara Peninsula. They were not with it. But I believe they now feel they have an agricultural community which might support them if they could now sham their way in an attack on the Conservative Party while still virtually on every occasion conscientiously voting with the Liberals?
It seems rather unjust that this debate should be taken on without any recognition of the contributions which have been made. Where were those members of the NDP, those heroes of the west today, at the point in time when a shipment of grain went from the European Economic Community and the subsidy paid for that shipment exceeded the price the Wheat Board was paying the western farmer? The subsidy alone exceeded the Wheat Board price for the grains exported on
that day. There was not a word of that from the NDP, not a word.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: We went to Brussels directly and we protested.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Not a single member of the NDP criticized the Liberal Party's stupid trade negotiations which permitted that to happen. But we took their apple juice to the detriment of the Niagara Peninsula.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: We ran against the Liberals in the election of 1980.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
You ran against the Liberals so you could get a chance to support them by your behaviour after you got elected.
I have to say that I have some sympathy with some of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins). I too saw some of the things he has related in his remarks. However, at that point in time it was the policy of both the Liberal and the Conservative Parties to keep the farmer in his place by recognition of his need with subsidies or price stabilization payments when the market was down. It was the Hon. Mr. Whelan as Minister of Agriculture who abandoned that. It was when the Trudeau Government took over this country that the Minister of Agriculture began to have no voice. That encouraged Canada, province by province, coast to coast, step by step, but not necessarily in order. It encouraged the Province of British Columbia to use its own treasury to support its agriculture. It encouraged Alberta at a later date to do the same thing, and it encouraged production of items which were already in surplus supply in Canada. It encouraged the Province of Saskatchewan to get a land bank and to support the increase in herds, which proved to be absolutely devastating to the cow-calf operation. Where was the NDP at that point in time? They were still voting with the Grits who mismanaged that structure as well. The NDP was still voting with the Grits, and the quicker it is known that this was an act of a chameleon, the quicker the public will know what this show is.
The New Democratic Party has not mentioned that the interest rates for FCC are now lower than they have been since 1979. It is not mentioned that certain emergent loans are made to the farmer at a rate of 2.5 per cent. It has not been mentioned that $750 million was paid out of the grain stabilization fund. It was not mentioned that $1 billion has been paid to the western farmer in addition to that.

That is the commitment that has been made but that has not been mentioned at any point in time in this or in any other debate.
I say again-and it has been repeated both in attack and in defense-the presentation by both the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party is totally and utterly misleading. It is recognized by every honest Member of the House that there are some people in the farming community who cannot ever, ever handle the debt load which they have undertaken. None are more willing to admit that than the farmers who have appeared in Saskatchewan before the appeal boards or the farmers who have appeared before other appeal boards under Farm Credit Corporation arrangements. None have been more willing to admit that than the farmer. It is absolutely and utterly impossible that every single last farmer can be held up. It is just not possible.
If members of the NDP want to heckle, let them remember their total inconsistency in terms of their support of the Liberal Party as it governed this country.

speechtext:
Do you suppose those fellows are run down yet, Mr. Speaker?
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) is quite knowledgeable, I think. I was very disappointed with the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville who should be knowledgeable in agriculture by who made a speech which was at best misleading and at worst-I guess I am not allowed to use the language that I would like to use in the House. Let us say that it was misleading and much, much more. It certainly did not depict the situation of agriculture in the west or in any other part of Canada. But the thing his speech did do is to ignore agriculture in every part of Canada except the the grain grower, and that is absolutely and utterly inexcusable. I say that because from Vancouver Island to St. John's, Newfoundland, there are farmers who need recognition, and they shall get it from this Government.
I want to repeat one of the remarks that I have made. If the NDP were conscientiously and historically interested in agriculture, why did it support the Liberal Party which failed to negotiate a deal with the GATT structure and which did not recognize the expenditure of billions of taxpayers' dollars to subsidize agriculture both for domestic consumption and for export? Why did members of that Party not upgrade the Liberal Party at the point in time when that subsidy exceeded the Wheat Board's payments of the day for the export of grain into our own markets?
I have seen hypocrisy, Mr. Speaker, but I submit to you that the NDP at this moment in time on the basis of its history and its present plaintive representations to Canada can very properly be accused on an historic basis of a hypocritical structure and a hypocritical presentation without the facts and of failing to recognize the contributions that have been made. It is quite proper that an opposition Party should ask for more. That, perhaps, may be the exact position that the Opposition

April 28, 1987
should take. But to fail to mention the assistance that has been extended to agriculture is not good moral behaviour which is expected by the Canadian population from a Party within the House.
When one tries to exploit the farmer when he is in difficulty by an about-face imposition and by a pursuit of the vote and the vote alone, I submit that that is the cruelest exploitation that the farmer of the country has ever experienced as it relates to the Liberals and their historic performance, and as it relates to the NDP and its support of the Liberals.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to stand and to speak to this very important topic today. I must say to the Hon. Member who just resumed his seat that I think it is quite an indication that he sees the New Democratic Party as a threat. Indeed, the polls should confirm that for him. I say that because he devoted his whole speech to a listing of references to the NDP. As the hon. gentleman who sits at the Table could tell him, most of the facts were, of course, distorted. However, I will not waste time in refuting them.
I wish to concentrate my remarks today on the impact of the economic situation with which the families of Canada are faced, which is stressful and which has become even more so this week. I would like to look at it from the point of view of the critic of social policy. I would also like to pay tribute to the many, many thousands of farm women across the country who face intolerable stress along with the rest of their families and who are carrying tremendous workloads.
We know that today we are very concerned. In fact, the reason this emergency debate went on all night last night and will continue to go on as long as this Party has speakers to put up is that we are extremely concerned at the announcement made this week that the Farm Credit Corporation will be given information to begin to foreclose on family farms. This comes, of course, as my colleagues have said over and over again, on a deepening crisis, where we have seen prices for Canadian grains plummet by 20 per cent last year, and a further 18 per cent this year.
This must be simply terrifying for farm families who already are coping with unbearable pressures and feelings of hopelessness. It is those pressures and sense of hopelessness that will be the theme of my remarks today.
A number of Hon. Members have spoken from their experience as farmers themselves, or having come from agricultural communities. I grew up in an agricultural community in southern Ontario, and I continue to share some of the very strong feelings that our rural population hold for their communities.
In my remarks today, I shall be speaking to the findings of some very significant authorities. Before getting into the main
theme of my remarks, I should like to repeat once again that the New Democratic Party is today calling for a commitment from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)-and I would hope that this commitment will be forthcoming-that, at the very least, Canadian grain farmers be provided with a guarantee that total grain receipts for crops planted in this crop year will equal at least those of last year, $1.5 billion to $2 billion, moneys which are so essential for our western grain producers.
We acknowledge that the Government is working on the international front, and that many of the problems can be attributed to what is happening on the international front. However, as Canadians, we cannot tolerate this threat to the basic economy of Canada.
As well, we hope that the Prime Minister and his Government will reverse the proposed lifting of the moratorium on foreclosures, at least until a deficiency program has been announced for the upcoming crop year.
It is important, also, to address the broad question of farm debt, much of which is still at very high interest rates, interest rates which were, of course, tolerated and in fact escalated by the previous Liberal Government.
Many thousands-not just a few families, as the Minister said earlier in this debate-of farm families will be adversely affected by the lifting of the moratorium on FCC loan foreclosures. In addition, we know that the banks, credit unions, trust companies, and other lending institutions will follow the lead of the FCC, thus leading to increased foreclosures.
This is a very serious problem. What I should like to do in the remainder of my time is to focus on this problem from the point of view of farm families and farm women. In that regard, I shall have reference to a report presented to the Standing Committee on Agriculture on May 12 of this year. This is a report prepared by Dr. Jim Walker, a research psychologist at Brandon University.
Dr. Walker and his colleagues carried out a very extensive study of farm families. During the course of their work, they heard farmers describe the "heartbreak of trying to cope with impossible economic situations". They heard from farm wives and husbands describing how their marriages are slowly falling apart; they mention the fact that they saw farmers break down in tears while filling out the survey.
In addition to the traditional stresses that our farmers bear, farming has now become an almost intolerably stressful occupation. The policies of this Government do not recognize this, nor do they deal with it. This Government, through its proposal to lift the foreclosure moratorium, is adding the additional threat of foreclosure.
This particular study highlighted a number of stress factors. It is a study that should be of great interest to those who are interested in human nature, human behaviour. The researchers found that rising expenses are at the top of the list when it comes to creating stress, followed by low commodity prices.
April 28, 1987

The lives of farmers are stressful because of their concern with the continued financial viability of their farm. They find that they have too much to do in too little time, particularly the stressful work at peak times.
These are all situations that cause stress in farm families. But even more important, and I note that this fact has been documented in other reports I have studied, up to 80 per cent of the respondents quoted Government policies and regulations as causing stress. Other factors are long work hours, weather and crop loss due to wet weather, not to mention equipment failure and the Government's cheap food policies. Those are just some of the factors that lead to stress in farm families.
The study to which I have reference was conducted over a year ago. Added to the stresses that those families were facing at that time is the additional stress that the current situation imposes on them. Day in and day out, farmers and their families have to deal with a great number of stresses, many over which they have little or no control. They are powerless to control many of these stresses.
Farmers are strong, independent and resourceful people, and today we see them turning to professional help as they never have before, and all because of the physical and psychological stresses they have to suffer.
I should like to highlight some of the situations outlined in the report. The report cites the example of a Saskatchewan farmer who complains of being under a lot of stress. It quotes him as saying, "I feel I have a lot of stress, and I am always so tired, without any reason". Fatigue is a common symptom of chronic stress. Of those surveyed, 49 per cent reported frequent fatigue.
The threat of stress to the family unit also shows itself in many different ways. One farm wife was quoted as saying, "I was 30 hours a week off the farm. The stress was incredible during peak periods. There is more stress than I can handle. I hope our marriage makes it, but I do not know that it will."
We have physical symptoms within families. I will not go into them. We have reports of serious disruption of sleep patterns, personality problems, health problems. Indeed, these stresses not only constitute a threat to the marital situation, but in fact lead to behavioural problems.
All of these things are related to family stress, stress which is caused by the intolerable economic situation in which our farm families are living.
Another farmer had this to say. "I often wonder what I would do or how our family would manage if we quit farming, or were unable to continue to farm. I am presently 32 years old. I have two pre-school children, and I really do not have any reliable farming future. We are just living to have three meals a day."
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) in his speech, spoke of the food banks in Saskatoon, and that is something that is astounding to me. Being from Vancouver I am used to seeing food-banks in that city. That in itself is an
immoral and deplorable situation. However, I had not realized that we now have members of our farming communities going to food-banks. The food producers have so little money to buy food for their table that they are now going to food-banks in Saskatoon and are in fact being turned away.

Getting back to the survey, another farmer is quoted as having asked those carrying out the survey whether they knew of anyone who wanted to buy a half section farm in the south western corner of Manitoba. That was a year, maybe two years ago. It may be that that farm has since been the subject of a foreclosure application, or perhaps it has been sold. In any event, my suspicion is that that farmer has now lost his farm.
It is little wonder that the members of our agricultural sector look to the future in despair. In fact, according to this survey, 11.4 per cent of those interviewed had in fact thought of killing themselves. According to the survey, the rate of suicides in farm communities is extraordinarily high. The instances of suicide in rural areas in Manitoba where the study was done were much higher than in urban areas. As I said, there has been a tremendous increase in people with mental and other health problems.
The report refers to another farmer who put it this way. "Many days I feel I cannot face another day". He indicated that it was extremely stressful to try to make ends meet and hold things together,that he had his best 30 years in the farm, and that if he lost it he would have worked all his life for nothing. Then he asked: "Does this make me a total failure?"
This farmer and his fellow farmers have not contributed to the situation. They contributed labour to their farm operations by working night and day over the years, yet they have no control over the situation. They have elected Members of Parliament from the west and from other parts of Canada to do something about it. The Members in the House can do something about the situation which is hurting these families. I appeal to my fellow Conservative colleagues to get to their Prime Minister today and to do something about it. They have the power to do it.

speechtext: He was here.

speechtext:
I hear them saying that he was here, but what did he say? He said nothing. He spoke for 40 minutes and made no commitments to the farmers of western Canada. I think it was absolutely immoral.
I also want particularly to mention the increase in violence occurring in rural communities. 1 have heard this from many women's organizations. We tend to think of it as an occurrence in urban communities. Transition houses for battered women have been set up. For instance, there is one in Brandon,

April 28, 1987
Manitoba, which has experienced a 50 per cent increase in the number of women who have sought shelter because of family violence in the rural community around that city. Also there has been a 70 per cent increase in the number of children who are in shelters because of family violence.
I have attended many hearings as my Party's critic for the status of women. Children who are battered now will grow up to be batterers. There are many long-term problems.
I hope Elon. Members will read this excellent survey in detail which was taken in May, 1986 before we had the present punitive policies and lack of action. It concluded as follows:
We believe the danger signals are all there. We believe it has reached the point where farm stress is killing people. We believe that the risk in the increase in the incidence of rural violence appears great. We believe we owe it to those who feed all of us in Canada to respond with action, with compassion and with humanity.
Again I appeal to the Government, particularly to the Prime Minister and the Minister responsible, to reverse its policies and to respond with action which will relieve the situation today, at least temporarily, until the more complex problems can be turned around. I appeal to the Government to ensure that the foreclosure policy is not allowed to go forward, so that we protect family farms and those who are facing devastating situations in their homes.
I should also like to refer to the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women. We do not usually think of this group being concerned with farmers, but it also talked about over a million people living on farms, less than half of whom are women. It dealt with the financial stress which is pressing in on farm families. Although the report was written a couple of years ago, it indicates that they are experiencing intolerable stress.
The number of family farms decreased by 13 per cent in 1981. While the net farm income in Canada decreased, total farm debt increased by 17.5 per cent over a 10-year period. It is much higher today. The 1984 survey by the Farm Credit Corporation showed that 17 per cent of farms were in severe financial difficulty. Surely it is up to almost 75 per cent today. In 1982, 19 per cent of farm families in Canada lived below the poverty line, as compared with 13 per cent of non-farm families who lived below that level.
I have attended child care hearings and Secretary of State hearings before which farm women have appeared. We have been told that they can hardly find enough money to buy groceries and about the nightmares they have because the bills are piling up. We were also told about the triple burden of farm women. Usually they are working with their partners on the farm in farm activities. Often they must take their children along with them on tractors. They are also carrying on traditional home-making roles in caring for the home and the children. In addition, they are often the ones who must go into nearby villages to work part time or full time so that there will be some cash to put food on the table. We talk about double discrimination and double disadvantage for women; these women are triply disadvantaged.
Let us add to the situation the current drop in farm prices this year, and the fact that there has been no commitment on the part of the Government to help farm families even as much as it did last year. We commend the Government for stepping in last year, but we must have it again this year. There must also be a commitment to do something about the foreclosure problem.
I see that my time is almost up. I had many more comments I wanted to make, but I should like to mention particularly the whole question of child care because it is a very current and important issue. We were told by many farm women, and also studies showed it, that there has been a very high incidence of accidents involving children on farms.
It is very critical that we have a different kind of child care for farm communities, one of the issues which was written up at length in the report of the Special Committee on Child Care. It recommended, in addition to normal funding, that Agriculture Canada should promote the safety of children.
Our own NDP report entitled "Caring for Canada's Children" strongly recommended that the federal Government establish a community initiatives fund which would receive $26 million this year and would be continued over the next five years, so that farm communities could develop innovative child care, such as buses picking up children or child care workers going to the farms. It must be a different kind of care than that in the cities.
In addition, we know that farm women share the concern about general agricultural problems. They also have concerns about equality from the point of view of their role on the farm. A whole new generation of farm women is adamant that they must be recognized as equal partners in both their marriage and their farm business. I am very glad to say that this is beginning to happen, with younger farmers particularly.
Farm women have many difficulties getting financial recognition in their own names. They must have land in their own names. They must qualify as operators. Farm women should be recognized for Prairie Grain Advance Payments and other farm assistance programs. I am glad to say that one of our Members has been working on that.
Stabilization plans and marketing boards should recognize both producers-the husband and the wife. Farm spouses cannot contribute to their own future under RRSPs. We are also very concerned about wages, contributions to the Canada Pension Plan, and unemployment insurance coverage. Rural women want a recognition in matrimonial property laws. I could go on and on and on. Farm women and support groups come out with recommendations and I hope when we have more time we will look at them.
[DOT] (M50)
I appeal again to the Government to rescind the decisions it has made that will increase the pressures on farm families, particularly on farm women, and to provide financial assistance, to make sure there will be no foreclosures either through

the Farm Credit Corporation or, even better still, something further.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak in the House today. As a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, I have had the honour and the privilege of listening to farmers from coast to coast talk about the problems and challenges they will be facing in the months and years to come. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) who spoke earlier mentioned the crisis situation and state of shock being experienced by families in western Canada. I agree, and I share her concerns. In any case, I must admit that unlike her colleagues, she showed some common sense in what she said, except where she referred to day care centres in rural areas. I think that logically, and if we want to be sensible, our priority should be helping farm families and not opening Government-supported day care centres, at a time when families are in such tremendous difficulty.
Mr. Speaker, since we are discussing agricultural problems, I would like to mention to the House that I toured the rural areas in my riding recently and met all the organizations in my riding, from the Outaouais to Mirabel.
I found that in my riding, at Notre-Dame-de-la-Paix which is not very far from here, potato farmers are having serious problems. They know how concerned I am about this, and I would like to remind them today that my riding office and I have taken steps to try and find ways to help these farmers.
Mr. Speaker, I think I can say with some pride that it may be thanks to my efforts that today, the Office du credit agricole du Quebec may be willing to help these potato producers.
Mr. Speaker, I come from a riding that has suffered a great deal as a result of the policies of the previous Government, and 1 would like to say that once again, we have been able to deal with a serious problem created by that Government. I am referring to the obscene expropriation of Mirabel farmland as a result of which at the time, hundreds of farm families in my riding were uprooted.
Mr. Speaker, the very Liberals who today claim to be the sole defenders of the poor and the homeless had no hesitation at the time in evicting for the purposes of their own shameless liberalism, entire farm families which have never fully recovered from those barbaric measures.
Today, many of these families have gone back to their homes and their land, feeling that at last, a Government has given them their due. Mr. Speaker, the people of Mirabel are no fools. They know that going back to farming after so many years is not easy, and that they will have to think of ways to find a niche within a controlled market such as the market for milk, for instance.
Mr. Speaker, Mirabel farmers have set their sights on objectives that may seem very ambitious today, but I am sure that in the medium and long term they will be vindicated. I am
referring to their export projects. The Mirabel UPA is about to develop a unique expertise in international agriculture. They intend to combine foreign expertise with their own and then export their methods to developing countries.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to emphasize these facts in the House today to indicate to what extent farmers in my riding, in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada can, as the Prime Minister said in his remarks this morning, be ingenious when we give them a chance to show what they can do.
The Government of the Progressive Conservative Party took action. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), bolstered by the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) leadership, made it a point to give top priority to the agricultural sector because of the war of subsidies between American and European producers which drove prices even further down and threatens our traditional markets. For quite some time now the farm commodity trade has been the weak point of GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, particularly so since 1955 when the Americans demanded exemptions with respect to their domestic production subsidies. The conference held in Uruguay made it possible to reach a compromise so that at least the matter will come up for debate. We are not satisfied with talking about it, Mr. Speaker, we take action.
Since yesterday I have been listening to the speeches of NDP and Liberal Members and I am quite simply bewildered by the paralogism of opposition Members who have the nerve to say that the Conservative Government has killed agriculture. They have the nerve to say that. Mr. Speaker, how can anyone be so blind, how can anyone stand still when listening to so much verbal trickery on the part of New Democratic Party Members who would have Canadians believe that if they were in office-Heaven forbid!-they would have done better than the Liberals. They would do better than the Conservatives or any other Government which would have been in power during times of such serious crisis as the one we are experiencing now. I can hardly wait to talk about such absurdities during the next election campaign. I am really looking forward to the day when the written and spoken press will at long last write and tell the truth about the economic illogicalness of this political Party which would go as far as bringing relations between men and women under state control.
It is unbelievable, Mr. Speaker, newspapers these days are full of articles about the contributions of opposition Members and their insanities. How do you explain the fact that the press does not even bother to mention the interventions of Government Members so that Canadian who are listening to this debate might have a better idea of what this Government has done? There is still room for improvement, of course, and nothing is perfect, as the Prime Minister said in his remarks this morning. Still, for the sake of equity, people must be made aware of our record. Mr. Speaker, I must tell you this, I think this House has become a sick place.

April 28, 1987
I regret having to say so, because it is incredible that no reference has been made to the tax rebate of 6.5 cents per litre of fuel in addition to a special discount of 1.5 cent granted to farmers as well as mortgages based on primary agricultural products, the setting up of committees to review farm debts, the Canadian rural transition program, reduced interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, the capital gain exemption of $500 000 on a farm, the Grain Advance Payments Act, the long-term dairy policy. No mention has been made of all that, because there was no scandal to be denounced. They are good news. Special programs worth several million and the most recent program worth 1 billion for grain producers, and I could go on. What is the matter, Mr. Speaker, with our parliamentary system? Lies make the headlines while true facts are not mentioned. People can talk through their hat in this House and any sensational news item is reported and when Canadians are wondering what is going on, we are unable to tell them the truth.
Farming is experiencing a serious crisis. I deeply regret it. Mr. Speaker, I am telling you from the bottom of my heart that we should help our western farmers who are indeed desperate, I know, having read and heard the many representations made. 1 think it is really unbelievable that because of farm debts, our colleagues representing other provinces should witness the breaking up of family farms which were the cornerstone of our western economy. Mr. Speaker, no government or elected member can remain insensitive to that. That is why we are part of this great country.
It is the "raison d'etre" of our Confederation. It is in times such as these that we should close our ranks and show generosity. Mr. Speaker, it is nobody's fault in Canada if the Americans and the European Economic Community subsidize unreasonably their respective farming communities, making it possible for purchasing countries to get the lowest prices imaginable.
Mr. Speaker, when our commitee on agriculture visited Washington last year, we met the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture. I asked him the following question: How can you say that you are our friends and extend to us such a warm welcome, when your Farm Bill is causing so much damage to the grain industry which is so dear to all Canadians? The Secretary replied that he understood my point quite well, but that Canadians themselves should try to understand the United States which is faced with huge farm problems.
The Prime Minister of Canada is not to blame. Mr. Speaker, I hope and trust that all Canadian voters, yours and mine, honourable friends, will realize that what the Opposition is saying is sheer nonsense. I am sure of that, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps I mention this unnecessarily, for Canadians are certainly much more enlightened than the Opposition gives them credit for.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that our trading partners cannot boycott European or American goods which are cheaper than ours just because their subsidies are hurting our farmers. These countries are faced with serious problems too. People
are all alike. When we go shopping, what do we do? We choose what is the least expensive. That is quite natural. How can a country as large, but as sparsely populated as Canada compete on an equal footing with the United States where the Government can collect revenues of billions of dollars each time a tax increases by one cent? We have a small population and limited resources. I find it quite incredible that we should talk about nationalizing. A commitment of $1 billion was announced a short time ago. After our Government hade made this commitment, the New Democrats and the Liberals immediately said: Give us another billion! This would make $2 billion. I do not even know where we can find $13 billion to subsidize day care. They speak about billions as though they were speaking about nickels and dimes. We have to be realistic. Matters are getting out of hand, Mr. Speaker. Fortunately, the Canadian public saw what was happening in 1984 and elected a Progressive Conservative Government with a Minister of Finance who knows about figures and who knows that one plus one make two.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, as I have not much time left, I would like to say that we, in Quebec, were proud to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announce a long term dairy policy. We were proud to be able to tell Quebecers recently that, for the first time ever, a Canadian Government had allocated $1 billion to Western farmers. This is not peanuts and this money was being spent in Canada. For the first time ever, $30 million will be spent in Quebec. That is a lot better that nothing! These are real initiatives, Mr. Speaker, these are real policies. We have taken action and we want people to know it. Perhaps more people would know about it if it were not for television reporting which gives the impression that there is no one on this side of the House. Yet, there are 211 of us. We speak, but no one ever reports what we say. The focus is on the Opposition Members who believe that they are the only ones who have anything worthwhile to say. There are limits, Mr. Speaker, and the truth has to come out. This is why I wanted to take part in this debate. I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture for two years. I have been listening to the Hon. Members and they do not even know what they are talking about. They should come and see what is going on in the Standing Committee on Agriculture. They would realize to what extent Canadian farm groups are supportive of what our Government has accomplished and that they keep on saying so week after week. Listen! I do not know where you get your stories, but if you bothered to drop in during the Standing Committee on Agriculture, you would realize that what you are saying does not make sense.
It was said in the Throne speech, Mr. Speaker-and I am very proud and honored to be a part of a government, of a political party, the Progressive Conservative Party, that does things .. . We do not only talk, Mr. Speaker, we do things. I would like to recall what the former Prime Minsiter said one day in a conversation. Prime Minister Trudeau was so arrogant in those days that he thought that he was the
April 28, 1987

permanent one man show. No one, he thought, could match his wits an his talent. So, one day, he asked western farmers how it was that they had to sell their grain. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, what brains it takes to utter such absurdities.
So it is easy for someone outside the ring, watching a boxing match-I love boxing-to say: "If I had been in his place, I would have pounced him, I would have done this, I would have done that!" But when you are inside the ring, it is not the same.
I look at the Hon. Member opposite who once was Solicitor General and who must remember from his time in office that things are much easier on the other side where Members can say whatever they want and pick at any small news from reporters who are themselves too busy to make their own research. A reporter I will not identify, Mr Speaker, said that he relies on what Opposition Members say to be part... Reporters have become the Opposition's researchers. Imagine! Opposition Members come to the House saying: "I have learned from a reliable source-" when, imagine, Mr. Speaker, the information appeared in the Toronto Star. They hold as the absolute truth whatever is published in the Toronto Star.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say the Government has acted. I am proud of the Prime Minister. For the first time, the agricultural matters are on the GATT table. For the first time, they were discussed when President Reagan came here. There are even some on the other side of the House who have no respect for visitors, who allow themselves to say anything at all, even to interrupt a speech by the President of the United States. That is going too far, Mr. Speaker. There will be an election, Mr. Speaker, and we will see then the effect of their behaviour if they keep this up. It will be fun, Mr. Speaker. I am anxious to start campaigning and reveal the truth.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Having had the pleasure to hear from beginning to end what the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) had to say, I intend to address some of the points she raised. I will not try to answer her questions about the Toronto Star article, for this newspaper did not seek my advice as to what it should print, and I said what I said to the Toronto Star reporter because I believed it to be the truth. The Hon. Member has made a few statements which I should like to repeat, for I believe they are quite funny. First, she said that farmers todays are happier than ever before. They appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture to say that they are happy. Then she said that they are faced now in western Canada with the worse disaster since the Great Depression of the 1930s. I just cannot see how farmers can be so happy when they are faced, as she said, with the worse disaster since the Great Depression. Third, she emphasized that the Prime Minister can do nothing. Why ask the Prime Minister to do nothing. Canada is a very small country compared with France which is now selling much more grain than Canada, and it is certainly not as large as the United States. Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with these statements as well as with others.
A final point which she raised is that Parliament is facing very hard times, that we are wasting our time with such a debate, that we should consider other matters and stop talking about this problem for which she feels there is no solution or at least about which the Prime Minister can do nothing.
There are no farms in my riding. There are no farmers living there. I am a city slicker, I suppose you could say. Why would someone from the city want to stand up and participate in a debate like this? I would like to begin by putting a marker on the farming industry of this country on behalf of city people.
We in the cities of Canada are very proud of our agricultural community. We are proud of the fact that this is a great agricultural power. We are disturbed to hear that France now produces more wheat than Canada. We are concerned that the price of wheat dropped 20 per cent this year after dropping 18 per cent last year.
We look across our country and see an industry hurting and people suffering. Yet we hear government supporters saying there is nothing that can be done about it. There is nothing the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) can do. They have given the farmers $1 billion and they should be content with that. That is not enough.
We in the cities of this country are not satisfied and we do not accept the fact that the Government just this week announced that foreclosures will begin on farmers who have defaulted on government-financed loans. We are taxpayers just as they are, but we do not accept that. We do not think the Government should be making the situation of the farmers worse and worse at a time when the Government has failed to announce whether there will be deficiency payments or not. You cannot expect a farmer in this terrible plight to just roll along, as in the 1930s, and go looking for private financing while being unable to tell the banks or the co-ops or the mortgage companies that there is going to be a deficiency payment and what it is going to be.
Another thing we know about farmers is that they are the biggest risk-takers in the public interest in the whole of the economy. I do not know a businessman or a worker in urban areas who takes the kind of risk that the farmer does. He has to decide whether to plant, what to plant and how much to plant. He has to sit back not knowing what his interest rate will be or the exchange rate on the Japanese yen, French franc or American dollar. He does not know what the weather will be. One or two rainfalls at the wrong time can make all the difference. Yet the agricultural sector takes those chances year after year with the backing of the Government, the Canadian Wheat Board and the backing of a certain set of policies which, to a certain extent, subsidize the risk they take. Yet this year, after a terrible year last year, the rug is pulled out from under them by the Government. City people, although we are not direct sufferers in the situation, do not like it, do not agree with it, and do not accept it.

April 28, 1987
I would now like to come to the Hon. Member's point concerning Parliament. Because there were not many Members on either side of the House at the time, I had the distinction of hearing the whole speech by the Prime Minister this morning.

speechtext: A good speech.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
It was a good speech. You could say it was a speech I listened to from one end to the other. However, what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) does not realize is that speaking is not good enough. It is not good enough for him to stand up and tell us what is wrong with us. It is not good enough to go on at great length insulting the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). That is not what Canadians want from the Prime Minister.
I agree that Parliament is a place where talking goes on. The opposition Parties talk; they have criticisms, ideas and questions. Yet there is only one Party here that can act-the government Party. After the last election that Party came into office with 211 seats and with promises to solve all the problems of the country, particularly those of the west were there is a deep sense of grievance. The Government brought with it from the west the great hope that its concerns were going to be the concerns of the Government.
I heard every government Member who stood up criticize Mr. Trudeau for asking, why should 1 sell your wheat? He said it. I read it after he said it. However, the Government of Mr. Trudeau sold wheat. He asked, why should I sell your wheat? He then went on to sell it in record volumes year after year after year. So much for talk. That Government is doing nothing but talk.
The only reason the opposition Parties are dragging this on is to get the Government to do something. What are we getting? The Government is not doing something. It is telling the country how terrible we and the NDP are, how terrible are the policies of the past. The Government is telling the Canadian people how much it loves the farmers. Every speaker has said that the farmers are the backbone of the nation, that we count on the industry, that farmers are needed, that we have a special mandate as a country to produce grain better than other countries who can do it only with subsidies. Yet what are we doing about it? Nothing.
We have to keep this up in spite of the objections of the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) until the Government stops talking and starts acting. It is the Party with the mandate to act. We are the ones, if you like, with the mandate to criticize, to make proposals, to carry on a debate, to surrender Question Period for a day to make a point. It is the Government that has to act.
We call on the Government to act. Not to tell us things which in its opinion have brought us to the situation we are in, things that we should have done while we were the Government, things that the NDP are doing or not doing in relation to the Liberals.
What does that have to do with the plight of farmers in western Canada who were told by the Government that they would be represented in this House and who have been betrayed in this one week by the opening of the door to a foreclosure process on government mortgages and a refusal to indicate whether there will be a deficiency payment and what that payment is going to be?
This is a terrible time for farmers. This morning my Leader referred to some figures dealing with what it means to a farmer to be paying interest at current rates. Members opposite jumped up and reminded us what interest rates used to be in the past. In some years they have been higher. However, there has not been a year when the real rate of interest paid by farmers over the Consumer Price Index at an annualized rate has been higher. In other words, the real interest rate that the farmers of Canada are paying on these mortgages is very, very high and growing. The Government has to take account of that as well, but it is not doing so. It is not looking at the burden farmers have to bear.
I listened with interest as well to the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) when he talked about how the farm situation was so terrible that we just had to let some farmers go down the drain. He said we just had to recognize that there would be farmers who would go down, family farms which would have to fold. That is just not good enough for the Government. That is fine for him to have as his opinion; people have opinions like that, but that is farmland which can be used.
The process of foreclosure and sale which is now being contemplated by the FCC will only result in some other farmer being on that land after the legal process is over. That is unfair, uncaring and wrong from a Government which made so many promises and has had so much support from western Canada.
The Government must do more. Before this debate is over it must stand up and put something concrete on the table, rather than this continuous criticism of us and this obsession about what is wrong with the NDP. The Government must put something on the table to support the farming industry which put so much confidence and faith in the Government.
I was looking at the story of the sugar-beet industry before I came in here. This is another example of a western agricultural application by a Government which gave that sector so much promise. The Conservative Government claims to be committed to western farmers, yet has still reached no agreement with the Manitoba sugar-beet farmers. They are at loggerheads. The farmers have done no seeding yet this year, or at least they had not a week ago when this material was prepared.
What excuse is there for the Government not getting on with solving the problems of the sugar-beet industry and the other problems which are being referred to by so many of us so well? As I keep saying, we can refer to them but only the
April 28, 1987

Government can do something about them. The time is now, today, for the Government to do something about them.
The Prime Minister wanted us to realize, and he explained very well, that there are a lot of international problems, that other countries are subsidizing their industry. I am not in favour of a world solution which will result in over-production and over-subsidization. That does not make sense to anyone. 1 understand that the Prime Minister wants to have such a policy ended in whatever countries practise it. However, Canada must recognize that until that is done, that is the kind of world we are in, that is the kind of international market in which our farmers are producing. If the competition is subsidizing their farmers and their production, I do not see how we can escape helping our own industry in the same measure.
A few weeks ago the most important politician in the world addressed this Chamber; the President of the United States. The United States is a great friend of ours and a great competitor of ours in a lot of industries including agriculture. The Prime Minister has made a great deal of the importance of having a good relationship with the United States and with the President of the United States. Canada has already paid a pretty high price to obtain, for the Prime Minister, that so-called good relationship with the President of the United States.
The United States can be criticized for a number of its policies in the agricultural field, policies which actually violate agreements which the United States has entered into and undertakings which the United States has given. One would have expected that the Prime Minister, who wants to help the agricultural industry in Canada and do no more subsidizing than he has to, would be working hard to get Canada's competitors, such as the United States, to reduce their unfair subsidies and unfair support and trade programs which are damaging the Canadian agricultural industry.
We heard the most important politician in the world stand in this place, make a long speech and say not one word about agriculture, not one word about wheat, nothing to indicate that the Prime Minister of Canada had made the point to him that our agricultural industry was suffering from unfair American policies, or even that the Prime Minister had raised the subject with him.
We know that Canadians have brought a long grievance list to the attention of American legislators. I want to draw your attention to a document put out recently by our Embassy in Washington. It is an unclassified document in which Ambassador Gotlieb makes point after point, in black and white, as clear as can be, ways in which the United States is unfairly competing with the Canadian agricultural industry. For example, with regard to food assistance, Section 616 of the American legislation provides that the American Secretary of Agriculture shall require that, in each food assistance agreement with a foreign country, the recipient country agree to give preference to the United States in future food purchases. That is in violation of a number of international commitments,
as the Ambassador says, including the principles of the Food and Agricultural Organization of Surplus Disposal and the Wheat Trade Convention under the International Wheat Agreement.
Did the Prime Minister raise that with the President of the United States when he was in town? We do not know, but we do know that the Americans are not doing anything about it. They have decided not to act and not to respond.
With regard to export enhancement, Section 622 of that same statute would extend the Export Enhancement Program, an export subsidy, for an additional two years, and the Americans are giving it an extra $1 billion in funding. Our Ambassador tells anyone who will listen to him that this measure will continue to depress world agricultural prices and increase the pressure on other countries to strengthen their own support measures. Our Ambassador says that Canada will not allow its traditional markets to be eroded through the use of such export subsidies of other countries, in this case, an export subsidy of the United States.
The Government has failed in many, many ways. It has failed the people who sent it to office. It has failed to keep its most important promises. It has failed to help its friends, because the agricultural industry in western Canada has certainly been a great friend and supporter of the Prime Minister and the Conservative Party. Today is the day that the Government should show that it cares and will not allow this industry to continue to suffer.
I see that my time is up, but I want to assure the Prime Minister that city people will not object and will not complain if he takes steps to bring the agricultural industry of western Canada through these tough, tough Tory times.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to explain our policies, the policies of the New Democratic Party, with respect to our farmers, both in western Canada and in Quebec.
Following numerous discussions with my party colleagues, I realized that basically, the problems facing Western farmers are the same as those facing farmers in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I also realized that my Party, the New Democratic Party, speaks for all Canadian farmers and is a Party that is historically rooted in the agricultural movement.
It is a fact that one out of every four Canadian farmers is facing serious financial problems. Today, and this has been going on for a number of years, we have a very serious crisis facing farm families and entire farming communities. We know that with free trade, the situation can only get worse. In fact, representations made by the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec were most emphatic in this respect. I have met with UPA representatives in my office in Repentigny, the riding of Terrebonne, and also in Ottawa. I can say that their fears are entirely justified, and that as far as our party is

April 28, 1987
concerned, we fully support their concerns. Free trade will have a direct impact on the entire marketing board system-
