subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, free trade will have a direct impact on the whole marketing board system. The direct impact will be felt by dairy producers in Quebec as much as by western farmers who need the Canadian Wheat Board. Free trade will have dire consequences for Quebec farmers in particular. This is why I entertain many doubts, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to say that there has been some double talk from the word go. In Quebec we talk about free trade, whereas the Government of Canada talks about freer trade. To put it another way, from the outset the Conservative Government has been using double talk, referring to free trade in Quebec and to freer trade in the other provinces of Canada.
Second, therefore, like all Quebec and Canadian farmers, I believe that all Canadians are entitled to know the basic facts concerning free or freer trade. Let me explain. Some economists will divide the various industries into 34 groups, more or less. What is needed before we take a position, contrary to what the Conservative Government is doing, is to know for each industry, first what firms cannot survive free trade, what firms or groups of firms will need an adaptation period to survive, and what firms can compete immediately. Then, at the level of each category of business and each particular business, we must know the human costs, which is the most important factor-the number of jobs that will be lost in any given industry, in any group of firms, in any given firm. Also, how many new jobs will be created, in order to make a value judgment.
Mr. Speaker, why have this debate today? Simply because the Conservative Government decided to lift the Farm Credit Corporation's moratorium on foreclosures, which in principle was to be effective this coming Friday.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we know that the banks in turn will now be in a position to foreclose on those farm loans. All they will need to do is follow the example set by the Farm Credit Corporation, in other words this Tory Government.
We also know that the price of wheat has come down 18 per cent this year, after declining some 20 per cent last year, and that, very soon if this is not already the case, prices will no longer cover production costs.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian farmers, Quebec farmers are going through a most difficult period. I feel that as a Government, in the case of such a basic industry as farming, we must take all
the steps needed to save our farmers, to save our family farms and to save that industry. We in the New Democratic Party, are saying that the Canadian Government must give farmers the assurance that their return this year will not be lower than it was last year. The agricultural economy of western Canada, the farmers' families and communities of western Canada, must be protected. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec farmers and the Quebec farm community are aware of the seriousness of the situation, not only for themselves, but also for their fellow farmers in western Canada and that they sympathize with them.
Quebec farmers also know that a solution has to be found to the problem of our debt, a $25 billion burden in Canada for our farmers. We know, and they know, that the problem of excessive interest rates for farmers is unjustified. In that respect, I wish to emphasize that about a year and a half or two years ago, in the Finance Committee, at about the same time in the House of Commons, we dealt with a number of specific points with respect to farmers, including Section 31 of the Act which deals with part-time farmers. We had suggested a number of solutions to help them.
There was also the tricky question of funding for Canadian farmers, in particular the matter of interest rates. There had been some discussion on a tax measure, an inadequate one by the way, which had been developed in the United States but which would not have been profitable to Canadian farmers because of a fiscal loss, and which was rejected. We had however suggested a direct approach by saying that to help our farmers, in Quebec as well as in western Canada, the Farm Credit Corporation should be allowed to take direct action by charging appropriate and reduced interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, one farmer out of four is faced with serious financial difficulties. I ask the Conservative Government: What will happen to them after the moratorium is lifted? What will the banks do? Follow the example of the Conservative Government?
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the farmers' debt load is too high. It must be reduced, and that is what our Party, the New Democratic Party of Canada, advocates.
I am proud, Mr. Speaker, to be taking part in this debate today, a debate that went on all night. I may point out that none of the Liberals saw fit to come and defend Canada's farmers, western farmers.

I also want to say that the problems of western farmers are very similar to the problems of farmers in Quebec. As a French-speaking Quebecer, I also want to say that French-Canadians, including farmers, whether they live in northern
April 28, 1987

Alberta, Manitoba or Saskatchewan, in Lafleche, St. Paul, St. Albert, Gravelbourg or elsewhere, have not been forgotten by the farmers and the people of Quebec, and that they can count on our support and the support of our Party.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the New Democratic Party of Canada, that its members, defended the interests of farmers yesterday, last night and today, as they have for so many years, and that we will continue to defend the interests of farmers in the west, in Quebec, in Ontario or in
any other province. It is now up to the Government to listen to us and to act accordingly.
